restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 3 Nephi 20:33-34 records the Savior's prophecy about 'backsliding children' being gathered and brought to know the Father. The language parallels Jeremiah's call. Mosiah 26:24-26 describes how even those who have turned away can return if they will repent—the ba'al relationship is never permanently severed for the repentant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:8-9 prophesies the gathering of the Lord's people from 'the four quarters of the earth,' echoing Jeremiah's vision of remnant return. D&C 133 is structured around the theme of gathering—'the gathering of Judah and the scattering of Israel'—which Jeremiah 3:14 anticipates.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The journey 'to Zion' is ultimately a journey to the temple, the place where covenant is renewed. In Latter-day Saint theology, temples scattered across the earth (like the gathering of 'one from a city, two from a clan') become miniature Zions—places where the scattered covenant people can experience God's presence without traveling to a central location.

commentary.christological_typology: God's willingness to gather even a tiny remnant ('one from a city, two from a clan') prefigures Christ's teaching that 'many are called, but few are chosen' (Matthew 22:14). Yet it also anticipates the Savior's particular attention to individuals—he knows his sheep by name. The ba'al relationship—simultaneously authoritative and intimate—becomes the paradigm for Christ as both Lord and intimate friend. His marriage to the Church (Ephesians 5:25-27) echoes this ancient covenant language.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members often think of repentance as a once-for-all transaction: confession, forgiveness, move on. Jeremiah's call to 'return' invites something more radical—recognition that our journey away from God can be reversed, that direction matters more than destination, and that God's authority over us is grounded in covenantal intimacy, not fear. The promise of gathering 'one from a city, two from a clan' speaks to modern diaspora Mormons: in a world where the faithful are scattered, God knows each one. You do not need to be part of a massive movement or cultural majority to matter to God. Your individual faithfulness—your willingness to turn back toward Zion—is known and valued. And like the ancient remnant, modern believers are gradually gathering to Zion, family by family, individually chosen.

text_kjv: And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.

commentary.narrative:
The promise of restored leadership follows naturally from the promise of gathered people. Israel scattered requires shepherds to tend her. God promises to give pastors 'according to my own heart' (ro'im kellibbi)—a deliberate echo of David, described in 1 Samuel 13:14 as 'a man after God's own heart.' This is not promise of return of David himself (though messianic interpretation has sometimes suggested this), but of a new generation of leaders shaped by God's own values and priorities. These leaders will be distinguished by a particular quality: they will 'feed' (ra'u) the people—the shepherd metaphor moves beyond political rule to nurturance and care. The specific form of nourishment will be 'knowledge and wisdom' (de'ah ve-haskeil).

This verse is crucial for understanding Jeremiah's vision of restoration. It is not merely return to old forms—old priesthood, old temple, old sacrificial system. The restored leadership will be qualitatively different: they will guide not through coercive power but through knowledge. The pairing 'knowledge and wisdom' is significant. De'ah ('knowledge') refers to information, discernment, understanding of God's ways. Haskeil ('wisdom') means skill, prudence, the ability to apply knowledge rightly in concrete situations. Together they describe leadership that understands God's heart (since they are chosen according to God's heart) and can communicate that understanding to the people.

The context is critical: in chapters 1-2, Jeremiah has indicted contemporary shepherds for failing precisely in this way. Jeremiah 23:1-4 will expand this critique: 'Woe unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!' The corrupt shepherds of Jeremiah's time fed themselves, not the flock. They led the people into idolatry and false confidence. The promise in 3:15, therefore, is not just of new leadership but of a leadership defined by the opposite qualities: knowledge of God, wisdom in guidance, care for the flock's spiritual nourishment. This verse hints at a fundamental institutional renewal—not just return to Zion, but transformation of how religious authority will function.

word_study.meaning: shepherds, pastors, leaders. The term can refer to literal shepherds of sheep, but in political/religious context denotes those who guide and care for a people. Kings, priests, and prophets all function as 'shepherds.'
word_study.significance: The shepherd metaphor runs throughout Jeremiah. It encompasses the full range of authority figures—political and religious. Jeremiah indicts corrupt shepherds and promises good ones. The metaphor emphasizes that leadership is fundamentally about care and guidance, not control.

word_study.meaning: According to my heart, according to my inner being, according to my character. The 'heart' (lev) in Hebrew represents the center of will, desire, understanding, and moral orientation—the true self.
word_study.significance: This phrase directly echoes 1 Samuel 13:14's description of David. The promise is not of David's return but of leaders shaped by the same divine values that shaped David. They will share God's priorities and concerns, not political expediency.

word_study.meaning: to feed, pasture, tend, guide. Used of shepherds tending sheep and metaphorically of leaders nourishing their people spiritually and politically.
word_study.significance: The shift from 'give you pastors' (passive receipt) to 'they will feed you' (active nourishment) emphasizes the quality of the new leadership. They will actively sustain, not merely rule.

word_study.meaning: knowledge, understanding, discernment. In biblical usage, often refers to experiential knowledge, not abstract information—knowing how things work, understanding God's character and ways.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'knowledge' (rather than 'knowledge' + 'understanding' as dual objects) suggests that this knowledge is specific and directed—knowledge of God's will and ways, not mere information.

word_study.meaning: wisdom, prudence, discretion, the ability to act skillfully. Related to seichel (reason, good sense). Describes the practical, applied dimension of knowledge.
word_study.significance: Pairing de'ah with haskeil creates a complete picture: knowing God's will (de'ah) plus the prudence to apply it wisely in concrete situations (haskeil). This is leadership that is both principled and practical.

cross_references.connection: David is described as 'a man after God's own heart.' Jeremiah's promise of pastors 'according to my heart' directly echoes this language, linking the ideal of Davidic leadership with the promised restoration.

Jeremiah pronounces woe on shepherds who 'destroy and scatter the sheep' and promises God will set over them 'pastors that shall feed them.' This verse expands and applies the same promise of renewed leadership.

Ezekiel prophesies that God himself will be shepherd to Israel and will raise up 'one shepherd' to feed them. Like Jeremiah, Ezekiel emphasizes nourishing, caring leadership as the mark of restoration.

Jesus identifies himself as 'the good shepherd' who 'knows his sheep by name' and lays down his life for them—a direct fulfillment of the shepherd-leader tradition that Jeremiah anchors in the promise of 3:15.

The Lord designates Joseph Smith as a leader and promises: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.'

commentary.historical_context: By Jeremiah's time, the priesthood and kingship were in crisis. King after king had led Judah toward idolatry and political disaster. The priests had become corrupt and complicit in false worship. Jeremiah's indictment of contemporary leaders (chapters 1-2) is scathing. The promise of new shepherds 'according to God's heart' would have been striking: not reformation of existing leadership structures, but replacement by leaders fundamentally aligned with God's values. In the post-exilic period, when Israel was restored, there was no king—the high priest became the central authority. This may be one of the ways Jeremiah's promise was fulfilled: leadership was reconceived around priestly rather than royal models, and the priesthood was reformed (with varying degrees of success) during and after the exile.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 23:14-15 describes wise leadership: 'And it came to pass that Alma did teach and establish order in the church; and thus the church began to have peace and to grow.' The principle of shepherds feeding the flock with knowledge appears throughout Book of Mormon leadership narratives. Alma 5:37-42 indicts corrupt leaders who 'scatter the flock' and promises restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 20:42-44 describes the role of the presiding elder (bishop): 'to preside over the church...to feed the flock of Christ.' The language directly applies Jeremiah's shepherd promise to latter-day Church leadership. D&C 84:111 promises that leaders called according to God's will will have knowledge poured upon them.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The feeding of the flock with 'knowledge and wisdom' occurs through temple ordinances and covenants. Latter-day temples are the places where God's knowledge is transmitted to his people through ritual, covenant, and revelation. The promise of shepherds sharing this knowledge connects to the role of temple presidency and stake leadership.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the ultimate fulfillment of this promise of shepherds 'according to God's heart.' He knows the Father's heart perfectly and feeds the flock with divine knowledge (John 10:11-14). The Sermon on the Mount, the Beatitudes, the parables—these are all instances of Jesus feeding the people with knowledge and wisdom. The transformation from Old Testament legal leaders to Christ as shepherd reflects the movement Jeremiah anticipates: from externally imposed authority to internalized, loving guidance.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern Church members to evaluate leadership—both ecclesiastical and familial. Are the leaders we sustain genuinely shepherds 'according to God's heart'? Do they feed rather than dominate? Do they offer knowledge (understanding of God's ways) and wisdom (prudent application in our lives)? Equally, if you hold any position of leadership—a calling in the Church, responsibility in your family, influence in your community—are you feeding the flock with knowledge of God and wisdom in application? The promise is not that perfect leaders will appear, but that God continually raises up leaders aligned with his values. Our responsibility is to recognize them and support them, and if we hold leadership roles, to seek alignment with God's heart rather than our own agendas.

text_kjv: And it shall come to pass, when ye be multiplied and increased in the land, in those days, saith the LORD, they shall say no more, The ark of the covenant of the LORD: neither shall it come to heart, neither shall they remember it; neither shall they visit it; neither shall that be made any more.

commentary.narrative:
This is one of the most theologically radical verses in the Hebrew Bible, and its radicalism requires careful reading. The ark of the covenant (aron berit-YHWH) was the holiest object in Israelite religious life—a wooden chest overlaid with pure gold, topped by the mercy seat (kapporet) where God's presence dwelt between two golden cherubim. Inside rested the Two Tables of the Law, and it was the center of Israel's entire religious system. To promise that this sacred object will not merely be lost or destroyed but will be actively, deliberately not rebuilt—that it will not even occur to future generations to reconstruct it—is extraordinary.

The fourfold negation creates cumulative force: (1) 'they will no longer say' its name; (2) 'it will not come to mind' (lo ya'aleh al lev—literally, 'it will not come up on the heart'); (3) 'they will not remember it'; (4) 'they will not miss it' or 'attend to it' (lo yifqodu). This is not loss through destruction but obsolescence through spiritual transformation. The ark was already missing by Jeremiah's time (its fate after the Babylonian destruction remains unknown), but this oracle goes further: it predicts that the ark will not be recreated because the covenant relationship will have fundamentally changed. The external mediator of God's presence will become unnecessary.

The condition for this radical shift is crucial: 'when you have multiplied and increased in the land'—this is restoration language. Only after Israel is restored, increased in population, and thriving territorially will the ark become unnecessary. This is not promise of a diminished covenant but of an intensified, internalized one. The current system—where God's presence is mediated through a physical object housed in a temple that can be destroyed or lost—will give way to something more durable and intimate. Later in Jeremiah (31:31-34), the prophet will articulate this explicitly: 'I will make a new covenant...I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.' This verse foreshadows that movement from external symbol to internal reality.

word_study.term_english: ark of the covenant of the LORD
word_study.meaning: Ark (aron): a wooden chest; Covenant (berit): binding agreement, the relational structure of Israel's faith. The ark was the physical repository of the covenant tablets and the seat of God's presence.
word_study.significance: This is the theological center of Israel's pre-exilic religion. Its proposed obsolescence signals a complete reorientation of how Israel relates to God. The Covenant Rendering's choice to emphasize the ark's abandonment (rather than its loss) highlights that this is deliberate spiritual evolution, not accidental loss.

word_study.meaning: To come up, ascend (alah); heart (lev), seat of consciousness, memory, intention. 'Come to heart' means to enter one's consciousness or memory—to be thought of.
word_study.significance: The phrase suggests that the ark will not merely be absent but will be psychologically forgotten. Future generations won't think to rebuild it because the internal reality of covenant will satisfy them completely. The heart's attention will be directed elsewhere.

word_study.meaning: To visit, attend to, care for, remember, or feel the absence of. In some contexts, 'to muster' or 'count.' The sense here is 'they will not miss it' or 'they will not attend to it.'
word_study.significance: This verb captures both psychological (not remember) and practical (not seek to rebuild) dimensions. The people will not even feel the loss of the ark because the covenant relationship will be complete without it.

word_study.meaning: To multiply, increase (rabah); to be fruitful, multiply (parah). The pairing echoes Genesis language of blessing—God's command to Adam and Eve to 'be fruitful and multiply.'
word_study.significance: Restoration is marked by fertility and abundance. The covenant innovation (life without the ark) comes not in a time of scarcity or loss but in a time of blessing. This suggests that spiritual maturity involves moving beyond external supports.

word_study.meaning: To make, do, create. The phrase negates future creation or construction of the ark.
word_study.significance: The explicit statement that the ark 'will not be made any more' (ve-lo yeiasah od) forecloses any attempt at reconstruction. This is not accidental loss but deliberate, divinely ordained obsolescence.

cross_references.connection: The explicit promise of the new covenant, where God writes the law on the heart rather than on stone tablets, directly fulfills this verse's prophecy. When the internal covenant is established, the external ark becomes unnecessary.

This apocryphal text reports that Jeremiah hid the ark before the Babylonian destruction, anticipating that it would be revealed when God gathered his people. The tradition recognizes that Jeremiah's prophecy leaves the ark's fate mysterious.
The New Testament describes the ark's furnishings and role in the old covenant tabernacle, then explains (10:1-18) how Christ's sacrifice fulfills and transcends these external types and shadows.

John's prologue about 'the Word made flesh' and 'the light that lighteth every man' describes the internalization of God's presence that Jeremiah anticipates—God's presence is no longer localized in a box but in the person of Christ.

The Lord explains how the fullness of the priesthood ('Aaronic priesthood') leads to the higher priesthood ('Melchizedek') and direct access to God, paralleling Jeremiah's movement from mediated (through the ark) to immediate divine presence.

commentary.historical_context: The ark of the covenant was physically present in the First Temple (built by Solomon around 960 BCE) until the Babylonian destruction in 586 BCE. Its fate afterward is unknown—it does not appear in the Second Temple built by the returning exiles (515 BCE). Rabbinic tradition suggests it was hidden or destroyed, and some sources claim it is still hidden beneath the Temple Mount. Jeremiah, prophesying before the destruction, makes a remarkable prediction: the ark will not be found or rebuilt because it will become unnecessary. This prophecy was 'fulfilled' not through dramatic divine removal but through quiet absence—no one bothered to rebuild it. The Jerusalem community returned and rebuilt the Temple, but they did not recreate the ark. This suggests that by the Second Temple period, religious consciousness had shifted toward the internalized covenant that Jeremiah predicted.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 3 Nephi 11:11 records the Savior's statement: 'I am the light and the life of the world.' This is the internalization Jeremiah predicts—God's presence is no longer mediated through a physical object but through Christ himself. Alma 36:24-26 describes how Alma experiences direct, interiorized access to God's presence without temple ritual.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:3-5 teaches that Christ 'is in all things, and through all things, and is the light of all things' and that he 'iswhere you are.' This is the fulfillment of Jeremiah's vision—God's presence is not confined to a shrine but is universal and internalized. D&C 109:2-4 (Kirtland Temple dedication) speaks of temples as places where God's presence is revealed, but the promise moves beyond temples as unique sacred spaces to temples as places where the already-internalized presence becomes consciously realized.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Paradoxically, Jeremiah's prophecy that the ark becomes unnecessary does not make temples unnecessary but reorients them. Latter-day temples do not house an ark or seek God's presence in a localized object. Instead, they are places where the internalized covenant is formally enacted and renewed. The temple is the place where the 'new covenant' promise of writing God's law on hearts is ritually affirmed. Modern temples make Jeremiah's vision concrete: they are centers where the covenant is internalized rather than mediated through external objects.

commentary.christological_typology: The ark was the ultimate type of Christ's atoning presence. The mercy seat (kapporet) where God's presence dwelt and where the high priest made annual atonement foreshadowed Christ himself as the 'mercy seat' or 'propitiation' (hilasterion in Greek, echoing kapporet) for all humanity. When the ark becomes unnecessary, it is because its type has been fulfilled—Christ is present, and his presence is accessible not through a physical shrine but through faith and covenant. Hebrews 9-10 makes this typological fulfillment explicit: the old covenant's external forms and shadows give way to Christ's presence 'in the most holy place' (literally, 'the holiest of holies').
commentary.application: This verse asks modern covenant members: Are you still seeking God primarily through external supports—buildings, rituals, authorities—or are you developing an internalized, direct relationship with him? Jeremiah's prophecy does not disparage temples or priesthood structures (they serve essential functions), but it calls believers toward maturity—toward a faith so deep and direct that external mediators become confirmations rather than necessities. For Latter-day Saints especially, this has profound meaning: temples are beautiful and essential, but the temple experience should deepen your personal covenant so that you carry God's presence with you beyond the temple walls. The promise is not that temples disappear but that your relationship with God becomes so immediate and personal that you would not 'miss' the temple if circumstances prevented you from attending—because you carry the covenant written on your heart.

text_kjv: At that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of the LORD; and all the nations shall be gathered unto it, to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem: neither shall they walk any more after the imagination of their evil heart.

commentary.narrative:
With the ark obsolete, what replaces it as the locus of God's presence? Jerusalem itself becomes God's throne (kisse'). This is extraordinary: not a temple building, not a sacred object within the city, but the entire city becomes the seat of God's sovereignty. The throne language is crucial—kisse' denotes the seat from which a ruler exercises authority. In ancient Near Eastern ideology, a god's throne was the physical manifestation of his rule and presence. By promising that Jerusalem itself will be called God's throne, Jeremiah envisions a complete reorientation: the city becomes the visible sign of divine sovereignty on earth.

This vision opens outward: 'all nations will gather to it, to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem.' This is universalism—not tribalism. The restored covenant is not for Israel alone but for all peoples. They gather 'to the name of the LORD'—seeking YHWH's reputation and presence—and this gathering occurs 'to Jerusalem.' The city becomes the magnetic center of religious pilgrimage and spiritual transformation. Earlier prophets (Isaiah 2:2-3, Micah 4:1-2) envision Mount Zion becoming the mountain to which all nations ascend. Jeremiah combines this with his own emphasis on internalized covenant: the gathering at Jerusalem is not primarily for sacrificial ritual (though the Temple will still function) but for encounter with God's presence that has become inseparable from the city itself.

The transformation's scope is then stated: 'They will no longer walk in the stubbornness of their evil hearts' (ve-lo yeilkhu od achrei sheririut libbam hara'). This is not mere behavioral reform but transformation of the human heart's orientation. The phrase 'stubbornness of their evil heart' (sheririut libbam hara') is Jeremiah's signature phrase for settled rebellion—the kind that refuses to hear God's voice (used in 7:24, 9:13, 11:8, 13:10). What the gathering at Jerusalem accomplishes is not external coercion but internal reorientation. Peoples come to Jerusalem not because they are forced but because they have been transformed by encounter with God's presence. This is the goal: not just restoration of Israel but transformation of human will itself toward alignment with God's purposes.

word_study.meaning: Throne, seat of authority and rule. In ancient Near Eastern ideology, a deity's throne was the symbol of cosmic sovereignty and the focal point of divine presence.
word_study.significance: The term moves from the literal throne-seat of a king to the metaphorical throne of God's sovereignty. By calling Jerusalem God's throne, Jeremiah claims that the city embodies and represents divine rule on earth. The Covenant Rendering's choice to render it 'the throne of the LORD' rather than 'the seat' captures the authority and sovereignty dimensions.

word_study.meaning: To gather together, assemble, congregate. The sense is of intentional gathering, not forced collection.
word_study.significance: The nations gather willingly—they are drawn by attraction to God's presence, not compelled by military conquest. This is a spiritual gathering, reflecting inner transformation rather than external domination.

word_study.term_english: to the name of the LORD
word_study.meaning: To the name of the LORD—'name' (shem) in biblical usage refers not merely to a label but to reputation, character, and manifest presence. 'Name' encompasses God's revealed nature and power.
word_study.significance: The nations gather not because they are forced to acknowledge a political power but because they are attracted to the Lord's character and reputation. This implies that God's character becomes universally known and attractive.

word_study.meaning: Stubbornness, obstinacy, hard-heartedness—the settled resistance of the will against God's voice. Related to the idea of a neck 'stiffened' against the yoke.
word_study.significance: This is the characteristic Jeremianic diagnosis of Israel's sin: not ignorance but willful refusal. Sheririut libbam hara' ('stubbornness of their evil heart') appears repeatedly (7:24, 9:13, 11:8, 13:10) as the spiritual condition that brings judgment. The promise that it will cease marks the deepest transformation.

word_study.meaning: Heart (lev)—the seat of will, desire, understanding, and moral orientation. 'The imagination/desire of their heart' refers to the settled inclinations and intentions that govern behavior.
word_study.significance: Transformation of the 'heart' is the deepest kind of change. External behavioral reform is possible without this; the promise is that internal orientation itself will be transformed.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah's parallel vision: 'The mountain of the LORD's house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and all nations shall flow unto it.' Jeremiah applies Isaiah's mountain vision to Jerusalem as God's throne.
Micah repeats Isaiah's vision of nations streaming to Zion to learn God's ways. All three prophets (Isaiah, Micah, Jeremiah) share this universalist eschatology.
Celebrates Jerusalem/Zion as 'the city of the great King' and 'the joy of the whole earth.' Jeremiah's vision transforms Jerusalem from historic capital to cosmic center of God's presence.

John's vision of the New Jerusalem coming down from heaven applies Jeremiah's promise to its ultimate fulfillment: a city where God dwells with humanity directly, and 'every nation' has access to 'the throne of God and of the Lamb.'

The Lord describes the destiny of Jerusalem and Zion in latter-day terms: 'Zion in the days of Jerusalem shall be kept from the overflowing scourge' and 'all nations shall behold her glory.' This applies Jeremiah's prophecy to modern restoration.

commentary.historical_context: Jeremiah's vision of Jerusalem as God's throne and the gathering of all nations is simultaneously grounded in ancient Near Eastern ideology and radically transformed. Ancient empires spoke of their capitals as cosmic centers where heaven and earth met (the ziggurats of Babylon, the temples of Egypt). Jeremiah appropriates this language for Jerusalem but with a crucial difference: the city is not the seat of human imperial power but of divine sovereignty. Moreover, the universalism—all nations gathering—reflects experiences of diaspora and later empire. As Israel was scattered under Assyrian and Babylonian rule, prophetic hope increasingly took universal form. The vision would have been particularly powerful for exiles: even in captivity, Jerusalem would become the spiritual center of the world, drawing all peoples toward God. This vision influenced later apocalyptic Judaism and Christianity's universalist theology.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 3 Nephi 21:23-29 records the Savior's prophecy that Israel will be gathered and 'become exceeding fair and white, becoming clean from all their filthiness,' and that 'all nations shall see the fulfillment of the covenant.' This applies Jeremiah's vision to the latter-day restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:42-43 prophesies that Zion will be 'the glory of the whole earth' when it is fully established. D&C 84:2-3 identifies the temple lot in Jackson County, Missouri as 'the foundation of Zion' and as 'the city of our God,' applying Jeremiah's vision of a city-throne to the American Zion. D&C 45:66-71 describes the Lord's protection of 'Zion in the days of Jerusalem' and the gathering of Judah to Jerusalem.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: If Jerusalem becomes God's throne, then temples (which house God's presence on earth) are the ritual enactment of this promise. Latter-day temples scattered across the world are simultaneously separate sacred spaces and extensions of the central Zion. They make Jeremiah's vision concrete: wherever a temple stands, Jerusalem's spiritual presence is renewed. The temple ordinances unite the faithful in covenant with Jerusalem's central promise.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus identifies himself as 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6), claiming to be the center to which all must come. His crucifixion in Jerusalem and his promise that 'all nations' would hear the gospel (Matthew 28:19-20) fulfills Jeremiah's prophecy: the gathering to Jerusalem is ultimately a gathering to Christ. The transformation of hearts ('neither shall they walk any more after the imagination of their evil heart') is precisely what the Savior effects through the gift of his Spirit—the heart is changed not by external compulsion but by internal conversion.
commentary.application: This verse invites meditation on what constitutes the center of your spiritual life. Jeremiah promises that there will be a place (Jerusalem) to which all are drawn, a city-throne where God's presence becomes undeniably evident. For Latter-day Saints, this has multiple layers: the Salt Lake Temple as the center of the faith community; Jerusalem itself as the place where Christ ministered and will return; and personally, the temples where you make covenant as your spiritual 'Jerusalem'—the place where heaven and earth meet in your own life. The promise also invites universalism: not mere ethnic or cultural nationalism, but a vision where 'all nations' are drawn to God's truth. How does your personal faith reflect this universalism? And practically: are you building toward a life where the 'stubbornness of your evil heart' is progressively transformed, so that your desires and intentions align with God's character rather than resisting it? Jeremiah's vision is ultimately about the magnetism of transformed hearts—that people are drawn toward God not by coercion but by the sheer attractiveness of his presence.

text_kjv: In those days the house of Judah shall walk with the house of Israel, and they shall come together out of the land of the north to the land that I have given for an inheritance unto your fathers.

commentary.narrative:
The vision concludes with concrete political restoration: the reunion of Judah and Israel. This was not a minor detail in ancient Jewish consciousness. The kingdom had been divided since Solomon's death (circa 930 BCE). When Assyria conquered the northern kingdom in 722 BCE, the ten tribes were scattered and largely lost to history (the 'lost tribes of Israel'). By Jeremiah's time, 'Israel' and 'Judah' were separate political entities, and the northern tribes seemed permanently exiled. Yet Jeremiah promises not merely the return of Judah from Babylonian exile (which would happen, beginning 539 BCE) but the restoration of the broken unity. Judah and Israel will walk together (yilkhu yachdav)—they will journey together as one people.

The phrase 'walk together' emphasizes companionship and shared purpose. This is not Judah absorbing Israel or vice versa, but a restoration of the original unity that existed under David and Solomon, before the dynastic split. The language 'come together from the land of the north' uses 'land of the north' (erets tsafon) as the direction of exile. Geographically, both Assyria (which deported Israel) and Babylon (which exiled Judah) lay northeast of Israel. The approach route for returning exiles was from the north. This concrete geographical detail grounds the prophecy in historical reality: exiles literally return from northern empires.

The destination is 'the land that I gave as an inheritance to your ancestors' (ha-aretz asher hinchalti et avoteikhem). The verb hinachalti uses the root nachal, which denotes permanent, heritable possession—land that belongs to a family not as rental but as ancestral inheritance. This is the land given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the land promised in the Abrahamic Covenant. The restoration is not merely return from exile but fulfillment of the original covenant promise. The exiles return not as refugees to a temporary shelter but as heirs to an inheritance. This reframes exile as temporary interruption of a permanent, covenantal relationship with the land.

word_study.meaning: To walk, go, travel (halakh); together (yachad). The combination emphasizes companionship and coordinated movement toward a shared destination.
word_study.significance: The verb 'walk' is characteristic of covenant language in the Bible—to 'walk with' someone is to be in covenantal relationship. The promise is not merely geographical co-location but renewed covenantal unity.

word_study.term_original: בֵית־יְהוּדָה / בֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל (beit Yehudah / beit Yisrael)
word_study.meaning: House (beit)—dynasty, kingdom, corporate entity. 'House of Judah' and 'House of Israel' denote the two separate political entities resulting from the post-Solomonic division.
word_study.significance: Using 'house' rather than merely 'Judah' and 'Israel' emphasizes the political and institutional dimensions of the split. The promise is not just cultural reunion but restoration of political and covenant unity.

word_study.meaning: Together, in unity, as one. Emphasizes oneness and coordinated action.
word_study.significance: The term appears twice in close proximity (v. 18, 'come together'/'yachad'). This repetition emphasizes unity as the central promise—the broken kingdom will be restored to singularity.

word_study.meaning: North, northland—in ancient Near Eastern geography, the direction from which invasions and empires came. Associationally, the direction of exile.
word_study.significance: 'Land of the north' is not a specific place but a directional reference. It encompasses both Assyrian exile (northern route) and Babylonian exile (northeastern route). The language grounds prophecy in historical geography.

word_study.meaning: To give as an inheritance, to bequeath. The root nachal carries the sense of permanent, familial possession—land that is passed down through generations as the family's own.
word_study.significance: This verb recalls the patriarchal covenants (Genesis 12:7, 15:7) where God promises the land to Abraham and his descendants 'for an inheritance.' The restoration is not a new gift but fulfillment of the original promise.

word_study.meaning: Fathers, ancestors, forebears—emphasizes continuity across generations and covenantal lineage.
word_study.significance: The promise connects the returning exiles to their patriarchal ancestors. The land belongs to them not as a new acquisition but as their ancestral inheritance. This is continuity across exile.

cross_references.connection: Ezekiel receives instruction to take two sticks (representing Judah and Israel) and join them into one, symbolizing the reunification Jeremiah promises. Ezekiel expands the promise: 'My servant David shall be king over them' and the covenant will be everlasting.

'The children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together' and 'they shall appoint themselves one head.' Hosea, an earlier prophet to the northern kingdom, similarly promises eventual reunification.
Historical account of Assyria's conquest and deportation of the northern kingdom (Israel). This is the exile that Jeremiah promises will be reversed through the return 'from the land of the north.'

Isaiah prophesies: 'I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west...Say to the north, Give up; and to the south, Keep not back...bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth.'
The Lord tells Joseph Smith that the keys of the gathering of Israel have been committed to him, relating to the fulfillment of prophecies about Israel's restoration and reunion.

commentary.historical_context: The reunification of Israel and Judah was never fully realized in ancient history. While some northern Israelites did return and were absorbed into the restored Judahite community (particularly after Josiah's reforms, 2 Kings 23), the ten northern tribes largely remained scattered. The historical record shows that when Judah returned from Babylonian exile (beginning 539 BCE), they returned as Judah, not as a reunited Israel-Judah. Yet the prophecy had profound theological significance: it kept alive the hope that God's covenant with all Israel was not permanently broken. In Jewish tradition and in later Christian and Latter-day Saint theology, the promise of Israel's reunion became an eschatological hope—to be fulfilled not in history but at the end of days when God would gather Israel 'from the four quarters of the earth' (D&C 29:8). Archaeological evidence from the Second Temple period suggests that some northerners had integrated into the Judahite community, but no systematic 'return' of the lost ten tribes occurred.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 30:8 prophesies: 'The Gentiles and the house of Israel shall flow together' in the latter days. 3 Nephi 20:31-33 records the Savior's prophecy: 'At that day when the Gentiles shall sin against my gospel, and shall reject the fulness of my gospel...then will I remember my covenant which I have made unto my people.' The Book of Mormon relocates Israel's restoration to the Americas while maintaining Jeremiah's theme of broken peoples being reunited in covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:8-9 explicitly quotes Jeremiah's language: 'The Lord shall utter his voice, and all the ends of the earth shall hear it; and all the nations of the earth shall mourn, and they that have laughed shall see their folly...Wherefore I say unto you, that I have sent unto you my servants the elders of my church, to lay the foundation of my house." D&C 110:11 states that 'the keys of the gathering of Israel' were given to Joseph Smith. D&C 133:26-34 speaks of the gathering of Judah to Jerusalem and the gathering of Israel to the land of their inheritance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gathering 'to the land of inheritance' is facilitated through temple work. Proxy ordinances allow scattered Israel (metaphorically, all humanity across time and space) to be spiritually gathered to covenant. The Salt Lake Temple sits on the land (Zion) toward which Israel gathers, and temples scattered globally bring the gathering to scattered peoples.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of the promise to 'walk together.' In John 17, Jesus prays for unity: 'That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us...I in them, and thou in me; that they may be made perfect in one.' The broken Israel of Jeremiah's time foreshadows the broken humanity that Christ came to reconcile—Jew and Gentile, Judah and Israel, all scattered peoples 'coming together' in him as the center of unity. The inheritance of the 'land given to your fathers' is ultimately the 'mansions' in the Father's house (John 14:2) that Christ prepares.
commentary.application: This verse concludes Jeremiah 3's promise of restoration with a call to unity. For modern believers, it raises questions about reconciliation and covenant renewal. Are there divisions in your life—broken relationships, estranged family branches, separated faith communities—that need the healing this verse promises? Jeremiah's vision is not naive unity (pretending differences don't exist) but genuine reunion ('walk together') grounded in shared covenantal inheritance. For The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, this verse has specific relevance: the restored church teaches that all of God's people, scattered across time and space, are being gathered into one family through covenant. Your personal gathering happens when you make sacred covenants in the temple—you are literally joining yourself to the 'land of inheritance' that belongs to all the faithful. Practically: are you part of building that gathered community, or are you allowing yourself to remain isolated? Jeremiah's promise is not merely about ancient Israel returning from Babylon but about the perennial human work of turning toward God and each other.

text_kjv: But I said, How shall I put thee among the children, and give thee a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the hosts of nations? and I said, Thou shalt call me, My father; and shalt not turn away from me.

commentary.narrative:
This verse pivots inward to God's heart, revealing His original intention for Israel before the covenant was broken. The rhetorical question 'How shall I put thee among the children' expresses not uncertainty but tender longing—God is deliberating how to honor Israel with the status of beloved child rather than servant. The 'pleasant land' and 'goodly heritage' reference the land of Canaan itself, but more profoundly, they represent the full covenant inheritance—not merely territory but relationship, protection, and divine favor. The phrase 'heritage of the hosts of nations' suggests Israel would inherit not just land but the choicest portion among all peoples, a position of unique favor.

The second half reveals what God hoped would follow: that Israel would address Him as 'My father' (avi), reversing the power dynamics of the master-servant relationship into the intimacy of child and parent. Crucially, this is God's desire stated as a promise or condition—'you will call me... and shall not turn away from me.' The emphatic repetition 'and I said' marks this as God's own deliberation, His inner hope for the relationship. Yet the verse is framed entirely in the past tense ('I said'), which creates a poignant tension: this was the original vision, but it has not come to pass.

word_study.meaning: The verb shith (שׁית) means 'to place, set, put'—not merely to locate but to establish in a position of status. The phrase ba-banim ('among the children') places Israel among God's children, not as an adopted servant but as a full son or daughter in the covenant household. The root carries the sense of permanent placement and legal standing.
word_study.significance: In Levantine family law and ancient Near Eastern adoption texts, to be 'set among the children' was a formal legal status conferring full inheritance rights. God is not offering charity but covenantal kinship—the highest relational status available.

word_study.meaning: Chemdah (חֶמְדָּה) derives from chamad, 'to desire, to covet'—the land is not merely good but desirable, an object of longing. It expresses both beauty and the aspiration it inspires. Combined with eretz ('land'), it denotes a land worthy of desire, precious in God's own estimation.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'desirable' over KJV's 'pleasant,' capturing the Hebrew sense that this inheritance is something to be yearned for, not simply pleasant—it is the object of rightful desire.

word_study.meaning: Nachalat (נַחֲלַת) means 'inheritance, possession'—a permanent, divinely allotted portion passed through covenant family lines. Tzevi (צְבִי) means 'beauty, splendor, glory'—the adjective form of a word suggesting aesthetic and spiritual brilliance. The phrase tzeva'ot goyim ('hosts/armies of nations') may refer to the multiplied wealth and strength of other nations, here offered to Israel as a heritage of surpassing beauty.
word_study.significance: The stacking of terms (nachalat + tzevi + tzeva'ot) creates an accumulation of beauty and worth—God is emphasizing not merely adequacy but superabundance. The inheritance offered transcends ordinary possession; it is heritage drenched in splendor.

word_study.meaning: From shuv (שׁוּב), the central verb of Jeremiah's theology meaning 'to turn, return, turn away.' Here in the negative—'you will not turn away'—it expresses the hope that the cycle of apostasy will finally break. The future tense ('will not') frames this as God's covenant expectation and condition.
word_study.significance: Shuv appears 44 times in Jeremiah; it is the prophet's dominant call and God's deepest longing. God's hope in verse 19 is that Israel will stop shuv-ing away (turning from Him) and only shuv back (returning to Him). The repetition of this root throughout the chapter links Israel's betrayal to the very possibility of restoration.

cross_references.connection: God calls Israel 'my son, even my firstborn,' establishing the father-child relationship that Jeremiah 3:19 recalls as God's original desire for the covenant people.

The parallel prophetic vision: 'When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt'—both Hosea and Jeremiah describe God's paternal love and the child-status He intended for Israel.
Moses rebukes Israel: 'Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? Is not he thy father that hath bought thee?'—the same father-child language with the same accusation of ingratitude.
Nephi describes the restoration of Israel as a return to the covenant status of beloved children, echoing the inheritance language of Jeremiah 3:19.

commentary.historical_context: The father-child relationship was central to ancient Near Eastern covenant theology, particularly in Hittite suzerainty treaties where the great king adopted vassal states as 'sons.' Israel's status as God's child (not merely servant) was exceptional and elevated. The 'pleasant land' reference to Canaan reflects the historical reality of the land grant as part of the Abrahamic covenant—the land was not merely territory but a tangible sign of divine favor and covenant belonging. The rhetorical question 'How shall I set you' reflects the idiom of deliberation found in Mesopotamian wisdom literature, where gods or kings weigh difficult decisions. God frames the covenant as His own heart's desire, not an imposed obligation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:12 speaks of Jesus taking upon Him the infirmities and sicknesses of His people, extending the healing covenant that Jeremiah pictures. Additionally, 1 Nephi 13-14 prophesies the restoration of all things, including Israel's return to covenant standing as God's children—the restoration of the very relationship Jeremiah 3:19 depicts.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:22 promises 'Peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come'—the same covenant hope that Jeremiah expresses. Also, D&C 29:17-20 emphasizes the Father's desire to gather and preserve His children, mirroring God's expressed longing in Jeremiah 3:19.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The father-child relationship is central to temple covenant theology. The adoption language of Jeremiah 3:19 ('put thee among the children') prefigures the sealing of families and the binding of children to parents in the new covenant of the Restoration. Modern revelation teaches that this familial covenant relationship—being sealed as God's children—is the highest ordinance.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah 3:19 points to the restoration of humanity's child-status before God through Christ. Just as God desired to set Israel among His children and receive their filial devotion, the gospel restores all believers to this position through Christ's mediation. The inheritance of the 'desirable land' becomes a type of the celestial kingdom—the inheritance prepared for those who remain covenant-faithful. Christ Himself is the ultimate 'son' whose faithfulness reverses the faithlessness of Israel (and all humanity), making possible the restoration of the father-child relationship that sin had severed.
commentary.application: Modern members of the Church are invited into this same covenant relationship—to be adopted as God's children through Christ and to inherit the 'desirable land' (the celestial kingdom). The challenge of verse 19 is personal: Will we call God 'Father' with genuine intimacy, or will we (metaphorically) 'turn away'? The verse invites deep meditation on whether our relationship with God is truly familial or merely transactional. Do we live as beloved children or anxious servants? The covenant hope is that we, like Israel, can move from estrangement to belonging—and remain loyal to that relationship.

text_kjv: Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
The verse pivots with devastating directness from the tenderness of God's desire in verse 19 to the harsh reality of Israel's betrayal. The word 'surely' (akin) signals a logical consequence or stark contrast—the dream of verse 19 stands opposed to the fact of verse 20. The marriage metaphor, established earlier in chapter 3 (verses 1-11), returns here at maximum intensity. God compares Israel's disloyalty to the act of a wife abandoning her husband—one of the gravest betrayals in ancient Near Eastern society, where marriage was a binding covenant of mutual obligation.

The phrase 'treacherously departeth from her husband' suggests not mere neglect but deliberate infidelity—a wife who leaves her legitimate husband for lovers. In Israel's case, the 'lovers' are the foreign gods and political alliances (see verses 1-2). The parallel structure—'as a wife... so have ye'—makes the comparison comprehensive: just as marital betrayal is a fundamental violation of covenant, so Israel's apostasy is a fundamental violation of the covenant with YHWH. The phrase 'O house of Israel' (not Judah, though Judah is mentioned elsewhere in the chapter) suggests this indictment applies to the entire covenant people, North and South alike.

word_study.meaning: Bagdah (בָּגְדָה) is from the root bagad, 'to betray, deal treacherously, break faith.' It carries not merely the act of leaving but the moral failure of covenant-breaking—infidelity in its deepest sense. The noun form bogdim ('traitors') appears throughout Jeremiah as a self-description. Me-re'ahah ('from her companion/husband') uses re'ah, which means both 'friend' and 'companion'—emphasizing that a husband is one's covenant partner, not a master.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures the distinction between bagad and simple departure (leaving). Bagad implies willful breach of a binding oath, not accidental separation. This is not a woman who fled in hardship but one who deliberately turned her back on her covenant oath. The same root was used in verse 11 for 'treacherous Judah' (bogdah)—now God applies it back to all Israel, indicting the entire nation.

word_study.meaning: The verb bagad with the preposition bi ('with me, against me') intensifies the sense of personal betrayal—it is not abstract infidelity but betrayal directed at God Himself. The second-person plural form (bagadtem) addresses Israel collectively, implicating the entire nation.
word_study.significance: The shift from 'a wife betrays her husband' (general case) to 'you have betrayed me' (direct accusation) makes the metaphor concrete and personal. God moves from illustration to indictment, centering Himself as the wronged party.

cross_references.connection: Judah is called 'treacherous' (bogdah) earlier in the chapter; verse 20 extends this indictment to all Israel, showing that the entire covenant people stand guilty of the same betrayal.

Hosea uses the same marriage metaphor: 'Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband'—both prophets employ marital betrayal as the supreme image of covenant-breaking.

Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem as a divorced wife—'Thy Maker is thine husband'—and promises restoration, showing how the prophets use the marriage covenant as a framework for understanding Israel's relationship to God.

Malachi condemns those who betray the wife of their covenant, applying the same language of bagad ('treachery') to interpersonal marriage, showing how covenant language extends from Israel's relationship with God to human relationships.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern law codes (such as the Code of Hammurabi), a wife who left her husband could be severely punished—even drowned in some formulations. Marriage was understood as a binding covenant with legal and religious dimensions. A wife's infidelity was not merely personal failure but a violation of family honor and social order. God's use of this metaphor would have struck with full cultural force: Israel's apostasy is not a policy error or religious drift but a violation of the fundamental covenant bond, as serious as marital infidelity. The metaphor would have resonated especially powerfully with Jeremiah's audience, who would have understood marriage as the binding covenant prototype. Prophetic marriage imagery (Hosea, Isaiah, Jeremiah) was likely shocking precisely because it invoked such intimate, personal betrayal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 2:30-35 uses similar marriage covenant language to condemn the people's infidelities, noting that God made the covenant 'that ye might raise up seed unto me'—emphasizing the procreative and covenantal dimensions of the marriage bond. The Book of Mormon prophets applied Jeremiah's marriage metaphor to their own people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:2 has the Lord saying, 'Verily I say unto you, the order of the house of the Lord'—part of a broader theology emphasizing that God's household is bound by covenant. D&C 52:15 addresses those who break covenant as those who reject the Lord Himself, extending Jeremiah's logic that covenant infidelity is personal betrayal of God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The marriage covenant—particularly the sealing covenant in modern temples—is understood as the earthly reflection of the covenant between God and His people. Jeremiah's use of marital betrayal as the image for Israel's apostasy invests the temple marriage covenant with prophetic weight; faithfulness or unfaithfulness in one's covenants is directly tied to one's ultimate relationship with God.

commentary.christological_typology: The betrayal of the covenant husband (YHWH) points typologically to Christ as the bridegroom whose people betray Him. The New Testament applies bridegroom imagery to Christ (John 3:29, Revelation 21:2), with the church as His bride. Just as Israel broke covenant, so humanity in its natural state breaks covenant with Christ. However, the gospel offers redemption and restoration—the betrayed bridegroom (Christ) extends reconciliation to His unfaithful people, offering a new covenant sealed in His blood. The severity of verse 20's accusation intensifies the grace of the gospel's offer of restoration.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 20 is a sobering invitation to examine our faithfulness to our covenants. The language of betrayal applies beyond sexual infidelity to include any act of covenant-breaking—placing other loyalties before God, pursuing false gods (whether material wealth, status, or ideology), or breaking the oaths we have made in baptism and temple ordinances. The verse teaches that covenant-breaking is not a neutral transgression but a personal affront to God, a violation of the intimate bond that God has initiated. Yet set in the context of chapter 3, which climaxes in offers of restoration and return, the verse calls us not to despair but to genuine repentance—to recognize betrayal, feel its weight, and return to covenant fidelity.

text_kjv: A voice was heard upon the high places, weeping and supplications of the children of Israel: for they have perverted their way, and they have forgotten the LORD their God.

commentary.narrative:
The scene shifts from divine accusation to the human response—a voice of weeping and supplication rises from the very 'high places' where Israel once prostituted herself (verse 2). This is poetic irony and redemptive reversal: the locations of Israel's idolatry become the locations of her repentance. The 'voice' (singular) represents Israel's collective lamentation, heard on the barren heights—the sacred landscape itself bears witness to the people's remorse. The 'weeping and supplications' (tahanunim) are the deep cries of those who recognize their sin and beg for mercy.

The verse provides both the form and the content of Israel's acknowledgment: she weeps, and she confesses two things—'they have perverted their way' and 'they have forgotten the LORD their God.' The first confession addresses the twisted nature of their path (they have taken a crooked course); the second addresses the underlying spiritual reality (they have severed themselves from knowledge of and relationship with their God). The verse does not yet record Israel's full repentance or return, but it marks the turning point: the recognition of sin precedes and enables repentance. The shift from direct divine speech to this auditory image of human weeping suggests that God is hearing His people's cry—the first movement toward restoration.

word_study.meaning: Shfayim (שְׁפָיִם), literally 'barren heights' or 'bare places,' refers to the elevated locations outside cities where idolatrous worship (particularly of Baal and Asherah) took place. The term carries a sense of exposure and desolation—these are not grand temples but bare hilltops.
word_study.significance: The repetition of shfayim from verse 2 ('upon the high places she hath played the harlot') creates a structural symmetry: Israel's shame was exposed on these heights, and now her repentance is also heard there. The same space becomes both the scene of idolatry and the scene of lamentation—suggesting that genuine repentance occurs at the very location of sin.

word_study.meaning: Bkhi (בְּכִי) means 'weeping, weeping sounds'—the audible expression of sorrow. Tahanunim (תַחֲנוּנֵי) from chanan means 'to supplicate, beseech, show mercy'—it is not mere crying but the pleading cry of someone who seeks mercy from one with power to grant or withhold it.
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'weeping' and 'supplications' suggests not passive grief but active petition—Israel cries out and simultaneously begs for mercy. The verb form indicates ongoing, repeated supplication.

word_study.meaning: He'ewu is from the root 'awah, meaning 'to bend, twist, pervert, distort.' It suggests that Israel's path was not merely wrong but fundamentally twisted out of its proper shape. Darkam ('their way') refers to the course or conduct of life—not a single sin but the entire trajectory of their choices.
word_study.significance: The verb 'awah suggests deformation rather than mere error—the path has been bent out of its original, intended shape. This is more serious than being lost; it is having deliberately distorted one's way.

word_study.meaning: Shakhah (שָׁכַח) means 'to forget,' but in Hebrew covenant theology, forgetting God is not mere cognitive lapse but the severing of relationship—the failure to maintain the remembrance and acknowledgment of covenant. It is volitional forgetting, the act of pushing God out of conscious recognition and loyalty.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'YHWH elohehem' ('the LORD their God') emphasizes the personal, covenant relationship—they have forgotten not an abstract deity but their God, the One who had entered into binding relationship with them.

cross_references.connection: The same 'high places' are mentioned as the location of Israel's idolatrous prostitution; verse 21 places her weeping at the same site, creating a reversal where shame becomes the birthplace of repentance.

The psalmist describes Israel's cycle of sin and restoration: 'Many times did he deliver them... Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry.'—The pattern of weeping cry leading to divine response matches Jeremiah's structure.
Jerusalem weeps: 'Mine eye runneth down with water... for the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me'—the same imagery of weeping as an expression of covenant loss and longing.
The sons of Mosiah, after their transformation, experience deep remorse and weeping; their tears of repentance precede their full return to God, mirroring the pattern in Jeremiah 3:21.

commentary.historical_context: The 'high places' were a persistent religious problem in ancient Israel and Judah. Despite Deuteronomic centralization reforms that attempted to consolidate worship in Jerusalem, local shrines on high places continued to flourish, especially in rural areas. Archaeological surveys have identified numerous Bronze Age and Iron Age cultic sites on elevated terrain throughout the Levant. These high places were not merely places of 'false worship' but often syncretic sites where Canaanite fertility religions (Baal, Asherah) were blended with Yahwistic practice. Jeremiah's audience would have been familiar with these locations and their association with idolatry. The image of weeping on the high places would have conveyed not only spiritual repentance but also visible, embodied remorse—tears on the very ground where unfaithfulness occurred.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:17-21 describes Alma's intense remorse and his cries for mercy in the depths of despair, followed by divine forgiveness. Like Jeremiah 3:21, Alma's weeping and pleading precede his restoration. Also, 2 Nephi 4:26-27 records Nephi's lament: 'O wretched man that I am!'—personal weeping leading to renewal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:15-16 describes Christ's suffering in Gethsemane: 'which suffering caused myself, even God the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore'—the cosmic resonance of repentant weeping. Also, D&C 121:1-6 records Joseph Smith's weeping cry from Liberty Jail, paralleling Israel's supplication in Jeremiah 3:21.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is understood in Restoration theology as a place where God hears the prayers and tears of His people. The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly emphasizes that the temple is a place where divine ears 'hear' human petitions. Jeremiah 3:21 prefigures the role of the temple as the place where sincere repentance is heard and answered.

commentary.christological_typology: The weeping and supplication of Israel in verse 21 point to Christ's own intercession for humanity. Just as Israel's tears of repentance rise from the 'high places' to be heard by God, so Christ's tears and blood cry out on humanity's behalf. Hebrews 5:7 describes Christ 'in the days of his flesh... with strong crying and tears' making supplication to God. The imagery of weeping as the language of covenant restoration finds its ultimate expression in Christ's redemptive tears and His role as mediator who brings humanity's repentance before the Father.
commentary.application: Verse 21 teaches that genuine repentance begins with honest acknowledgment—not hiding shame but weeping it out, speaking it aloud, letting it be heard. It affirms that the willingness to recognize sin and confess it ('they have perverted their way, they have forgotten the LORD') is itself the beginning of restoration. Modern members are invited to practice this honesty: to weep over real faithlessness, to articulate genuine remorse, and to voice sincere supplication. The verse also teaches that God hears such weeping—He is not distant from the repentant soul but attentive to its cry. The fact that Israel's voice rises from the very places of her shame suggests that repentance need not be hidden or performed in a sanitized setting; it happens where the sin was—in the midst of real life, real failure, real need.

text_kjv: Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings. Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the LORD our God.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 22 is the turning point of the entire chapter—a voice (identified as God's, though not explicitly labeled) calls Israel to return, and Israel immediately responds, 'Here we are, we come unto thee.' The structure itself is dramatic: God's command and Israel's obedience happen in the same verse, suggesting the immediacy and power of genuine repentance. The call 'Return, ye backsliding children' reframes Israel not as irredeemable traitors but as wayward children who can come home. The language shifts from accusation (verses 20-21) to invitation (verse 22)—God offers not punishment but healing.

The promise 'I will heal your backslidings' is revolutionary: apostasy, which seemed like a crime warranting death, is reframed as a sickness that can be cured. The Hebrew meshuvotekhem ('your faithlessness, your turnings-away') are all the accumulated departures from God—they are treated as a disease rather than a legal violation requiring retribution. Crucially, God does not ask Israel to heal herself; He offers His own healing power. The people's response—'Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the LORD our God'—marks the completion of the repentance cycle: recognition of sin (verse 21), acceptance of invitation (verse 22), and confession of God's identity and authority ('thou art the LORD our God'). The use of 'we' signals communal repentance, not individual conversion.

word_study.meaning: Shuv (שׁוּב), the root meaning 'to turn, return,' appears three times in this verse: shuvu ('return!'), shvavim ('backsliding ones'—literally 'turning-away ones'), and meshuvotekhem ('your turnings-away'). Each form of shuv carries the full weight of the chapter's theological vocabulary. The noun banim ('children') recalls verse 19—these are not enemies but God's own children, addressed with a mixture of rebuke and affection.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that no English translation can capture the intensive wordplay: the command to shuv (turn-back) is directed at the shvavim (the turn-away ones), and God promises to heal the meshuvot (the turnings-away). It is a linguistic embodiment of the message itself—the very sound and structure of the Hebrew enacts the call to reverse course.

word_study.meaning: Erpa (אֶרְפָּה) from the verb rapha ('to heal, cure, restore to health') suggests that God approaches apostasy not as a judge but as a physician. Meshuvotekhem (מְשׁוּבֹתֵיכֶם) is the noun form of shuv, literally 'your turnings-away,' but here it functions as the disease to be healed. The verb is first-person singular ('I will heal'), emphasizing God's active, personal agency in restoration.
word_study.significance: The medical metaphor reframes repentance: Israel is not guilty of a crime but sick with a disease. Healing requires not punishment but cure—medicine, time, and the physician's skill. This is extraordinarily compassionate language, especially given the severity of Israel's betrayal in verse 20.

word_study.meaning: Hinnenu ('behold us, here we are') is an emphatic affirmation of presence and commitment. Atanu ('we come, we go') uses the causative form, suggesting active motion toward God. Lakh ('to you') designates God as the destination. Together, the phrase means 'Here we are—we come to you,' expressing both present reality and deliberate movement.
word_study.significance: The people's response is immediate and corporeal—they do not merely assent to words but declare their physical, emotional, and spiritual arrival at God's presence. This is covenant language of approach and reconciliation.

word_study.term_english: for thou art the LORD our God
word_study.meaning: Ki ('for, because') provides the logical ground of their return: because YHWH is eloheinu ('our God'), they belong to Him and He to them. The assertion 'Thou art YHWH' (the singular personal name) and 'our God' (the covenant identifier) is a full confession of faith in God's identity and power.
word_study.significance: The people do not base their return on their own deservingness but on the reality of who God is. They return because they remember (or realize) that YHWH is their God—the covenant remains valid, and they belong to Him regardless of their wandering.

cross_references.connection: Earlier in the chapter, God says, 'Turn, O backsliding children'—verse 22 echoes this earlier call, suggesting repeated, patient invitations to repentance.

Hosea calls Israel to 'Return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity'—and promises healing: 'I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.' The parallel structure and language suggest a shared prophetic theology of repentance and restoration.

Isaiah offers the same structure—recognition of sin, God's invitation to return, and the promise of restoration: 'though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.' The pattern of call-response-healing appears throughout the prophets.
Modern revelation echoes Jeremiah's structure: 'Wherefore, I am in your midst, and I am the good shepherd'—God locates Himself with His people and invites their return to wholeness.

commentary.historical_context: The medical metaphor for repentance would have resonated with ancient audiences familiar with both Mesopotamian and Egyptian healing practices. The verb rapha ('to heal') appears in texts from across the ancient Near East, suggesting it was a widely understood metaphor for restoration and cure. In ancient covenant law, a breach of covenant was typically punishable by curse, exile, or death—not by healing. God's reframing of Israel's apostasy as sickness rather than crime was theologically radical and mercy-oriented. The communal nature of the response ('we come') reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding that covenants were collective, not merely individual; the entire people would be healed together or not at all.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:12 describes Christ's role: 'And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people'—extending the healing promised in Jeremiah 3:22 into the redemptive work of Christ. Also, Enos 1:8 records Enos's return to God: 'Behold, I went to hunt beasts in the forests; and the words which I had often heard my father speak concerning eternal life, and the joy of the saints, sank deep into my heart'—a personal parallel to Israel's corporate return.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 95:1 records: 'Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you whom I love, and whom I love I also chasten'—the pattern of calling wayward people to repentance through the voice of love, not judgment. D&C 6:16 offers 'Peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come'—the healing and wholeness promised in Jeremiah's restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is portrayed in Latter-day Saint theology as the place of reconciliation and healing for covenant people. The temple ceremony enacts return and restoration—the journey back to God's presence through ordinances. Jeremiah 3:22's promise of divine healing is fulfilled through the healing ordinances of the temple, particularly for those who have fallen away.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 22 prefigures Christ's role as the healer of humanity's apostasy and faithlessness. Jesus explicitly identified Himself with the healing function in Luke 4:18 ('to heal the brokenhearted') and Matthew 9:12 ('They that be whole need not a physician; but they that are sick'). Christ is the physician who treats the disease of sin not with death but with life-giving medicine. His call to 'Return' in verse 22 is echoed in the gospel's call to repentance, and His promise of healing is fulfilled in the Atonement—the cosmic restoration that makes possible humanity's return to covenant standing.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 22 offers two profound invitations. First, it teaches that the path back to God is always open—no sin, no departure, no failure is so final that return is impossible. The call 'Return, ye backsliding children' is not conditional on earning God's favor but is an unconditional invitation based on His nature and covenant. Second, it teaches the power of honest confession: 'Here we are, we come unto thee' is not a plea for mercy based on self-justification but a bare acknowledgment of presence and commitment. Modern members are invited to practice this kind of return—not waiting to be perfect before approaching God but coming as they are, declaring 'Here we are,' and trusting God's healing power. The verse specifically teaches that healing is God's prerogative, not something we must accomplish through our own effort. This frees the repentant from the burden of self-condemnation and opens the way to genuine restoration.

text_kjv: Truly in vain is salvation hoped for from the hills, and from the multitude of mountains: truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 23 continues Israel's confession and marks a crucial theological clarification. Having declared 'Here we are,' Israel now explicitly repudiates the false sources of salvation she had pursued—the 'hills' and 'mountains' where idolatrous worship occurred. The verse contrasts two paths: the false hope placed in high places (where Baal and other gods were worshipped) and the true salvation found in YHWH alone. The structure is parallel and emphatic: 'Truly in vain... truly in the LORD...' The double 'truly' (akin) signals that what follows is not opinion but absolute reality.

The phrase 'salvation hoped for from the hills' captures Israel's earlier strategy: she had sought salvation, prosperity, and protection from the Baals and gods associated with the high places. The 'multitude of mountains' suggests not merely the physical geography but the vast system of false worship scattered across the land. The second half of the verse asserts that salvation belongs to God alone—not as a hopeful wish but as a statement of theological fact. The phrase 'salvation of Israel' (teshu'at yisra'el) uses the covenantal language of deliverance; YHWH alone possesses the power to save His people from their enemies, their sins, and their exile. The verse represents Israel's intellectual and spiritual reorientation—a complete reversal of the theological assumptions that had led her into apostasy.

word_study.meaning: Sheqer (שֶׁקֶר) means 'falsehood, deception, lie'—not merely futility but conscious deception. The preposition la ('from, in') suggests seeking from falsehood, or seeking what is intrinsically false. The phrase lasheqer carries the sense 'in a lie' or 'from a lie'—the salvation hoped for from the hills is not merely disappointing but fundamentally false, built on deception.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures the distinction: 'The hills are a delusion, the commotion on the mountains is a lie.' The 'hills' are not neutral territory but sites of deception—the worship that occurs there promises salvation but delivers only emptiness.

word_study.meaning: Shfayim (שְׁפָיִם) refers to the barren heights, the high places of idolatry (as in verses 2 and 21). Harim (הָרִים) means 'mountains,' the elevated terrain itself. Together they represent the geographical and spiritual locus of Israel's false religion.
word_study.significance: The repetition of high places throughout the chapter (verses 2, 21, 23) creates structural emphasis—these locations are the scenes both of Israel's sin and of her repentance and restoration. The physical landscape is implicated in the theology.

word_study.meaning: Hamon (הָמוֹן) means 'multitude, throng, commotion, tumult'—specifically, the noise and activity of a crowd. In religious contexts, it can refer to the tumultuous activity of cultic worship, the noise of festivals, sacrifices, and celebrations.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'multitude of mountains' may suggest both the numerous mountains (geographical extent) and the tumultuous noise of worship on those mountains (religious excess). The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'the commotion on the mountains is a lie.'

word_study.meaning: Teshu'ah (תְּשׁוּעָה) from the root yasha means 'deliverance, salvation, rescue.' It refers to YHWH's action of saving His people from enemies, affliction, and death. In covenant theology, teshu'ah is the distinctive prerogative of God—He alone can deliver and restore.
word_study.significance: The use of teshu'ah twice in verse 23—negatively ('salvation hoped for from the hills') and positively ('salvation of Israel')—creates a theological pivot. True salvation is not a commodity available from multiple sources but the unique action of God, available only through Him.

cross_references.connection: Earlier, God condemned Israel's multiplied gods and idols: 'But where are thy gods that thou hast made thee? let them arise, if they can save thee in the time of thy trouble'—verse 23 echoes this challenge, affirming that the idols cannot save.

'I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD'—the psalmist looks to mountains but finds salvation in YHWH alone, paralleling Jeremiah's movement from false hope in hills to true salvation in God.
'Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song'—the same affirmation of God alone as source of salvation and strength.
'Counsel with the Lord in all thy doings, and he will direct thee for good'—the Book of Mormon affirms that counsel (and salvation) comes from God, not from any other source.

commentary.historical_context: The critique of high place worship and the affirmation of YHWH as sole savior reflect the historical struggle between Yahwism and Canaanite religion throughout Iron Age Israel and Judah. Archaeological evidence from sites like Khirtan and Arad shows cultic installations at high places and smaller sanctuaries away from the central Jerusalem temple. Many Israelites and Judahites seemed to have practiced a syncretic religion, calling on both YHWH and Baal depending on the context—YHWH for national security, Baal for agricultural fertility. Jeremiah's theological assertion that YHWH alone saves challenges this syncretism head-on. The 'multitude of mountains' reflects the real, widespread presence of these cult sites throughout the land. From Jeremiah's perspective and within Deuteronomic theology, centralization of worship in Jerusalem was essential precisely because divided worship led to divided loyalty and false confidence in false gods.
