restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes both blessing and cursing—the endowment presents the consequences of covenant-breaking. Verse 20 represents the fulfillment of the curses that accompany covenantal violation. The unquenchable fire echoes temple imagery of divine justice and purification.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's teachings about final judgment employ similar fire imagery (Matthew 13:36-42, where Jesus explains the parable of the tares and describes the end-time burning of the wicked). However, Christ adds an element of mercy absent in Jeremiah's immediate pronouncement: the opportunity for repentance before judgment falls. The 'unquenchable fire' in Christian theology becomes associated with hell—the final state of those who reject Christ's redemption. In this way, Jeremiah's warning becomes a type of the ultimate judgment Christ Himself will execute.
commentary.application: For modern members, this verse serves as a sober reminder that covenant membership brings accountability. The destruction of Jerusalem was not arbitrary divine caprice but the inevitable result of sustained covenantal violation. The principle applies to individuals and institutions: those who have entered into sacred covenants face more serious consequences for violations than those without such commitments. The comprehensiveness of judgment—affecting not just the guilty but the entire social and natural order—reminds us that sin has ripple effects beyond the immediate actor. A leader's hypocrisy, a parent's unfaithfulness, or a community's drift from covenant principles creates collateral damage. The call is not to fear-based obedience but to recognize that faithfulness to covenant is the only way to avoid judgment's reach.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices, and eat flesh.

commentary.narrative:
This verse pivots sharply in tone—from the terrifying pronouncement of judgment to biting sarcasm. God commands: 'Add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices and eat the meat yourselves!' The sarcasm is devastating because it works through the inversion of a fundamental law of sacrifice. In the Levitical system, the burnt offering (olah) was completely consumed by fire on the altar. Unlike peace offerings or sin offerings, which provided portions of meat for the priests and worshippers to eat, the burnt offering was entirely God's. To eat from a burnt offering was unthinkable—it violated the whole structure of the sacrifice.

But Jeremiah, speaking for God, sarcastically commands them to do exactly that. The point is that the distinction between what belongs to God and what belongs to the people has become meaningless in their practice. Their sacrifices have been emptied of spiritual significance; they have become nothing but a pretext for meat consumption. God is saying, in effect: 'You are already acting as though sacrifice is just a meal. Stop pretending otherwise. Go ahead and eat the whole thing. Your ritual performance is so hollow that maintaining the form of the law is pointless.' This is caustic rejection not of the sacrificial system itself (which God established) but of the people's approach to it—ritual without repentance, form without substance, mechanical observance without covenant commitment.

word_study.meaning: Plural of olah, 'burnt offering.' The term derives from a root meaning 'to ascend,' reflecting the rising smoke of the sacrifice toward heaven. The olah was unique in that the entire animal (except the hide) was consumed by fire—nothing was eaten by the worshipper or priest.
word_study.significance: The choice of olah (rather than other sacrifices) is deliberate. God singles out the one sacrifice that required total surrender. To mock it by calling for it to be eaten is to mock the highest form of devotion and complete self-surrender. The Covenant Rendering's translation of olot as 'burnt offerings' captures the distinction from other sacrifices. By commanding them to eat even these, God highlights the depths of their spiritual corruption—they cannot distinguish between what they owe to God and what they owe to themselves.

word_study.meaning: Sacrifices, specifically offerings whose meat is shared among priests and worshippers (as opposed to the wholly burned olah). These included peace offerings and meal offerings.
word_study.significance: The contrast is key: zebachim were already shared meals. God is saying, 'Mix in the burnt offerings too. Turn the entire system into a meal.' This exposes the instrumentalization of sacrifice—using it for its meat rather than as an expression of covenant obedience.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'and eat meat.' The reduction of sacrifice to mere meat-eating, stripped of its ritual and relational significance.
word_study.significance: The bluntness of basar ('flesh') emphasizes the purely physical, carnal dimension. Where sacrifice should involve the whole person—body, soul, and spirit offered to God—their version has reduced it to appetite. This is Jeremiah's repeated critique: the people have externalized religion, making it a matter of mechanics rather than covenant devotion.

cross_references.connection: Samuel rebukes Saul with the principle that obedience to God's word is better than sacrifice, and listening than the fat of rams—establishing the priority of relational faithfulness over ritual performance.
God declares 'I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings'—a parallel condemnation of sacrifice divorced from genuine covenant love.
Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 in response to Pharisaic criticism, emphasizing that God's desire is mercy and genuine relationship, not the external observance of ritual law.

Teaches that while we should remember to keep the Sabbath day holy, the Lord's work is to 'bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man'—giving priority to spiritual substance over ceremonial form.
Describes the law of the burnt offering, which was entirely consumed by fire—providing the legal background that makes Jeremiah's sarcastic command to 'eat' the olah so caustic.

commentary.historical_context: By Jeremiah's time (late 7th century BCE), Jerusalem's Temple had become increasingly corrupted. Kings like Ahaz and Manasseh had introduced Canaanite religious practices into the Temple precincts. Even during reforms (such as under Hezekiah or later Josiah), the outward performance of sacrifice continued while the people's hearts remained oriented toward false gods and unjust practices. The temple may have been crowded with worshippers and heavily perfumed with incense, yet the city was full of violence, theft, adultery, and false swearing (as Jeremiah details in verses 5-6). Archaeological and textual evidence suggests that Judean religious practice in this era involved significant syncretism—the blending of Yahweh worship with Canaanite fertility religion. Jeremiah's sarcasm targets this disconnect: the religious institution is operating smoothly while the society is morally bankrupt.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 26:29, Nephi prophesies that some will say, 'We have received the word of God,' yet will rob the poor and deny the Holy Ghost. This reflects Jeremiah's principle: people can participate in religious forms while abandoning covenantal substance. Alma 31 depicts the Zoramites engaging in elaborate synagogue prayer while oppressing the poor—their ritual life completely divorced from justice.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:119 emphasizes that in the Lord's house, all things should be done 'in order.' Yet D&C 50:18-24 warns that many will be deceived, thinking they work for God while walking in darkness. The principle is that form without substance, order without spirit, is a snare rather than a salvation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes covenants of obedience and sacrifice. Jeremiah's rebuke applies to any temple member who treats temple participation as a ritual obligation divorced from genuine commitment to live the covenants made there. The endowment is not 'work' to be gotten through but an embodiment of principles to be lived.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus's cleansing of the Temple (Matthew 21:12-17, Mark 11:15-19) represents a parallel moment of prophetic rejection of externalized religion. Jesus overturns the money-changers' tables and drives out those who buy and sell—essentially saying the Temple has become a marketplace rather than a house of prayer. Like Jeremiah's sarcasm, Christ's action communicates that form without relational authenticity is not merely inadequate; it is an affront to God. Both prophets insist that true worship requires the alignment of the heart, not mere external conformity.
commentary.application: This verse challenges members to examine the gap between their religious participation and their daily conduct. Do we treat covenant practices (Temple attendance, sacrament participation, home teaching, etc.) as obligations to be fulfilled, or as expressions of genuine devotion to Christ? Jeremiah's sarcasm suggests that going through the motions of religion while harboring an unrepentant heart and engaging in unethical behavior is not just inadequate—it is something God actively rejects. The application is not to abandon ritual (which has real power and meaning) but to ensure that ritual participation flows from and reinforces genuine covenantal commitment. As one general authority has observed, the most important meeting in the Church is not in the chapel but around the family dinner table—because living the covenant matters infinitely more than the frequency of religious observance.

text_kjv: For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices:

commentary.narrative:
This verse contains one of the most provocative statements in the Hebrew Bible, one that appears to directly contradict the extensive sacrificial legislation found in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. On the surface, God claims He never commanded the fathers concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices when He brought them out of Egypt. But this seems impossible—Exodus 12 describes the Passover sacrifice, and Exodus 20 is followed by extensive instructions for the Tabernacle, priests, and sacrifices.

The key to interpreting this passage lies in the phrase 'in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt.' This temporal marker is crucial. God is not claiming that He never instituted sacrifices; rather, He is claiming that sacrifices were not His primary demand at the moment of deliverance from Egypt. When God met Israel at Sinai immediately after the Exodus, His first words were the Ten Commandments—the moral law, not the ceremonial law. The Ten Commandments establish the relationship: obedience to God's moral will. The sacrificial system, by contrast, was remedial—a means of addressing violations of that primary covenant. Jeremiah's point is that later generations (and indeed the religious establishment of Jeremiah's own time) have inverted the priority. They have treated sacrifice as the core of religious obligation, when in fact it was always secondary to relational obedience. The word 'commanded' (tzivviti) appears twice in this verse and the next, setting up a contrast: 'I commanded them' not about sacrifice but about obedience. This is Jeremiah's theological reorientation of the entire system.

word_study.term_original: לֹֽא־דִבַּ֣רְתִּי / לֹ֤א צִוִּיתִים (lo dibbarti / lo tzivvitim)
word_study.meaning: Dibbarti derives from 'dabar' ('word,' 'speak'); tzivvitim from 'tzavah' ('command,' 'order'). The first emphasizes communication; the second, authoritative directive. Together they deny both that God spoke about sacrifice and that He authoritatively commanded it as a priority.
word_study.significance: The double negation is emphatic. It's not that God merely neglected to mention sacrifice; He actively did not command it at the foundational moment of covenant relationship. The Covenant Rendering's use of 'declare' and 'command' preserves this distinction between communication and authoritative ordering.

word_study.term_english: in the day that I brought them out
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'in the day [that] I brought them out.' This refers to the immediate aftermath of the Exodus, the moment of Sinai and the giving of the law.
word_study.significance: This phrase anchors the statement temporally. God is making a claim about the priorities at the foundational covenantal moment—not denying that sacrifice was later instituted, but insisting that sacrifice was never the first principle. This is consistent with the historical sequence: Exodus 20 gives the Ten Commandments, and it is only after the people's covenant commitment to the moral law that detailed sacrificial legislation follows.

cross_references.connection: The Ten Commandments, given immediately after the Exodus, establish moral obedience as the foundation of covenant, preceding detailed sacrificial law.
The detailed sacrificial legislation that follows the commandments, illustrating that the ceremonial law was given after and as supplementary to the moral law.
Samuel delivers the principle that 'to obey is better than sacrifice'—directly echoing Jeremiah's reorientation of priorities.
God declares 'I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings'—affirming Jeremiah's principle that relational obedience precedes ritual.
Amulek explains that the sacrifices and performances of the law pointed to Christ and were never meant as ends in themselves, but as types of the final sacrifice.

commentary.historical_context: From a historical-critical perspective, biblical scholars recognize that the Torah (Pentateuch) reached its final form during or after the Babylonian exile. Jeremiah prophesied during the years immediately preceding and following Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BCE. From this vantage point, Jeremiah may be critiquing the received sacrificial legislation—not denying its validity but questioning whether the institution had become an end in itself rather than a means to relational faithfulness. In the temple-centered religion of Judah, especially after the Josian reform (621 BCE) which centralized sacrifice exclusively in Jerusalem, the sacrificial system had become professionalized, economically significant, and institutionally powerful. Priests depended on sacrifices for their livelihood; the Temple was the economic center of Jerusalem. Jeremiah's prophetic critique cuts through institutional interests to recover what he sees as the original covenant demand: obedience, not performance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's commentary in 2 Nephi 25:24-27 is directly relevant: 'And notwithstanding we believe in Christ, we keep the law of Moses, and look forward with steadfastness unto Christ, until the law shall be fulfilled... for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.' The Book of Mormon clarifies that the law of Moses—including sacrifice—was a type pointing to Christ and was never meant to be the foundation of salvation. The foundation is grace and repentance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:40-42 teaches that Christ is 'the brightness of [God's] glory, and the express image of his person,' and that through His blood we gain eternal life. This prioritizes Christ's redemption over ceremonial observance. D&C 97:15-16 connects this to the temple: the temple becomes holy when its inhabitants are holy—the priority again is the people's covenantal integrity, not the building's ceremonial functions.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the Restoration, the temple is understood through the lens of personal covenants rather than institutional sacrifice. Members make covenants of obedience, sacrifice, and consecration—not through animal offerings but through alignment of will with God's will. The temple embodies Jeremiah's priority: relational commitment precedes and underwrites ritual. The question for temple participants is whether they approach the temple as a transformative covenantal experience or merely as an observance to be completed.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse points forward to the abolition of the sacrificial system through Christ's perfect sacrifice. In Hebrews 10:1-10, the author argues that the law with its sacrifices was 'a shadow of good things to come' and that Christ's single offering 'hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.' Jeremiah's claim that God's primary demand was always relational obedience finds its ultimate expression in Christ, who teaches that the greatest commandments are love of God and neighbor (Matthew 22:37-40). The sacrifice of Christ is not merely another ritual in a series; it is the completion and replacement of the entire sacrificial system, because it accomplishes what all sacrifices pointed to: the reconciliation of humanity to God through perfect obedience.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites deep examination of the distinction between form and substance. Do we approach religious practice—temple attendance, sacrament participation, callings, missionary work—as ends in themselves, or as means of deepening covenantal relationship with God? Jeremiah warns that it is possible to be religiously active while spiritually distant. The principle applies to families and communities as well: a family that prays together but lacks genuine love and honesty has confused form with substance. A ward that holds regular meetings but lacks compassion and genuine fellowship has made Jeremiah's error. The application is to recover the primacy of relational obedience—keeping the commandments not from duty but from love, engaging in religious practice not to satisfy obligation but to strengthen covenant bond with God and neighbor.

text_kjv: But this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you.

commentary.narrative:
This verse presents the positive counterpoint to verse 22. If God did not primarily command sacrifice at the Exodus, what did He command? The answer is relational obedience expressed through the covenant formula. The structure of this verse is dense with theological significance: it contains the foundational covenant proclamation ('I will be your God and you will be my people'), linked to a double command ('Obey my voice' and 'Walk in all the ways that I have commanded you'), with a promise attached ('that it may be well unto you').

The covenant formula 'I will be your God and you will be my people' (ani lekhem le'elohim ve'attem tihyu li le'am) appears throughout scripture as the essence of the covenantal relationship. It establishes mutuality: God commits to being in relationship with this specific people, and they commit to being God's particular people. This is not transactional (you perform sacrifice, I accept it), but relational and exclusive. To be God's people means to listen to God's voice (shim'u beqoli) with genuine responsiveness, not merely formal compliance. 'Walking in all the ways' (halakhtem bekhol-haderekh) picks up the metaphor of covenant as a path—not a collection of isolated duties but an integrated way of living. The promise 'that it may go well with you' (lema'an yitav lakhem) reframes obedience not as arbitrary submission but as practical wisdom. Following God's way leads to flourishing; departing from it leads to ruin. This verse represents Jeremiah's attempt to restore the covenant to its proper foundation: not the machinery of the Temple but the heart-level alignment of the people with their God.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'hear in/by my voice.' Shema ('hear') in Hebrew often means more than passive auditory reception; it implies responsive listening, compliance, and obedience. Beqoli ('by my voice') emphasizes that God speaks—that revelation is dynamic and ongoing.
word_study.significance: This is covenant language. The foundational Jewish prayer, the Shema Yisrael ('Hear, O Israel'), begins with this same root, establishing that the core religious obligation is responsive listening to God's self-revelation. For Jeremiah, sacrifice is peripheral to this primary relationship.

word_study.term_english: I will be your God and you shall be my people
word_study.term_original: וְהָיִ֤יתִי לָכֶם֙ לֵאלֹהִ֔ים וְאַתֶּ֖ם תִּהְיוּ־לִ֣י לְעָ֑ם (ve-hayiti lakhem le'elohim ve'attem tihyu li le'am)
word_study.transliteration: ve-hayiti lakhem le-Elohim ve-attem tihyu li le-am
word_study.meaning: The classic covenant formula. Hayiti ('I will be') and tihyu ('you will be') use the simple future tense, expressing commitment. Le'elohim ('as God') and le'am ('as people') establish the specific relational identity.
word_study.significance: This formula appears in Exodus 19:5-6, Leviticus 26:12, and throughout the prophets. It is the backbone of biblical covenant theology. God commits His identity (to be *their* God, not just any god) and they commit theirs (to be *His* people, not pursuing independent allegiance). The Covenant Rendering's preservation of this exact English formulation is important for recognizing its resonance throughout scripture.

word_study.term_original: וַהֲלַכְתֶּ֗ם בְּכָל־הַדֶּ֙רֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֲצַוֶּ֣ה אֶתְכֶ֔ם (va-halakhtem bekhol-haderekh asher atzavveh etkhem)
word_study.meaning: Halakhtem ('you shall walk') from halak ('to go,' 'to walk'). Derekh ('way,' 'path') is a metaphor for conduct and way of life. The command is for total, not partial, alignment with God's instruction.
word_study.significance: The 'way' (derekh) language pervades prophetic and wisdom literature. Jeremiah employs it repeatedly to show that covenant is not a collection of rules but a trajectory, a direction, an integrated approach to living. This anticipates Christ's claim to be 'the way, the truth, and the life.'

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'in order that it may be good/well for you.' Yitav ('it will be good') is the simple future, indicating consequence not reward—if you walk in God's ways, well-being naturally follows.
word_study.significance: This is not bribery ('if you obey, I'll give you stuff') but wisdom teaching. God's way is the path of genuine flourishing. Departure from it inevitably leads to harm. This aligns with the wisdom tradition and with Jeremiah's repeated counsel that turning toward God is Israel's only path to restoration.

cross_references.connection: Contains the original covenant formula that Jeremiah echoes here, establishing that covenant relationship is the foundational commitment preceding all other obligations.

Moses presents the choice: 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live.' This echoes Jeremiah's promise that obedience leads to well-being.

Describes the righteous person who walks not in the counsel of the wicked but delights in God's law, and whose way will prosper—reflecting the same principle of well-being following from obedient alignment.
Jeremiah repeats this exact covenant formula in another oracle, emphasizing its centrality to his theology and prophecy.
Teaches that there is a law upon all things, and those who keep God's laws receive blessings, while those who break them receive cursings—the same principle of natural consequence.

commentary.historical_context: The covenant formula that Jeremiah invokes here carries weight in Judah's remembered history. It appears in Exodus at the moment Israel accepts the covenant at Sinai. It appears in Leviticus as the promise attached to observing the law. Deuteronomy recounts a covenant renewal ceremony where Moses presents Israel with a choice: life or death, blessing or curse—and urges them to choose life by turning toward God. In Jeremiah's own era, the memory of the Josian reform (621 BCE) was still fresh. King Josiah had carried out extensive religious reforms, attempting to purify the Temple and centralize worship in Jerusalem. Yet despite this external reformation, Jeremiah saw that the people's hearts remained uncommitted. The formula Jeremiah quotes here is meant to call them back to genuine covenant relationship, not merely external reformation. Historically, the Babylonian threat was looming (the final destruction would come 586 BCE), and Jeremiah is offering a path to restoration: turn back to genuine covenantal commitment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 2:41, King Benjamin teaches: 'And now, I would that ye should understand that these are the conditions that were laid down by the angel of the Lord and the Lord Jesus Christ, that whoso should repent of his sins and desireth to be baptized in my name, even so shall ye receive of my blood, which was shed for you... And now I say unto you, my brethren, you that have desired to come into the covenant of God, I would that ye should consider the mighty change which is required of you; for I do not mean to apply harsh things unto you. For I say unto you that the good shepherd doth call after you.' The covenant relationship, not the mechanical observance of law, is the heart of salvation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 59:5-7 teaches: 'That thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day; For verily this is a day appointed unto you to rest from your labors, and to pay thy devotions unto the Most High; Nevertheless thy vows shall be offered up in righteousness on all days and at all times.' The principle is that religious observance is meant to deepen covenantal relationship, not replace it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment ceremony centers on covenants of obedience—not to earn salvation but to align oneself with God's will. The temple teaches that the covenant relationship ('I will be your God and you will be my people') is the foundation, and the specific covenants of obedience, sacrifice, and consecration flow from and serve this fundamental relationship. The temple is the place where this formula is embodied and renewed.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse directly points to Christ's own embodiment of perfect covenant obedience. In John 1:1-2, Jesus is identified as the Logos ('Word'), the one through whom all things were made and who is the source of revelation. In Matthew 3:15-17, when baptized by John, Jesus fulfills all righteousness and hears the voice of God saying, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' Jesus perfectly 'hears' God's voice and 'walks' in God's ways. His covenant with His disciples is the new covenant (Luke 22:20), which perfects and replaces the old. The formula 'I will be your God and you will be my people' finds its ultimate expression in Christ's promise to His followers: 'I will not leave you orphans... I will come to you' (John 14:18).
commentary.application: This verse calls modern covenant members to examine whether their religious commitment is rooted in relational love for God or in obligation and habit. Jeremiah's promise—'that it may go well with you'—reframes obedience not as submission to an external authority but as alignment with the path of genuine flourishing. The application is personal and communal: individuals are called to walk continuously in God's ways, not merely to comply with specific rules; families are called to build their homes on covenantal values that create genuine belonging; communities and wards are called to foster cultures where the covenant relationship with God is the animating principle rather than institutional maintenance. The question for each member is: Is my religion an external obligation I perform, or an internal transformation of how I relate to God and neighbor? Do I 'hear' God's voice with genuine responsiveness, or do I offer formal compliance? Do I see God's commandments as obstacles to freedom or as the pathway to true flourishing?

text_kjv: But they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear, but walked in the counsels and in the imagination of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward.

commentary.narrative:
This verse pivots from the covenantal offer—'hear my voice, walk in my ways, and it will go well with you'—to the tragic response: they refused. The structure of refusal is presented in escalating terms. First, the people did not 'hearken' (shama'u) or 'incline their ear' (hitu et-'oznam). These are the opposite of the 'obey my voice' demanded in verse 23. The double negation emphasizes complete rejection. Second, instead of following God's commandments, 'they walked according to the schemes of their evil heart' (yalekhu bemo'atzot bisheririut libam hara). This is not mere passive resistance but active rebellion oriented toward destruction. Third, the spatial metaphor concludes the verse: 'they went backward, not forward' (va-yihyu le'achor velo lefanim). In biblical thought, history moves forward as a narrative of covenantal progress. Israel should be advancing toward God's purposes, fulfilling its role as God's people. Instead, the nation regresses—repeating the patterns of earlier generations who also rejected God.

This verse names the fundamental pathology that Jeremiah diagnoses throughout his ministry: a 'hardened heart' (sheririut) that has lost the capacity for repentance. The people are not merely making mistakes; they are locked in willful rebellion. They have convinced themselves that their own 'counsel' (mo'atzot)—their schemes, their plans, their understanding—is superior to God's instruction. This is the essence of the pride Jeremiah repeatedly attacks. What makes this verse particularly tragic is that it describes not a momentary lapse but a habitual condition. The perfect tense ('they went' va-yihyu) suggests completed action, as though this backward motion is now their permanent trajectory.

word_study.term_original: וְלֹ֤א שָׁמְעוּ֙ וְלֹא־הִטּ֣וּ אֶת־אָזְנָ֔ם (ve-lo shama'u ve-lo-hittu et-'oznam)
word_study.meaning: Shama'u ('they heard') from shama ('to hear, obey, listen responsively'). Hittu et-oznam ('they inclined their ear') is literally 'they bent/turned their ear'—the gesture of receptive listening.
word_study.significance: The double refusal mirrors the double command in verse 23 (shim'u beqoli, 'obey my voice'). They refused to listen, refused to incline themselves toward God's word. This is not deafness but deliberate rejection—a turning away.

word_study.meaning: Mo'atzot ('counsels,' 'schemes,' 'plans') from ya'atz ('to counsel,' 'to advise'). The phrase describes people following their own or others' schemes rather than God's instruction.
word_study.significance: In Jeremiah's theology, human schemes that reject God's word are inherently destructive. The juxtaposition with verse 23's 'walk in all the ways that I have commanded you' is sharp: the people chose to walk in their own counsel instead of God's. This is the core of Jeremianic rebellion.

word_study.meaning: Sheririut ('stubbornness,' 'stiffness,' 'hardness') derives from a root suggesting something twisted, hardened, or locked in place. Lev ('heart') refers to the seat of will and understanding. Hara ('evil') qualifies the heart as oriented toward destruction.
word_study.significance: Sheririut is Jeremiah's signature diagnosis of Israel's condition. It appears repeatedly (3:17, 9:13, 11:8, 13:10, 16:12, 18:12, 23:17). The image is of a heart that has calcified—it can no longer bend, listen, or change direction. It is locked into a destructive trajectory. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'stubbornness' captures the willful dimension—this is not mere weakness but deliberate resistance.

word_study.term_original: וַיִּהְי֥וּ לְאָח֖וֹר וְלֹ֥א לְפָנִֽים (va-yihyu le'achor velo lefanim)
word_study.meaning: Le'achor ('backward,' 'to the back') and lefanim ('forward,' 'to the face'). The spatial metaphor depicts time and covenant as a forward trajectory.
word_study.significance: This is one of Jeremiah's most profound theological images. Covenant history should move forward—from Abraham, through Moses and the wilderness, into the land, toward the fulfillment of God's purposes. Instead, Israel regresses. They are going 'backward' toward the patterns of idolatry and moral corruption from which God should have freed them. The tragedy is not mere stagnation but active regression.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah uses the same term 'sheririut libam' (stubbornness of their heart) to describe Israel's condition—establishing that this calcified resistance is habitual, not occasional.
Isaiah writes that the people 'rebelled and grieved his holy Spirit'—depicting the same pattern of deliberate rejection of God's voice and presence.
Paul cites Isaiah to describe Israel's hardening: 'God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that should not see and ears that should not hear'—though Paul insists this hardening is not final.

Alma teaches that if people harden their hearts, 'the judgments of God shall come upon them; therefore, he cannot dwell with them.' This echoes Jeremiah's principle that hardened resistance to God has inevitable consequences.

The Lord warns in the Doctrine and Covenants: 'The weak things of the world shall come forth and break down the mighty and strong things... that man should not counsel his fellow man, neither trust in the arm of flesh.' This affirms Jeremiah's rebuke of those who follow their own counsel rather than God's.

commentary.historical_context: By the time Jeremiah delivers this oracle, the pattern of Israel's rejection has centuries of history behind it. The people had repeatedly rejected prophetic warnings during the monarchy. The Northern Kingdom had fallen to Assyria in 722 BCE. Now, in Jeremiah's time (late 7th century BCE), the Southern Kingdom of Judah faces the same trajectory. Archaeological and textual evidence suggests that despite religious reforms under kings like Hezekiah and Josiah, the underlying spiritual condition of the people—what Jeremiah calls 'the stubbornness of their evil heart'—remained unchanged. The leadership continued to trust in political alliances with Egypt rather than in covenant relationship with God. The wealthy continued to oppress the poor. The Temple continued to be corrupted with idolatrous practices imported from neighboring nations. Jeremiah watched as the nation backed further away from genuine covenantal fidelity even as it maintained the external forms of religion. From his perspective, the nation was literally 'going backward'—repeating the sins of the wilderness generation instead of advancing toward the fulfillment of covenant promises.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon recounts multiple cycles of this same pattern. In Helaman 12, Mormon writes: 'And thus we see that except the Lord doth soften the hearts of the children of men, and except they humble themselves and turn to the Lord their God, they must unavoidably perish.' The people of Nephi repeatedly move from covenant faithfulness to backsliding, their hearts hardening with prosperity. The metaphor of going 'backward, not forward' appears explicitly in Mormon's summary of the people's trajectory.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:33-34 teaches: 'But he that breaketh a covenant... that same is not exempted from the buffetings of Satan unto the day of redemption. And thus, with the sword and by bloodshed the inhabitants of the earth shall mourn.' The principle that covenant-breaking results in self-imposed separation from God's protection is consistent with Jeremiah's diagnosis.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment ceremony includes a covenant to 'obey the law of God.' The ceremony's logic reflects the same principle Jeremiah outlines: those who hearken to God's voice, who turn toward the light of revelation, who walk in the path of righteousness, progress forward. Those who harden their hearts and turn away move backward into darkness. The temple teaches that this is not arbitrary punishment but natural consequence—the structure of spiritual reality itself.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse describes the trajectory of those who reject Christ's message, a pattern developed throughout the New Testament. In John 8:31-47, Jesus distinguishes between those who abide in His word and those who refuse—describing the latter as slaves to sin. In Matthew 13:13-15, Jesus quotes Isaiah about those who 'seeing see not; and hearing they hear not'—their hearts have 'waxed gross' (become hardened). The image of going 'backward' rather than 'forward' finds its counterpart in Philippians 3:13-14, where Paul describes 'forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before'—the opposite of Jeremiah's regression. Christ offers redemption from this backward motion: the power to turn around (repent), to have the heart softened, to move forward toward the Father.
commentary.application:
This final verse of the passage serves as a dire warning and an invitation to self-examination. Jeremiah's diagnosis of 'stubbornness of heart' (sheririut libam) is the fundamental spiritual condition he addresses throughout his ministry. For modern readers, the question is: In what areas of my life have I hardened my heart? Where have I refused to 'incline my ear' to God's voice? Where am I following 'the counsel' of my own limited understanding or the world's values rather than God's instruction? The spatial metaphor 'backward, not forward' invites reflection on the trajectory of one's spiritual life. Am I progressing in faithfulness, deepening commitment, and alignment with covenant? Or am I regressing—returning to old patterns of selfishness, pride, or compromise?

The verse also applies communally. A ward, a family, or an institution can experience the same hardening. External forms of religious observance can persist while genuine covenantal commitment erodes. The solution Jeremiah offers (though not explicitly in this verse) is repentance—the softening of the heart, the turning back toward God's voice, the reorientation toward the covenant relationship. The application is urgent: recognize the signs of regression, respond to the prophetic call to repentance, and turn forward again toward genuine fidelity to God and neighbor.

text_kjv: Since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them.

commentary.narrative:
God's complaint against Judah deepens here with a historical sweep that spans the entire covenant history of Israel. From the moment the Exodus liberated the ancestors from Egypt until the present moment of Jeremiah's ministry, God has persistently sent prophetic messengers. The phrase "rising up early and sending" (hashkem veshaloch in Hebrew) is not mere literary repetition—it is an idiomatic expression for relentless, continuous effort, like a master who rises early each day to dispatch servants on errands. This is not God's first attempt at correction or His first warning; it is centuries of sustained intervention.

The emphasis falls on God's faithfulness and consistency in fulfilling His covenantal obligation to speak through prophets. This is important context for understanding Jeremiah's own mission: he is not an anomaly or an emergency measure, but the latest in an unbroken line of witnesses. Yet the very need for such persistence hints at the tragedy that follows—all this effort has yielded little fruit. The covenant people have had every opportunity, every warning, every prophetic voice. The failure lies entirely with Israel's refusal to listen, not with any lack of divine communication.

word_study.meaning: A Hebrew idiom expressing persistent, repeated action—literally 'to rise early' (wake before dawn) and 'to send forth.' In ancient Near Eastern context, the early riser was the diligent master; the phrase together expresses tireless, continuous effort. The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'sending them persistently, day after day.'
word_study.significance: This idiom recurs throughout Jeremiah (11:7, 25:4, 26:5, 29:19, 35:15, 44:4) as God's signature phrase for His unrelenting prophetic mission. It reframes covenant relationship as not transactional but relational—God sends prophets not as legal notices but as constant overtures of faithfulness. For modern readers, it challenges the notion that God is distant or silent; the problem is always Israel's deafness, never God's neglect.

word_study.meaning: God's prophets are called His 'servants' (avadim)—the same term used for slaves or devoted subordinates. This emphasizes the prophets' subordinate role to God's will and their function as instruments of divine speech rather than autonomous speakers.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah himself is a 'servant of the LORD' in this same sense. The term elevates the prophetic office by making it a form of service to God, not self-promotion. It also underscores that these men and women are not acting on their own authority but are sent with a message that transcends their personal will.

cross_references.connection: Amos declares that God 'will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets'—affirming that prophetic communication is God's standard mode of covenant interaction.

The Northern Kingdom is judged because 'the LORD testified against Israel, and against Judah, by all the prophets, and by all the seers, saying, Turn ye from your evil ways'—showing this pattern of persistent prophetic witness applied across generations.

The Lord tells Joseph Smith that the scriptures 'are given unto you that you may be sanctified by them' and promises to speak through prophets—establishing the same principle of continuous divine communication through prophetic instrumentality.
Alma testifies that God 'sendeth more prophets unto this people...to testify unto them of their iniquities and the traditions of their fathers,' mirroring Jeremiah's role in a different dispensation.

commentary.historical_context: The Exodus from Egypt (mid-13th century BCE on most scholarly dating) was the foundational event of Israel's covenantal identity. Jeremiah's audience would have known this story intimately—recited at Passover, embedded in their law codes, the narrative core of their identity. By referencing 'the day your fathers came out of Egypt,' Jeremiah is invoking the most sacred moment in Israel's memory and asking: 'Given this redemptive history, how have we fallen so far?' The very idea that prophets have been sent 'daily' since then would have seemed hyperbolic to modern ears but resonated with the historical reality of prophetic activity throughout the monarchy (Samuel, Nathan, Elijah, Elisha, and numerous other court and wilderness prophets). This verse thus serves as a theological argument: the failure is not God's but Israel's persistent, generational rejection of divine counsel.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's testimony in 2 Nephi 33:4-5 echoes this pattern: prophets have spoken from Adam onward, and those who harden their hearts reject the repeated witness of the Spirit. The Book of Mormon presents the same covenant history lens—prophets sent, warnings given, but 'this people' chooses darkness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:17-22 summarizes the same pattern in Latter-day Saint dispensational history: God has called prophets in every age, and the responsibility for covenant keeping rests with the hearer, not the sender.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple serves as the ultimate sign of God's continued presence and willingness to dwell with His people. That the prophets are sent to a people who possess the Temple—God's house—yet refuse to listen deepens the tragedy: they have access to both the prophets' voice and the place of God's presence, yet remain deaf and blind.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is Himself the final and greatest of the prophets sent to Israel (Hebrews 1:1-2). The history of rejected prophets culminates in the rejection of the Prophet par excellence. In John 12:37-41, John reflects on Isaiah's vision and connects it to the rejection of Jesus—the people would not believe despite 'all these miracles.' Christ embodies the pattern: He is the ultimate 'servant sent' in God's relentless courtship of His covenant people.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse challenges the assumption that God's voice is distant or unclear. Like Jeremiah's audience, we live in an age of prophetic communication—through living prophets, scripture, and the Holy Ghost. The question Jeremiah poses is not 'Has God spoken?' but 'Will I listen?' The persistence of God's efforts to communicate through His servants (the prophets, then and now) places responsibility squarely on the hearer. Each generation must decide whether to 'hear the voice of the LORD' or follow the trajectory of Judah—a spiral of worsening rebellion masked by religious formalism.

text_kjv: Yet they hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear, but hardened their neck: they did worse than their fathers.

commentary.narrative:
This verse pivots from God's sustained efforts to Israel's sustained refusal. The structure is emphatic: three negative clauses build the case. They did not listen, they did not lean their ear forward (a gesture of receptivity), and most dramatically, they "stiffened their neck." The image is visceral—an ox resisting the yoke by going rigid, refusing to bend to the plow. This is not passive inattention but active resistance.

But the final clause contains the crushing indictment: "they did worse than their fathers." This is not a plateau of rebellion; it is a trajectory of escalation. Each generation surpassed the previous one in wickedness. This suggests that Judah's history is not a steady state of unfaithfulness but a downward spiral—a corruption that compounds. What fathers broke, children shattered further. What fathers rationalized, children magnified. The implication is that by Jeremiah's time, Judah has reached a nadir from which recovery may no longer be possible. This is covenant language: the covenant people are not merely failing to obey; they are progressively severing themselves from the covenant relationship itself.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'to incline/turn the ear.' In ancient Near Eastern communication, the posture of the ear is crucial—leaning the ear forward is the physical gesture of receptive listening. The verb here is in the negative ('they did not incline'), emphasizing that they refused even the posture of attention.
word_study.significance: The Hebrew does not simply say 'they did not hear' but focuses on the deliberate refusal to orient oneself toward speech. This suggests culpability—hearing is not merely passive reception but an act of will. Jeremiah's audience could have chosen to bend their ear; they actively refused to.

word_study.meaning: The verb qashah means to 'harden' or 'make stiff'; the 'neck' (oref) is the physical locus of this stubbornness. Combined, the phrase depicts an ox or mule that refuses the yoke by going rigid, resisting the pull of the reins. This is not intellectual disagreement but physical, embodied rebellion.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves this image vividly. The 'stiffened neck' becomes Jeremiah's signature descriptor for Judah's condition (3:17; 17:23; 19:15). It is a powerful metaphor for covenantal rebellion: just as a draft animal refuses to be guided, Judah refuses to bend to God's will. The metaphor suggests that their resistance is instinctive, habitual, almost physical—not reasoned dissent but stubborn disobedience bred into the culture.

word_study.meaning: The verb ra'a (in the Hiphil form) means to 'make bad' or 'do evil.' The comparison 'from/than their fathers' (mi-avotam) establishes that each generation's wickedness exceeds the previous.
word_study.significance: This is covenant language of the most serious kind. The Mosaic covenant threatened curses for violation (Deuteronomy 28), but the trajectory suggested here is that each generation's curse-worthiness compounds. Jeremiah is not merely diagnosing the present; he is tracing a pattern of degeneracy that makes the present moment an extreme liability.

cross_references.connection: After the golden calf incident, the LORD describes Israel to Moses as 'a stiffnecked people' (am qshei-oref)—establishing this phrase as Israel's defining weakness from the beginning of the covenant.
Moses prophesies to Israel at the end of his life: 'I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck'—suggesting that stubborn refusal of God's will is Israel's perennial character flaw.
The chronicler summarizes: 'The LORD...sent to them by his messengers...but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words'—a parallel summary of the same pattern of rejection.

Alma describes a similar trajectory among the Nephites: each generation that rejects the prophets becomes more entrenched in wickedness, with 'this people' growing harder in their hearts despite repeated warnings.

In a Latter-day Saint context, the Lord warns that those who persist in hardening their hearts against the prophets will eventually have the Spirit withdrawn—a direct parallel to Jeremiah's concept of escalating covenant violation leading to divine withdrawal.

commentary.historical_context: The history of the Judahite monarchy from the United Monarchy through the divided kingdom (c. 930-586 BCE) does show cyclical patterns of religious reform and relapse. Hezekiah's reforms (late 8th century) were followed by Manasseh's radical apostasy (mid-7th century), which was then partially corrected by Josiah's reforms (late 7th century). By Jeremiah's time (late 7th to early 6th century), Josiah is dead and his reforms are being reversed. Jeremiah can thus point to a multigenerational pattern: the people do seem to be doing 'worse than their fathers' in terms of institutional idolatry and covenant violation. The archaeological record shows evidence of widespread syncretistic religious practice, suggesting that the population at large—not just a small aberrant faction—had absorbed foreign religious practices.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon traces a nearly identical pattern. The righteous prophets (Nephi, Jacob, Enos, Jarom) are followed by generations of increasing wickedness. By the time of Mormon's writing, the civilization has spiraled into genocide and self-destruction. Mormon himself comments on the pattern: each generation that receives the word and rejects it becomes harder to reach than the last (Mormon 3:2-3).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 95:3-8 describes the Saints' failure to build the Temple and warns that 'a zion cannot be built up unless it is by the principles of the law of the celestial kingdom; otherwise I cannot receive it unto myself.' This parallels Jeremiah's point: there is a trajectory of violation that eventually makes repentance structurally difficult—the people become so habituated to covenant-breaking that reform becomes almost impossible.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the visible sign of God's presence and His covenant with the people. When a generation rejects the prophets who represent that covenant, they are rejecting access to the Temple's sanctifying power. Jeremiah 7:10-11 will reveal that Judah still frequented the Temple even while practicing abominations—they had severed the Temple from its covenantal meaning.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'stiffened neck' that refused to bend to God's will is the opposite of the posture Christ models. In Gethsemane, Jesus says 'not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42)—the complete surrender of the neck, so to speak. Matthew 11:28-30 presents Christ as offering a yoke that is 'easy' and a burden that is 'light,' in direct contrast to the yoke Israel refuses. The hardened-neck people are precisely those who cannot submit to Christ's gentle yoke.
commentary.application: This verse diagnoses a spiritual condition: the hardening of resistance to God's voice is not a sudden event but a progressive one. Each time we refuse to listen, each time we incline our ear away from prophetic counsel, we reinforce a pattern. The warning is that a culture of resistance—in a family, congregation, or individual soul—compounds over time. Today's 'I'll ignore this counsel from the prophet' becomes tomorrow's habitual dismissal, and eventually, a posture of resistance that becomes nearly impossible to reverse. The call to modern covenant members is not merely to avoid rebellion but to actively practice receptivity—to incline the ear, to bend the neck in humility. The alternative is the Judahite trajectory: progressive spiritual hardening that leads to covenant rupture.

text_kjv: Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a pivot from historical reflection to prophetic commission—and it is perhaps the most painful commission in scripture. God tells Jeremiah plainly: "You will speak to them. They will not listen. You will call to them. They will not respond." The words "all these words" refer to everything God has been saying in this chapter—the indictment of false worship, the appeal to justice, the covenant history. Jeremiah is being sent to deliver a message he is assured in advance will be rejected.

The parallel structure—"speak... will not hearken" / "call... will not answer"—is not poetic embellishment but a theological statement. God is not sending Jeremiah on a futile errand; God is sending him on a *known* futile errand. This is extraordinarily difficult. It strips away any illusion that prophetic success can be measured by audience reception. Jeremiah's faithfulness will be demonstrated not by winning hearts but by speaking truth regardless of reception. Yet there is also mercy embedded here: God tells Jeremiah this *in advance*, so that when rejection comes (and it will), Jeremiah will not be shattered by surprise. God prepares His prophets for the conditions they will face.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew verb shama' means both 'to hear' and 'to obey'—these are not distinguished in Hebrew as they are in English. To 'hear' (literally receive sound) and to 'obey' (act on what is heard) are aspects of the same verb.
word_study.significance: When God says they 'will not shama',' He means they will refuse both to hear and to comply. The refusal is not one of auditory reception but of obedience. This deepens the tragedy: it is not that Jeremiah's words are inaudible but that the people refuse to let those words govern their behavior.

word_study.meaning: The verb qara' means to 'call out' or 'summon.' When used with 'el' (to/toward), it suggests calling out a question or appeal. The verb can carry the sense of urgent, even desperate summoning.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah's calling will not be serene or one-directional. He will cry out to the people, appealing, pleading, desperately trying to reach them. Yet even this passionate calling will meet with silence—they will not 'answer him' (ya'anu). The image is of someone crying into the void.

word_study.meaning: The verb anah means to 'answer' or 'respond'—to return a response to one who has spoken. In the negative ('will not answer'), it means a refusal of reciprocal communication.
word_study.significance: The covenant relationship is, at its core, reciprocal communication. God speaks; Israel responds. But here, Israel severs that reciprocity. They will not engage, will not dialogue, will not even acknowledge Jeremiah's words by responding to them. This is a breakdown of the basic grammar of covenant relationship.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah is told: 'Hear ye indeed, but understand not... lest they...be healed'—God explicitly instructs Isaiah that his message will harden rather than soften his audience, a foreknowledge parallel to Jeremiah's commission.

Ezekiel is commissioned to speak to 'a rebellious house,' with God declaring 'whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear' (i.e., regardless of their response), Ezekiel must deliver the message—emphasizing prophetic duty as independent of audience reception.

Jesus warns: 'Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you'—inverting the expectation that popularity validates truth-telling. True prophetic witness often invites rejection rather than acclaim.

The Lord promises Joseph Smith: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful...Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same' (D&C 1:37-38)—the covenant people are bound to receive the prophetic word regardless of the prophet's apparent success in the world.

After being driven out and beaten by the people of Ammonihah, Alma is told by an angel: 'Blessed art thou, Alma; therefore, lift up thy head and rejoice; for thou hast faithful friends who stand by thee'—suggesting that prophetic faithfulness is validated not by crowd approval but by covenantal standing before God.

commentary.historical_context: Jeremiah lived through the final decades before Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BCE. He would have witnessed the reforms of King Josiah (c. 640-609), which showed some responsiveness to prophetic correction, followed by a rapid reversal after Josiah's death. Kings like Jehoiakim (609-598) openly opposed Jeremiah's message and sought to suppress it (Jeremiah 36). This historical context makes God's advance warning comprehensible: Jeremiah would minister in an era when political leadership was hostile to the prophetic word, when court factions opposed him, and when the population at large was invested in religious syncretism and false optimism. The 'call' that goes unanswered is not hypothetical; it is the actual condition Jeremiah would face.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi experiences this same foreknowledge when his father gives him the brass plates record and tells him the Nephites will reject his teachings (2 Nephi 1:18-26). Mormon faces it when he records: 'I had supposed that the Lamanites had been true that one to another; but behold, they were leading my people forth into the land northward' (Mormon 3:9)—each wave of prophetic hope meets resistance and hardening.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:5 records: 'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord'—the principle is that righteousness measured by outcome (how many forgive you) is false; righteousness is measured by faithfulness to principle regardless of reception.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the place where the community gathers to hear the covenant terms repeated. Jeremiah's commission to speak words that will not be heard means he stands outside the circle of accepted Temple prophecy—he is a prophet whose message is rejected by the institutional religion, foreshadowing how the prophetic voice often stands in tension with institutional religion that has become formalized and disconnected from covenantal substance.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse foreshadows Christ's ministry more directly than perhaps any other passage. Jesus is sent with a message of repentance and covenant renewal (Matthew 4:17). He teaches in parables 'lest they should see, and hear, and understand, and be converted' (Matthew 13:13, quoting Isaiah 6:9-10)—His own teaching is given in forms designed to both reveal and conceal, depending on the hearer's openness. Most tragically, He is rejected: 'He came unto his own, and his own received him not' (John 1:11). Yet He continues His mission to completion. The 'call' that receives no answer becomes the cry from the cross: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34)—but that cry is the completion of redemption, not its failure.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, especially those called to positions of teaching or witness, this verse offers hard wisdom: the measure of your prophetic or teaching faithfulness is not how many people agree with you or change because of you. The measure is whether you speak the word faithfully regardless of reception. This applies to parents teaching children who may later reject the faith, to missionaries serving in areas with few converts, to leaders giving counsel that will be disregarded. The culture often teaches that success equals results; covenant life teaches that success equals faithfulness. The hard peace of this verse is that you may be completely faithful and completely rejected. That is not failure; that is the condition of authentic prophetic witness. The comfort is that God knows this in advance and commissions you anyway—which means your standing with God is never dependent on crowd approval.

text_kjv: But thou shalt say unto them, This is a nation that obeyeth not the voice of the LORD their God, nor receiveth correction: truth is perished, and is cut off from their mouth.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah is given a specific proclamation to deliver: a diagnosis of Judah's condition. The words 'This is a nation' introduces a formal pronouncement—a prophetic summary statement that encapsulates Israel's spiritual status. Three elements comprise the diagnosis: (1) they do not obey God's voice, (2) they refuse correction (musar—instruction, discipline, reproof), and (3) most damaging, faithfulness (emunah) has perished from their lips. This is not merely behavioral failure; it is the collapse of the basic structure of covenant language and truth-telling.

The phrase 'truth is perished' (abedah ha-emunah) requires careful attention. The Hebrew word emunah does not mean abstract truth but covenantal faithfulness—trustworthiness, reliability, the quality of standing firm in one's commitments. When emunah 'perishes,' it means the living reality of faithful commitment between God and people has died. And crucially, it is 'cut off from their mouth'—severed from their speech. They no longer speak faithfully; they no longer voice the commitments that bind them to God. This is not merely a failure to act rightly; it is a corruption of language itself. The people speak, but what comes from their mouths is not truth-speech (dabar emunah) but hollow, unfaithful words. The covenant breaks down when covenant language dies.

word_study.meaning: From the root aleph-mem-nun (to be firm, steady, enduring). Emunah means 'steadfastness,' 'reliability,' 'faithfulness'—not intellectual belief or abstract truth, but living covenantal loyalty that persists and can be depended upon. The Covenant Rendering's choice to render this as 'faithfulness' rather than the KJV's 'truth' captures this relational, covenantal dimension more accurately.
word_study.significance: Emunah is the opposite of the 'stiffened neck' of verse 26. Where that was active resistance, emunah is active loyalty. Its disappearance from the people's lips means they have lost the very language of covenant commitment. They can no longer speak reliability or trustworthiness. This is catastrophic because language shapes action: if emunah has left the mouth, it has left the heart. Speech-act theory here proves profound—by ceasing to speak faithfully, the people have killed faithfulness itself.

word_study.meaning: The verb abad means to 'perish,' 'be lost,' 'disappear,' often with the sense of irretrievable loss. It is the condition of something destroyed or dead.
word_study.significance: This is not temporary lapse but permanent loss. Emunah is not merely suppressed; it has 'perished'—died, vanished, become extinct. The metaphor is terminal.

word_study.meaning: The verb karath means to 'cut off' or 'sever'—often used of cutting a covenant (karath berit), but here used to describe the severance of emunah from speech. The image is surgical or violent: something living is severed from the body.
word_study.significance: The metaphor suggests emunah was once integral to the people's speech and has been violently separated. It is not that they never had it; it is that they have cut themselves off from it. The voice of the people is now amputated from its source of faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: Musar means 'discipline,' 'instruction,' 'reproof'—it is the corrective teaching that leads to wisdom. To refuse musar is to refuse the pedagogical discipline of the covenant.
word_study.significance: Musar is how the covenant people learn obedience. To reject it is to reject the very mechanism of spiritual growth. It suggests not merely that Judah disobeys but that they have become unreachable—closed to the very possibility of correction.

cross_references.connection: The lips of the righteous 'feed many,' while 'fools die for want of wisdom'—contrasting faithful speech with foolish silence, parallel to Jeremiah's diagnosis of emunah cut off from the mouth.

Isaiah opens with a similar diagnosis: 'I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me... the ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib; but Israel doth not know'—covenant people degraded below the level of domestic animals in their failure to recognize their covenant Lord.

Hosea brings a charge: 'Hear the word of the LORD... for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land'—similar indictment of covenant collapse into faithlessness.

The Lord indicts the Saints: 'They seek not the Lord to establish his righteousness, but every man walketh in his own way, and after the image of his own god'—the same pattern of refusal of divine instruction and substitution of self-will.

Mormon teaches that 'by the power of the Holy Ghost ye may know the truth of all things,' but this requires faith and openness to correction—inversely, those who close themselves to the Spirit lose access to truth.

commentary.historical_context: By Jeremiah's time (late 7th/early 6th century BCE), Judahite religion had become thoroughly institutionalized and syncretistic. Archaeological evidence from the Iron Age II suggests widespread practices of household idolatry, consultation of mediums and spiritists (cf. 8:19), and incorporation of Canaanite fertility religion into the ostensibly Yahwistic Temple cult. The royal courts patronized multiple religious traditions and were reluctant to enforce strict covenant loyalty. Meanwhile, prophets like Jeremiah were marginal figures, often opposed by court prophets (Jeremiah 28). In this context, Jeremiah's diagnosis is not merely religious but social: the language of the covenant—the very way the people spoke about their relationship with God—had become corrupted by syncretism, false oaths, and accommodations to political pressure. The 'mouth' from which emunah was cut off was the mouth of priests, kings, false prophets, and the people themselves.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon diagnoses a similar condition in his people: 'And there was nothing save it was exceedingly harshness, and continual wars, and bloodsheds...and the hearts of the people were exceedingly hardened' (Mormon 2:7-8). The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows how loss of covenant language precedes loss of covenantal reality.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:80 teaches: 'Let all thy things be done in order'—and D&C 88:119 emphasizes that the Zion community must speak with 'one heart and one mind.' When the language of faithfulness disappears, community itself becomes impossible. The Lord warns in D&C 84:54-57 that 'they have not understood it' because 'they receive not the light'—without emunah in the mouth, the people cannot speak or hear covenant truth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the place where covenant language is rehearsed and renewed—through blessing, praise, and the articulation of covenantal commitment. When emunah is cut off from the people's mouth, the Temple becomes an empty building. The sacrifices continue, but the covenantal speech that gives them meaning has died. This explains why Jeremiah will later pronounce judgment on the Temple itself (verses 11-14).

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is 'the faithful and true witness' (Revelation 3:14)—He embodies emunah incarnate. His entire mission is to restore covenant language and covenantal reality. The Gospel of John emphasizes 'truth' (Greek aletheia) repeatedly, but it is not abstract but relational truth—the truth that God's word is reliable and His covenant is being fulfilled in Christ. In John 8:32, 'the truth shall make you free'—but this freedom comes only to those who abide in His word (John 8:31), who restore emunah to their lips and lives.
commentary.application: This verse diagnoses a condition that can afflict modern covenant communities: the corruption of covenant language. When members speak faithfully about their covenants—in families, in the Church, in personal testimony—they reinforce the reality of covenant commitment. But when the language becomes hollow (we say the words of covenants but do not mean them, we make promises we have no intention of keeping, we speak piously but act selfishly), the covenant itself dies. This applies to marriage covenants spoken without intention to cherish, temple covenants rehearsed but not lived, testimonies borne without real belief. Jeremiah calls modern members to restore emunah to our mouths—to speak with faithfulness, to make our speech match our hearts, to use covenant language as more than ritual formula but as the living expression of our commitment to God and each other.

text_kjv: Cut off thine hair, O Jerusalem, and cast it away, and take up a lamentation on high places; for the LORD hath rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.
text_kjv_alt: Gaze upon thy baldness; throw it away and lift up a lament on the barren heights, for the LORD has rejected and abandoned the generation that provoked his wrath.

commentary.narrative:
The verse shifts to performative, embodied prophecy—a command to Jerusalem (personified as a woman) to enact a ritual of mourning. The cutting of hair is a sign of deep grief and, more specifically, of the breaking of a sacred vow. In Israelite practice, uncut hair was a sign of consecration (associated with Nazirite vows and with dedication to God). To cut one's hair was to sever that sign of consecration, to declare that the covenant relationship has been terminated. This is not merely private sorrow but public, visible mourning—Jerusalem is to appear bald in the sight of all, her shame and her grief on display.

But the command contains layers of tragedy. Jerusalem is told to 'cast it away'—throw the cut hair away, dispose of it as refuse. The hair that once signified consecration to the LORD becomes waste matter. She is then to 'take up a lamentation on high places'—the same high places where idolatry had been practiced (4:11; 11:16). Now those high places become sites not of false worship but of genuine lamentation. The final clause—'the LORD hath rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath'—gives the theological reason for the mourning: this is not a temporary discipline but a decisive rupture. God has rejected (ma'as) and forsaken (natash) His people. The covenant has been terminated. The generation is identified as 'the generation of his wrath'—they are the ones who provoked God's anger through centuries of refusal and escalating unfaithfulness (verse 26).

word_study.meaning: The verb gazaz means to 'shear' or 'cut hair.' Nizrek appears to be imperative form addressing Jerusalem. The imperative form is startling—God commands Jerusalem to cut her own hair, as if she must participate in her own humiliation.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern mourning practice, cutting hair (or in extreme cases, shaving the head) was an act of self-mortification expressing grief. But here it has additional covenantal meaning: the nezer (consecrated hair) was the visible symbol of dedication to God. To cut it is to unmake that visible sign. The Covenant Rendering's 'Cut off your hair' captures the directness of the command more vividly than many renderings.

word_study.meaning: Ma'as means to 'reject,' 'despise,' 'refuse to accept.' Natash means to 'leave,' 'abandon,' 'desert.' Together they form a pair describing complete relational rupture—not just disapproval but abandonment.
word_study.significance: These are not verbs of temporary correction but of ultimate separation. When God 'rejects and forsakes' a people, it suggests He withdraws His protection, His guidance, His presence. This is the antithesis of covenant. Covenant means God remains present even in judgment; abandonment means the relationship itself is severed.

word_study.meaning: Dor means 'generation' or 'age'; ebrah (divine wrath) is the anger of the LORD. The phrase 'generation of his wrath' identifies this particular generation as the target and cause of God's wrath.
word_study.significance: This is not abstract judgment but personal—this generation has exhausted God's patience through their own choices. The plural trajectory established in verse 26 ('they did worse than their fathers') culminates here: the present generation has become the 'generation of wrath,' the breaking point, the moment when God's patience reaches its limit.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'high places.' Bamot (high places) were locations of worship—often hilltops or raised areas. In Jeremiah's time, they were associated with both legitimate worship of the LORD and with syncretistic, idolatrous practices.
word_study.significance: The same high places where Judah worshipped idols and false gods (4:11; 19:5) now become sites of lamentation. The irony is severe: the places of false religious devotion become places of true mourning. Jerusalem's lament on the high places is an inversion of the false worship that occurred there.

cross_references.connection: The Nazirite vow requires that 'all the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head'—uncut hair signifies consecration to God, making the cutting of hair in Jeremiah 7:29 a symbolic ending of that consecration.

In the lament over Moab, 'he is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba...on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off'—showing that baldness was a standard mourning practice in the ancient Near East.

In the covenant curse-list, the LORD threatens: 'And thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword, among all nations'—Jerusalem's public baldness and lamentation make her a visible sign of covenant rupture.

The Lord teaches that covenants kept bring blessings but violation brings withdrawal of blessings: 'When men are called unto mine everlasting gospel and covenant which I have sent forth to commit unto you...and refuse and reject it, they are left unto themselves'—the pattern of rejection and forsaking.

Lehi's vision shows those who eat the fruit of the tree of life but then wander away into darkness, ashamed and lost—a parallel image of a people who once had covenant relationship but have fallen into separation from God's presence.

commentary.historical_context: The command to cut hair and mourn would have been immediately recognizable to Jeremiah's audience as both a literal mourning practice and as a symbolic act. Ezekiel, Jeremiah's contemporary, performed similar symbolic actions (cutting hair in Ezekiel 5:1-4 as a sign of judgment). The high places referenced here are likely the worship sites on hilltops throughout Judah where both YHWH and other deities were honored—sites mentioned in 2 Kings 23 as targets of Josiah's reforms and likely sites of renewed syncretistic practice by Jeremiah's time. Archaeologically, evidence of cult practices at high places (figurines, altars, votive offerings) has been found throughout the Iron Age II in Judah, confirming their cultural significance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar images of covenant rupture. In Alma 5:1-3, Alma calls the people to repentance, warning that the Lord can withdraw His Spirit. In 3 Nephi 8-9, the destruction that follows the crucifixion involves darkness and the apparent withdrawal of the Lord's presence—a literal enactment of rejection and forsaking until the risen Christ appears.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 86:3 teaches 'the field is white already to harvest' but D&C 82:3-4 warns that when covenants are broken, 'the church cannot be sanctified unless they abide [the law]'—the principle that covenant violation leads to withdrawal of divine sanction and presence.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the place of God's presence (Exodus 25:8, 'Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them'). When God 'rejects and forsakes' the people, it means He withdraws from the Temple. Jeremiah will later symbolically enact this when he records God's departure from the Temple (Ezekiel 11:23, though that is Ezekiel's vision, the same pattern applies). The cutting of hair and lamentation on the high places is a sign that the Temple has become an empty shell.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ underwent a form of this same humiliation. He was stripped naked on the cross (Matthew 27:35), exposed in His shame, rejected and forsaken ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'—Mark 15:34). But whereas Jerusalem's cutting of hair signifies the end of her covenant relationship, Christ's stripping and forsakenness becomes the means of covenant renewal. He takes upon Himself the role of the rejected generation and through His atonement makes restoration possible. The image of baldness—visible shame—prefigures not Christ's shame but His willingness to endure shame for the covenant people.
commentary.application: This verse presents a terrifying possibility: that a covenant people can so thoroughly reject their covenant that God withdraws His protection, presence, and relationship. For modern Latter-day Saints, this is a call to take seriously the covenant made in the Temple. The cutting of hair here is a physical sign of the spiritual reality: when we refuse to live covenantally, we are severing the sign of our consecration to God. This is not about external appearance but about internal reality—are we living in fidelity to our covenants, or are we allowing the culture of worldliness to strip away our commitment? The high places where false worship occurred become places of mourning—a warning that the very places where we thought we were secure (our institutions, our assumed righteousness, our familiarity with religious practice) become sites of lamentation when the covenant is broken. The call to modern members is to guard the visible signs of consecration—not just hair but time, attention, resources—and to ensure that these signs continue to reflect genuine inner commitment to God.

text_kjv: For the children of Judah have done evil in my sight, saith the LORD: they have set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to pollute it.

commentary.narrative:
