This final verse of the section provides the specific reason for the judgment announced in verse 29: the pollution of the Temple itself. The "house which is called by my name" is the Temple in Jerusalem—the place where God's presence was believed to dwell, where sacrifices were offered, where the covenant was renewed. But the people have 'set their abominations' (shiqquts, detestable idols) within this sacred space. This is not merely worshipping other gods elsewhere; this is installing idolatrous objects in the LORD's own house, defiling the place of His presence with the very things He most abhors.

The verb 'to pollute' (tame') carries cultic weight. In Levitical terms, tame' means to make ritually unclean, to introduce contamination that requires purification (or that makes purification impossible). An idol placed in the Temple is not merely an aesthetic affront or a theological error; it is a ritual defilement that makes the Temple unfit for the presence of the Holy God. The covenant relationship is structured around the Temple as the locus of divine-human encounter. When abominations are placed there, that encounter becomes impossible. God can no longer dwell in a house defiled by what He abhors. This verse thus explains the trajectory: the people who have cut themselves off from covenant language (verse 28), who refuse the prophetic word (verse 27), who do worse than their fathers (verse 26), have now crossed the line into Temple defilement—the gravest violation possible. The covenant structure itself collapses when the Temple, its center, is polluted.

word_study.meaning: A term for something detestable or abhorrent, often specifically idols or idolatrous objects. Unlike to'evah (which means 'abomination' more broadly), shiqquts refers specifically to objects that provoke revulsion—typically carved idols.
word_study.significance: The choice of shiqquts rather than to'evah is significant. Jeremiah is referring not to abstract sins but to concrete, physical idols placed inside the Temple. These were visible abominations—objects that any visitor to the Temple would see and recognize as violating the covenant.

word_study.meaning: The verb sum means to 'place,' 'set,' 'put.' It is a simple verb of positioning, but in this context it carries the weight of deliberate action—the idols were intentionally installed in the Temple.
word_study.significance: This is not accidental defilement but willful violation. The people knew what they were doing when they placed these objects in the Temple. It is an act of conscious rebellion against the covenant.

word_study.term_english: house which is called by my name
word_study.term_original: bayit asher-niqra shemi alav (בַּבַּיִת אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָא־שְׁמִי עָלָיו)
word_study.meaning: The house 'upon which the name of the LORD is called' or 'over which my name is invoked.' In Hebrew covenant language, to have God's name called upon a place means that place is claimed as sacred, as God's possession, as the locus of His presence.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'the house which is called by my name' is used multiple times in this chapter (verses 11, 14, 30) and emphasizes that the Temple is not merely a building but a place that carries the divine name. To defile it is to directly affront God's name and God's honor. It is a violation not just of covenant law but of covenant honor.

word_study.meaning: To make ritually unclean, to introduce contamination that violates holiness codes. In Levitical law, to 'tame' something is to make it unfit for sacred use or presence.
word_study.significance: The Levitical system distinguishes between clean and unclean (tahor and tame'). To pollute the Temple is to introduce tame' into a place that must remain tahor—that must be kept clean for the presence of the Holy God. It is the ultimate violation of the purity codes that structure the covenant relationship.

cross_references.connection: King Manasseh 'built altars in the house of the LORD...and set a graven image of the grove that he had made in the house' and set up 'an image of the grove in the Temple'—a specific historical instance of Temple defilement that Jeremiah's generation may have witnessed or inherited.

The law commands that pagan altars 'ye shall quite pluck down, and break in pieces, and burn with fire their groves'—establishing that the Temple must be kept free from any objects associated with pagan worship.

The covenant law states: 'Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness; that they die not in their uncleanness, when they defile my tabernacle that is among them'—emphasizing that defilement of the sanctuary results in death, both spiritual and physical.

Ezekiel receives similar judgment language: 'Wherefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD...I will also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity'—the defilement of the Temple triggers God's complete withdrawal of mercy.

The Lord teaches: 'Organize yourselves; prepare every needful thing; and establish a house, even a house of prayer, a house of fasting, a house of faith, a house of learning'—the Temple must be organized according to covenant principles, and defilement violates its entire purpose.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeological and biblical evidence suggests that by the late 7th century BCE (Jeremiah's time), the Jerusalem Temple housed not only the traditional furnishings but also altars and cult objects associated with other deities. 2 Kings 21:1-18 describes how King Manasseh (697-642 BCE) 'wrought much evil in the sight of the LORD' by setting up pagan altars in the Temple; though his son Josiah later (640-609 BCE) attempted to purify the Temple, the reforms were not sustained after Josiah's death. By Jeremiah's time (c. 628-586 BCE), idolatrous objects may have been reinstalled. The phrase 'high places' in verse 29 likely refers to alternative worship sites where this syncretistic practice was most extreme, but verse 30 indicates that the pollution had reached even the Temple itself. Inscriptional evidence (the Khirbet el-Qom and Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions) suggests that some Israelites worshipped 'Asherah' alongside the LORD, possibly installing Asherah symbolism even in orthodox contexts.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon presents a parallel situation in Alma 4:7-10, where corrupted Church leaders 'set themselves up for teachers, and began to teach the people openly' false doctrines, polluting the sacred institution of the Church. Similarly, in Alma 31:16-17, the apostate Zoramites had created a false synagogue-house of worship. The pattern is consistent: when the people place false teachings or false objects in the sacred house, they defile it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 68:30 teaches that 'he that hath got nothing...is he that is at fault.' But more directly, D&C 109:20 (from the Kirtland Temple dedication prayer) emphasizes that the Temple must be 'sanctified' and kept holy. When members of the modern Church introduce teachings or practices contrary to the covenant into sacred spaces (including in the Temple), they risk a form of spiritual defilement. The Lord's emphasis throughout the Doctrine and Covenants on 'holiness to the Lord' (D&C 97:15) is a warning against the Jeremianic situation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the pinnacle of the covenant. To defile it is the ultimate covenant violation. In the Latter-day Saint Temple, covenants are renewed and God's name is invoked over the ordinances performed. When individuals approach the Temple with divided hearts, with unrepentant sin, or with intentions contrary to the covenant, they introduce a form of spiritual defilement. The modern application is that covenant-keeping extends into the Temple itself—how one prepares to enter, what one brings into the Temple spiritually, and how one conducts oneself there.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is Himself both the Temple and the One who cleanses the Temple. In John 2:14-16, Jesus drives out those who defile the Temple with commerce and corruption ('my house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves'). But more profoundly, in John 2:19-21, Jesus identifies Himself as the Temple: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up'—He is the true Temple, the true locus of God's presence. When He is crucified, the veil of the Temple is rent (Matthew 27:51), signifying that the old Temple system is ending and Christ Himself becomes the way of access to God. His body becomes the Temple that cannot be defiled because it is the sacrifice that cleanses all defilement.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse raises uncomfortable questions about the state of our spiritual 'temples'—both the literal Temple buildings and the Temple of the body. Paul teaches that 'your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you' (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). To 'set abominations' in this temple means to introduce addictions, lustful thoughts, pride, dishonesty—the spiritual equivalents of idols. It means to treat our bodies and minds as places where false gods can be enthroned. Similarly, on a community level, the question is: Are we, as a Church, maintaining the sanctity of Temple worship? Are we guarding against false teachings being 'set' within our sacred institutions? Are we collectively maintaining holiness? The call to action is at three levels: (1) personally, to guard the temple of the body from defilement, (2) familially, to ensure that family life (the domestic temple) is kept free from practices and teachings that violate covenant, and (3) ecclesiastically, to support and sustain the institutions of the Church as places of holiness and to resist the infiltration of worldly values and false teachings.

text_kjv: And they have built the high places of Tophet, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded it not, neither came it into my heart.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah now moves from general indictment of false worship to the most horrific specific crime: child sacrifice. The high places of Topheth were not merely pagan altars but sites of systematic infanticide carried out under the guise of religious devotion. This was not a marginal practice—archaeological and textual evidence suggests child sacrifice was an occasional but recurring phenomenon in Jerusalem during periods of religious apostasy, particularly during threats of siege when desperation led parents and priests to attempt to appease foreign gods or invoke extreme divine intervention. The valley of Ben-Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom), located south of Jerusalem, became the symbolic center of this abomination.

God's response is emphatic: 'I commanded it not, neither came it into my heart' (lo aletah al libbi). This is not mere prohibition—it is ontological denial. The practice is not simply forbidden; it is incomprehensible to God's character. The phrase 'never entered my mind' represents the strongest possible disavowal in Hebrew moral language. God is saying that the very concept of child sacrifice is antithetical to his nature and will. This stands in sharp contrast to the religious rationale the people must have constructed for themselves—perhaps they believed they were following ancient Canaanite custom, perhaps they thought they were making an ultimate sacrifice to secure God's favor in crisis. Yet God declares the entire enterprise a fabrication born of human perversity, not divine instruction.

The theological irony cuts deep: the people had just been rebuked for claiming to possess God's Temple as insurance against judgment (7:4). Now Jeremiah exposes the moral bankruptcy of their entire religious system—they have built altars to burn their own children. The juxtaposition is intentional: if they will not repent of their fundamental ethical violations, the Temple itself becomes complicit in their wickedness. This verse sets up the catastrophic consequence that follows: the very valley where they murdered their children will become their mass grave.

word_study.meaning: Elevated shrines or hilltop altars, typically places of illicit worship or syncretistic practice. The term carries connotations of religious deviation from the centralized Temple worship that Deuteronomy commanded.
word_study.significance: Throughout Jeremiah, bamot represent the persistent problem of decentralized, uncontrolled religious practice that led to syncretism and moral corruption. The bamot of Topheth are worse than merely irregular—they are sites of abomination.

word_study.meaning: The etymology likely derives from a root meaning 'fireplace' or possibly 'drum.' Translator notes suggest drums (toph) may have been beaten during rituals to drown out the screams of the victims. By Jeremiah's time, Topheth had become the iconic name for the most degraded form of human sacrifice.
word_study.significance: This place-name would later become corrupted into Greek Gehenna (γέεννα), becoming Jesus's primary metaphor for final judgment and separation from God. The Restoration understanding of Gehenna carries the weight of this original Jeremianic condemnation—a place of fire, death, and ultimate consequence for moral rebellion.

word_study.meaning: A ravine south of Jerusalem. 'Ben-Hinnom' may refer to a family or person who owned property there, or may derive from older Canaanite place-name traditions. The valley's literal geography becomes inseparable from its moral significance.
word_study.significance: This geographic location became so associated with abomination that its name was transformed into an eschatological concept. Modern visitors to Jerusalem can still identify this valley, making the historical reality of this condemnation geographically verifiable and theologically sobering.

word_study.term_english: neither came it into my heart (lo aletah al libbi)
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'it did not go up into my heart/mind.' The Hebrew uses עָלָה (alah, 'to ascend/go up') with לֵב (leb, 'heart/mind') to express that something never even occurred to the speaker. This is stronger than mere prohibition.
word_study.significance: God's disavowal is absolute: not only did he not command this, he could not conceive of it. This language protects God's character against any suggestion that he might tolerate such practices under certain conditions or circumstances. The practice is fundamentally irreconcilable with divine nature.

cross_references.connection: Moses explicitly forbids the practices of Canaanite nations, warning 'thou shalt not do so unto the LORD thy God: for every abomination to the LORD, which he hateth, have they done unto their gods; for even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire of their gods.' Jeremiah's indictment shows that Judah has fallen into precisely the idolatry that Deuteronomy warned against.

The Levitical law explicitly prohibits passing children through fire to Molech. Jeremiah's contemporary audience would have known this law, making their practice not merely a lapse but a willful transgression of covenant law.

King Josiah defiled Topheth so that no one could make their son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech. This historical reference shows that Josiah's reform attempted to eradicate this exact practice, but Jeremiah's prophecy comes later when the practice has returned or persists despite reform efforts.

Isaiah similarly condemns the people's sacrifices and offerings, declaring that God takes no pleasure in blood sacrifices when they are offered without righteousness. Both prophets diagnose the same disease: religious practice divorced from moral transformation.
Jeremiah returns to this condemnation of Topheth and child sacrifice, reinforcing that this theme is central to his prophetic message and God's judgment against Judah's religious apostasy.

commentary.historical_context:
Child sacrifice in the ancient Near East was practiced by various Canaanite and Phoenician peoples, typically in times of extreme crisis (siege, famine, plague) as an attempt to appease national gods or procure divine intervention. Excavations at Carthage and other sites have revealed evidence of systematic child sacrifice (tophet sites). In Judah, such practices appear to have been episodic rather than institutionalized, emerging during periods of religious syncretism or national emergency.

The specific mention of Topheth and the Valley of Ben-Hinnom suggests this was not theoretical but an actual location where such practices occurred. The valley's southern location, outside the city proper, would have made it an ideal site for such clandestine or marginalized worship. Jeremiah's condemnation indicates that by his era (late 7th century BCE), this practice had either returned or persisted in isolated communities despite Josiah's earlier reforms.

The use of drums during the ritual (as translator notes suggest from the Topheth etymology) would represent an attempt to mask the horror—a chilling detail that emphasizes how deliberately the people had to suppress their moral intuitions to carry out such acts. This is not accidental evil but choreographed abomination.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar warnings against child sacrifice and the corruption of religion through syncretism. In Alma 14:10-11, those who reject the word of God face divine judgment, and in Mosiah 11:1-6, King Noah's wickedness leads to spiritual and eventually political destruction. The pattern is consistent: religious apostasy combined with moral perversion invites swift judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:31-32 establishes the foundational principle: 'For I the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance; Nevertheless, he that repents and does the commandments of the Lord shall be forgiven.' This passage in Jeremiah 7:31 shows God's absolute refusal to entertain explanations or excuses for child sacrifice. There is no threshold of desperation that would make such an act acceptable. D&C 132:19 teaches that covenant-breaking has consequences; Jeremiah's people had broken the most fundamental covenant—the sanctity of life and the protection of the innocent.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The people had trusted in the Temple as a place of protection (7:4), yet simultaneously they were committing abominations in the valley near Jerusalem. The Restoration teaches that temples are places of sacred covenant-making and purification. The juxtaposition of Temple confidence with child sacrifice reveals the hollowness of their worship. In Latter-day Saint understanding, the Temple is the place where we covenant to build up God's kingdom and protect life. The inverse of this was what Judah was doing—using religious frameworks to justify the destruction of life.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse does not present positive typology but rather demonstrates the condition that makes Christ's atonement necessary. Christ himself spoke of Gehenna (the Greek form of Ge-Hinnom) as the ultimate consequence of rejecting righteousness (Matthew 5:22, 29-30). The judgment announced here—that the place of child sacrifice becomes a place of mass death—foreshadows the ultimate separation from God that Christ came to overcome through repentance and redemption. The people's willingness to sacrifice their own children represents the ultimate inversion of God's love; Christ's willing sacrifice of himself represents the true offering that redeems all who accept it.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern readers with a piercing question: In what ways do we, as individuals or societies, sacrifice what we claim to treasure most—our children, our families, our moral convictions—on the altars of false gods? Jeremiah's indictment is not primarily about ancient Canaanite religion but about the human capacity for self-deception and moral inversion. We rationalize practices antithetical to our deepest values by framing them within elaborate belief systems. The principle applies to any compromise of fundamental ethics in the name of security, prosperity, or social conformity. For Latter-day Saints, this verse calls us to examine whether our religious practice (attendance, service, rhetoric) is matched by genuine moral transformation and protection of the vulnerable. Are we truly building Zion, or are we merely maintaining religious appearances while tolerating injustice?

text_kjv: Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that it shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter: for they shall bury in Tophet, till there be no place.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 32 pronounces the divine reversal and judgment. The place where children were ritually murdered becomes the place where the murderers themselves will be slaughtered en masse and buried. This is not merely poetic justice but covenant consequence—the Deuteronomic curse made manifest in specific geography. The renaming from 'Valley of Ben-Hinnom' (or Topheth, the fireplace) to 'Valley of Slaughter' (Ge ha-Haregah) inverts the valley's function entirely. What was a site of false worship and child sacrifice becomes a mass grave of the judgment that such wickedness invokes.

The phrase 'they shall bury in Tophet, till there be no place' conveys catastrophic mortality. This is not the death of a few rebels or a limited military defeat. The imagery is of such overwhelming carnage that the burial ground itself becomes insufficient—the dead are piled beyond capacity. This language echoes the curses pronounced in Deuteronomy 28:26, where exposure of bodies to scavengers is the ultimate covenant violation. Here, however, Jeremiah combines two horrors: bodies are buried in Topheth, yet there is eventually no room for proper burial, suggesting that many will remain unburied, exposed to the elements and scavengers.

The mechanism of judgment is not arbitrary divine wrath but the natural consequence of religious apostasy combined with political rebellion. Jeremiah prophesied during the final decades before the Babylonian siege and destruction of Jerusalem (586 BCE). The 'days are coming' would be fulfilled within his audience's lifetime. The valley south of Jerusalem would literally become a burial ground as the city fell and its inhabitants were killed or died of starvation and plague during the siege. The specificity of this prophecy—that the valley will be so filled with corpses that burial space becomes exhausted—reflects the horrific reality of siege warfare and the collapse of social order that followed. Yet this is not mere historical accident; it is judgment for covenant violation.

word_study.meaning: The Valley of the Slaying/Killing. The term הֲרֵגָה (haregah) derives from הָרַג (harag, 'to kill/slay'). This is a renaming that completely inverts the valley's identity and function.
word_study.significance: The renaming itself is a prophetic act—in Hebrew thought, names carry ontological significance. To rename something is to declare its new reality and meaning. The valley's new name declares its future destiny. This echoes the prophetic renaming tradition where new circumstances demand new designations (e.g., Abram to Abraham, Saul to Paul).

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine plural perfect of קָבַר (qabar, 'to bury'). The verb appears in a passive sense here—'they shall be buried,' with the active agent left ambiguous. In the context of siege and destruction, this implies burial by whomever survives or by officials attempting to manage the catastrophe.
word_study.significance: Burial was a central covenant concern in ancient Israel. Proper burial ensured rest and dignity; denial of burial was a curse. Here, there is burial, but it is in the place of abomination, and it is insufficient—there is simply too much death to manage.

word_study.meaning: There is no place/space. Literally, 'space' or 'location' is exhausted. The term מָקוֹם (maqom) can mean physical location, status, or position.
word_study.significance: This phrase conveys both the literal reality (the valley fills with so many corpses that there is no more ground to dig in) and the metaphorical reality (there is no place/no standing, no position, no dignity for this people anymore). The doubling effect suggests total collapse of social order and burial capacity.

word_study.meaning: Participle of בוֹא (bo', 'to come/arrive'). Used here in the sense of 'days are coming'—future events that approach with inevitability.
word_study.significance: The predictive certainty of this language—not 'might come' but 'are coming'—emphasizes that this judgment is not a conditional threat but a fixed future consequence. The covenant has already been broken; the judgment is already set in motion.

cross_references.connection: The covenant curse explicitly states: 'Thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away.' Jeremiah's prophecy of mass unburied death invokes this exact Deuteronomic curse as the consequence of covenant violation.

Jeremiah repeats this curse later: 'They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried; but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth.' The consistency of this judgment across Jeremiah's prophecies underscores its centrality to his message.

Written after the fall of Jerusalem, Lamentations describes the aftermath: children killed in streets, mothers and infants in the sanctuary. This verse fulfills the prophecy of Jeremiah 7:32, showing how the prediction came to pass during the siege of 586 BCE.

Jeremiah's later symbolic action at Topheth repeats and expands this prophecy, declaring that the valley will become 'the valley of slaughter' and that the Lord will make the city's people fall by the sword of their enemies.

The historical record of the Babylonian siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE provides the historical fulfillment of these prophetic judgments. The siege resulted in mass death, starvation, and overwhelming casualties.

commentary.historical_context:
The late 7th and early 6th centuries BCE were times of extraordinary upheaval in Judah. The Assyrian Empire had already devastated the northern kingdom of Israel (722 BCE), and Judah faced mounting pressure from Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II. The Babylonian siege of Jerusalem (597-586 BCE) was catastrophic—the city was encircled, supplies depleted, and surrender led to mass casualties and deportation. Historical and archaeological records confirm that during such sieges, death tolls were enormous, burial practices broke down, and mass graves became necessary.

The specific mention of Topheth as a burial ground may reflect historical reality: after the siege, the valley south of Jerusalem (already a place of shame due to its association with child sacrifice) would have served as a burial area. The valley's pre-existing negative associations made it a fitting place for mass graves. Jeremiah's prophecy demonstrates precise knowledge of geography and social practice—he is not speaking in vague abstractions but prophesying specific historical consequences.

The renaming of Ge-Hinnom to Ge ha-Haregah reflects a prophetic pattern in which future judgment inverts present shame. The place of the people's religious abomination becomes the place of their judgment and death. In this way, the land itself becomes a witness to covenant violation and consequence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently describes the pattern of religious apostasy leading to societal collapse and mass death. In Helaman 13:1-14, Samuel the Lamanite prophesies that the Nephites' rejection of the Lord will lead to their destruction. In 3 Nephi 8-10, the destruction of the wicked at Christ's coming is described with imagery of fire, collapse of cities, and mass death. The parallel is consistent: covenant violation leads to judgment that is both sudden and overwhelming.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 97:22-28 establishes that Zion is built up through righteousness and that those who reject the covenant will face judgment. The inversion principle appears in D&C 121:22—'No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' Judah had twisted religious authority to justify abomination; they faced the consequence of that inversion. The principle remains: misuse of sacred things invokes judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple was meant to be a place of covenant-making and purification. The fact that Topheth (a place of abomination) became a burial ground while the Temple stood in Jerusalem emphasizes the separation between true and false worship. In Latter-day Saint understanding, those who reject the covenant made in the Temple face spiritual death. The physical prophecy of Topheth becoming a grave is a shadow of the spiritual reality: rejection of the covenant leads to spiritual death and separation from God's presence.

commentary.christological_typology: The principle of reversal—the place of death for the innocent becoming the place of death for the guilty—foreshadows Christ's vicarious sacrifice. Christ took upon himself the judgment that humanity deserved, reversing the flow of condemnation. Where Jeremiah's prophecy shows the guilty falling under judgment in the very place of their abomination, Christ's atonement shows the innocent bearing the weight of the guilty so that the guilty might be redeemed. The specificity of the judgment pronounced here emphasizes why Christ's redemptive work was necessary—without repentance and acceptance of the atonement, the consequences of covenant violation are inexorable.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that consequences are not arbitrary or abstract but are often worked out in concrete, historical ways. For modern covenant people, this is a sobering reminder that religious identity alone (being called by God's name, possessing the Temple, claiming covenant status) does not guarantee protection from judgment if fundamental moral violations are tolerated or rationalized. The principle applies to individuals and communities: moral and spiritual consequences often manifest in real social, psychological, and relational consequences. Latter-day Saints are called to examine whether their faith leads to genuine moral transformation or merely to external observance. The 'valley of slaughter' becomes a warning: communities that tolerate injustice in the name of religious stability face judgment that is both swift and overwhelming. The application today might be: In what ways do we, as a people, rationalize injustice or tolerate abuse under the guise of institutional loyalty? Do our real practices match our stated values? If not, are we not building on the same unstable foundation that Judah was?

text_kjv: And the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and none shall fray them away.

commentary.narrative:
This verse specifies the grotesque detail of the judgment: not only will the people die in overwhelming numbers, but their bodies will be left exposed to scavengers, denied the dignity of burial. This is the literal application of the Deuteronomic curse—the ultimate degradation. In ancient Near Eastern understanding, exposure of a corpse to birds and wild animals was not merely disrespectful; it was a spiritual catastrophe. It meant denial of proper burial rites, denial of rest, denial of honor. The phrase 'none shall fray them away' (ein macharid) contains a particular horror: there will be no living person left who cares enough or has the capacity to drive away the scavengers. Not only are the dead exposed, but the living are so few, so broken, or so indifferent that they cannot perform even this minimal act of respect.

This verse also contains a theological inversion of the opening of Jeremiah. In Jeremiah 1, God called Jeremiah to be 'a prophet unto the nations' and promised him that before he was born, God had sanctified him. Now, in chapter 7, that same God declares that the people—once called to be God's covenant nation—will be abandoned to the vultures and jackals like common carrion. The dignity promised to Israel as God's people is stripped away through judgment. They are not merely dead; they are dishonored, degraded, left as food for scavengers.

The historical reality underlying this prophecy is grimly specific. During siege warfare, especially the prolonged Babylonian siege of Jerusalem, plague and starvation killed enormous numbers. As the city's defenders weakened and social order collapsed, the proper management of corpses became impossible. Bodies accumulated faster than they could be buried. The weak and dying were left where they fell. After conquest, mass casualties meant that burial could not keep pace with death. The poetic image in this verse—carcasses as food for birds and beasts—reflects the actual horror of siege and aftermath. Jeremiah's prophecy is not hyperbole; it is a precise description of what happens when a city falls.

word_study.meaning: Plural construct of נִבְלָה (niblah), 'carcass/corpse.' The term is used specifically for dead bodies of animals or humans in a degraded state. It carries connotations of filth, decay, and ultimate dishonor.
word_study.significance: The use of nibelat rather than a more neutral term for the dead emphasizes the degraded, dishonored state of the bodies. This is not merely death but desecration. The word choice itself—applied to the people—emphasizes the lowest possible social status and dignity.

word_study.meaning: Food or fare. The preposition לְ (le) means 'for' or 'to serve as.' Combined, the phrase means 'to serve as food for.' This language reduces human bodies to the status of prey or carrion.
word_study.significance: The reduction of human remains to 'food' strips away human dignity entirely. This is the ultimate image of degradation—the reversal of the food chain, with humans at the bottom as prey. In covenant terms, this is what happens when the people reject their covenant status as God's beloved.

word_study.meaning: Birds, fowl. In biblical usage, birds of the sky often represent judgment or defilement (see Leviticus 11, which lists unclean birds; or Deuteronomy 28:26).
word_study.significance: The pairing of birds with beasts emphasizes the completeness of exposure and defilement. No creature—whether of air or earth—is excluded from feasting on the dead. The use of 'fowls of the heaven' echoes Deuteronomy 28:26 directly, invoking the covenant curse tradition.

word_study.meaning: To frighten away, to shoo, to cause to flee. The verb חָרַד (harad) means 'to tremble/be afraid,' so the causative form (hiphil) means 'to frighten/drive away.' The negative construction 'none shall fray them away' is critical.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes not just that bodies are exposed, but that no one survives or cares to interrupt the process. The absence of someone to perform even this minimal act of respect implies either mass death (there are no survivors) or such utter societal collapse that survivors no longer maintain normal human practices of respect. This is total civilizational breakdown.

cross_references.connection: The foundational curse passage explicitly states: 'The LORD shall cause thee to be smitten before thine enemies... thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away.' Jeremiah 7:33 is the direct fulfillment of this covenant curse for violation.

Goliath's threat to David—to leave his corpse for birds and beasts—was understood as the ultimate insult and degradation in ancient Near Eastern culture. By contrast, David's God protects him. Jeremiah's prophecy shows what happens when a people turn from that protective God.

The psalmist laments that enemies have defiled the Temple and left 'the dead bodies of thy servants meat for the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth.' This psalm likely reflects the reality that Jeremiah prophesied—the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall.

Jeremiah repeats this specific curse language: 'They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried; but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth.' The consistency across passages underscores its centrality to Jeremiah's prophetic message.

The Teacher reflects on the return of the spirit to God and the body to dust, emphasizing the vanity of human striving. Jeremiah's prophecy of unburied corpses is the inverse image—where humans are denied even the dignity of returning to proper rest in the earth.

commentary.historical_context:
Ancient Near Eastern burial practices were deeply significant. Proper burial was not optional but essential—it ensured the deceased's rest, honored the family, and maintained social stability. Denial of burial was a severe punishment, reserved for the worst criminals or enemies. The Hittite laws, Egyptian practices, and Mesopotamian customs all attest to the central importance of proper burial.

During siege warfare in the ancient Levant, normal burial practices often broke down catastrophically. The Assyrian and Babylonian armies, when they conquered cities, were known to leave bodies exposed as a terror tactic—a visual demonstration of power and a warning to other cities. The Assyrian reliefs depicting siege warfare show bodies being thrown from walls. The historical record of Judah's Babylonian siege in 586 BCE suggests massive casualties from both combat and starvation.

Jeremiah's prophecy reflects precise knowledge of what happens during and after siege warfare. His specificity—birds and beasts, no one to drive them away—suggests either eyewitness experience or detailed understanding of siege dynamics. The valley south of Jerusalem, already associated with shame, would become a place of uncontrolled decay. Whether Jeremiah witnessed such scenes or drew on knowledge of Assyrian siege warfare (which had devastated the northern kingdom in 722 BCE), his prophecy demonstrates the harsh realism of biblical prophecy: not moral abstractions, but concrete historical consequences.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar imagery of covenant violation leading to degradation of the bodies of the wicked. In 1 Nephi 12:4, Nephi sees in vision that after the Savior's crucifixion, the righteous Nephites will be taken up to heaven, but the wicked will be destroyed. The contrast is stark: the righteous are taken up in glory, the wicked are left in degradation. In 3 Nephi 8:8-10, during the destruction of the wicked at Christ's coming, the earth opens and swallows some, others are burned, and the land is left desolate.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:32-40 describes the fate of those who reject the testimony of the Son of God—they are assigned to outer darkness and a kingdom of little glory. The principle of covenant rejection leading to degradation runs through revealed doctrine. D&C 84:24 warns that those who reject God's word 'have strayed from my statutes.' The consequence is diminishment—both spiritual and ultimately physical.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple represents God's presence and the covenant people's standing before him. Defilement, denial of burial rights, and exposure to degradation represent the ultimate spiritual consequence of covenant rejection—separation from God's presence and from the dignity that covenant membership provides. In the Restoration, we understand that those who reject the covenant made in the Temple face the ultimate loss: exile from God's presence. The physical imagery of Jeremiah—exposure, degradation, lack of honor—shadows this spiritual reality.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse demonstrates why Christ's atoning sacrifice was necessary. The curse pronounced here—degradation, denial of dignity, abandonment—is the natural consequence of covenant violation. Christ, who had no covenant violation, voluntarily accepted degradation and death to bear the curse on behalf of humanity. His burial in a rich man's tomb (Matthew 27:57-60) stands in contrast to the degraded exposure Jeremiah prophesies for the wicked. Yet Christ's resurrection reverses both the physical indignity and the spiritual consequence—those who accept his atonement are no longer abandoned to degradation but are raised to dignity and life. The contrast between this verse (exposure and shame) and the promise of resurrection through Christ (dignity and restoration) is the Gospel's central message.
commentary.application: For modern readers, this verse is a stark reminder that covenant rejection has consequences that are not merely spiritual or abstract. The degradation and shame Jeremiah describes are the natural fruit of a broken covenant. For Latter-day Saints, this raises urgent questions: Are we maintaining our covenants? Do our practices reflect our promises? The warning is not primarily about literal birds and beasts (though the literal history of Jerusalem's siege shows that prophecy can be grimly exact), but about the inevitable social, relational, and spiritual collapse that follows from systemic moral corruption. The principle applies to communities and individuals: communities that tolerate injustice or moral compromise face not only divine judgment but the natural social consequences of those violations. Individuals who break covenants face spiritual and relational degradation. The application might be: What compromises have I rationalized? What covenants am I neglecting? What is the trajectory I am on, and where will it lead if I do not repent? The severity of Jeremiah's language is meant to wake us from complacency.

text_kjv: Then will I cause to cease from the cities of Judah, and from the streets of Jerusalem, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride: for the land shall be desolate.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 34 brings Jeremiah 7 to its devastating conclusion. After laying out the specific sins (false reliance on the Temple, idolatry, child sacrifice) and the specific consequences (mass death, exposure of corpses, burial grounds overwhelmed), Jeremiah now pronounces the ultimate judgment: the silencing of normal human life. The fourfold repetition of 'voice' (qol—qol sason, qol simcha, qol chatan, qol kalla) creates a litany of loss. Joy, gladness, bridegroom, bride—these are the sounds of life continuing, of celebration, of hope, of family continuity. Their absence means the death not merely of individuals but of society itself.

This verse uses a formula that Jeremiah returns to throughout his prophecies (16:9; 25:10) and that his contemporary Zechariah later reverses as a sign of restoration (33:11). The specific pairing of bridegroom and bride is particularly poignant—marriage represents the future, continuity, hope. The silence of wedding celebrations means no future, no new generation being born into the covenant community, no expectation of restoration. The repetition of 'voice' emphasizes that this is not merely visual desolation but auditory—a silence so complete that the listener would become aware of the absence of normal human sound.

The final phrase, 'for the land shall be desolate' (ki lacharbah tiheye ha'aretz), gives the reason. The land becomes a wasteland not through natural disaster but through the withdrawal of human civilization. The wilderness does not silence; people do. This is the inverse of creation: where Genesis describes a land filled with life and God walking with humans, Jeremiah describes land emptied of human voice and presence. The desolation is both cause and consequence—the land is desolate because the people are dead or exiled; the people experience desolation because the land is empty of the markers of normal life.

Historically, this prophecy was fulfilled in the years after the Babylonian siege of 586 BCE. Jerusalem was destroyed, the Temple was burned, the leadership was deported to Babylon, and Judah became a devastated, depopulated region. Archaeological evidence confirms the scale of destruction: burned buildings, collapsed walls, abandoned sites. For a generation, the cities of Judah would indeed be silent—no wedding celebrations, no public gladness, only survival or exile.

word_study.meaning: First person singular hiphil of שׁבת (shabat, 'to cease/stop/rest'). The hiphil causative form means 'I will cause to cease' or 'I will put an end to.' The prefix וְ (ve) means 'and' and connects this action to the preceding judgment.
word_study.significance: God is not merely allowing silence to happen; he is actively causing it. This emphasizes divine agency in judgment. The silencing of celebration is a specific act of God, not a passive consequence. This active causative language throughout Jeremiah emphasizes that God is the agent of judgment, not merely a passive observer.

word_study.meaning: Voice, sound, noise. The term can refer to literal sound or metaphorically to proclamation or message. The fourfold repetition (qol sason, qol simcha, qol chatan, qol kalla) creates a cascading rhythm that emphasizes the completeness of the silencing.
word_study.significance: The Hebrew Bible uses qol to represent both human utterance and divine Word. The silencing of human voices is presented as a judgment—the land becomes silent before God. This echoes the principle that where God's word is rejected, human voice becomes empty and eventually ceases altogether.

word_study.meaning: Joy, gladness, exultation. A strong positive emotion, often associated with celebration, festivity, and communal gathering. The term appears frequently in Isaiah 35:10 and 51:11 as part of eschatological restoration.
word_study.significance: Sason represents not merely individual emotion but communal celebration—the shared joy of a thriving people. Its absence marks social collapse. Notably, Isaiah uses the restoration of sason as a sign of messianic renewal, making this verse's silencing of sason particularly significant for understanding judgment and restoration dialectically.

word_study.meaning: Joy, gladness, happiness. Similar to sason but with slightly different connotations—simcha is more personal and internal, while sason is more outward and celebratory. Together they form a comprehensive picture of human joy.
word_study.significance: In Latter-day Saint usage, simcha (Hebrew cognate) remains a familiar term in Jewish contexts and carries the weight of Jewish spiritual tradition. The loss of simcha from the cities represents the spiritual death of community—not merely economic hardship but the loss of the capacity for joy itself.

word_study.meaning: Bridegroom, bridegroom-to-be, son-in-law. In biblical usage, chatan represents youth, hope, the future, family continuity. The voice of the chatan is the voice of male joy and anticipation.
word_study.significance: The bridegroom represents the male line of descent and the future of the people. His silence marks the termination of generational continuity. This is why the term appears so prominently in prophecies of both judgment (here) and restoration (33:11, 16:9).

word_study.meaning: Bride, newly married woman. Kalla represents fertility, new life, the incorporation of new members into the covenant community. Her voice—whether singing, celebrating, or crying out—is the voice of the future generation.
word_study.significance: The silencing of the bride's voice means the silencing of female joy and also the silencing of fertility and futurity. The pairing of chatan and kalla is not merely romantic but fundamentally about the continuation of the people. Their silence is civilizational death, not merely personal loss.

word_study.meaning: Waste, ruin, desolation. The word חָרַב (charab) means 'to be laid waste' or 'to become dry.' The feminine form חָרְבָּה (charebah) is often used of Jerusalem or the land in its desolated state.
word_study.significance: This word becomes the theological signature of covenant judgment throughout the prophets. It represents not merely physical destruction but the emptiness that results from abandonment—by God, by the people, by civilization itself. It is the opposite of the land flowing with milk and honey promised to the covenant people.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah repeats this judgment formula: 'For thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will cause to cease from this place in your eyes, and in your days, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride.' The repetition across multiple contexts reinforces that this silencing is central to Jeremiah's message of judgment.

In a judgment prophecy against all nations, Jeremiah includes: 'Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the candle.' The expansion of the formula to include millstones and candles emphasizes the completeness of civilizational collapse.

In a later prophecy of restoration, Jeremiah reverses this judgment: 'Thus saith the LORD; Again there shall be heard in this place... the voice of joy, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the voice of them that shall say, Praise the LORD of hosts.' The reversal of this formula is the sign that restoration has come. This shows that the absence and presence of these voices frame Jeremiah's entire prophecy.

The covenant curse specifies: 'Thou shalt betroth a wife, and another man shall lie with her: thou shalt build an house, and thou shalt not dwell therein: thou shalt plant a vineyard, and shalt not gather the grapes thereof.' The inability to celebrate marriage, build, and sow are all aspects of the covenant curse Jeremiah is invoking.

After Jerusalem's fall, the Lamentation describes: 'All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?' The fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy is described in Lamentations—the city that once had 'voice of gladness' is now a mockery and ruin.

commentary.historical_context:
Wedding celebrations in ancient Near Eastern societies, particularly in Israel, were major communal events lasting multiple days (Genesis 29:27, Judges 14:12-17). The wedding feast included music, dancing, feasting, and public rejoicing. The presence of a wedding was a sign of peace, prosperity, and the social order functioning normally. The absence of weddings and the silencing of the wedding celebration would have been immediately apparent to contemporary observers—it would signal civilizational breakdown.

During the Babylonian siege and destruction of Jerusalem (597-586 BCE) and in the aftermath of conquest, weddings would indeed have ceased. The young men were killed or deported; women and survivors faced famine and exile. For decades, the land experienced this silence. Archaeological evidence shows that many sites in Judah were depopulated or sparsely inhabited for generations after the Babylonian destruction. The silence Jeremiah prophesies is not poetic exaggeration but an accurate description of what post-conquest desolation meant.

The formula of silenced celebration also appears in prophetic texts from other ancient Near Eastern cultures, suggesting a widespread recognition that the cessation of normal life sounds (celebration, work, daily activity) was a sign of profound social collapse. Jeremiah's use of this formula is thus both culturally grounded and theologically resonant—his audience would immediately understand that the silencing he describes is the ultimate marker of judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon describes similar patterns of judgment where the sounds of a thriving society are silenced. In 3 Nephi 8:8-10, during the destruction at Christ's coming, the land is shaken, cities burned, and the sounds of normal life cease. Later, in 3 Nephi 27-28, the Nephite society is restored and celebrates Christ's ministry, with the sounds of celebration and normal life returning. The pattern is consistent with Jeremiah: silence is judgment; the restoration of sound is redemption.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:29-30 establishes God's pattern: 'The church which I have established and called forth out of the wilderness... shall no more be moved out of her place.' For those who keep covenant, stability and continuation are promised. Conversely, for those who break covenant, the pattern Jeremiah describes unfolds. D&C 84:24 warns that those who reject God's word 'have strayed from my statutes, and have not kept my commandments.' The consequence, Jeremiah shows, is the silencing of celebration and the end of normal life.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple was the place where God's voice and presence dwelt with his people. The silencing Jeremiah prophesies is in part the silencing of God's presence—when the people reject covenant, God withdraws, and the land becomes desolate. In Latter-day Saint understanding, the temples dot the earth as places where God's voice and presence can be accessed. The opposite of desolation is the land dotted with temples where the voices of joy and gladness continue because the covenant is honored and God's presence remains. The contrast between verse 34's silence and the temples as centers of continued voice and presence is stark.

commentary.christological_typology: The silencing of the voice of the bridegroom and bride foreshadows the silencing of Christ—his arrest, trial, crucifixion, and the seeming end of his mission. Yet as Jeremiah's prophecy of silence is followed by restoration (33:10-11), so Christ's apparent defeat is followed by resurrection and the continuation of God's voice through the Church. Christ is the ultimate Bridegroom (Revelation 21:2, Ephesians 5:25-27), and his voice is restored after the resurrection, bringing joy and gladness to those who accept his atonement. The restoration formula in Jeremiah 33:11—where the voice of the bridegroom is restored as a sign of redemption—is ultimately fulfilled in the Restoration of the Gospel through Joseph Smith, where the voice of God speaks again through prophets and the bride (the Church) is again established.
commentary.application:
For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse poses a penetrating diagnostic question: Are we maintaining the markers of a thriving covenant people, or are we slipping toward the silence Jeremiah describes? The voice of the bridegroom and bride represents hope, futurity, family continuity, and normal life flourishing. For individuals, the application might be: Am I maintaining hope? Am I honoring marriage and family? Do I engage in genuine celebration and joy, or have those become foreign to me? For communities, the question is whether we are building Zion or allowing the slow erosion of the markers of covenant community—celebration, family formation, public joy in righteousness.

The severity of Jeremiah's language should wake us from spiritual complacency. The silence he describes comes not suddenly but gradually, as covenant violations accumulate and are rationalized. The prevention of desolation is not the work of a single dramatic action but of sustained commitment to covenants, protection of the vulnerable, and genuine moral transformation. The principle is clear: communities that maintain their covenants maintain their voice; communities that break covenant face silence and desolation. The application for 2026 readers: As you engage with Come, Follow Me and the restored scriptures, examine whether your individual faith and your community's practice are trending toward covenant fidelity (voice, celebration, hope) or toward compromise and silence. Repentance is the way to restore the voice—both individually and communally.

text_kjv: The word of the LORD came also unto me, saying,

commentary.narrative: This verse opens with the standard prophetic reception formula—the formula Jeremiah uses repeatedly throughout his ministry to signal that what follows originates not from human reasoning but from divine command. The phrase 'word of the LORD came to me' establishes the absolute authority of what follows. Unlike visions or dreams, which Jeremiah also receives, 'the word of the LORD' carries the weight of direct, unambiguous divine speech. In the Hebrew prophetic tradition, this formula marks the boundary between the prophet's own thoughts and God's irrevocable utterance. Jeremiah is about to receive a command that will reshape his entire life—not as suggestion or invitation, but as binding divine instruction.
commentary.narrative_cont: The TCR rendering omits the phrase 'also unto me' found in the KJV, reflecting a more direct translation of the Hebrew le'mor ('saying'), which typically introduces direct speech rather than being translated as a separate clause. This small difference matters: the Hebrew construction is purely formulaic, introducing the divine word without editorial comment. Jeremiah's personal involvement ('unto me') is implicit in his role as recipient, not explicitly emphasized. The simplicity of the formula masks its radical nature—the prophet is about to be told to remain single in a culture where marriage and children are not personal choices but covenantal obligations, markers of full participation in the community's continuity.

word_study.meaning: word, matter, thing, utterance; in prophetic literature, 'the word of the LORD' represents God's active, creative utterance that accomplishes its purpose (cf. Isaiah 55:11). Not mere information but efficacious speech.
word_study.significance: In prophetic formula, davar haYHWH carries covenantal weight—it is not advisory but binding, not negotiable but determinative of reality.

word_study.meaning: and it came to pass, and there was; the conjunction vav ('and') + hayah ('to be/become'). Common narrative transition marker, but in prophetic contexts signals a divinely ordained event.
word_study.significance: The verb does not describe Jeremiah seeking God's word; rather, the word 'came' to him—emphasizing divine initiative and Jeremiah's receptivity. This passive construction is theologically significant: the prophet does not manufacture divine speech.

cross_references.connection: Uses the identical formula 'the word of the LORD came unto me,' establishing this as Jeremiah's consistent way of marking divine communication throughout his prophetic career.
Ezekiel uses the same prophetic reception formula, showing this was the standard convention for marking genuine divine utterance across the prophetic corpus.
Establishes that 'the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets'—the word coming to the prophet is God's established means of revealing his purposes.

Modern revelation affirms that the Lord's word comes to his spokesmen: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.'

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, divine communication typically occurred through oracles, divination, or dreams. The Hebrew prophetic tradition established a distinctive form: direct word-transmission, where the prophet receives speech directly attributable to the deity. This elevated the prophet's authority immensely—the prophet was not interpreting signs or meditative experiences, but conveying God's own words. The formula 'the word of the LORD came to me' became so standardized that its presence or absence determined whether a claim to prophecy would be taken seriously by the community. Jeremiah uses this formula deliberately to establish legitimacy for what many in Jerusalem will find outrageous: that God has commanded him to remain unmarried.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi uses a parallel construction when receiving divine direction: 'And it came to pass that the voice of the Lord spake unto me' (1 Nephi 3:2), showing the Book of Mormon maintains the same prophetic convention for marking God's direct speech.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 68:4 applies this principle to all who speak by divine authority: 'And whatsoever they shall speak when moved upon by the Holy Ghost shall be scripture, shall be the will of the Lord, shall be the mind of the Lord, shall be the word of the Lord, shall be the voice of the Lord, and the power of God unto salvation.' The Restoration affirms that divine words transmitted through prophets carry full scriptural weight.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, the pattern of direct divine communication to the covenant-keeper parallels the prophetic reception formula—God speaks directly to his people when they are in the proper frame of receptivity.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's receptivity to the word coming to him prefigures the incarnational principle: Jesus is called 'the Word' (John 1:1)—God's ultimate self-disclosure in flesh. Just as Jeremiah opens himself to receive God's word, the Incarnation represents God's word becoming fully enfleshed in human reality.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members receive direction through channels of divine authority: through scriptures (the word given to past prophets), through living prophets and apostles, through personal revelation by the Holy Ghost. This verse invites us to recognize how divine direction typically comes—often unexpectedly, often challenging conventional assumptions about what a good life looks like, always carrying the weight of divine authority rather than mere human opinion. The question Jeremiah faces immediately (should he marry or not?) mirrors questions modern members face: How do I distinguish between my legitimate desires and God's direction? Am I truly listening for God's word, or am I listening for confirmation of what I already want?

text_kjv: Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place.

commentary.narrative: This is the most radical command in Jeremiah's call narrative—radical precisely because it strikes at the deepest social and religious expectations of ancient Israel. In that culture, marriage and childbearing were not optional lifestyle choices but covenantal obligations rooted in God's original blessing to Abraham: 'Be fruitful and multiply' (Genesis 1:28). To remain unmarried was to cut off one's name, to refuse the fundamental way a man participated in Israel's ongoing covenant story. A man without sons had no heir, no legacy, no continuation of his father's house. The phrase 'in this place' adds an eschatological dimension: not a temporary prohibition during Jeremiah's training, but a lifelong enforced celibacy as a permanent prophetic sign. The TCR rendering sharpens the point: 'You must not take a wife for yourself'—the reflexive form emphasizes Jeremiah's personal claim and possession; he is forbidden even to claim marriage as his own possession.
commentary.narrative_cont: The context immediately following this verse will explain God's reason: the coming destruction will make family life not only undesirable but impossible. Children will die of disease, parents will not be able to mourn them, and the whole social fabric that makes family continuity meaningful will be torn apart. So Jeremiah's enforced celibacy becomes a living parable—his empty house testifies in advance to the desolation coming. Unlike other prophets (Hosea, Isaiah, Ezekiel) who had marriages and children that symbolically enacted their messages, Jeremiah's symbolic message was the absence of family itself. This was a radical claim on God's part: the prophet's personal life becomes subordinated entirely to his prophetic function. He is not called to live an exemplary life that others might imitate; he is called to live a countercultural life that witnesses to catastrophe.

word_study.meaning: to take, seize, accept, marry. In the context of marriage, it is the standard Hebrew verb for a man taking a wife. The root conveys active acquisition and assumption of responsibility.
word_study.significance: The verb laqach for marriage emphasizes the man's active role in establishing the covenantal bond. God forbidding Jeremiah to 'take' a wife means forbidding him the most basic adult male role in Hebrew society.

word_study.meaning: woman, wife; from the root 'ish (man), suggesting the correlative relationship—a wife is she who belongs to and with the man as his counterpart.
word_study.significance: The term ishshah encompasses both the woman herself and her social role as wife and mother. For Jeremiah to be denied a wife meant being denied access to the most fundamental social identity available to an adult Hebrew male.

word_study.meaning: sons and daughters; the pairing covers all offspring regardless of gender. In covenant language, sons represent lineage and inheritance; daughters represent the continuation of the family through marriage alliances.
word_study.significance: The comprehensive pairing—not just sons (heirs) but daughters (who bear the next generation)—emphasizes that every avenue of family continuity is cut off. This is total denial of the blessing to 'be fruitful and multiply.'

cross_references.connection: God's original blessing to humanity: 'Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.' Jeremiah is commanded to refuse the most fundamental blessing given to God's people, making his obedience a complete reversal of normal covenantal expectation.

'There shall not be male or female barren among you'—a blessing promised to the faithful covenant people. Jeremiah's enforced childlessness thus becomes a counter-sign that the blessings are being withdrawn.

God commands Hosea to marry Gomer, a prostitute, so that his marriage enacts the unfaithfulness of Israel. Jeremiah's situation is the inverse: he is forbidden marriage so that his singleness enacts the coming judgment.

Paul discusses remaining unmarried for the sake of undivided devotion to the Lord's work. Jeremiah's celibacy parallels this principle—his unmarried state frees him entirely for prophetic service while simultaneously making him a sign of coming desolation.

The Lord speaks to Emma Smith acknowledging the sacrifice of Church leaders' families in the work of restoration: 'Wherefore, my dearly beloved, let thy virtues and thy faithful diligence, and thy devotion unto all righteousness be constant.' While not forbidding marriage, the principle of sacrificing family peace for prophetic work echoes Jeremiah's situation.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the household was the fundamental unit of both social organization and religious practice. A man without a wife was incomplete, even suspect—he could not fully participate in the Passover ritual (which required a household) or maintain an inheritance (which passed through sons). The denial of marriage was more than personal deprivation; it was social excommunication. Jeremiah would have been viewed as either religiously deficient or under a curse. Archaeological evidence from family tombs in the Levantine region shows how deeply genealogy and family continuity mattered—extended family burials ensured that the deceased remained part of the ongoing family story. By forbidding Jeremiah to have sons, God was cutting him off from this most basic form of continuity. The timing is significant: this command comes during Josiah's reign (639-609 BCE), when the nation still enjoyed relative stability and prosperity. Jeremiah's lonely celibacy would thus be a stark, visible contradiction to the apparent normality around him—his empty house a daily testimony that something was gravely wrong.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes sacrificing family relationships for covenant duty: Nephi leaves his father Lehi's house and later separates from Laman and Lemuel; Alma the Younger is separated from his family by persecution. Yet none of these figures is explicitly forbidden family life as a prophetic sign. Jeremiah's situation is thus uniquely stark.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:8-9 teaches that in the last days there will be 'great tribulations' and 'weeping and wailing.' The principle that prophetic witness sometimes requires personal sacrifice for the sake of testifying to coming judgment is embedded in covenant theology. The Joseph Smith History records that Joseph was commanded to take multiple wives, which was a different kind of family sacrifice—but like Jeremiah, it was framed as a peculiar command that testified to principles beyond normal social expectation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant involves relinquishing earthly claims and placing one's life entirely at God's disposal. Jeremiah's renunciation of family life parallels the temple principle of giving 'all that [we] have' to the Lord (D&C 97:8), though Jeremiah's sacrifice is unique in being permanent and visible.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus himself remained unmarried, living out a version of Jeremiah's celibacy. Yet Jesus's singleness pointed not to judgment (as Jeremiah's did) but to his complete identification with the kingdom—his 'marriage' was to the Church, his children were those he redeemed. Jeremiah's enforced childlessness testifies to judgment; Christ's celibacy testifies to redemption and covenant renewal.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members rarely face Jeremiah's specific command, but the principle is present: sometimes God calls us to relinquish what is legitimately good (marriage, family, security) for the sake of a larger prophetic witness. The question Jeremiah's command raises is not 'Is marriage good?'—it clearly is in Hebrew covenant theology—but 'Is obedience to God's specific word for my life more important than fulfilling my own legitimate desires?' For some modern members, this might mean remaining single to serve a mission or calling; for others, it might mean accepting infertility or remaining childless when children were desired. For all, it asks: Am I willing to allow God's purposes to override my personal life plans?

text_kjv: For thus saith the LORD concerning the sons and concerning the daughters that are born in this place, and concerning their mothers that bare them, and concerning their fathers that begat them in this land;

commentary.narrative: This verse serves as the heading for the apocalyptic oracle that follows. God now explains why Jeremiah must remain unmarried: the coming destruction will obliterate family life entirely, rendering procreation itself a curse rather than a blessing. The fourfold repetition—sons, daughters, mothers, fathers—is not merely stylistic elaboration but theological comprehensiveness. Every participant in the family structure, every generation, every sex, will be swept up in the coming judgment. The phrase 'that are born in this place' and 'that begat them in this land' emphasizes that we are not speaking of distant future generations, but of people currently alive or about to be born. The destruction is imminent enough that those born now will live to see the judgment. The TCR rendering clarifies that this verse is a heading: the colon after 'in this land' is not a period but an announcement that judgment details follow.
commentary.narrative_cont: The structure here is crucial for understanding how Hebrew prophecy works. God does not say, 'Therefore you cannot marry because I am angry.' Rather, God says, 'I will tell you what will happen to families. That is why you will have no family.' Jeremiah's celibacy is not punishment for his own sin or a test of arbitrary obedience. It is a prophetic sign—a living embodiment of the judgment that is coming. Just as a street sign points to something beyond itself, Jeremiah's empty household points to the devastation heading toward Jerusalem. This is a far more demanding form of prophecy than simply speaking warnings. Jeremiah must enact the prophecy in his body, in his family structure (or lack thereof), in the social death of remaining unmarried. His very existence becomes the message.

word_study.meaning: born; passive participle of yalad (to bear, give birth). The passive form emphasizes that these are the recipients of birth, not active agents—they are brought into the world only to face destruction.
word_study.significance: The use of the passive participle suggests innocence or at least powerlessness. These children being 'born' are not guilty parties who deserve judgment; they are brought into existence within a doomed nation. This compounds the tragedy.

word_study.meaning: bearing, giving birth; feminine participle of yalad. Emphasizes the mothers' active role in bringing children into the world through the pain and vulnerability of childbirth.
word_study.significance: The term yoldot carries the weight of maternal sacrifice and hope—a mother bears a child through suffering in the expectation of a future. This makes the coming destruction of those children more poignant.

word_study.meaning: siring, begetting; masculine participle of yalad. Emphasizes the fathers' role in procreation and their covenantal obligation to raise heirs.
word_study.significance: The parallelism of yoldot (mothers bearing) and molidim (fathers siring) shows that both parents equally participate in family creation—and both will be swept up in the judgment. Neither sex can escape.

cross_references.connection: This verse introduces the curse-language oracle, describing how the sons, daughters, and parents mentioned here will die of disease, famine, and sword—unproperly buried and unlamented.

Part of the covenant curses: 'Thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away.' Jeremiah's oracle directly echoes this covenant curse language.

The book of Lamentations describes the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall: 'The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets...When they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, they poured out their souls into their mothers' bosoms.' This is the lived reality of the judgment Jeremiah announces.

Ezekiel announces similar judgments: 'When I shall send upon them the evil arrows of famine...I will increase the famine upon you, and will break your staff of bread.' Both prophets announce combined judgments of disease, famine, and sword.

Modern revelation echoes this principle: when the covenant people turn from God, judgment comes upon 'all people' in a community, affecting 'the children, and the beasts of the field, and the fowls of the heaven.'

commentary.historical_context: The verse's reference to 'this place' (Jerusalem/Judah) and 'this land' (the land of promise) carries heavy covenantal weight. The land was never simply real estate—it was the sacramental center of God's covenant with Israel. To announce that judgment will devastate the land and its inhabitants was to announce the breaking of the covenant relationship itself. Archaeological evidence from the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem (597-586 BCE) shows exactly the kind of destruction Jeremiah announces: mass graves, evidence of disease and starvation within the walls, and the systematic destruction of the temple and civic structures. The timing matters: Jeremiah lived through the reign of Josiah (639-609 BCE), a time of religious reform, and then through the reigns of Josiah's sons, when the nation spiraled into political chaos, alliances with foreign powers, and religious apostasy. By the time Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, multiple prophetic warnings had gone unheeded. Jeremiah's announcement of death affecting 'sons and daughters, mothers and fathers' reflects the actual demographic catastrophe that would soon occur.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi witnesses the future destruction of Jerusalem (1 Nephi 10:7-9) and announces that 'the children of men shall not perish' but only those who remain in unbelief. The Book of Mormon places the burden of the judgment on rejection of God's word rather than inevitable doom—there is always a way of escape for the repentant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:8-9, 17-21 prophesies that in the last days there will come 'great tribulations' and that 'the hour cometh that I will drink of the fruit of the vine with you on the earth.' The principle that judgment affects entire families and communities is part of Latter-day Saint eschatology, though always with the promise of redemption for the faithful.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that families are eternal covenants. Jeremiah's announcement that earthly families will be destroyed testifies to the principle that without the restored covenant of eternal families (restored through temple sealing), human relationships are ultimately fragile and subject to mortality. The judgment Jeremiah announces is precisely what makes the restored doctrine of eternal families so precious.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's announcement that the mothers and fathers of Jerusalem will be destroyed points to Christ as the one who reverses this judgment. Jesus is born of Mary, who will witness his death, but then resurrects—not to bodily death but to eternal life. Christ restores what the judgment destroys: the family relationship, redeemed and perfected.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern readers to contemplate the spiritual state of their own communities. When prophetic voices announce judgment, they are typically announcing not arbitrary punishment but the natural consequences of collective turning away from God. The question for us is: Am I listening to contemporary prophetic voices warning of spiritual dangers? Am I living in a way that keeps my family (spiritual and literal) within the covenant, or am I among those who dismiss warnings and assume that 'it can't happen to us'? The verse also teaches that judgment, when it comes, does not discriminate by age or innocence—entire communities suffer together. This calls covenant members to prayer and repentance not just for personal salvation but for the spiritual welfare of their families, wards, and nations.

text_kjv: They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried; but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth: and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine; and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.

commentary.narrative: This is among the most graphically devastating verses in the prophetic corpus. The oracle piles curse upon curse with relentless specificity: death from disease, refusal of mourning, denial of burial, exposure of corpses, consumption by famine and sword, and desecration by scavenging animals. Each element represents a specific violation of ancient Near Eastern funeral practice and covenantal shame. The TCR rendering 'deaths of deadly diseases' (memotei tachaluim, a plural construct form) suggests multiple kinds of gruesome illnesses—plague, pestilence, perhaps cholera or dysentery, diseases of the siege.
