word_study.significance: The imperative places the command squarely on God. Jeremiah does not petition gently but demands healing as a covenant right, yet in absolute dependence on God's willingness to act.

word_study.meaning: Cohortative form expressing consequence and determination: 'then I will be healed.' The passive voice indicates that Jeremiah's healing is God's action, not his own.
word_study.significance: The cohortative creates a promise: if God acts, then Jeremiah will be healed. This expresses the biblical principle that salvation is God's work received by human faith and obedience.

word_study.meaning: My praise, my song of praise. Derived from the root HLL (to praise, shine). Tehilla is not praise offered to someone but praise as the substance itself—what one celebrates.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah's statement 'thou art my praise' means God is the very content of his celebration. Not 'I praise you' but 'you are what I praise.' This is radical: God is the object, subject, and substance of Jeremiah's worship.

cross_references.connection: Part of Jeremiah's prophetic crisis: he wishes his head were 'a fountain of tears' because of the sin he must proclaim. Verse 14 shows his movement from lamentation to petition—from sorrow over others' condition to personal prayer for healing.
'Bless the LORD, O my soul...Who healeth all thy diseases.' This psalm shares the same theological affirmation: God is the sole healer, and praise (tehilla) is the appropriate response.

The Suffering Servant passage: 'with his stripes we are healed.' Jeremiah's plea for healing anticipates the Messianic promise that healing comes through one's wounds—a pattern Jeremiah himself embodies as a rejected prophet.

The Lord's revelation on healing in the Restoration: 'And whosoever among you are sick, and have not faith to be healed, but believe, shall be healed.' The principle of faith dependent on God's power mirrors Jeremiah's structure.

Jesus's high priestly prayer: 'Father, glorify thy son, that thy son also may glorify thee.' Like Jeremiah, Jesus makes God the substance of his praise and the sole source of his authority and healing.

commentary.historical_context: The structure of verse 14—imperative followed by consequence—reflects both biblical prayer formulae and Ancient Near Eastern petition traditions. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian prayer literature, petitions to deities often followed the pattern 'Do X for me, that I might achieve Y'—establishing a causal connection between divine action and human outcome. Jeremiah's prayer follows this formal structure while inverting it theologically: he is not negotiating with God as an equal but acknowledging absolute dependence. The incorporation of this verse into the Amidah (likely after the Second Temple period) reflects Jewish recognition of its theological centrality and its applicability to corporate prayer.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:26-27 echoes the same principle: 'And now, my brethren, I would that, after ye have received so many blessings from the hand of the Lord your God, that ye should render all thanks unto him. And I would that ye should remember, that whatsoever thing ye ask in faith, believing that ye shall receive in the name of Christ, ye shall receive it.' The structure parallels Jeremiah's: ask (faith) / receive (God's action).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:34 reiterates: 'Wherefore, I have sent you out to preach repentance and redemption through Jesus Christ unto all people, in all nations, kindreds, tongues and languages.' The healing Jeremiah seeks is healing from the spiritual disease that verse 9 diagnosed—a disease only God can cure through covenant renewal and obedience.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, covenants involve the repeated pattern of promise and blessing: the member makes covenants (human action), and God bestows blessings (divine action). Jeremiah's prayer mirrors this covenant structure—he petitions for healing as a covenantal right, grounded in Israel's relationship with God.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's prayer for healing is a type of Christ's redemptive work. As the Great Physician, Jesus comes not for the healthy but for the sick (Matthew 9:12). His atonement is the ultimate healing: 'He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities' (Isaiah 53:5). Jeremiah's willingness to be healed—to acknowledge disease and depend on God—models the repentance that Christ's healing requires. The phrase 'thou art my praise' anticipates the New Testament's vision of Christ as the 'author and finisher of our faith' (Hebrews 12:2), the one who is celebrated as the substance of the faithful's hope.
commentary.application: Jeremiah's prayer invites modern believers to examine their relationship to healing and deliverance. The verse distinguishes sharply between self-help and true healing: Jeremiah does not strategize his own recovery but surrenders it to God. In contemporary Latter-day Saint practice, this has concrete implications. Members often oscillate between fervent faith that God will heal and anxiety that takes healing into their own hands. Verse 14 calls for both: petition (demonstrating faith and desire) and surrender (acknowledging that the outcome rests with God). Furthermore, the declaration 'thou art my praise' challenges the modern tendency to praise God for blessings while remaining distant from God as a person. Jeremiah's theology insists that God himself—not his gifts—is the proper focus of praise. In personal prayer and fasting, in seeking guidance for difficult decisions, in confronting persistent sin or weakness: this verse teaches that the healing comes from God, not from technique, and that God himself is worthy of celebration regardless of circumstance.

text_kjv: Behold, they say unto me, Where is the word of the LORD? let it come now.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah's prayer is immediately interrupted by the voice of his mockers. Verse 15 represents the constant taunt that plagued his ministry: the demand that his prophecies prove themselves true, and if they have not yet been fulfilled, they are fraudulent. The phrase 'Where is the word of the LORD?' (ayeh devar YHWH) is not a sincere inquiry but a challenge to prophetic credibility. Jeremiah's enemies are essentially saying: You claim to speak for God. We see no judgment. Where is it? The addition 'let it come now' (yavo na) intensifies the sarcasm—come on then, let's see it. The taunt is deeply personal; it is directed at Jeremiah as much as at his message.

This mockery reflects a genuine theological problem for Jeremiah's audience. His prophecies of destruction took decades to materialize. Jeremiah began prophesying around 627 BCE, but Jerusalem did not fall until 586 BCE—forty years later. For much of that period, the city appeared stable under King Josiah's reforms and subsequent reigns. To ordinary Jerusalemites, Jeremiah looked like a false prophet whose dire warnings had proven empty. This delay in fulfillment is not addressed in scripture as a mere inconvenience but as a genuine crisis of prophetic authority. The mockers in verse 15 represent what must have been widespread skepticism: if Jeremiah speaks for God, why hasn't God acted? The demand 'let it come now' mocks the notion that God might work on a timeline different from human expectation.

Yet from the Hebrew perspective preserved in The Covenant Rendering's note, the taunt carries spiritual danger. To mock a true prophet is to mock God himself. The participle 'omrim ('they keep saying') suggests this is not a one-time comment but ongoing, repeated harassment. Jeremiah must endure not just the burden of an unpopular message but constant, daily mockery from those who claim his words are false.

word_study.term_english: Where is the word of the LORD?
word_study.meaning: 'Where is the word of YHWH?'—an interrogative demanding proof. 'Word' (devar) means both the spoken message and its actualization/fulfillment.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, the 'word' of God is not merely information but an agent of change—it 'goes forth and does not return empty' (Isaiah 55:11). To ask 'where is the word' is to deny that it has power, suggesting it remains unfulfilled and therefore false.

word_study.meaning: Imperative with the particle na (please, I pray), but in this context used ironically. 'Let it come'—go ahead, bring it on (sarcasm).
word_study.significance: The particles na intensifies the demand, but the context makes clear it is a taunt, not a sincere plea. The mockers are challenging God's word to materialize; they do not genuinely expect it.

word_study.meaning: Present participle: 'saying,' 'keep saying,' 'continually saying.' Indicates ongoing, repeated action.
word_study.significance: This is not isolated criticism but a constant refrain. Jeremiah must endure not a single taunt but the tireless repetition of doubt about his prophetic authority—a psychological and spiritual assault.

cross_references.connection: In another confession, Jeremiah expresses the interior pain of being mocked: 'O LORD, thou hast deceived me...I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me.' Yet he cannot refrain from prophesying, though the message brings only scorn.

The Torah's test for false prophecy: 'When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, then that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken.' The mockers in verse 15 are implicitly applying this test—and Jeremiah's delayed fulfillment made it appear he failed.

Peter's warning about end-times scoffers: 'Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were.' The New Testament echoes this ancient struggle with divine patience versus human expectation of immediacy.

A parallel taunt directed at Isaiah: 'Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it.' The mockers challenge God's judgment to come quickly, a universal prophetic burden across scripture.

Jacob teaches: 'Wherefore, brethren, seek not to counsel the Lord, but to take counsel from his hand.' The mockers in Jeremiah 17:15 exemplify exactly what Jacob warns against—demanding that God act on human timeline and logic.

commentary.historical_context: The taunt in verse 15 reflects a real historical challenge. Jeremiah's prophecies did not come to pass during the reigns of Josiah (639-609 BCE) or the early reigns of his successors. The fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE was four decades away from Jeremiah's early ministry. In ancient Near Eastern culture, prophets were expected to produce immediate results or face dismissal as false. The fact that Jeremiah was allowed to continue prophesying despite this delay speaks to the power of his personality and the respect he commanded; yet it also explains the virulence of opposition. Furthermore, the period between Josiah's death and the exile saw several false prophets arise, claiming that God would not destroy Jerusalem (cf. Jeremiah 23:16-22). These competitors mocked Jeremiah's pessimism, telling people what they wanted to hear. Against this backdrop, Jeremiah's mockery by ordinary citizens and competing prophets reflects a genuine theological crisis: how to distinguish true prophecy from false when the fulfillment is delayed?

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 13:3-8 describes a similar situation: the prophet Samuel, speaking in the name of the Lord, pronounces judgments on the Nephites. Verse 5 notes: 'Nevertheless, the people did harden their hearts, for they were of a stiff neck and a stiff people.' The mockers in Jeremiah 17:15 parallel those who hardened their hearts against Samuel's word—both prophets experience the burden of being mocked while speaking unwelcome truth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 reasserts: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled. What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; and I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away.'' This Restoration assurance directly answers the mockers' challenge in verse 15—God's word will be fulfilled, though heaven and earth pass away first.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, members promise to 'sustain the Church and its leaders.' This covenant directly relates to verses like 17:15: sustaining the prophets means believing their word even when its fulfillment is not immediate, and trusting that God acts according to divine timeline, not human demand.

commentary.christological_typology: The mockers who demand 'Where is the word of the LORD?' prefigure the mockery of Christ on the cross. Matthew 27:42-43 records: 'He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.' The taunt mirrors verse 15's sarcasm: 'let it come now.' Christ endures the same challenge Jeremiah faces—the demand for immediate proof, the mockery that claims that if God's word were true, it would be evidently fulfilled. Yet Christ's resurrection vindicated his word, just as the fall of Jerusalem vindicated Jeremiah's prophecy.
commentary.application: Modern members of the Church face analogous challenges to both Jeremiah and his mockers. Testimony often comes before understanding; faith must sometimes precede proof. The verse teaches the danger of demanding that God's word prove itself on an accelerated timeline. In personal life, members may receive revelation—a prompting to move, to serve, to forgive, to commit to a relationship—yet the fruits may not be immediately evident. Verse 15 warns against the sophisticated mockery of doubt that masquerades as rationality: 'If this is true, I should see results now.' Conversely, the verse calls members to the faith that Jeremiah exemplifies: to proclaim and live by truth even when mockers surround, trusting that God's word will ultimately be vindicated. In the modern context of opposition to the Church, verse 15 reminds members that skepticism ('Where is the proof?') is not a new challenge to faith but as old as prophecy itself.

text_kjv: As for me, I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee: neither have I desired the woeful day; thou knowest: that which came out of my lips was right before thee.

commentary.narrative:
In verse 16, Jeremiah defends himself directly before God, acknowledging the profound tension of his calling. The verse opens with a personal assertion: 'As for me' (va'ani)—establishing that Jeremiah speaks to God about his own integrity and faithfulness. He then denies two charges that his mockers implicitly level. First, 'I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee' (lo atsti mero'eh acharekha). The language is crucial: Jeremiah did not 'rush away' from his role as shepherd of God's people. The metaphor of 'shepherd' (ro'eh) is not one Jeremiah applies to himself explicitly elsewhere in the book, making this statement remarkable. He is asserting that despite the burdens of prophetic ministry—despite the rejection, the mockery, the physical danger—he has not abandoned his post. He has continued to shepherd God's flock in the direction God commands, even when doing so was costly.

Second, Jeremiah denies that 'I have desired the woeful day.' The phrase 'day of calamity' (yom anush) echoes verse 9's diagnosis of the 'desperate wickedness' of the human heart. To desire the 'day of calamity' would be to secretly wish for the disaster he prophesies—perhaps from a motive of vindication ('I told you so') or vengeance. Jeremiah insists he harbors no such desire. He does not relish the thought of Jerusalem's destruction; he prophesies it only because God commands it. This is a profound statement about the prophetic burden: to warn of judgment without desiring it, to speak the hard word from obedience rather than from personal malice.

The final assertion is perhaps the most significant: 'that which came out of my lips was right before thee.' The phrase 'motsa sefatai' (literally 'the going forth of my lips' or 'what came from my mouth') refers to his prophecies. 'Right before thee' (nokhach panekha, 'before your face') means these words were spoken in God's presence, witnessed by God. Jeremiah appeals to God as the ultimate judge of his prophetic authenticity. He does not defend himself before the mockers but before God, claiming that his words have been uttered in God's presence and are therefore true, regardless of whether the mockers believe them.

word_study.meaning: Shepherd, one who tends a flock. The verb ra'ah means to pasture, tend, guide. Used metaphorically for leaders who care for their people.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah reclaims the shepherding role despite its costs. In Jeremiah 2-3, God criticizes the false shepherds of Israel; here, Jeremiah asserts he has been a true shepherd, following God's direction even when it leads to unpopularity.

word_study.meaning: I did not rush, did not press forward, did not hasten. The verb uts means to press, hurry, or rush away.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah emphasizes perseverance despite pressure. He has not fled his role even when circumstances demanded it; he remains at his post as shepherd.

word_study.meaning: Day of sickness, illness, calamity, incurability. Anush relates to a hopeless, desperate condition—echoing verse 9's diagnosis of the incurable heart.
word_study.significance: The same linguistic field ('anush' / 'desperately wicked') connects verse 16 to verse 9. The 'day of calamity' is characterized by the same spiritual desperation that marks the unregenerate human heart. To desire it would be to wish spiritual death on Israel.

word_study.term_english: that which came out of my lips
word_study.meaning: The going forth, the utterance, what proceeded from my lips. Motsa denotes what exits or issues forth.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah's words are not his own inventions but what God has caused to issue forth. The phrase appeals to the divine origin and authority of his prophecies.

cross_references.connection: God's initial commission to Jeremiah includes a warning of opposition: 'they shall fight against thee.' Verse 16 shows Jeremiah's faithfulness to that original call despite the opposition he now faces.

Jeremiah condemns the false shepherds of Israel: 'Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep.' In verse 16, Jeremiah asserts he has been a true pastor, not one who scatters or destroys.

Ezekiel similarly condemns false shepherds who feed themselves rather than the flock. By claiming he did not 'hasten from being a pastor,' Jeremiah aligns himself with true shepherding as defined by scripture.

Jesus identifies himself as the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. Jeremiah's assertion that he remained faithful to his shepherding role prefigures Christ's ultimate model of prophetic fidelity.

The role of shepherds (bishops, leaders) in the Restoration is to 'watch over the Church and be to it a savior.' Jeremiah's defense of his shepherding aligns with this Restoration definition of pastoral responsibility.

commentary.historical_context: The metaphor of the shepherd was common in ancient Near Eastern political language. Mesopotamian kings styled themselves as shepherds of their people; Egyptian pharaohs bore similar titles. In Israel, the king was ideally the shepherd of God's flock (2 Samuel 5:2). By the time of Jeremiah, however, 'the shepherds' (a term for leaders, especially kings and priests) had become corrupt. Jeremiah's assertion that he did not 'hasten from being a pastor' is therefore countercultural—he is claiming the authority and responsibility of true shepherding while rejecting the false shepherds who dominated Jerusalem's leadership. Additionally, Jeremiah's defense 'before God's face' reflects the ancient Near Eastern practice of temple oaths, where a person would make a solemn protestation of innocence in God's presence, invoking divine judgment on themselves if they lied.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:37-40 presents a similar shepherding model: Alma asks the Saints, 'If ye have experienced a change of heart, and ye have felt to sing the song of redeeming love, I would ask, have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances?' Alma, like Jeremiah, remains at his pastoral post despite the Church's challenges, calling the people to faithfulness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 describes the role of the Church president (the 'shepherd'): 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' The principle of faithful shepherding, obedience to God, and personal integrity before God defines both Jeremiah's claim in verse 16 and the Restoration's understanding of prophetic leadership.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The language 'right before thee' and 'before thy face' (nokhach panekha) is temple language—it refers to standing in God's presence. Jeremiah's appeal is fundamentally a temple prayer: he stands before God's face and asserts his faithfulness. This connects to modern temple worship, where covenants are made 'before God and these witnesses.'

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's defense of his shepherding fidelity despite rejection prefigures Christ's role as the true shepherd. In John 10:12-13, Jesus contrasts the true shepherd (who lays down his life for the sheep) with the hireling (who abandons the sheep when danger comes). Jeremiah's assertion that he did not 'hasten from being a pastor' even when facing mockery and threat exemplifies true shepherding. Moreover, Christ's willingness to speak truth before the Jewish authorities and face mockery ('Where is the word of the Lord?') parallels Jeremiah's faithfulness despite opposition.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, verse 16 speaks directly to Church leaders and to all members who bear responsibility for others' spiritual welfare. Jeremiah's claim 'I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee' sets a standard: faithfulness to one's calling despite pressure to abandon it. In contemporary contexts, pastors, Sunday School teachers, youth leaders, and parents regularly face the temptation to relax their standards, to 'hasten away' from their shepherding role when it becomes unpopular or burdensome. A child questions why they should follow Church teachings; a class member challenges a doctrinal point; a colleague mocks religious commitment. In these moments, verse 16 calls for steadfast shepherding—not defending oneself to the mockers but appealing to God as witness to one's faithfulness. Additionally, the refusal to 'desire the woeful day' teaches members to distinguish between prophetic truth-telling and personal malice. It is possible to uphold difficult doctrines (such as standards of modesty, sexuality, or media consumption) while genuinely desiring the spiritual welfare—not the destruction—of those who oppose them.

text_kjv: Be not a terror unto me: thou art my hope in the day of evil.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 17 marks a dramatic shift in tone from defense to vulnerability. Having asserted his faithfulness in verse 16, Jeremiah now admits a fear so profound it borders on theological scandal: he is afraid that God himself might become 'a terror' to him. The plea 'Be not a terror unto me' (al tihyeh li lemechittah) is not a prayer for protection from enemies but a prayer that God not become Jeremiah's enemy. This is not anxiety about persecution from mockers or hostile kings, but terror of God's judgment—the possibility that God might turn against Jeremiah himself.

Why would Jeremiah fear this? The book of Jeremiah presents the prophet as bearing the weight of God's wrath against a sinful nation. Repeatedly, God assures Jeremiah that he is with him (1:8, 1:19, 15:20), yet also assigns him the burden of pronouncing judgment that no one wants to hear. The prophet internalizes the divine anger he must proclaim; he bears witness to God's fury against sin. In this context, Jeremiah's fear is understandable: might not the God who is enraged at Jerusalem's idolatry and injustice become similarly enraged at Jeremiah for his faltering faith, his moments of despair, his expressions of doubt? The word mechittah ('terror, ruin, dismay') suggests not mere fear but shattering—the prophet fears being broken by the God he serves.

Yet the verse does not end in despair. Immediately after the plea comes the counter-assertion: 'thou art my hope in the day of evil' (machasi attah beyom ra'ah). The word machasi ('refuge, shelter, place of safety') is the same used in the Psalms to describe God as protection from enemies. Jeremiah simultaneously fears God and trusts God as his refuge. This is not a contradiction but the deepest paradox of faith: the God who is terrifying in holiness is also the only refuge from terror. In 'the day of evil' (yom ra'ah)—which could refer to the coming judgment on Jerusalem or to any time of distress—Jeremiah has nowhere to turn but to God. This tension between terror and refuge, between fear of God's judgment and trust in God's protection, defines the prophet's spiritual landscape.

word_study.term_english: Be not a terror unto me
word_study.meaning: Do not become a source of terror, ruin, or dismay to me. Mechittah denotes not just fear but breaking, shattering, overwhelming distress.
word_study.significance: The plea acknowledges that God could be terrifying, that divine judgment could fall on Jeremiah himself. This is bold honesty about the prophet's psychological and spiritual state.

word_study.meaning: My refuge, my shelter, my place of safety. The root means to take refuge, to flee for protection. Common in the Psalms to describe God as protection.
word_study.significance: Despite his fear, Jeremiah has nowhere else to turn. God is simultaneously the source of potential terror and the only refuge from it. This captures the essence of prophetic faith.

word_study.meaning: Day of calamity, disaster, evil. Can refer to personal distress or collective judgment.
word_study.significance: For Jeremiah, 'the day of evil' encompasses both the coming destruction of Jerusalem and his personal persecution. In all such days, only God is refuge.

cross_references.connection: God's promise to Jeremiah at the beginning of his ministry: 'Be not afraid of their faces...I am with thee.' Yet by chapter 17, Jeremiah's fear has shifted: he fears not men but God himself.
'When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.' Jeremiah echoes this psalmic sentiment: when all earthly support fails and God appears terrifying, God alone is refuge.
'Be merciful unto me, O LORD, for I am in trouble...thou art my refuge.' This psalm shares Jeremiah's dual recognition: fear and refuge co-exist in the same prayer.

'Fear ye not their fear...Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear.' Isaiah presents a similar paradox: fear God rather than men, making God's holiness both the terror and the security.

'Therefore, fear not, little flock; do good; let earth and hell combine against you, for if ye are built upon my rock, they cannot prevail.' This Restoration promise echoes Jeremiah's dual motion: fear God, not the world; trust God as refuge.

commentary.historical_context: Jeremiah's fear of God must be understood in the context of Ancient Near Eastern conceptions of divine power. The gods were understood as powerful, often arbitrary, and capable of both help and harm. To draw near to a god (as a prophet does) was to risk divine anger as well as divine favor. The Hebrew Bible presents this with particular intensity: God's holiness is described as consuming fire (Exodus 33:5, Isaiah 33:14). Jeremiah, having been called to carry God's word, stands closer to this divine fire than most. His fear is not cowardice but spiritual realism. Additionally, in the context of his confessions, Jeremiah has just endured mockery (verse 15) and has defended his faithfulness (verse 16); now he admits the deeper fear beneath social opposition—the fear of standing before a holy God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:3-11 presents a similar crisis: Alma describes being 'racked with eternal torment, for my soul was harrowed up to the greatest degree and racked with all my sins.' Yet verse 11 reverses this: 'And it came to pass that I saw a light...I believed that it was the Son of God.' Alma's experience mirrors Jeremiah's—terror before God transformed into refuge in God through faith.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-6 records Joseph Smith's anguish: 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion that covereth thy hiding place?' Yet verse 7 promises: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment.'' Joseph's prayer, like Jeremiah's, moves from terror to assurance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, members make promises before God and invoke both blessing and cursing—'if you keep these covenants, you will be blessed; if you break them, you will suffer.' Verse 17 captures the psychological reality of covenant relationship: standing in God's presence is both terrifying (the weight of covenant obligation) and comforting (God is one's refuge for covenant-keeping).

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's fear of God and his refuge in God finds ultimate expression in Christ's experience in Gethsemane. In Matthew 26:38-39, Jesus says 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death' and prays 'if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.' Jesus experiences something akin to Jeremiah's terror—the weight of bearing God's judgment. Yet he concludes 'thy will be done,' finding refuge in obedience to God even in the face of divine judgment. On the cross, Christ experiences the full weight of God's wrath against sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), yet he is simultaneously the ultimate refuge for those who believe in him.
commentary.application: Verse 17 gives permission for a confession that modern faith often suppresses: it is possible to fear God and yet depend on God completely. The contemporary tendency is to downplay God's holiness in favor of God's love, making God safer and more approachable. But this verse insists that mature faith includes reverential fear—not terror or anxiety, but the profound recognition that one stands before a power vastly greater than oneself. In personal prayer, especially when facing moral failure or spiritual crisis, verse 17 teaches that the first movement is not to deny fear but to express it: 'Do not let me be broken by your judgment.' The second movement is immediate assurance: 'Yet you are my only refuge.' This pattern—honest fear followed by radical trust—characterizes genuine covenant relationship. Modern members might apply this when facing consequences for sin: the fear is real, but the refuge is also real. When facing unanswered prayers, verse 17 teaches that the prayer itself can become refuge—the act of bringing one's terror before God and claiming God as shelter, even while the answer remains unclear.

text_kjv: Let them be confounded that persecute me, but let not me be confounded: let them be dismayed, but let not me be dismayed: bring upon them the day of evil, and destroy them with double destruction.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 18 is Jeremiah's imprecatory prayer—his formal petition for God to judge his persecutors. The structure is strikingly formal, employing chiasm (parallelism arranged in reverse order) to create a balanced petition. The pattern is: 'Let them A, but not me A; let them B, but not me B; [then detailed curse].' This formal structure reflects Jewish liturgical tradition (the verse became influential in later Jewish prayer), and it creates a vivid moral distinction: Jeremiah and his persecutors are on opposite sides of a divide. One will be blessed (not confounded); the other cursed (put to shame).

The first petition uses the verb bosh ('be put to shame, be confounded'). To be 'put to shame' is not merely to experience embarrassment but to be publically discredited, to have one's reputation destroyed and one's identity undermined. Jeremiah asks that this fate fall on his pursuers (rodepai) but not on himself. The word rodepai ('my persecutors') is active and hostile—they actively hunt Jeremiah, seeking to destroy him. Similarly, the request to let 'them be dismayed, but not me be dismayed' uses the verb chatu ('be terrified, be shattered'). The emotional intensity escalates: beyond shame comes shattering terror. Yet Jeremiah's prayer maintains a careful symmetry: whatever falls on his enemies must not fall on him.

The prayer culminates in the imprecatory formula: 'Bring upon them the day of evil' (habi aleihem yom ra'ah). This echoes verse 15's taunt ('Where is the word of the LORD?') and verses 9 and 16's references to the 'day of calamity.' The 'day of evil' is the day of judgment. The final phrase—'destroy them with double destruction' (mishneh shivron shavrem)—intensifies the request beyond mere justice. The word mishneh ('double') and the repeated verb shavar ('break, shatter') create a rhythm that emphasizes emphatic, doubled judgment. Jeremiah is not asking for measured retribution but for overwhelming judgment.

This imprecatory prayer disturbs modern sensibilities. How can a righteous prophet ask God to 'double' destroy his enemies? Yet this prayer must be understood in its context. Jeremiah has just asserted his faithfulness and his fear of God; he has exposed the constant mockery he endures. The imprecatory prayer is not vindictiveness but the final honest expression of pain and the appeal to God for vindication. Moreover, it follows the structure of biblical lament psalms (Psalms 35, 55, 69, etc.), where the psalmist brings unbearable suffering before God and asks for divine intervention. In this literary form, the intensity of the curse reflects the intensity of the suffering. Jeremiah does not hate his persecutors in the sense of wishing them ill for personal satisfaction; rather, he asks that God vindicate the truth by distinguishing between prophet and persecutor, between God's messenger and God's enemies.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine plural imperfect: let them be put to shame, let them be confounded. Bosh means to be shamed, disgraced, or discredited.
word_study.significance: To be 'put to shame' in biblical usage is more than embarrassment—it is to be publicly marked as wrong, discredited, and spiritually rejected. The curse is for public vindication of Jeremiah's righteousness.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine plural imperfect of chatu: let them be terrified, broken, shattered. The emotion is one of overwhelming distress.
word_study.significance: Beyond shame comes terror—a psychological and spiritual breaking. The verb captures not just fear but the shattering of one's sense of security and identity.

word_study.meaning: Those who pursue me, hunt me, persecute me. The participle form suggests ongoing, active persecution.
word_study.significance: Rodepai are not passive opponents but active hunters. They pursue Jeremiah with intention and violence. The term justified Jeremiah's fear and grounds his prayer for divine intervention.

word_study.meaning: A doubling of breaking, a twofold breaking, emphasizing intensity and multiplied judgment. Shivron comes from shavar (to break, smash, shatter).
word_study.significance: The 'double' is not proportional justice but emphasized, intensified judgment. This reflects the emotional intensity of the lament and Jeremiah's desperation for vindication. The repetition of the root shavar (shivron shavrem, 'breaking, break them') creates a rhythmic, almost incantatory effect that was likely meant to be pronounced or chanted.

word_study.meaning: Day of calamity, disaster, judgment. The same phrase appears in verse 17.
word_study.significance: The 'day of evil' becomes the divine instrument of Jeremiah's vindication. What his persecutors demanded ('Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!') Jeremiah now invokes: let God's judgment day come upon them.

cross_references.connection: A parallel imprecatory prayer: 'Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me...Let them be confounded and put to shame that seek after my soul.' The structure and language closely mirror Jeremiah 17:18.

Another imprecatory psalm with similar intensity: 'Let their table become a snare...let them be blotted out of the book of the living.' Like Jeremiah, the psalmist seeks God's vindicating judgment on persecutors.

In another confession, Jeremiah appeals to God: 'But, O LORD of hosts, that judgest righteously...let me see thy vengeance on them.' This repeated theme throughout Jeremiah's confessions shows the consistency of his imprecatory prayer.
'To me belongeth vengeance and recompence.' Jeremiah's prayer implicitly acknowledges this: he does not take vengeance himself but commits his cause to God's justice.

Paul cites Deuteronomy 32:35 in the context of the Gospel: 'Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves...for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.' The New Testament transforms the imprecatory prayer from a petition for curse into a call to trust God's justice.

commentary.historical_context: Imprecatory prayers appear throughout the Ancient Near Eastern literature, not only in the Bible but in Egyptian texts, Mesopotamian prayers, and Hittite curses. The formal structure—the balanced curse, the appeal to deity for vindication, the repeated parallelism—reflects literary conventions of ancient prayer. The intensity of the 'double destruction' request is not unique to Jeremiah; comparable formulations appear in Mesopotamian curses inscribed on boundary stones and temple walls. These prayers were understood not as wishing ill for private satisfaction but as formal appeals for divine justice. In the context of ancient Israel, where formal curses and blessings had legal and religious force, Jeremiah's imprecatory prayer was a recognized form of legal appeal before God. Moreover, the prayer must be contextualized within Jeremiah's historical situation: he has endured decades of mockery, opposition, and physical danger (he was thrown into a cistern to die, beaten by priests, etc.). By the time he speaks verse 18, his persecutors have not merely disagreed with him; they have actively sought his death. The intensity of his prayer reflects the intensity of his suffering.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 14:22-27 describes Alma and Amulek witnessing believers being burned alive by anti-Christs. Alma prays for intervention, and God responds with calamity ('the earth shook, and the walls of the prison were rent in twain'). Like Jeremiah, Alma combines passive suffering with formal petition for God's vindicating judgment. The result is that God's word is confirmed through divine action—Jeremiah's persecutors will ultimately witness the fall of Jerusalem, confirming his prophecy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:21-28 records a judgment against those who oppose Zion: 'Those that have been scattered by their enemies...shall be gathered again...those that have been driven out...shall be brought again into their lands.' The Restoration principle is that God vindicates his people against persecutors, not through human vengeance but through divine justice working in history.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Imprecatory prayers were part of ancient covenant enforcement. When one made a covenant, one invoked blessings for faithfulness and curses for violation. The temple context would have made Jeremiah's prayer resonant: standing in God's presence (as implied in verse 16), one appeals to God as judge and enforcer of covenant obligations. Those who persecute God's prophet are persecuting a covenant partner and deserve covenant curses.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's imprecatory prayer contrasts sharply with Christ's attitude toward his persecutors. In Luke 23:34, Christ prays on the cross: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.' Rather than curse those who persecute him, Christ asks for their forgiveness. Yet Christ's prayer does not negate Jeremiah's; rather, it transforms it. Where Jeremiah asks for God to 'double' destroy his enemies, Christ intercedes for their salvation. The final judgment—the 'day of evil' for those who reject God—still comes, but Christ's intercession offers an alternative: repentance and forgiveness. Christ embodies a higher fulfillment of the imprecatory prayer: rather than destroyer of enemies, he becomes savior of enemies through his atonement.
commentary.application:
Verse 18 is challenging for modern covenant members who are taught to forgive enemies and pray for those who despitefully use them. Yet the verse offers something important: validation that the pain of persecution is real and that it is appropriate to bring that pain before God in honest prayer. The modern tendency to suppress or spiritualize pain ('I should not feel anger at my persecutors') can itself become spiritually dishonest. Verse 18 says: bring the full weight of your suffering before God. Ask God to vindicate the truth. Trust God's justice rather than taking vengeance yourself.

Yet the verse must be held in tension with New Testament teaching. The progression from Old Testament imprecatory prayer to Christ's intercession for enemies represents spiritual maturation. As members grow in faith, they may move from asking God to curse persecutors toward asking God to save them. Yet even this higher prayer is built on the foundation of verse 18: the honest acknowledgment that persecution is wrong, that justice matters, and that God—not the persecuted—is the judge.

In practical application: when facing opposition for one's faith or principles, verse 18 teaches the power of formal, honest prayer. Rather than nursing resentment or plotting private revenge, the believer brings the case before God: 'Vindicate the truth. Let those who oppose your word see the consequences of their choice. Let my name be cleared.' This prayer releases the burden of vindication from the believer to God, where it belongs. Moreover, the prayer's formal structure—the careful balance, the measured language—can help transform raw emotion into organized petition, making space for God's justice to work rather than human reaction.

text_kjv: Thus said the LORD unto me; Go and stand in the gate of the children of the people, whereby the kings of Judah come in, and by the which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem;

commentary.narrative:
The LORD commands Jeremiah to take his message to the most public place in Jerusalem—the gates where the kings and all citizens pass through daily. This is not a temple proclamation or a private message to the elite; it is a street-level confrontation with the entire social order at the point where they are most vulnerable to the prophet's word. Gates in the ancient Near East functioned as civic centers where law was administered, commerce conducted, and communal decisions made. By positioning Jeremiah at the gate, God ensures that the message cannot be ignored or confined to religious circles. The kings of Judah, mentioned specifically, represent both legitimate authority and the regime's responsibility before God. The repetition—"whereby the kings come in, and by the which they go out, and in all the gates"—emphasizes the comprehensiveness and inescapability of the confrontation. This is a showdown between Jeremiah's word and the people's ordinary business-as-usual mentality.

The phrase "gate of the children of the people" (sha'ar benei ha'am) is rendered in The Covenant Rendering as simply "the gate of the people," suggesting a specific, identifiable gate known to Jeremiah's audience. This was likely the Benjamin Gate or the Gate of the Sheep, primary thoroughfares through Jerusalem's walls. The location matters not primarily for historical reconstruction but for understanding the narrative strategy: Jeremiah is placed where he cannot be dismissed as marginal or extremist. He stands where power passes, where ordinary life unfolds, where the boundary between the sacred (Jerusalem, the holy city) and the secular (commerce, civil authority) is most visible. The word of the LORD will meet Judah exactly where it has learned to ignore him.

word_study.meaning: Gate; opening in a wall; a place of assembly and judicial authority. In biblical usage, gates were not mere entrances but institutional spaces where elders sat to judge, merchants traded, and public proclamations were made. The gate was the interface between the city proper and the outside world, between order and disorder.
word_study.significance: By standing in the gate, Jeremiah positions himself at the hinge of Jerusalem's existence—the place where the boundary between inside and outside, sacred and secular, is negotiated daily. This is not a remote, holy place but a crowded, commercial space, making the prophetic word inescapably present to every class of society.

word_study.meaning: Kings of Judah; rulers with legitimate authority over the southern kingdom. The plural form may suggest the ongoing dynasty or may be a formal address encompassing both past and present authority. Political leadership is the first category mentioned, indicating that the message targets those with power to implement or reject covenant obedience.
word_study.significance: The explicit mention of kings underscores that this is not merely individual piety but a corporate, political crisis. Jeremiah's message is not spiritually neutral—it challenges the state apparatus to align itself with God's demands for Sabbath observance and social justice.

cross_references.connection: The original commandment to remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy, which forms the foundation for Jeremiah's call to the people to obey this ancient covenant requirement.

An earlier oracle where Jeremiah also stands at a gate of the LORD's house to confront the people's false reliance on the temple, showing a pattern of public confrontation at structurally important locations.
Another prophet confronting the people at their gathering places, demonstrating the prophetic tradition of interrupting public commerce with divine demands for justice and obedience.
Moses' reiteration of the Sabbath law in the covenant renewal, grounding Jeremiah's command in the foundational Torah obligation to all Israel.

commentary.historical_context: Gates in Iron Age Jerusalem served multiple functions: they were the entry/exit points through the city walls (essential for defense), sites of judicial assembly (where elders heard cases and administered law per Deuteronomy 21:19), centers of commerce (where merchants set up stalls and conducted trade), and spaces of social gathering. Archaeological evidence from excavations of Iron Age gates shows benches along the interior walls where people sat—these were not merely narrow passages but open areas capable of holding groups. The mention of kings entering and leaving suggests a royal procession, perhaps a daily or regular occurrence that drew crowds. The context of Sabbath violation indicates that Jerusalem's economy in the late 7th century BCE had become increasingly commercialized; the Sabbath law, once culturally normative, had become a burden to merchants and traders. Jeremiah's confrontation occurs at the flashpoint where religious obligation meets economic pressure—exactly where cultural erosion of covenant identity is most visible.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's experience in 1 Nephi 3-4 shows a similar prophetic confrontation with Jerusalem—standing in the city and calling its people to repentance while institutional powers (Laban, the community) resist. Both prophets are positioned to address entire populations and confront the political and spiritual authorities with unyielding divine demands.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:1-2 reflects a similar pattern: the Lord's voice is raised to 'all people' through his servants, beginning with a specific location or address. D&C 29:1 emphasizes God's communication to every 'nation, kindred, tongue, and people'—suggesting that the gate serves the same function in Jeremiah's era as the written revelation does in the Restoration: a unavoidable confrontation with divine will.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gates of Jerusalem frame the boundary between the sacred (the temple and holy city) and the ordinary. Sabbath observance is presented not as a temple ritual but as a marker of holiness that extends into ordinary life—into commerce, household labor, and daily movement. This prefigures the Restoration teaching that all of life, not merely temple ordinances, constitutes proper covenant living.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah standing in the gate foreshadows Christ's public teaching at the temple gates and in the marketplace—places where all classes encounter the word. Christ, like Jeremiah, confronts religious and political authority at the intersection of sacred and secular space. The call to Sabbath observance points forward to Christ as the fulfillment and Lord of the Sabbath (Matthew 12:8), whose teaching redefines what true Sabbath holiness means beyond mere external compliance.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members should recognize that prophetic witness is not confined to Sunday worship or to private spiritual experience. The prophets speak through channels (general conference, official statements) that reach into the ordinary spaces of life—much as Jeremiah's message meets people at the gate where they conduct daily business. The question each member faces is whether the demands of covenant living will be taken seriously at the gates where we enter and exit—in our workplaces, our financial decisions, our use of time. Standing in 'the gate' today means allowing God's word to reshape how we move through ordinary life, not sheltering it safely within religious practice alone.

text_kjv: And say unto them, Hear ye the word of the LORD, ye kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that enter in by these gates:

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah is now given the precise words to speak—a direct address to a stratified audience: the kings (political elite), all Judah (the nation as a whole), and all inhabitants of Jerusalem (the urban population). The tripartite address moves from political rulers to the collective nation to the urban residents, encompassing all levels of society and ensuring that no one can claim ignorance or exemption. The phrase "Hear ye the word of the LORD" (shim'u devar YHWH) is the prophetic formula used throughout the book—a summons to listen with understanding and obedience, not merely to hear sound. The repetition of "gates" anchors this abstract address in concrete location and concrete people: these are not hypothetical inhabitants or theoretical subjects but real persons entering through real gates on a real day.

The specificity of the address is striking. Rather than proclaiming from the temple or addressing a gathered congregation, Jeremiah confronts people in passing—at a threshold moment when they are neither fully engaged in prayer nor fully absorbed in commerce. The address to "those who enter in by these gates" suggests that the people have a choice at this moment: they can listen or they can pass by; they can receive the word or they can ignore it. Yet by placing them in the gate, Jeremiah denies them the comfort of anonymity. In a crowd, each person is still individually confronted. The "you" of the address is simultaneously corporate (all Judah) and individual (all inhabitants) — a rhetorical move that brings collective responsibility home to individual conscience.

word_study.meaning: Imperative form of 'to hear'; implies not merely auditory reception but attentive listening with understanding and intended obedience. In prophetic contexts, shim'u is a call to covenant hearing—the kind of listening that binds one to accountability.
word_study.significance: The command 'Hear the word of the LORD' is not optional—it is a summons that presumes authority and expects response. To hear God's word is already to be placed under obligation; there is no neutral stance toward it.

word_study.meaning: The utterance, speech, or message of the LORD; what God has commissioned the prophet to speak. In Hebrew thought, God's word is not merely communication but action—it accomplishes what it intends (Isaiah 55:10-11).
word_study.significance: To hear 'the word of the LORD' is to encounter God's will as active and effective, not as optional advice. This phrase carries the weight of divine authority and divine efficacy.

word_study.meaning: The entire nation of Judah; used to denote collective national identity and collective responsibility before God. The word 'all' emphasizes that no segment is exempt.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah is addressing not merely Jerusalem but the entire southern kingdom, suggesting that Sabbath observance is a national covenant matter, not a local urban issue. The breach extends throughout the body politic.

cross_references.connection: An earlier address to 'all Judah' in which Jeremiah recalls their initial covenant relationship and fidelity, providing a baseline for understanding their current failure to obey the Sabbath command.

Isaiah also addresses rulers and inhabitants together, calling them to 'hear the word of the LORD'—a pattern in prophetic rhetoric of engaging all levels of society simultaneously with divine demands.
Moses' covenant renewal address is similarly framed to include all Israel—men, women, children, and strangers—emphasizing that covenant obligation is comprehensive and inescapable.
Another address by Jeremiah to the house of David and the kings of Judah, showing that political leadership is always the first category targeted by prophetic accountability.

commentary.historical_context: The stratification of Judahite society by the late 7th century BCE was pronounced. The monarchy represented centralized power and international trade relationships; the 'all Judah' represented rural and urban populations with varying economic interests; and 'all inhabitants of Jerusalem' specifically refers to the urban elite, merchants, administrators, and their families. Archaeological evidence suggests that Jerusalem in the reign of Josiah (641-609 BCE, during or just after Jeremiah's likely period of prophetic activity) was experiencing economic expansion with increased international commerce. The Sabbath law, which had long been observed, was increasingly seen as an obstacle to profit in a commercializing economy. Jeremiah's confrontation at the gate reflects the real tension between traditional covenant identity (grounded in Sabbath observance as a sign of Israel's peculiarity) and new economic pressures (grounded in international trade and urban commerce). The gate address format ensured that the message reached merchants, officials, and ordinary travelers in a setting where economic pressures were most visible.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:35 and the broader Nephite emphasis on hearing and obeying prophetic counsel parallels Jeremiah's summons. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows prophets addressing all levels of society—Nephite rulers, common folk, and dissidents—with the expectation that all are bound by covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:4-5 describes the Lord's voice going forth to 'all people' without exception; D&C 88:81 emphasizes that the Lord's commandments 'are not given to be withheld from the heads of I have appointed to lead my people.' The principle is that covenant instruction is comprehensive and hierarchically accountable—leaders first, then all.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The call to Sabbath observance is framed here not as a temple practice but as a sign of covenantal identity to be practiced in ordinary life. In Restoration theology, Sabbath observance connects to the temple covenant but is not limited to the temple. All spaces and all times must be sanctified.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's charge to the Twelve in Matthew 28:19-20—'Go and make disciples of all nations'—echoes the prophetic pattern of comprehensive address. Jeremiah's word confronts all Judah as Christ's gospel confronts all nations. Both involve a call to hear and obey that is inescapable and universal in scope.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, there is no escaping the prophetic word through claims of ignorance or irrelevance. Like the inhabitants of Jerusalem at the gate, members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints are addressed comprehensively—from leadership (bishops, stake presidents, general authorities) through all membership (rich and poor, educated and simple, urban and rural). The question is not whether the message applies to me, but whether I will hear it as the word of the LORD and respond with obedience, particularly in the ordinary spaces where my life is lived—in work, commerce, family, and daily time management.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD; Take heed to yourselves, and bear no burden on the sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem;

commentary.narrative:
The prophetic word now becomes specific: absolute prohibition on carrying burdens (goods, cargo, merchandise) through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath. The opening phrase "Thus saith the LORD" (koh amar YHWH) signals that what follows is not Jeremiah's opinion or interpretation but divine command with the full weight of God's authority. The phrase "Take heed to yourselves" (hishameru benafshoteikhem) is striking—The Covenant Rendering captures the sense precisely as "Guard your lives." This is not legalistic nitpicking about Sabbath rest; this is presented as a matter of life and death. The Hebrew word nefesh (נפש) means 'soul, life, self, essence'—the command is to guard one's fundamental existence, implying that violation of the Sabbath threatens not merely external consequences but the very person of the violator.

The focus on burdens (massa) entering through the gates is deliberately targeted. The gates are not private spaces but public thoroughfares; they are not religious spaces but commercial ones. By prohibiting the carrying of goods through them on the Sabbath, the command attacks the very heart of commercialization—the extension of market activity into every corner of life and every moment of time. If goods cannot pass through the gate on the Sabbath, then commerce itself must stop; the economic machinery must come to rest. This is not a minor restriction affecting a few traders; it is a systemic challenge to an economy built on continuous exchange and production. The Babylonian world (into which Judah was increasingly drawn through trade and political alignment) operated on a continuous commercial calendar. Israel's Sabbath represented a radical counter-claim: one day in seven, all exchange stops; all labor ceases; human beings step outside the economy and affirm that they belong first to God, not to the market.

word_study.meaning: 'Guard yourselves', 'be watchful over your souls/lives'; from the root sh-m-r (guard, keep, preserve). The phrase is emphatic—it stresses active, attentive protection of one's fundamental being.
word_study.significance: This framing elevates Sabbath observance from external ritual to existential necessity. To violate the Sabbath is not merely to break a rule; it is to destroy one's own soul. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on 'guard your lives' makes clear this is about survival of the self, not mere legal compliance.

word_study.meaning: A load, burden, cargo, or weight that is carried or transported; specifically, goods being conveyed for commercial purposes. The root m-s-' means 'to lift, carry, bear'.
word_study.significance: The term is carefully chosen—it refers not to personal necessities (eating, going to family) but to commercial goods. The Sabbath law targets the economic sphere specifically, not all activity. The prohibition on burden-carrying distinguishes between movement for human need and movement for commercial profit.

word_study.meaning: The gate-complex of Jerusalem; the literal and symbolic boundary points through which all traffic enters and exits. In biblical literature, gates are both physical structures and institutions of authority.
word_study.significance: By specifying the gates of Jerusalem rather than 'any gate' or 'the gates of Judah,' Jeremiah targets the capital—the center of political, economic, and religious power. This is where the breach of covenant is most visible and where its remedy is most crucial.

cross_references.connection: The foundational Sabbath commandment in the Decalogue, upon which Jeremiah's demand is explicitly based; establishing that Sabbath rest is a perpetual sign of the Sinai covenant.

In the post-exile period, the returned community explicitly covenants not to buy goods on the Sabbath, showing that Jeremiah's demand for Sabbath commercial cessation remained a crucial covenant marker even after exile.

Amos condemns merchants who circumvent Sabbath restrictions through sleight of hand ('when will the Sabbath be over, that we may buy and sell?'), showing the same prophetic opposition to commercialization of the Sabbath.

The expanded covenant version of Sabbath law, which emphasizes rest not merely as abstinence but as restoration—a day set apart for remembering God's deliverance and for allowing human beings and animals to recuperate.

Isaiah's vision of true Sabbath observance involves 'not doing thy own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure,' paralleling Jeremiah's insistence that the Sabbath must be fundamentally different from ordinary commercial activity.

commentary.historical_context: Iron Age Jerusalem, particularly during Jeremiah's prophetic ministry (late 7th century BCE), was experiencing increased commercial activity. Archaeological evidence from the city suggests growing trade networks and mercantile activity, particularly with Phoenician and Babylonian merchants. The Assyrian Empire had recently fallen (609 BCE), and Babylonia was rising as the regional superpower. Judah found itself caught in geopolitical and economic currents that pressured traditional covenant practices. The Sabbath law, once organically observed in an agrarian society, became increasingly difficult to maintain in an urbanized, commercialized context where just-in-time production and continuous trade were becoming normative. Jeremiah's command to stop all commercial movement through the gates on the Sabbath was thus not merely a pious restatement of old law but a radical counter-cultural demand in a context of accelerating economic change. The carrying of loads through gates was precisely what an expanding mercantile economy required; the prohibition thus constituted a prophetic rejection of the economic trajectory Jerusalem was following.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 16 describes the Nephites' practice of cease from labor on the Sabbath as a sign of covenant identity. The same principle appears in D&C 59:9-13, where Sabbath observance is framed not as restriction but as a holy day set apart for spiritual nourishment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 59:9-16 addresses the Sabbath day in the Restoration: 'And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day.' The prohibition on 'worldly work' (v. 13) parallels Jeremiah's focus on preventing commercial activity on the Sabbath. Both emphasize that the Sabbath must be qualitatively different from other days—a separation from ordinary labor and commerce to focus on God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: While the Sabbath in Jeremiah's oracle is not explicitly temple-focused, it functions as a covenant sign analogous to temple worship. In Restoration thought, both Sabbath observance and temple worship serve the same function: marking time and space as set apart for God. The Sabbath is the weekly renewal of covenant identity; the temple is the periodic renewal of covenant ordinances. Both require cessation from ordinary commercial pursuits.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ as the fulfillment of the Sabbath (Colossians 2:16-17) came to internalize the Sabbath principle: rest from self-directed labor in reliance on God's work. The prohibition on burdens becomes in Jesus's teaching a spiritual reality—the call to 'come unto me all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28). Christ is the true Sabbath-rest, toward which all Sabbath observance points.
commentary.application: For modern members, the command to guard one's life through Sabbath observance means asking seriously: how does my keeping of Sunday (and the broader rhythm of weekly rest) actually differ from my secular week? Does commerce still dominate my mind even when I'm not working? Does the Sabbath function as a true escape from the marketplace and from economic anxiety, or is it merely another scheduled activity among many? The principle extends beyond literal cargo through gates—it asks whether I am willing to let go of economic productivity and profit-seeking, at least for one day, and affirm through my actions that I belong to God, not to the market. The metaphor of the gates remains relevant: at the threshold of Sunday, will I carry my burdens through, or will I leave them outside?

text_kjv: Neither carry forth a burden out of your houses on the sabbath day, neither do ye any work, but hallow the sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers.

commentary.narrative:
The prohibition now extends from the public gates to the private sphere—prohibiting the carrying of burdens out of houses themselves. This movement from external gates to internal houses encompasses the totality of life: the boundary is closed both outwardly (no goods through the gates) and inwardly (no goods leaving the home). The verse then makes a crucial grammatical and theological shift. After two prohibitions ("neither carry...neither do any work"), the verse pivots to a positive command: "but hallow the sabbath day" (ve-qiddashtem et yom ha-shabbat). The word "hallow" (qiddesh, from the root q-d-sh meaning 'holy, set apart') transforms what could be merely negative restriction into positive consecration. The Sabbath is not simply a day of avoidance; it is a day actively set apart for God.

The final phrase—"as I commanded your fathers"—grounds this command in the original covenant at Sinai, establishing unbroken continuity between the ancient Decalogue and Jeremiah's contemporary demand. This is not a new rule introduced to address current crises; it is the restatement of an eternal covenant obligation that the current generation is violating. The fathers received the command at Sinai; that same command remains binding on their descendants. The failure to hallow the Sabbath is thus not merely contemporary negligence but covenantal betrayal—a breaking of the bond that connects the people to their ancestors and to God. The appeal to ancestral obedience implicitly shames the current generation: if your fathers kept this commandment, why do you abandon it? The verse thus moves from prohibition (what not to do) through consecration (what to do positively) to accountability (living up to the standard your ancestors established).

word_study.meaning: 'Do not bring out a load/cargo'; the verb y-ts-' means 'to go out, bring out, send out.' The negative (lo) is emphatic—complete prohibition, not restriction.
word_study.significance: The extension of the prohibition from the gates to the houses themselves creates comprehensive coverage. No sphere of life—public commerce or private domestic activity—is exempted from Sabbath rest.

word_study.meaning: 'All work, all labor'; melachah refers to productive labor or craft work—the kind of activity that generates material goods or accomplishes material tasks. The word encompasses everything from manual labor to administrative work.
word_study.significance: The absolute prohibition on 'any work' makes clear this is not about rest from heavy labor only but cessation of all productive activity. The Sabbath is a complete stop to human striving and labor.

word_study.term_original: וְקִדַּשְׁתֶּם אֶת־יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת (ve-qiddashtem et yom ha-shabbat)
word_study.meaning: 'And you shall consecrate/set apart the Sabbath day'; the verb qiddesh (from q-d-sh, 'holy') means to make holy, to set apart from ordinary use or time. The Hiphil form (causative) suggests an active making-holy rather than mere recognition.
word_study.significance: This is the positive content of Sabbath observance—not merely the absence of work but the active consecration of time to God. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes this: to consecrate is to 'recognize [the day] as qualitatively different from other days — set apart for God and removed from the sphere of ordinary labor and commerce.' The Sabbath is created through our action of setting it apart; it does not exist passively but is actively consecrated by covenant practice.

word_study.term_original: כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוִּיתִי אֶת־אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם (ka-asher tzivviti et avoteikhem)
word_study.meaning: 'Just as I commanded your fathers'; tzavah means 'to command, charge, instruct.' The phrase connects present obligation to ancestral covenantal history.
word_study.significance: This appeal to continuity with the fathers makes the Sabbath law not a new demand but the reiteration of an eternal covenant obligation. The current generation is being called to faithfulness to the same standard their ancestors received—implying both that they know this standard and that they are failing to keep it.

cross_references.connection: The original Decalogue prohibition: 'Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work.' Jeremiah reiterates this foundational command.

The Sabbath is described as 'a sign between me and you throughout your generations,' emphasizing that Sabbath observance is the visible marker of Israel's covenant identity—which makes its violation a public denial of that identity.

The Deuteronomic restatement adds the rationale: 'That thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou,' emphasizing that Sabbath rest is a matter of justice and compassion, not merely ritual.
Isaiah's prophecy concerning those who 'keep the sabbath from polluting it' and 'hold fast my covenant'—showing that even in exilic times, Sabbath observance remained a primary covenant sign.

Nehemiah's reform after the exile includes vigorous enforcement of Sabbath rest by closing the gates on the Sabbath day—a direct implementation of Jeremiah's command to stop commercial activity through Jerusalem's gates.

commentary.historical_context: By the late 7th century BCE, the practice of Sabbath observance may have experienced significant erosion, particularly in Jerusalem and other urban centers. The pressure of international trade, the need for continuous production to maintain competitive advantage, and the gradual secularization of urban life all worked against the traditional Sabbath rhythm. Jeremiah's appeal to 'your fathers' (the Sinai generation or the generation of the patriarchs) represents an effort to restore what had been lost or abandoned. The specific mention of both carrying from houses and carrying through gates suggests that Sabbath violation was systemic—both domestic production and commercial trade were continuing on the seventh day. Jeremiah's command thus represents not merely religious instruction but an attempt to restore the entire covenant framework upon which Judah's identity depended. The reference to this practice occurring later in Nehemiah 13 (after the exile, during the restoration period) shows that this was indeed a persistent problem requiring repeated prophetic and leadership intervention.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 13:16-19 contains King Benjamin's address invoking the same Sinai commandment regarding Sabbath observance, showing that even in Book of Mormon times, the Sabbath remained a crucial covenant marker. The Nephite covenant community maintained Sabbath observance as a sign of their fidelity to God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 59:9-16 provides the Restoration parallel: 'And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day; And on this day thou shalt do none other thing, only let thy food be prepared with singleness of heart.' The language of 'keeping thyself unspotted from the world' echoes Jeremiah's insistence that the Sabbath must be qualitatively different from ordinary days. Additionally, D&C 107:17 states that the president of the Church 'shall not depart from the office...except the Lord shall otherwise direct.' This suggests that even leadership rest is structured and accountable—there is a rhythm to covenant life that cannot be abandoned even for urgent matters.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In LDS theology, Sabbath observance and temple worship both serve to consecrate time and space to God. The Hebrew word qiddesh used here for 'hallow' is the same root from which Kadesh derives—and 'qadosh' (holy) is the fundamental category for understanding the temple. The Sabbath makes weekly space holy; the temple makes dedicated space holy. Both require cessation from ordinary commerce and labor.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's resurrection on the first day of the week (Sunday) reorients the Sabbath toward its fulfillment rather than its abolition (Colossians 2:16-17). The Christian Sabbath becomes not a day of legal restriction but a day of Gospel rest—entering into Christ's finished work (Hebrews 4:9-11). Yet the principle of consecrating a day to God, of stepping outside economic productivity to affirm covenant identity, remains central to Christian practice. The 'hallowing' that Jeremiah demands becomes in the New Testament the sanctification of all time through redemption in Christ.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 22 presents a profound challenge to contemporary life. We live in an economy that operates continuously—7 days a week, 24 hours a day. Our phones, computers, and communication devices keep us perpetually connected to work and commerce. The command to 'hallow the Sabbath day' requires asking: What work am I truly resting from? Is my Sunday genuinely different from my Monday through Saturday, or have I allowed commercial consciousness to penetrate my Sabbath? The principle of not carrying burdens 'out of your houses' has a modern equivalent: not checking work emails, not conducting business, not allowing the pressure of production to enter your home on Sunday. More positively, 'hallowing' the Sabbath means actively consecrating the day—through worship, family time, spiritual renewal, and deliberate withdrawal from the world's economic demands. This is not passive rest but active covenant practice.

text_kjv: But they obeyed not, neither inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff, that they might not hear, nor receive instruction.

commentary.narrative:
The prophetic word shifts from command to diagnosis: the people have not obeyed and will not obey. The verse catalogs their resistance through a triple refusal that escalates from passive non-response to active defiance. First, "they obeyed not" (lo shame'u)—they did not listen, did not hear. Second, "neither inclined their ear" (lo hittu et oznam)—they did not turn their attention toward the word, did not make themselves receptive. Third, and most dramatically, "they made their neck stiff" (vayyaqshu et orpam)—they actively hardened themselves against the word. The metaphor of the stiff neck is drawn from agricultural experience: an ox that hardens its neck refuses to turn when the yoke is pulled; it resists control and instruction. In biblical theology, this image suggests willful defiance, not mere forgetfulness or inadvertent neglect. The people are choosing stubbornness. The final phrase—"that they might not hear, nor receive instruction" (lebilti shemo'a ulebilti qahat musar)—reveals the intentionality of this resistance. They actively work to avoid hearing, to prevent themselves from receiving correction (musar). The Hebrew musar carries the sense not merely of instruction but of discipline and chastisement—they reject both teaching and correction alike. This is the pathology of covenant breach: not merely failure to obey but refusal to hear, active resistance to the prophetic word.

The verse functions as a transition between the divine command (vv. 21-22) and the consequences (vv. 24-26). Before presenting the conditional promise, Jeremiah must establish that this command is not new—it has already been proclaimed and refused. This historicizes the refusal; it is not a hypothetical non-compliance but a documented pattern. The people have been offered the word and rejected it. They bear responsibility for this rejection. The triple escalation (not listening—not turning ear—stiffening neck) suggests a process of hardening: initial indifference becomes deliberate inattention becomes active defiance. Each stage is a choice.

word_study.meaning: 'Did not listen, did not hear'; shama means 'to hear, listen, obey.' The combination of hearing and obedience is intrinsic to the Hebrew concept—to truly hear is already to accept obligation.
word_study.significance: The first stage of refusal is passive: they simply did not listen. This could theoretically be blamed on inattention or distraction, but the following phrases make clear it was chosen.

word_study.meaning: 'Turned their ear'; from the root n-t-h meaning 'to turn, incline, stretch.' To incline one's ear is to actively position oneself to listen—it is deliberate receptivity.
word_study.significance: The second refusal is the failure to turn toward the word. They did not merely fail to hear; they refused to position themselves to hear. The 'ear' is both physical organ and metaphor for willingness to receive.

word_study.meaning: 'Hardened their neck'; qasah means 'to be hard, stiff, stubborn'; oref means 'neck, nape.' The image is of an ox refusing to turn because it has stiffened its neck against the yoke.
word_study.significance: This is active, visible defiance. Not merely a failure to turn but a hardening against the very possibility of turning. The neck as a seat of stubbornness appears frequently in prophetic literature (Exodus 32:9, 33:3, 33:5; Acts 7:51). It represents the point at which human will asserts itself against divine will.

word_study.meaning: 'To take/receive discipline, instruction, correction'; musar means discipline, chastisement, or correction—not merely neutral instruction but correction aimed at behavioral change. From the root y-s-r, 'to discipline, chasten.'
word_study.significance: The refusal extends not merely to hearing but to accepting discipline. This suggests the people reject both the teaching (what they should know) and the correction (what they should change). They refuse accountability.
