When Nineveh repents at Jonah's preaching, God relents from the threatened destruction. This verse illustrates that the principle in Jeremiah 18:8 applies to foreign nations as well—divine judgment is conditional regardless of national identity.

Lehi teaches his sons that God has promised that if they keep His commandments they shall prosper, but if they transgress they shall be carried away captive. This expresses the bilateral conditionality that Jeremiah is establishing.
The Lord teaches that He will forgive those who confess and repent, yet the wicked shall be punished. This modern revelation restates the principle: judgment is responsive to human repentance.

Later in Jeremiah, the people are told, 'amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the LORD your God; and the LORD will repent him of the evil that he hath pronounced against you'—a direct application of the principle stated here.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature often portrayed divine judgment as inevitable and mechanistic. Mesopotamian omen texts and divination practices often treated the future as fixed, discernible only through reading signs. The Israelite prophetic tradition introduces a radical alternative: the future is not fixed but conditional upon human response. This made prophecy a moral act, not merely a predictive one. Jeremiah's contemporaries would have found this teaching either liberating (if they took repentance seriously) or infuriating (if they preferred to blame circumstances beyond their control). The Babylonian threat was real and growing during Jeremiah's ministry, yet he insisted that Judah's fate was not determined by geopolitical realities alone but by their moral response to God's word.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon is thoroughly saturated with this principle. Lehi's prophecies to his sons, the cyclical rise and fall of Nephite and Lamanite civilizations, and the recurring pattern of prophetic warning followed by either repentance or destruction all illustrate the conditionality of divine judgment. See particularly Helaman 5:10-11, where the people's repentance brings divine protection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:32-33 teaches that God's judgments are 'just and true,' and that they operate according to fixed principles: 'He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.' Yet D&C 58:42-43 immediately offers the path of repentance and forgiveness. The conditionality is structural to the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint theology, the principle of conditional judgment underlies the entire temple experience. Covenants are conditional—the temple patron makes promises and receives corresponding blessings, but the blessings remain contingent on ongoing faithfulness. This reflects the principle Jeremiah announces: God's favor is responsive to human obedience.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the truth of this verse in His ministry. He comes not primarily as a judge pronouncing irreversible doom, but as a Savior offering repentance and redemption. His crucifixion itself is the ultimate expression of this principle: God's willingness to relent from justice when offered a sacrifice on behalf of the transgressor. In Matthew 3:2 and throughout the Gospels, John the Baptist and Jesus Himself preach repentance 'for the kingdom of heaven is at hand'—the offer of mercy contingent on turning from evil. Jesus is the embodiment of God's relenting: He offers to bear the judgment so that those who turn to Him may be spared.
commentary.application: This verse offers profound hope to anyone in sin or living contrary to God's way. The prophetic threat is not a curse upon the disobedient but an instrument of mercy—an announcement designed to provoke repentance before disaster comes. For covenant members, this means: (1) When prophetic warning comes, recognize it as an act of love, not condemnation. (2) Repentance is never too late; God's relenting is immediate when the turn is genuine. (3) We should not despair about our communities, nations, or personal situations as though they are fixed in disaster. The future remains open to those who will turn. (4) Conversely, we should not presume that past blessings guarantee future favor if we cease to repent and turn. The conditionality works both ways.

text_kjv: And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it;

commentary.narrative:
The verse completes the theological symmetry begun in verse 7. Just as God can, in a single instant, pronounce judgment against a nation, so too can He pronounce blessing. The verbs 'build' and 'plant' are the positive counterparts to 'pluck up,' 'pull down,' and 'destroy.' Where judgment unmakes and dismantles, blessing constructs and establishes. The parallel structure (verse 7 and verse 9 both begin with 'at what instant' and speak 'concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom') is intentional: God's power over nations is as absolute in blessing as in judgment.

Critically, this verse introduces the second axis of conditionality. Verses 7-8 established that threatened judgment can be averted by repentance. Verses 9-10 (which will follow) establish the obverse: promised blessing can be revoked by disobedience. The theological principle is bilateral—neither judgment nor blessing is automatically fixed. God's governance of nations is dynamic and responsive to the moral character and choices of peoples. This is not a diminishment of God's sovereignty but its fullest expression: true sovereignty includes the freedom to respond wisely to changed circumstances.

word_study.meaning: To build, construct, establish. Can refer to literal construction or to the establishment of institutions, families, or nations.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in Jeremiah's commissioning (1:10), where God gives him authority over nations 'to build and to plant.' Here, the positive application of that authority is shown. Building suggests the construction of stability, order, prosperity, and institutional strength. The Covenant Rendering's 'build' is direct and clear.

word_study.meaning: To plant, to set in place (as of trees, crops, settlements, or populations). In agricultural contexts, to establish something that will grow and bear fruit.
word_study.significance: Planting is inherently future-oriented—the planter expects growth, harvest, and fruitfulness. When God 'plants' a nation, He establishes it with the expectation that it will flourish and produce blessing. This is an act of creation and investment, not temporary accommodation.

word_study.meaning: A moment, an instant; emphasizes immediacy and divine sovereignty over time.
word_study.significance: The repetition of regha from verse 7 underscores the symmetry: God's blessing is as swift and sovereign as His judgment. Neither requires preparation or extended deliberation; a single divine word effects either judgment or blessing.

cross_references.connection: God's commissioning explicitly pairs the destructive verbs (uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow) with the constructive verbs (build, plant), indicating that Jeremiah has authority over nations in both dimensions.

The Psalmist celebrates how God raises the poor from dust and 'setteth him with princes,' illustrating the constructive and elevating aspects of divine blessing that correspond to the 'building' and 'planting' mentioned here.
Amos prophesies that the Lord will 'plant' Israel in their land and they shall not be uprooted anymore, expressing confidence in the permanence of blessing when God speaks it.
Nephi explains that the righteous branches of Israel will be 'nourished' by the Lord and 'planted in a good soil,' using the identical agricultural metaphor for divine blessing.
The Lord speaks of building His kingdom and establishing it in the latter days, using the language of construction and planting that parallels Jeremiah's vision of God's creative authority.

commentary.historical_context: The historical realities of Jeremiah's era included both the rise and fall of kingdoms. Some nations prospered under divine favor and good governance; others fell into exile and ruin. Jeremiah's contemporaries would recognize in this verse a description of actual historical patterns: some nations seemed blessed with fertility, population growth, and prosperity; others faced famine, depopulation, and collapse. The prophet's insight is that these patterns are not merely the product of geography, military strategy, or luck, but of divine governance responding to moral conditions. Ancient peoples often attributed national prosperity or failure to divine will, but Jeremiah makes explicit that this divine response is conditional—it is neither arbitrary nor does it override human responsibility.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly illustrates the principle stated here. The Jaredite and Nephite civilizations are 'built and planted' by the Lord when they remain righteous, experiencing material prosperity and population growth. Helaman 13:8-10 describes a land that is blessed with wealth and prosperity when its inhabitants are righteous.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:17-20 speaks of the Lord's power to build and establish His kingdom, and D&C 105:5 teaches that Zion shall be built up according to the principles of the celestial kingdom. The pattern of conditional blessing appears throughout: the Lord will build and establish His work, but the success of individual members and stakes depends on faithfulness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is itself a place where God 'builds and plants'—it is the house of the Lord, established on earth as a standing symbol of divine blessing and an ordinance house where salvation is made available. The temple endowment teaches that God's creative power builds and establishes all things in wisdom.

commentary.christological_typology: Just as this verse establishes God's power to build and plant nations, Christ is described as the foundation of the Church that is built upon Him. In Matthew 16:18, Jesus says, 'upon this rock I will build my church.' Christ is also the one who plants His Father's vineyard (Matthew 21:33-41)—He is the agent through whom God's constructive, redemptive work is accomplished in the world. In the resurrection, Christ will build and plant a renewed creation (Revelation 21:4-5).
commentary.application: For individuals and communities seeking God's blessing, this verse establishes that prosperity, growth, and establishment are divine gifts, contingent upon alignment with God's purposes. This counters both despair (the mistaken belief that setbacks or difficulties are permanent) and presumption (the false confidence that past blessings guarantee future favor regardless of behavior). If God can 'build and plant' a nation in an instant, then: (1) The future is open to transformation and blessing for those who position themselves to receive it. (2) Growth in spirituality, family, or community requires ongoing alignment with divine principles, not merely present righteousness. (3) We should pray not only for protection from judgment but for God's active blessing—His building and planting work in our lives and communities.

text_kjv: If it do evil in my sight, so that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them.

commentary.narrative:
The theological circle is now complete. Verse 10 is the inverse of verse 8: just as threatened judgment can be averted by repentance, so too can promised blessing be revoked by disobedience. The nation that receives divine blessing—prosperity, strength, and establishment—must recognize that these gifts remain conditional. If the nation turns to evil and refuses to obey God's voice, then God will 'relent' (the same verb nicham from verse 8) from the good He had purposed for them.

This verse introduces a stark reality often overlooked in prosperity-focused theology: God's blessing is not a permanent possession but a relationship. A nation that enjoys God's favor and then deliberately chooses evil while refusing to hear His prophetic voice forfeits that favor. The parallel structure emphasizes the symmetry of divine conditionality: (1) If you turn from evil, I will relent from judgment (v. 8). (2) If you do evil and refuse to obey, I will relent from blessing (v. 10). The bilateral character of this covenant principle means that no nation can presume upon past blessings or assume that present disobedience will not be met with withdrawal of divine favor. This is not caprice but justice: the gifts of God are conditional upon the recipient's alignment with His purposes.

word_study.meaning: Evil, wrongdoing, moral wickedness, or the harmful consequences thereof. Here specifically moral wickedness.
word_study.significance: The repetition of ra'ah from verse 8 establishes the center of the conditionality: the nation's moral character. Obedience and righteousness preserve blessing; disobedience and wickedness forfeit it.

word_study.meaning: To hear, listen, obey. When used of hearing the voice of the Lord, it means to listen attentively and comply with what is heard.
word_study.significance: Shama' appears frequently in Jeremiah as the test of obedience (e.g., 7:23, 11:4). Refusal to shama' God's voice through His prophets is the cardinal sin. The Covenant Rendering's 'not obeying my voice' captures the active dimension—it is not merely that they do not hear, but that they hear and refuse to comply.

word_study.meaning: To relent, change one's mind about a course of action, to reconsider a decision.
word_study.significance: The use of nicham here parallels its use in verse 8, but now applied to the withdrawal of blessing rather than the withdrawal of judgment. God's relenting works symmetrically: when circumstances change from disobedience to obedience, judgment is withdrawn; when circumstances change from obedience to disobedience, blessing is withdrawn. This demonstrates that the verb does not mean God made an error but that God's announced intentions are responsive to human behavior.

word_study.meaning: Good, goodness, blessing, benefit. Can refer to moral goodness or to beneficial circumstances and gifts.
word_study.significance: Here, tov refers to the benefits and blessings God had purposed to provide—prosperity, peace, stability, fruitfulness. These are not automatic but contingent upon the nation's faithfulness.

cross_references.connection: The covenant formula that undergirds all of Jeremiah's prophecy. Deuteronomy 28:1-14 promises blessings for obedience; verses 15-68 threaten curses for disobedience—establishing the bilateral conditionality that Jeremiah restates.

Samuel tells Israel, 'if ye do well, ye shall continue...but if ye do wickedly, ye shall be consumed.' This expresses the same principle: blessing is conditional, and disobedience forfeits divine favor.

After the dedication of the temple, the Lord tells Solomon that if he and his sons turn away to serve other gods, then He will cut off Israel from the land. Promised blessing is revoked by disobedience.

Alma teaches that those who 'turn from their evil ways' shall 'have mercy extended unto them through Christ,' but implicitly, those who persist in wickedness will not. This expresses the conditionality of divine blessing.

Mormon warns that if the Nephites continue in sin, God will withdraw the riches and prosperity that had been given them, illustrating the principle that blessing, once forfeited, may not be easily regained.

commentary.historical_context: The historical experience of Israel and Judah serves as the backdrop for this verse. Both kingdoms had experienced periods of great prosperity and blessing under righteous kings (David, Solomon, Hezekiah, Josiah) and periods of decline under wicked kings (Manasseh, the later Judahite kings). Jeremiah's own era witnessed the decline of Judah from the time of King Josiah (who attempted extensive religious reform) through successive kings who returned to idolatry and injustice. The prophet could point to these historical patterns and argue: the blessings your ancestors enjoyed were real, but they were conditional. When your nation turned to idolatry, injustice, and refusal to hear the prophets, those blessings were withdrawn. The current crisis is not a surprise betrayal of Israel's destiny but the predictable consequence of national apostasy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon is structured as a demonstration of this very principle. The Nephite civilization repeatedly receives God's blessing—prosperity, military success, good government. But when they turn to pride, corruption, and rejection of the prophetic voice, blessings are systematically withdrawn: famines, wars, internal strife, and eventual destruction follow. See Helaman 13:4-14 for Mormon's explicit prophecy of the withdrawal of blessings from a people who forget God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:32 teaches that the Lord's 'arm is stretched out still' to gather Israel, but D&C 1:34-35 promises 'war, pestilence, and famine' to nations that refuse to hear His voice. This symmetry between conditional blessing and conditional judgment parallels Jeremiah 18:8-10.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant itself embodies this bilateral conditionality. Temple patrons receive promises of blessings (endowment, sealing, exaltation) contingent upon their faithfulness to their covenants. If one breaks covenants, the promises are not automatically maintained. This reflects the principle: blessing is contingent upon obedience.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's ministry repeatedly emphasizes this principle. In the Gospels, He teaches that those who hear His voice and follow Him will receive abundant life (John 10:27-28), but those who reject Him and refuse to obey will face judgment. In Hebrews 12:25-26, the author warns that those who 'refuse him that speaketh' from heaven will find no escape from judgment—God's blessing, once extended, can be withdrawn from the disobedient. Yet Christ also offers the possibility of restoration through repentance and atonement (1 John 1:9).
commentary.application: This verse offers a necessary corrective to false confidence or spiritual complacency. Blessings received from God—whether spiritual maturity, family prosperity, church position, or community influence—must never be assumed to be permanent possessions. They are held in trust, conditional upon ongoing faithfulness and obedience to the prophetic voice. For members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: (1) Testimony, spiritual gifts, and divine favor are not self-sustaining; they require continuous cultivation through obedience. (2) History (both scriptural and personal) demonstrates that the withdrawal of blessings is rapid and comprehensive when one turns to evil while refusing to hear prophetic counsel. (3) The solution is not to live in fear of losing blessings but to maintain vigilant obedience and active listening to the voice of the Lord through His chosen servants. (4) If you have experienced the withdrawal of blessings, know that Jeremiah's message also includes the possibility of restoration through genuine repentance and return.

text_kjv: Now therefore go to, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a device against you: return ye now every one from his evil way, and make your ways and your doings good.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah's abstract theological teaching about the conditionality of divine judgment now becomes urgently concrete and personal. The Lord commissions Jeremiah to deliver a specific word to the people of Judah and Jerusalem: God is actively 'framing' and 'devising' disaster against them. The use of the potter's vocabulary (yotser, 'framing'—literally, the one who forms on the potter's wheel) connects directly to the parable of the potter in verses 1-6, which precedes this chapter. Just as the potter forms a vessel on the wheel, God is forming calamity on His wheel, shaping it with His hands, crafting it with divine purpose.

Yet the announcement of formed disaster is immediately followed by an urgent appeal to repentance. The imperatives 'return' (shuvu) and 'make good' (heitivu) call each person individually ('every one of you') to turn from the evil way and set right their ways and deeds. This is not a resigned announcement of inevitable doom but an explicit offer: if you turn now, before the formed calamity is released, it will not come upon you. The timing is critical—the disaster is still being formed, still on the potter's wheel. It has not yet been fired in the kiln or released into the world. Repentance now can still alter its course. This verse is the climax of Jeremiah's argument: the abstract principle of conditional judgment (verses 7-10) meets the lived reality of Judah in crisis (verses 11-12).

word_study.meaning: One who forms or shapes; the potter. The verb form (yatzar) means to form, shape, fashion, typically on the potter's wheel.
word_study.significance: This word is loaded with meaning in Jeremiah. It echoes the creation account (God 'formed' mankind from dust in Genesis 2:7). The Covenant Rendering's 'shaping' captures the sense of intentional, deliberate craftsmanship. God is actively, skillfully forming disaster—not waiting passively but actively shaping it. Yet the theological irony is that the disaster is still in formation, still responsive to changed conditions.

word_study.meaning: To devise, think, plan, consider. Suggests active intellectual engagement in forming a plan.
word_study.significance: This verb emphasizes intentionality. God is not reacting emotionally but thinking through, devising, a plan. This plan is a machteshavah (a 'device' or deliberate design). The repetition emphasizes that this is no mere threat but a genuine plan, actively worked out.

word_study.meaning: Evil, wrongdoing, calamity, disaster. Here, ra'ah refers to the calamitous judgment God is forming in response to Judah's evil.
word_study.significance: The ambiguity of ra'ah is theologically important. The word carries both moral and consequential meaning. Judah has practiced ra'ah (moral evil); God is forming ra'ah (calamitous consequences) in response. The disaster is the natural, just response to the wickedness.

word_study.meaning: Return, turn back, turn around. Imperative form calling for immediate action.
word_study.significance: This is the key repentance verb. Here it appears as an urgent imperative—not a gentle invitation but a command calling Judah to immediate reversal of direction. This is the verb Jeremiah used in his earlier prophecies; now it reaches its climactic application. The Covenant Rendering's 'Turn back' captures the directional, urgent sense.

word_study.meaning: To make good, do well, set right, improve. Often contrasted with 'doing evil' (ra'ah).
word_study.significance: This verb calls for more than mere cessation of evil; it calls for positive action—actually making one's ways and deeds good, not merely less bad. The Covenant Rendering's 'set right' captures this sense of deliberate correction.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah was commissioned 'over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.' This verse is the application of that commission—Jeremiah is now speaking God's word over Judah.
Jeremiah urges the people to 'amend your ways and your doings' if they wish to remain in the land, using language almost identical to verse 11's call to make their ways and doings good.

Jeremiah earlier announced, 'If thou wilt return, O Israel...then shalt thou not remove.' This verse uses the same repentance vocabulary (shuv) and offers the same possibility: if you turn, the threatened judgment will not come.

When Nineveh turns from evil and repents, 'God saw their works...and God repented of the evil that he had said he would do unto them.' This is the practical fulfillment of the principle Jeremiah announces: repentance averts announced judgment.

The Lord teaches that He forgives those who confess and repent, 'and I, the Lord, will not lay any more charges against that one.' This modern revelation echoes the mercy offered in Jeremiah's call to repentance.

commentary.historical_context: Jeremiah's ministry spans approximately 627–586 BCE, and this prophecy likely comes from the middle period of his career, after the Babylonian threat had become undeniable but before the final fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE. Jeremiah is one of the few prophets whose ministry is extensively recorded in a biographical narrative (particularly in the later chapters of his book), and this gives us insight into the reception of his message. The people of Judah repeatedly refused his call to repentance, even as they watched the northern kingdom fall to Assyria decades earlier. They maintained false confidence in the Temple, believing God would never allow His house to be destroyed, despite the prophet's repeated warnings. This verse represents Jeremiah's last-ditch effort to call them to repentance before the judgment he had so long announced would finally fall.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly records prophets making similar appeals. Lehi calls his sons to repent before judgment comes (1 Nephi 2:23-24). Abinadi stands before King Noah and calls the people to turn from their evil ways (Mosiah 11:20-25). Jacob preaches repentance to the Nephites (Jacob 2:1-11). The pattern is consistent: prophets announce judgment and simultaneously offer the pathway to avert it through immediate repentance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:4-5 states that the Lord has sent His word to the world 'to the inhabitants thereof' so that they might hear and repent. The missionary work of the Restoration embodies this principle: the announcement of the Restoration is simultaneously an urgent call to repentance before the Lord's judgments are poured out (see D&C 29:14-21).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint theology, repentance is central to entering into covenant with God and receiving the blessings of the temple. The call to repentance is not merely a warning but an invitation—a pathway to transformation and blessing. This reflects Jeremiah's urgent appeal: turn now, and the evil God is forming against you will not come upon you.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's entire earthly mission is an embodiment of this verse. He comes as God's final messenger, announcing both judgment and mercy. In Matthew 3:2, John the Baptist proclaims, 'Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' Christ Himself begins His ministry with the call to repentance (Matthew 4:17) and repeatedly calls individuals and the nation to turn from evil (Luke 13:3, 5). He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its rejection of the prophetic voice (Matthew 23:37-39) while simultaneously offering the possibility of redemption through repentance and faith in Him. His crucifixion can be understood as the ultimate expression of this principle: God forms judgment (the cross) not as an end in itself but as the means to offer salvation and the possibility of restoration to all who turn to Him.
commentary.application: This verse brings home the urgent, personal nature of prophetic warning. Jeremiah does not speak in abstractions to a distant future generation but addresses 'the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem'—his contemporaries, his neighbors, people he knew by name. Similarly, the prophetic voice in each generation speaks to that generation's specific circumstance and calls for immediate response. For modern members: (1) The call to repentance is not a sign of God's anger but of His care—He warns through prophets because He desires our salvation, not our destruction. (2) The announcement of judgment often comes with a narrow window for response. When prophets warn against specific evils or call for specific reforms, the time to respond is now, not later. (3) Each person must respond individually ('every one from his evil way')—no one can hide behind collective identity or the faith of others. (4) True repentance includes both turning from evil and actively 'making good one's ways and doings'—it is transformative, not merely regretful.

text_kjv: And they said, There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart.

commentary.narrative:
The immediate response to Jeremiah's urgent call to repentance is a stunning act of defiance. Rather than accepting the prophet's word or even arguing about whether judgment is truly coming, the people declare 'there is no hope' (no'ash). But this cry of hopelessness is not despair in the sense of weakness or passivity—it is the conscious, deliberate rejection of God's offer of mercy. They are saying, in effect, 'God's way is hopeless; we refuse it. We will instead walk after our own maḥshavot (plans, devices, thoughts).' They reject God's maḥshavah (His devised plan; v. 11) and embrace instead their own desires.

What follows is a remarkable moment of self-indictment. The people explicitly adopt the very diagnosis Jeremiah has applied to them. They quote—or at least echo—the language of Jeremianic judgment, using it to describe themselves: 'each of us will act according to the sheririut of his evil heart' (sheririut meaning 'stubbornness'—a hardened, calcified will). The phrase 'sheririut libbo hara' ('stubbornness of his evil heart') becomes the people's own motto, their badge of identity. They have moved beyond merely practicing evil to embracing evil as their settled posture. The tragedy is complete: God offers life through repentance; the people choose death through deliberate rebellion. Jeremiah's prophecy has become a narrative of diminishing options—each refusal of repentance narrows the pathway to salvation, until finally the people have locked themselves into resistance.

word_study.term_english: hopeless / in vain / it is useless
word_study.meaning: To despair, lose hope, consider something to be in vain or useless. The root 'ush means to be despaired of, impossible.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'It is hopeless!' captures the defiant tone. This is not the despair of someone who has given up but the cynicism of someone who has decided to defy God's offer. The people are declaring that God's offer of mercy through repentance is 'hopeless'—but the deeper meaning is that they consider submission to God hopeless and prefer to follow their own will.

word_study.meaning: To walk after, follow, pursue; to go in the direction of something or someone. In Jeremianic language, typically means to follow false gods or rebellious courses.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'walk after our own devices' is direct language for abandoning God and pursuing self-will. The verb halak suggests a committed course of action, not a momentary lapse. They are setting their faces toward rebellion.

word_study.meaning: Thoughts, plans, devices, schemes. Plural of maḥshavah, emphasizing the multiplicity and variety of self-directed purposes.
word_study.significance: This is the plural of the same word used in verse 11: God is 'devising' (maḥshavah) a plan against Judah, and Judah is deliberately choosing to 'walk after' their own maḥshavot instead. The contrast emphasizes the conflict of wills: God's unified, wise plan versus humanity's scattered, self-directed schemes.

word_study.meaning: Stubbornness, hardness of heart, obstinacy. The root sharar means to be stiff, rigid, unyielding. A characteristic condition of heart that resists divine correction.
word_study.significance: This is Jeremiah's signature term for the spiritual condition that prevents repentance. It appears repeatedly in Jeremiah (3:17, 7:24, 9:13, 11:8, 13:10, 16:12, 23:17)—always as a diagnosis of the people's refusal to turn from evil. The Covenant Rendering's 'stubbornness' is perfect. Sheririut is not a passing mood but a hardened disposition, a spiritual rigidity that has become constitutional. The remarkable thing about verse 12 is that the people themselves use this word about themselves—they have internalized Jeremiah's diagnosis and made it their identity.

word_study.meaning: Evil heart; the center of will, emotion, and intention that is oriented toward evil rather than good.
word_study.significance: In biblical anthropology, the lev (heart) is the seat of the will and consciousness. An 'evil heart' is one in which the will has been oriented toward wickedness as a fundamental posture. The people are acknowledging that they will act 'according to' their evil hearts—their actions follow from their inmost orientation.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah earlier diagnosed the same stubborn heart (sheririut lev) in the people who walked after false gods, using the identical terminology that appears in verse 12.

Jeremiah laments that Israel 'walked in the counsels and in the imagination of their evil heart' (sheririut libam)—the same phrase the people now apply to themselves, suggesting that this stubbornness is a persistent pattern in Israel's history.
After the golden calf incident, the Lord describes Israel as 'a stiffnecked people' (kesef oref), using parallel language for the same phenomenon of hardened resistance that Jeremiah calls sheririut.

Paul describes the progression toward reprobate thinking: those who reject God's revelation are given over to a 'reprobate mind' and practice all manner of wickedness (v. 29-32). This is the Christian parallel to the Jeremianic diagnosis of sheririut.

King Benjamin warns his people that those who rebel against God and become 'carnal, sensual, and devilish' will find no redemption. This echoes Jeremiah's warning that those who embrace evil stubbornness as an identity have foreclosed the possibility of repentance.

The Lord describes those who 'deny the truth' and 'defy my power' as those who have become 'sons of perdition.' Their defiance of God's offer is so complete that they lose the possibility of any degree of salvation. This parallels the people's rejection in Jeremiah 18:12.

commentary.historical_context: This verse reflects a historical reality that ancient Judah experienced. Despite decades of Jeremianic prophecy, warnings from other prophets, and the living memory of the northern kingdom's fall to Assyria, the Judahite ruling class and populace chose not to repent. Instead, they pursued alliances with Egypt and Babylon, engaged in idolatry, and trusted in false prophets who promised peace and security. When the Babylonian siege came in 586 BCE, Jerusalem fell, the Temple was destroyed, and the population was exiled—precisely as Jeremiah had warned. The defiance recorded in verse 12 is historically rooted. Jeremiah's contemporaries actually did reject his call to repentance and embrace courses of action that led to their own destruction. The prophet was not exaggerating or fabricating; he was recording the actual response of the people to God's offer of mercy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly documents this identical pattern. The people of the land refuse the prophetic call to repentance and embrace their own devices (see Helaman 5:2-3, where the people reject Samuel the Lamanite's warning). Mormon specifically laments that the Nephites 'did harden their hearts' and 'did reject all the words of the prophets' (3 Nephi 2:1-2). The book of Ether records similar cycles where peoples refuse repentance and are destroyed. The pattern suggests that verse 12 is not unique to Jeremiah's era but represents a recurring tragedy in human history—peoples who choose self-will over submission to God's word.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:14-16 teaches that many 'hearken not to the voice of the Lord' and instead 'walk in the pride of their hearts.' This is the modern equivalent of Judah's choice in Jeremiah 18:12. D&C 5:7-9 describes those who will 'take up arms against you' and 'will not hear the words of the Lord'—explicitly connecting refusal to hear the prophetic word with destruction.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology teaches that covenants offer a pathway to exaltation but only for those who accept them. Those who reject the covenant offer and choose instead to 'walk after their own devices' place themselves outside the saving ordinances. The tragedy of Jeremiah 18:12 is that the people are explicitly rejecting God's covenant offer—the possibility of repentance and restoration—and choosing instead a path that leads to destruction.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's rejection by His own people (John 1:11; Matthew 21:37-39) is the ultimate fulfillment of this pattern. Christ comes as God's final offer of mercy and repentance (Luke 24:46-47), yet the religious and political leaders reject Him and choose instead to pursue their own power and devices. They choose Barabbas over Jesus, they choose the counsel of the chief priests over the words of the prophets, and they 'defy' God's ultimate messenger. The result is destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE—just as Jeremianic defiance led to destruction in 586 BCE. Yet even in rejection, Christ offers the possibility of repentance and restoration (Acts 2:38, where Peter calls the very people who rejected Jesus to repent and receive forgiveness). This shows that the pattern Jeremiah describes is not inevitable or irrevocable in the way the people believe—redemption remains possible even after apparent rejection, but only for those who turn.
commentary.application: Verse 12 presents a sobering portrait of how human defiance of God's offer operates. Several insights emerge: (1) Rejection of prophetic warning often does not come from ignorance but from conscious choice. The people are not confused about what God is offering; they are deliberately refusing it. (2) There is a dangerous progression from isolated acts of rebellion to a settled posture of defiance. Over time, the act of refusing God's word can crystallize into an identity—'I am the type of person who walks after my own devices.' When this happens, repentance becomes psychologically more difficult because changing course means changing identity. (3) The language of 'hopelessness' and 'no hope' can mask a kind of perverse hope—hope placed in one's own plans and devices rather than in God. (4) For modern members, the question is urgent: Are we cultivating an attitude of listening to the prophetic voice, or are we gradually hardening ourselves against it? Are we, like the people of Jeremiah's day, beginning to embrace 'the stubbornness of our evil heart' as an identity? The remedy is to consciously, repeatedly, choose to turn and listen to God's word before the hardening becomes complete.

text_kjv: Therefore thus saith the LORD; Ask ye now among the heathen, who hath heard such things: the virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing.

commentary.narrative: Jeremiah issues a challenge that reverses normal expectations: if you want to understand how shocking Israel's behavior is, ask the pagan nations themselves. This is rhetorical genius. The surrounding nations, who embrace idolatry as standard practice, would still find Israel's betrayal of her God incomprehensible. Israel was supposed to be devoted exclusively to the LORD—a covenant partner with singular allegiance—yet she has abandoned him for worthless idols. The comparison to 'the virgin of Israel' (betulat Yisra'el) is not merely poetic; it is a covenant epithet. A virgin is pledged to one husband alone. Israel's infidelity thus violates the most intimate and binding of relationships.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'a very horrible thing' (sha'arurit) appears in only three places in Scripture (here, Jer 5:30, and 23:14), suggesting an extraordinary act of moral outrage. The Lord is essentially saying: This sin is so unnatural, so contrary to the order of creation and covenant, that even pagans—whose theology is fundamentally different—recognize its perversity. The appeal to 'the heathen' as judges of Israel's behavior emphasizes how completely Israel has violated not just divine law but the basic bonds of loyal relationship. This sets up the following verses, which use natural imagery to show how Israel's infidelity defies even the laws of nature itself.

word_study.meaning: A virgin; more broadly, a young woman in her prime, especially one pledged to exclusive covenant relationship. In prophetic literature, it becomes an epithet for Israel as the bride of God, devoted and undefiled.
word_study.significance: The title 'virgin of Israel' carries covenantal weight—Israel was to be devoted exclusively to the LORD as a wife to her husband. The use of this term in contexts of infidelity (cf. Amos 5:2) emphasizes the violation of intimate trust. The Covenant Rendering preserves this covenantal meaning, marking Israel not as politically young but as relationally bound.

word_study.meaning: Appalling, horrifying, an act that makes the hair stand on end (from se'ar, 'hair'). A rare word appearing only in Jer 18:13, 5:30, and 23:14—each time describing idolatry as shockingly wrong.
word_study.significance: The rarity and intensity of this term underscore how completely Israel's idolatry violates the natural and moral order. It is not merely sin but an outrage against reality itself. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'utterly appalling' captures both the moral and visceral force of sha'arurit.

word_study.meaning: To ask, inquire, request; often in the sense of seeking counsel or opinion. Here it carries the sense of making inquiry among witnesses.
word_study.significance: The imperative form 'Ask ye now' (shilahu-na) is urgent and emphatic—Jeremiah is calling Israel's judges (the pagan nations) to testify to the enormity of the crime. The Lord invites examination, confident that the evidence is overwhelming.

cross_references.connection: The vineyard metaphor: 'Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine?' Israel was planted as pure, devoted stock but has degenerated into idolatry.

The same imagery of Israel as an unfaithful wife: 'Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband.' The covenant language of spousal infidelity runs throughout the prophets.

Israel's unfaithfulness directly: 'Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD.' The virgin epithet emphasizes the betrayal of exclusive devotion.
A similar appeal to witnesses: 'Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth' — Isaiah also calls creation itself to witness Israel's rebellion against her God.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the relationship between a god and his people was understood through the lens of covenant loyalty. Israel's singular monotheistic commitment to the LORD was radically counter-cultural; surrounding nations practiced polytheism and syncretism as normal. The irony Jeremiah emphasizes—that pagan nations would find Israel's betrayal shocking—reflects this: even people without Israel's covenantal revelation understand the fundamental wrongness of a committed relationship being abandoned for worthless alternatives. The 'virgin of Israel' epithet draws on ancient Near Eastern marriage customs, where virginity was a sign of loyalty and exclusive devotion. The appeal to gentile nations as judges also reflects a common prophetic strategy: invoking the testimony of outsiders to amplify the severity of Israel's guilt.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, similar language of covenant infidelity appears. Nephi describes the waywardness of covenant Israel using spousal imagery (1 Nephi 21:4, citing Isaiah 49:4), and the Nephites themselves are presented as a covenantal community whose unfaithfulness brings judgment. The concept of a 'virgin' people devoted to God also resonates in D&C 113, where the bride imagery describes the Lord's faithful people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 speaks of the Lord's covenant with the Church and the danger of turning aside from his word. The principle that covenant violation brings judgement is central to Doctrine and Covenants understanding of God's relationship with his people. D&C 121:45 emphasizes the contrast between divine favor and the withdrawal of blessing—mirroring the face-hiding judgment Jeremiah announces.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of Israel as the virgin bride of God foreshadows New Testament temple symbolism, where the Church becomes the Bride of Christ. In latter-day revelation, the temple represents the covenant space where exclusive devotion to God is renewed. The violation of covenantal exclusivity—idolatry—is the ultimate profanation of that sacred bond.

commentary.christological_typology: While not directly messianic, the covenant relationship Jeremiah defends—the exclusive devotion demanded between God and his people—finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ as the bridegroom of the Church (Ephesians 5:25-27). Christ's faithfulness complements and redeems humanity's unfaithfulness. The scandal of Israel's betrayal of her covenant with God in the Old Testament is answered by Christ's perfect and unshakeable faithfulness to his covenant with the Church. The 'virgin of Israel' epithet prefigures the Church as the undefiled Bride of Christ.
commentary.application: This verse confronts us with the seriousness of covenantal commitment. Like Israel, members of The Church of Jesus Christ have entered into a covenant relationship with God—not through the law of Moses, but through baptism and temple ordinances. The question Jeremiah raises implicitly: What would outsiders say if they witnessed our faithfulness—or unfaithfulness—to our covenants? Have we, like Israel, abandoned the 'ancient paths' for the worthless things the world offers? The call to ask 'among the heathen' is a call to honest self-examination: Is our devotion to God singular and exclusive, or have we diluted it with competing allegiances? Repentance begins when we acknowledge, with Jeremiah's prophetic clarity, that covenant infidelity is not a small thing but 'something utterly appalling.'

text_kjv: Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon which cometh from the rock of the field? or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken?

commentary.narrative: Jeremiah shifts from condemning Israel's moral failure to asking a question about nature's reliability—and in doing so, highlights the unnaturalness of Israel's infidelity. The snow of Lebanon was proverbial in ancient Israel: it covered the highest peaks, endured for months, and fed the streams that watered the land. The 'cold, flowing waters from distant sources' (possibly referring to underground springs or the waters of the Hermon massif) were constant, dependable, and life-sustaining. Jeremiah's rhetorical questions expect a simple answer: No, the snow does not abandon the mountain; no, the springs do not cease to flow. Nature is faithful to its created purpose.
commentary.narrative_continued: This is an argument from creation itself. If mountains keep their snow, if springs keep flowing, if nature maintains its appointed order, how can Israel abandon the LORD, who created all of this? The comparison is devastating precisely because it is so simple. An inanimate mountain is more faithful to its function than Israel is to her God. A spring that has flowed for millennia does not suddenly stop; yet Israel, who has been in covenant relationship with the living God for over a thousand years, has turned away. The verse sets up the contrast with verse 15: nature's faithfulness versus human unfaithfulness, creation's loyalty versus covenant-breaker's betrayal.

word_study.meaning: Snow, understood as a symbol of purity, permanence, and blessing in the Mediterranean climate. The snow of Lebanon's peaks was legendary for its durability and abundance.
word_study.significance: In biblical imagery, snow represents both permanence and purity. That Lebanon's snow should 'abandon' the rock is absurd—it is as fixed to its place as anything in creation. The Covenant Rendering's question 'Does the snow vanish from the rocky crags of Lebanon?' captures the impossibility inherent in the premise.

word_study.meaning: Rock, cliff, crag; also used metaphorically for God as refuge and strength. The rocky peaks of Lebanon were immovable and eternal.
word_study.significance: The irony is thick: mountains of rock, which the Bible often uses as metaphors for God's steadfastness (Psalm 18:2, 'my rock and my fortress'), remain faithful to their nature. Israel should remain as steadfast as Lebanon's peaks are permanent. The use of tsur here invokes that theological resonance.

word_study.term_original: mayim zarim qarim nozlim (מַיִם זָרִים קָרִים נוֹזְלִים)
word_study.meaning: Waters from foreign/distant sources that are cold and flowing. The adjectives emphasize both origin (distant, from elsewhere) and perpetual nature (cold = refreshing, nozlim = flowing, continuous).
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's rendering 'cold, flowing waters from distant sources' captures the permanence and reliability of natural hydrology. Even water that originates from far away does not cease its flow. The word zarim ('foreign, distant') may carry a subtle irony—even waters not native to the speaker still remain faithful to their course.

cross_references.connection: The Lord is called a rock: 'The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer.' Mountains and rocks are biblical symbols for God's unchanging faithfulness.

Earlier, Jeremiah urges: 'Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein.' The contrast between nature's faithfulness to its ancient ways and Israel's abandonment of the ancient paths.

A reference to digging wells and bringing forth waters: ancient hydraulic technology relied on the constancy of mountain springs—a reliability that natural sources provide but Israel fails to exhibit.
'The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.' Even nature fades, but God's word and covenant faithfulness endure—Israel should mirror this eternal constancy.

commentary.historical_context: The snow of Lebanon was not merely a poetic reference; it was a geographic fact central to Levantine water systems. The anti-Lebanon and Lebanon mountain ranges collect snow that feeds the Jordan River system and numerous springs throughout the Levant. In Jeremiah's time, these water sources were known to be remarkably constant—reliable enough to support agriculture and settlement. The ancient Near East valued water sources as life itself; a spring that ceased to flow would be catastrophic. Jeremiah's appeal to this geological reality reflects ancient understanding: certain natural phenomena are so reliable that to expect them to cease would be absurd. By extension, Israel's abandonment of her God is portrayed as defying the very laws of nature.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 12:24, there is emphasis on the enduring nature of the Lord's law: 'And thus we see that all things as to their time are appointed unto man; wherefore they have their agency given unto them.' The laws of nature reflect God's eternal order. The Nephites also experience cycles of faithfulness and apostasy, mirroring Israel's failure to maintain constant devotion.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:42-47 describes the order and faithfulness of creation: 'The earth abideth the law of a celestial kingdom... the stars abide the law of a telestial kingdom.' Creation obeys eternal law; covenant Israel should obey as faithfully. The principle that creation maintains its appointed order becomes a rebuke to those who break their covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple teaching, the order of creation reflects divine order and eternal law. The temple landscape often invokes natural elements (water, stone, vegetation) as symbols of eternal principles. Israel's covenant violation is thus not merely a breach of contract but a defiance of the cosmic order itself—a profanation of the sacred order the temple represents.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the fulfillment of covenantal fidelity. Hebrews 13:8 states, 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever'—an immutable constancy. Where Israel was like water that dried up and mountains that crumbled, Christ is the rock (1 Corinthians 10:4) that never ceases to sustain his people. His faithfulness to the covenant (Hebrews 8:6) is permanent and unchanging, unlike Israel's wavering devotion.
commentary.application: This verse calls modern covenant Israel to examine our constancy. We live in an age of rapid change and distraction. Loyalty to God requires the same permanence Jeremiah attributes to mountains and springs—not a seasonal or circumstantial devotion, but a continuous, flowing commitment. The question Jeremiah poses is ultimately about us: Will we, who have made covenants with God, prove less reliable than inanimate nature? The challenge is to cultivate a devotion as constant as a spring that has never stopped flowing, as permanent as snow that returns to the peaks year after year. In a cultural moment that celebrates novelty and change, fidelity to our covenants—to temple promises, to the restored Gospel, to the living God—should be as natural and as reliable as water flowing downward from a mountain source.

text_kjv: Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up;

commentary.narrative: This verse moves from nature's faithfulness to Israel's active betrayal. 'Forgotten me' (shekhahunim) is not accidental amnesia but willful disregard—a turning away from covenantal memory. What follows is a sequence of descent: first, they burn incense to shav ('vanity, emptiness, nothingness')—idols that literally do not exist as sources of divine power. Second, they are 'caused to stumble' (the reflexive form suggests they have allowed themselves to be misled) from the ancient paths (shvilei olam—'paths of eternity,' the tested ways of covenant obedience) onto side trails and ungraded roads (nativot, derekh lo selulah—literally paths that have not been built up or maintained).
commentary.narrative_continued: The imagery is of leaving a well-maintained highway for wilderness. The 'ancient paths' echo Jeremiah 6:16, where the prophet urges Israel to 'stand at the crossroads and look; ask for the ancient paths, where is the good way, and walk therein.' Israel had been offered a choice—faithfulness or apostasy—and chose the ungraded road. This verse explains the mechanism of Israel's fall: forgetting the covenant, worshiping nothingness, and losing their footing on the path of obedience. The phrase 'they have been caused to stumble' suggests both personal responsibility and the seductive power of idolatry—they have allowed themselves to be led astray. By verse 16, this stumbling leads to complete desolation.

word_study.meaning: To forget, to disregard, to cease to remember. In covenantal language, it often means to abandon or neglect one's commitments.
word_study.significance: The forgetting is not passive. In Hebrew thought, to forget God means to cease honoring the covenant relationship. It is an active breach. The prophets use this language repeatedly to describe Israel's apostasy as a turning away, not mere lapse of memory.

word_study.meaning: Emptiness, nothingness, worthlessness, falsehood. Often used to describe idols—things that have no real power or substance. The Covenant Rendering renders this 'worthless things' to capture the notion that idols are literally nothing.
word_study.significance: Shav appears frequently in prophetic condemnation of idolatry (Jeremiah 10:8, 'brutish and foolish; the stock is a doctrine of vanities'). To burn incense to shav is to offer worship to nonexistence. The contrast with the God who exists and acts is devastating. Israel exchanges the real for the unreal.

word_study.meaning: To stumble, to fall, to fail; often used metaphorically for moral or spiritual failure. The reflexive form (hikkashilu, 'they have been made to stumble') suggests both passivity and complicity.
word_study.significance: The verb captures the disorientation and loss of footing that comes from abandoning the established path. Stumbling leads inevitably to falling; moral stumbling leads to destruction.

word_study.meaning: Paths of eternity, ancient paths, the tested ways. Olam can mean 'world' but often carries the sense of 'forever' or 'ancient times.' These are not merely old routes but paths proven by time and divine order.
word_study.significance: The phrase invokes the long covenantal history of Israel and the reliability of obedience. The 'ancient paths' are the ways that generations of faithful Israel have walked. To abandon them is to reject the wisdom of the fathers and the guidance of God's revealed law.

word_study.meaning: To raise up, to grade, to build up (a road). A salaluach (graded way) is a properly constructed path, smooth and maintained; a derekh lo selulah is an ungraded, unmaintained, potentially dangerous trail.
word_study.significance: The contrast between the maintained highway (selulah) of covenant obedience and the ungraded wilderness paths (lo selulah) of idolatry captures the practical consequences of apostasy. The well-maintained path implies safety, direction, and divine provision; the ungraded trail implies danger, disorientation, and abandonment.

cross_references.connection: 'Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein: and ye shall find rest for your souls.' Jeremiah had offered the choice; Israel refused, opting instead for the ungraded paths of verse 15.
A description of those who 'leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness,' who 'forget the paths of the Lord.' This is the fruit of forgetting covenant and choosing vanity.

'Arise, get thee down quickly from hence; for thy people which thou hast brought forth out of Egypt have corrupted themselves.' Israel's forgetting of covenant is described as corruption from their first moments of freedom.
'But my people would not hearken to my voice; and Israel would none of me.' A parallel lament over Israel's willful forgetting and rejection of divine guidance.

Alma 37:12 teaches about maintaining 'the records which shall be kept and shall be handed down from one generation to another.' The 'ancient paths' of covenant knowledge require active transmission and remembrance.

commentary.historical_context: The religious geography of ancient Israel is important here. The 'ancient paths' likely refer to both the literal pilgrimage routes to the temple in Jerusalem and, more broadly, the traditional practices of Yahweh worship established in the time of Moses and David. Idolatry—'burning incense to vanity'—was not aberrant but widespread in the ancient world. Every Near Eastern nation practiced syncretism and veneration of multiple deities. What made Israel's apostasy uniquely shocking (as verse 13 emphasized) was that Israel had committed herself uniquely to the LORD. The reference to 'side trails' and 'ungraded roads' may reflect the chaos of the late pre-exilic period, when Judah was religiously fractured between competing centers of worship (the Asherah poles in the high places, the temple in Jerusalem, the shrines of foreign gods). The ungraded road is the religiously chaotic path.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 8, Lehi's vision describes those who 'began to get ashamed, because of those that were scoffing at them; and they fell away into forbidden paths and were lost.' The imagery of leaving the straight and narrow path for ungraded wilderness paths is central to Book of Mormon theology. Alma 39:4 speaks of Corianton abandoning 'the way which is just, to go into the ways of this wicked man' and being 'overcome by the temptations of the devil.' The principle of forgetting the ancient paths and stumbling into apostasy is a recurring Book of Mormon theme.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:2 states that the revelations came so that 'the fulness of my gospel might be proclaimed by the weak and the simple unto the ends of the world.' The 'ancient paths' in Restoration context are the restored truths—the pathway laid out by Joseph Smith and continuing in the living prophets. D&C 21:4-6 warns against turning aside from the word of the Lord. D&C 132 emphasizes covenantal exclusivity, echoing the theme of devoted paths versus wandering into 'another way.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the initiate walks a specific path through the house of the Lord—a graded and maintained way that represents covenant progression. To abandon this path is to 'stumble' spiritually. The temple endowment emphasizes the ancient paths of divine knowledge and covenant, contrasting with the 'ungraded roads' of worldly philosophy and false teachings.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). He is the ultimate fulfillment of the ancient paths—the straight way that leads to God. Where Israel stumbled from the path and was lost in wilderness, Christ remained on the path of obedience and becomes the way back. His perfection on the ancient path of covenant obedience makes him the Mediator who restores those who have stumbled and been lost. Hebrews 12:2 describes Christ as 'the author and finisher of our faith,' the one who keeps the path perfect when others falter.
commentary.application: Modern readers must ask themselves: Are we maintaining the 'ancient paths' that the Restoration has recovered? These include the covenants of baptism, temple endowment, and sealing; the principles of revelation through living prophets; the practices of family home evening and family prayer; the discipline of Sabbath observance and regular scripture study. Or have we allowed ourselves to be distracted by the 'ungraded roads' of worldly thinking—the notion that covenant is optional, that revelation has ceased, that personal preference trumps divine law? Verse 15 diagnoses apostasy as a three-step process: forgetting, idolatry (worship of what is empty and powerless), and stumbling. We prevent apostasy by active remembrance (maintaining family history, studying the scriptures, honoring our baptismal and temple covenants), by directing worship exclusively to God (not to wealth, status, or ideology), and by staying on the maintained paths our prophets and scriptures lay out for us. The 'ancient paths' are not antiquated—they are eternally true, and every generation must choose to walk them.

text_kjv: To make their land desolate, and a perpetual hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished, and wag his head.

commentary.narrative: This verse describes the judgment that follows apostasy: complete desolation and perpetual shame. The land, which was meant to be the fulfillment of covenant promise (flowing with milk and honey), becomes a wasteland. More than mere physical ruin, it becomes an object of scorn—a 'perpetual hissing' (sheriqot olam). The word sheriqot captures the sound a person makes when confronted with shocking devastation: a sharp intake of breath, a low whistle of horror and disbelief. Every traveler who passes the ruined land will be 'astonished' (shamem—stunned, appalled) and 'wag his head' (yanid bero'sho—a gesture of disapproval and mourning). The desolation is not temporary; it is 'perpetual,' marking the land forever as a monument to divine judgment.
commentary.narrative_continued: This represents the ultimate reversal of blessing. In the wilderness wanderings, Israel was the wonder of the nations—manna from heaven, water from the rock, divine presence in a pillar of cloud. By Jeremiah's time, Israel faces becoming a spectacle of ruin instead of a spectacle of blessing. Every passerby becomes a witness to the consequences of covenant-breaking. The 'perpetual hissing' suggests that Israel's desolation will be so complete and so long-lasting that it becomes legendary. The shaking of the head is both mourning (for what Israel was) and warning (to others who might consider similar apostasy). This verse anticipates the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile, which would indeed make Judah a byword among the nations.

word_study.meaning: To be desolate, waste, ruined; to be appalled or horrified. As a noun, shimah refers to desolation. The verb carries both the sense of physical devastation and the emotional reaction to it.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering uses 'desolation' to capture both the state and the astonishment it provokes. When a land is shamah, it is not merely empty but catastrophically destroyed—a place that provokes horror in those who see it.

word_study.term_english: perpetual hissing / object of perpetual scorn
word_study.meaning: A hissing (the sound of sharp intake of breath or low whistle) that is perpetual/eternal. Sheriqot suggests both the sound and the attitude—a dismissive or horrified reaction. Olam means 'eternity' or 'perpetually.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'object of perpetual scorn' captures the ongoing, legendary quality of Israel's shame. It is not a temporary disaster but a permanent marker. Every generation that passes will shake their head. This is the prophetic equivalent of infamy.

word_study.meaning: To be desolated, appalled, horrified. The same root as shamah (desolation), but here describing the emotional response of those who witness the ruin.
word_study.significance: Israel's land becomes not only desolate but a source of desolation to those who behold it. The witness to ruin becomes themselves horrified, rendered mute or trembling by what they see.

word_study.meaning: To shake one's head; a gesture of disapproval, mourning, or warning. The verb nud means 'to shake, rock, or wave.'
word_study.significance: In biblical culture, the head-shake is a multivalent gesture—it can express pity, disapproval, disbelief, or warning. In this context, it is the reaction of a witness to catastrophe. The physical gesture becomes a wordless sermon to all who pass: 'This is what covenant-breaking brings.'

cross_references.connection: 'And thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword, among all nations whither the LORD shall lead thee.' The covenant curses include becoming a byword—exactly what Jeremiah describes.

'All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?' A direct parallel describing Jerusalem's ruin as an object of mockery and head-shaking.

Solomon is warned that if the house is rejected, 'this house, which is high, every one that passeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss.' This is a prophecy of exactly the scenario Jeremiah describes.
'We are become a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and derision to them that are round about us.' The psalmist laments this very condition of becoming a byword among the nations.

commentary.historical_context: The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BCE would indeed make Judah a desolation and a byword. Travelers on the ancient trade routes would pass the ruins of the temple and the walls. The land would be depopulated and economically devastated for generations. Archaeology confirms the violence and completeness of the destruction. Beyond the physical reality, the theological impact was enormous: a nation that believed itself chosen and covenanted with God had been utterly defeated and exiled. This raised profound questions about whether God had abandoned them. The 'perpetual hissing' would echo through the centuries—the destruction became a fixed point in memory, referenced in rabbinic literature and in the consciousness of diaspora Judaism forever after.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar cycles of blessing and desolation. When the Nephites are faithful, their land prospers; when they apostatize, they face destruction. Helaman 13 describes the pronouncement of ruin on Zarahemla: 'the sword of justice hangeth over you.' The pattern of covenant-keeping leading to blessing and covenant-breaking leading to desolation is a central Book of Mormon theme. The scattering of Israelites from their covenanted land is a recurring consequence of apostasy (1 Nephi 13:12-14).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:66 promises that those who 'seek in sincerity of heart' will be numbered with the righteous 'in the day that I come,' but D&C 63:32 warns of 'desolations' for the wicked. The principle that covenant-breaking brings desolation is central to Doctrine and Covenants theology. D&C 121:37 emphasizes that when priesthood holders become 'covered with the robe of my righteousness,' their works are known to God, but those who break covenants lose this protection.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the covenant relationship at its most intimate. When a people breaks covenant, they are barred from the temple. The destruction of the temple—first by the Babylonians, later by the Romans—represents the ultimate desolation: the breaking of the covenant connection between God and his people. In latter-day revelation, the building and dedication of temples is a sign of the Lord's favor, while their destruction would signal withdrawal of blessing.

commentary.christological_typology: While not directly messianic, the desolation Jeremiah describes points to the necessity of Christ's atonement. Humanity's covenant-breaking creates a desolation—a spiritual wasteland—that only Christ's redemption can restore. The imagery of a land made perpetually desolate parallels the spiritual death that results from sin, which Christ overcomes through his resurrection. Where the old covenant was broken and the land made barren, Christ establishes a new covenant (Hebrews 8:6-13) where blessing is restored and the wasteland blooms again (Isaiah 35).
commentary.application: This verse should sober modern covenant Israel. The consequences of covenant-breaking are not abstract or theoretical but concrete and perpetual. When a person, a family, or a community breaks their covenants with God, the consequences are not temporary setbacks but lasting desolation. Consider: How many people have walked away from the restored Gospel, and how their communities have been affected? How many families have been rent apart by apostasy and sin? The 'perpetual hissing' and head-shaking are real—they are the judgment of heaven and the recognition of those who witness that covenant violations have consequences. But the inverse is also true: covenant faithfulness brings blessing that is equally perpetual. The challenge is to choose the path of covenantal fidelity, not for fear of judgment alone, but because the covenant is the pathway to divine presence, protection, and exaltation. Modern Israel must understand that what we do with our covenants will determine not only our individual salvation but the blessing or desolation of generations.

text_kjv: I will scatter them as with an east wind before the enemy; I will shew them the back, and not the face, in the day of their calamity.

commentary.narrative: God now explicitly announces the method and meaning of judgment. First, Israel will be 'scattered as with an east wind' (ke-ruach qadim). The east wind—the khamsin or sirocco—is the scorching desert wind that desiccates and destroys. It is not a gentle breeze but a destructive force that withers vegetation and disorients travelers. Jeremiah uses this image to convey military defeat: as an enemy is scattered like dust before the wind, so Israel will be scattered before her enemies. But there is a deeper meaning: the scattering before the enemy is a manifestation of God's judgment. It is God who will scatter them—the human enemy is merely the instrument.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second part of the verse is even more profound: 'I will show them the back, and not the face, in the day of their calamity.' This reverses the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26: 'The Lord bless thee, and keep thee: The Lord make his face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.' When God's face shines upon his people, it means blessing, protection, and peace. When God shows his back, it means he is turning away—withdrawing his presence and protection. This is not merely military defeat but spiritual abandonment. In Israel's darkest moment—the day of calamity—they will discover that God is not facing them but has turned away. The verse thus announces both judgment (defeat before enemies) and its spiritual cause: the withdrawal of divine favor.

word_study.meaning: The east wind; in the ancient Near East, this referred to the hot, dry, destructive winds from the desert. Qadim means 'east' or 'before,' and ruach means 'wind' or 'spirit.'
word_study.significance: The east wind is not merely weather but a symbol of divine judgment and desolation throughout Scripture. In Exodus 10:13-15, it brings the locusts; in Ezekiel 17:10, it withers and dries up the vine. It is a force of nature that cannot be resisted. The image conveys the totality and inevitability of Israel's dispersion.

word_study.meaning: To scatter, disperse, or spread out (like chaff before the wind or grain scattered by threshing). The verb implies both separation and purposelessness—the scattered people lose cohesion and direction.
word_study.significance: The verb is active: God is the agent doing the scattering. This is not random military defeat but purposeful divine judgment. The Covenant Rendering's 'scatter them' captures this active divine agency.

word_study.meaning: Oref = back, nape of the neck; panim = face, front, presence. The contrast is absolute: facing someone means engagement and presence; showing one's back means withdrawal and rejection.
word_study.significance: In biblical thought, God's face (panim Adonai) is the ultimate expression of his favor and presence. The priestly blessing emphasizes this: 'The Lord make his face shine upon you' (Numbers 6:25). To experience God showing his back is to lose the covenant presence. This is not merely emotional rejection but the removal of divine protection and guidance.

word_study.meaning: The day of their ruin, disaster, or calamity. Eid refers to destruction or ruin; yom is 'day' in the sense of a specific time of crisis.
word_study.significance: The 'day of calamity' is eschatological language pointing to a specific moment when judgment is executed—the fall of Jerusalem. It is a day when all will be revealed: Israel's apostasy and God's withdrawal of his protective presence.

cross_references.connection: The priestly blessing: 'The Lord make his face to shine upon thee...and give thee peace.' This is the inverse of what Jeremiah announces—God's face withdrawn is the curse that undoes the blessing.

Moses prophesies: 'They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God...and I will hide my face from them, and will see what their end shall be.' Hiding or showing one's back is equivalent to withdrawing the covenant presence.

'Hear, O LORD, when I cry with my voice...hide not thy face far from me; put not thy servant away in anger.' David pleads precisely against what Jeremiah announces—the hiding or turning away of God's face.

'There is none that calleth upon thy name, that stirreth up himself to take hold of thee: for thou hast hid thy face from us, and hast consumed us, because of our iniquities.' The removal of God's face leads to consumption and judgment.
Later in Jeremiah, God says 'they have turned unto me the back, and not the face' (a partial reversal of 18:17). Israel shows God her back; God, in turn, shows Israel his back.

commentary.historical_context: The east wind as a judgment motif appears throughout Mesopotamian literature and the Bible, reflecting the terrifying reality of the desert wind to Levantine peoples. The military destruction of Judah by Babylon would have felt exactly like this: overwhelming, irresistible, and complete. The Babylonian campaign under Nebuchadnezzar (605-586 BCE) devastated Judah, with the final siege and destruction of Jerusalem being particularly catastrophic. From the perspective of the exiles, this would have felt like the removal of divine presence—the temple destroyed, the king executed or exiled, the land laid waste. The concept of God 'showing his back' would have resonated deeply: the people experienced divine abandonment as a concrete reality. Yet, crucially, this is not permanent. Later in Jeremiah (29:10-14), God promises restoration after seventy years—the back is shown only during the exile; the face will return in restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:27, Alma rejoices that he has not been left as 'a vagabond and a wanderer,' having kept his covenants. The scattering 'as with an east wind' mirrors the dispersion the Lamanites inflict on unfaithful Nephites. The principle that apostasy leads to scattering and divine withdrawal appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Mosiah 7:25-30 describes the Nephite refugees suffering judgment as exiles—experiencing the removal of divine protection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:33 states, 'I the Lord... will visit upon the wicked their own doings.' D&C 121:37 teaches that when priesthood holders abuse power, 'Amen to the priesthood or the authority of that man.' The withdrawal of authority parallels the withdrawal of God's face. D&C 64:7 emphasizes that 'I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.'—restoration of the divine face requires reconciliation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple ordinances, the face-to-face encounter with God (symbolized in the endowment and celestial room) represents the ultimate restoration of divine presence. Conversely, being barred from the temple (the consequence of breaking covenants) represents the withdrawal of the divine face. The temple is where Israel encounters the face of God; its destruction represents the ultimate desolation of covenant breach.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's crucifixion includes the cry, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Matthew 27:46). Here, Christ experiences the withdrawal of the divine face—bearing the weight of human sin and covenant-breaking. But his resurrection reverses this: the face of God is restored, not to the old covenant community, but to a renewed covenant community in Christ. Hebrews 10:19-22 speaks of approaching God 'by a new and living way... by the blood of Jesus,' having confidence to enter 'into the holiest by the blood of Jesus' because 'the vail of the temple' is rent. Through Christ, the divine face is turned toward humanity again, and the covenant presence is restored.
