commentary.application: This verse confronts us with a hard truth: covenant-breaking has consequences that include the withdrawal of divine presence and protection. It should provoke deep reflection: Do we sense God's face shining upon us, or do we feel abandoned? The answer depends not on circumstance but on our faithfulness. Modern Israel must understand that sin and apostasy do not merely result in external judgment but in an internal experience of separation from God. When we break our temple covenants through immorality, lies, or disloyalty; when we turn away from the restored Gospel; when we neglect prayer and scripture study—we experience, in essence, God's turning of his back toward us. But the inverse is equally true: when we keep our covenants with exactness and devotion, we experience the divine countenance shining upon us. We sense his presence, his guidance, his protection. The challenge is to choose faithfulness—not to avoid judgment alone, but to maintain the intimate presence of the divine face throughout our lives. This is the foundation of both personal spiritual life and community blessing.

text_kjv: Then said they, Come, and let us devise devices against Jeremiah; for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words.

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the beginning of Jeremiah's fourth confession (18:18-23) and reveals the response of Israel's leadership to the prophet's judgment. They plot against Jeremiah, but their reasoning is telling: they believe that instruction (torah) will always come from the priest, counsel from the wise, and the word from the prophet. In other words, they believe the institutional structures of religious guidance are so established that one dissenting voice—Jeremiah—can be safely eliminated without consequence. This reveals a fundamental theological error: they assume the sources of divine guidance are automatic and perpetual, regardless of the condition of the people. They do not believe that God would withdraw his presence through prophet, priest, and sage.
commentary.narrative_continued: The enemies plot to 'attack him with the tongue' (nakkeihu vallashon)—not physical violence, but a campaign of slander, mockery, and denunciation. They will engage in character assassination, undermining his credibility so thoroughly that 'we need not give heed to any of his words.' The phrase 'attack with the tongue' suggests the kind of social ostracism and public ridicule that can be more devastating than physical violence. By silencing Jeremiah's words, they believe they can silence God's judgment. What follows (verses 19-23) is Jeremiah's anguished response to this conspiracy—his lament that he is being persecuted for faithfully delivering God's word.

word_study.meaning: To devise, plan, scheme, or invent. The noun form (machshavot) refers to schemes or thoughts. The repetition 'devise devices' is emphatic—they are plotting carefully and with intent.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests deliberate, calculated opposition—not spontaneous anger but premeditated conspiracy. The Covenant Rendering's 'plot schemes' captures this intentional malice. This is not a momentary reaction but an organized effort to eliminate Jeremiah's influence.

word_study.meaning: Instruction, law, teaching; originally the priestly instruction (torah) given at the temple. It later came to refer to the written Torah scroll, but in Jeremiah's time, it meant the living guidance that priests provided.
word_study.significance: The enemies claim that torah will not perish from the priest—but this assumes the priest remains loyal to God and the covenant. As Jeremiah announces judgment that may include the destruction of the temple and exile of the priesthood, their assumption is shown to be false. The Covenant Rendering's 'instruction' preserves the broader sense of torah beyond written law.

word_study.meaning: Counsel, advice, plan, or wisdom. The wise (chachamim) were counselors and strategists whose advice guided kings and communities.
word_study.significance: The enemies assume that human wisdom, embodied in the counsel of the wise, will always be available. Yet Jeremiah's prophecy includes the judgment that wisdom will fail in the crisis of invasion and exile (Jeremiah 8:9). Their confidence in the wise is misplaced.

word_study.meaning: Word, matter, thing, utterance. In prophetic context, it refers to the word or utterance of the prophet—the divine message.
word_study.significance: The enemies acknowledge that the prophetic word should exist—they just deny that Jeremiah's particular word has validity. They assume prophecy will continue to flow, not recognizing that Israel's apostasy might lead to the silence of God (cf. Amos 8:11-12).

word_study.term_english: attack him with the tongue / attack with the tongue
word_study.meaning: To strike/smite with the tongue; to use harsh words, slander, and denunciation as a weapon. The 'tongue' is the instrument of social destruction through lies and mockery.
word_study.significance: This is a particularly insidious form of persecution: the enemies do not need physical weapons because the tongue is deadlier. Social ostracism, mockery, and the spreading of lies can destroy a person's reputation and influence. The Covenant Rendering's 'attack him with the tongue' preserves the immediacy of verbal violence.

word_study.meaning: To listen, pay attention, or give heed. The negative form 'let us not give heed' means to deliberately refuse to listen.
word_study.significance: The enemies plan a two-fold strategy: slander Jeremiah and then dismiss his words. By destroying his credibility, they believe they can silence his message. But what they are really trying to do is silence God, who speaks through the prophet.

cross_references.connection: In Jeremiah's earlier confession: 'But I was like a lamb or an ox that is brought to the slaughter; and I knew not that they had devised devices against me.' This is the first indication of persecution; verse 18:18 shows it escalating into organized conspiracy.

'Who whet their tongue like a sword, and bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words: That they may shoot in secret at the perfect: suddenly do they shoot at him, and fear not.' A parallel description of persecution through the tongue.

'The wise men are ashamed, they are dismayed and taken: lo, they have rejected the word of the LORD; and what wisdom is in them?' Jeremiah's prophecy that the wisdom of the wise will fail—directly undermining the enemies' confidence in verse 18.

'Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread...but of hearing the words of the LORD.' The prophetic word may indeed perish if Israel refuses to hear it—another challenge to the enemies' assumption.

In the Book of Mormon, Nephi is bound and nearly killed by his brothers; later (1 Nephi 21:23), the Lord promises that those who oppose his servants will not prevail. The persecution of the faithful servant is a recurring pattern.

The Lord tells Joseph Smith: 'And if thou art cast into the pit, or into the hands of murderers, and the sentence of death passed upon thee...know thou, my son, that all these things shall give thee experience.' Divine assurance that persecution of God's servants is allowed but ultimately purposeful.

commentary.historical_context: Jeremiah's persecution by the leadership is historically grounded. The book of Jeremiah records multiple instances of his arrest, beating, and attempted execution (Jeremiah 20:1-2, 26:8-15, 37:11-21, 38:1-6). The leadership—priests, false prophets, officials—genuinely believed that Jeremiah's prophecies of destruction were treason and falsehood. Their logic in verse 18 reflects an institutional confidence: the system of temple, priesthood, and court prophets had served Judah for centuries; why should they believe this one lone voice over the established authorities? This was not unreasonable from a human perspective. But it was profoundly mistaken spiritually. The enemies do not perceive what Jeremiah sees: God is withdrawing his presence precisely because of Israel's infidelity. The institutional structures they trust—priest, wise counselor, and official court prophet—are compromised by apostasy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records persistent patterns of persecution against prophets and faithful believers. In Jacob 4:14, Jacob laments that the Jews 'despise the words of plainness, and kill the prophets, and seek for things that they cannot understand.' The enemies of truth in the Book of Mormon use character assassination and mockery—the 'tongues' of verse 18—against the servants of God. Alma 1:26 describes how Alma's detractors use slander to try to discredit him. The pattern is identical: silence the prophet by destroying credibility and spreading lies.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 31:4 warns that the servant of God will face 'tribulation,' but D&C 31:5-6 promises 'nevertheless, the Holy Ghost shall be a comforter unto you...and I will go before you.' When the enemies plot against Jeremiah using words, they fail to account for the Spirit. D&C 101:4-5 emphasizes that persecution comes because 'the inhabitants of the earth are asleep, and they know not when the evil one cometh.' Those who plot against God's servants do not perceive divine reality. D&C 123:12 instructs that 'by the power of our testimony' the persecutors 'shall be judged in all things, notwithstanding their hypocrisy.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple imagery and revelation, the priesthood and the covenant are inseparable. The enemies in verse 18 assume the priesthood will endure—but if the covenant is broken, the priesthood is voided. Doctrine and Covenants 121:37 teaches: 'Behold, all those who preach my gospel, and keep not my commandments...shall lose their power.' The institutional structures (priest, wise counselor, prophet) cannot continue if the people break covenant. The temple covenant is the foundation that sustains all other priesthood functions.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's persecution prefigures Christ's, though Jeremiah survives to witness judgment while Christ is executed. Yet the pattern is similar: the institutional leaders (chief priests, scribes, Pharisees) plot against the one who speaks God's authentic word. In Matthew 12:34, Jesus says, 'Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh,' and in Matthew 15:10-11, he teaches that words from the mouth defile a person. The enemies attack Jesus 'with the tongue'—through slander, false accusation, and mockery (Matthew 26:59-68, 27:29-44). Yet Christ's word cannot be silenced by the tongue of enemies; his resurrection vindicates his word. Ultimately, it is the enemies whose words perish, while Christ's word endures forever (Matthew 24:35).
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to modern disciples who bear testimony of the restored Gospel. Like Jeremiah, we live in an age when the prophetic word is contested. The enemies of the Church use the 'tongue'—media, social criticism, and institutional opposition—to try to undermine the credibility of the prophet and the message. The pattern is identical: the opposition assumes that institutional structures (academia, government, popular opinion) are self-sustaining and that one voice (the prophet) can be safely dismissed. But the central issue is not the strength of institutions but fidelity to God's covenant. The Church does not endure because of superior human wisdom or institutional muscle but because it maintains covenantal relationship with God. For individual members, this verse offers both warning and promise. Warning: be cautious about joining in character assassination or spreading slander against God's servants (Doctrine and Covenants 76:103 warns against those who 'lie and deceive'). Promise: those who stand with the prophetic word, even when attacked by the tongue, are standing on the side of truth. The enemies of Jeremiah could not prevent his word from coming to pass; the judgment he announced occurred, vindicating him. Similarly, the word of living prophets will prove true, and those who opposed it will be judged. Our responsibility is to sustain the prophet and the priesthood, defend them against slander, and refuse to be silenced by the 'tongues' of the world. In an age of information warfare and rapid spread of lies, defending the prophetic voice requires active loyalty and refusal to participate in character assassination.

text_kjv: Give heed to me, O LORD, and hearken to the voice of them that contend with me.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah abruptly shifts from the narrative account of the potter's house into direct, desperate prayer. The potter passage (verses 1-17) has just illustrated God's power to reshape nations and the futility of Judah's rebellion. Now Jeremiah himself becomes the supplicant, crying out for God's attention in the face of active hostility. This transition is crucial: the prophet who has been announcing God's judgments is now himself under attack from those who reject his message. He appeals to the divine judge to 'pay attention' to him, using language that frames his opponents as legal adversaries in a formal proceeding.

The word yerivai ('my accusers, those who contend with me') imports legal terminology into prayer. In the ancient Near Eastern understanding, a 'riv' is not merely a personal quarrel but a formal lawsuit or formal dispute that requires adjudication by a higher authority. By using this language, Jeremiah is doing what a persecuted prophet must do: he is bringing his case before the ultimate judge. He is not asking for sympathy or comfort, but for God to hear the voice of his legal opponents so that God can render judgment. The prophetic tradition often portrays the prophet standing in God's presence as an advocate—here Jeremiah stands as a defendant seeking vindication.

word_study.meaning: To listen intently, to incline the ear, to pay careful attention. From qashav, meaning to listen with focused intention. The imperative form expresses urgency and desperation.
word_study.significance: This is not a polite request but an urgent plea. The verb suggests that Jeremiah is demanding God's undivided attention in a crisis. In prayer language throughout the Psalms, haqshivah appears when the psalmist is in mortal danger and needs God to listen now.

word_study.meaning: Those who engage in a legal dispute (riv) with me; my adversaries in a lawsuit or formal contention. Riv encompasses both the verbal conflict and the formal legal proceeding.
word_study.significance: By using covenant lawsuit terminology, Jeremiah frames his enemies not as personal opponents but as parties in a formal legal dispute before God. This elevates the conflict to the divine court, where God serves as judge. The Covenant Rendering's translation of 'accusers' captures the prosecutorial dimension of this term.

cross_references.connection: David uses nearly identical language ('Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me') when under persecution, establishing a psalmic pattern of appeal to God as the ultimate arbiter in legal disputes.
Jeremiah later expresses the internal conflict of being called to prophesy while facing rejection and violence from those he was sent to warn, deepening the context of this prayer.
Nephi describes his brethren's contention against him, using similar covenant-legal language, showing how Book of Mormon prophets faced the same pattern of persecution as Old Testament prophets.
Joseph Smith's petition to God from Liberty Jail uses similar urgent language calling God to 'hear' his plea, establishing a pattern of latter-day prophetic petition under persecution.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern legal contexts, bringing a case before a deity was the highest appeal. Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts show litigants appealing to gods to judge their cases. Jeremiah's use of this language would have been understood by his contemporaries as placing his accusers on trial before the divine court. The prophet, as God's mouthpiece, would have enjoyed a unique status in such proceedings—his authority derived from standing in God's presence. However, his enemies would have disputed both his prophetic credentials and his message, making this appeal urgent. The phrase 'voice of them that contend with me' suggests multiple opponents—not a single rival but a coalition of hostile voices.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon prophets—Abinadi, Alma, and Nephi—all faced similar persecution from those who rejected their messages. They too had to appeal to God for vindication. Alma's experience in Ammonihah (Alma 8-14) parallels Jeremiah's situation: a prophet rejected and threatened by those he tried to save.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 63:5 presents a similar principle: 'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord.' The legal imagery of standing before God as judge appears throughout D&C sections on persecution and vindication.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The language of standing before the Lord (amdi lefanekha in verse 20) evokes the temple context where prophets and priests stood before God's presence to intercede. Jeremiah's prayer positions him in a temple-like posture—standing in God's presence as an advocate.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's position as a rejected prophet whose message was despised prefigures Christ's rejection by those he came to save. Like Christ in Gethsemane, Jeremiah must appeal to God the Father while facing death threats from those who should have received his witness. The legal language of the riv (lawsuit) anticipates the trial of Jesus, who is the ultimate arbiter of all legal disputes before God.
commentary.application: Members facing opposition or rejection for their faith can learn from Jeremiah's example of bringing the matter directly before God in prayer. Rather than responding to attacks with retaliation or despair, Jeremiah appeals to the divine court. This teaches us that God is aware of contentions against His servants and that prayer is the appropriate response when human adversaries cannot be persuaded. The urgency of 'give heed' and 'hearken' invites us to press our own petitions to God with earnest intensity, trusting Him to know all our circumstances and to judge justly.

text_kjv: Shall evil be recompensed for good? for they have digged a pit for my soul. Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah now presents his case with two devastating arguments. First, he poses a rhetorical question that appeals to divine justice: 'Should evil be repaid for good?' This is not merely personal complaint but an appeal to a fundamental principle of covenant morality—that God's justice requires proportional response. Jeremiah has acted with goodness toward his enemies; they have responded with evil. The imbalance cries out to heaven. Second, he reminds God of his own intercession on behalf of the very people now attacking him. He had 'stood before you to speak on their behalf, to turn your wrath away from them.' This is the heart of the lament: Jeremiah has played the role of mediator, pleading with God to spare Judah, yet those he saved are now seeking his death.

The metaphor of digging a pit is vivid and ancient. In the ancient Near East, hunters and warriors would dig deep pits to trap enemies or wild beasts, then cover them with branches and dirt so the victim would fall in unaware. Jeremiah's enemies have done this to him—secretly plotting his downfall. But the pit is also a symbol of Sheol, the grave, the realm of death. By digging a pit for his soul (nephesh), they are attempting to consign him to death itself. The cruelty is compounded because Jeremiah has stood before God interceding for these very people. The ingratitude is cosmic in scope.

word_study.meaning: They have dug / excavated a pit or trap-pit. Karu is the past tense of karah (to dig, to bore). Shuchah refers to a deep hole, particularly a trap-pit used for hunting or warfare. The imagery suggests deliberate, premeditated harm.
word_study.significance: This metaphor appears throughout biblical literature for setting traps for enemies (Psalm 35:7, 57:6, 119:85). It expresses the sense of hidden, calculated danger. The verb karu implies sustained effort—this is not a sudden attack but a deliberate plot. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the trap metaphor, making clear that Jeremiah's enemies are engaged in planned destruction.

word_study.meaning: I stood in your presence, I took my stand before you. Amad means to stand, to take a position, to assume a role. Standing before God in this context is technical language for prophetic intercession—the mediatorial posture of one who stands in God's presence on behalf of others.
word_study.significance: This phrase is crucial for understanding the prophet's role in covenant life. To stand before God (amad lefanei YHWH) is to occupy the position of intercessor, advocate, and mediator. Moses stood before God to intercede for Israel (Exodus 32:11); Jeremiah does the same for Judah. The phrase appears in 15:1 and 23:18, marking the authentic prophet as one who has access to God's presence and uses that access to plead for others. Standing before God is an earned privilege of the righteous mediator.

word_study.meaning: To speak goodness/blessing on their behalf, to utter words of favor or intercession for them. Daber means to speak or utter; tovah means good, blessing, welfare. Combined, this means to advocate for someone's welfare before God.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah emphasizes that his intercession was active and intentional—he used his prophetic voice to speak blessing on Judah. This is the opposite of what Jeremiah's public message was often required to be (judgment, warning, threat). But in his private intercession, he switched roles to become their advocate. This shows the complexity of the prophetic calling: publicly announcing judgment while privately interceding for mercy.

word_study.meaning: To turn back, to reverse, to cause to return. Cham means heat or wrath; matekha is 'your' in construct. The phrase means to avert or deflect God's burning anger away from the target.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah claims to have been an effective intercessor—his prayers actually 'turned away' God's wrath. This implies that without his intercession, God's judgment would have fallen. By reminding God of this, Jeremiah is saying: 'Your mercy toward this people came through my advocacy. And now they attack me.'

cross_references.connection: The psalmist uses identical pit-imagery ('Let destruction come upon him at unawares') and asks God to judge those who dig traps for the righteous, providing a parallel psalmic prayer structure.

God tells Jeremiah, 'Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind could not be toward this people'—establishing that even the greatest intercessors have limits, which makes Jeremiah's current powerlessness less shocking.

Moses stands before God to intercede for Israel after the golden calf incident, using similar mediatorial language and successfully turning away God's wrath—establishing the biblical precedent for prophetic intercession.

Samuel intercedes for Israel and offers a burnt offering, and God responds with deliverance—showing that prophetic intercession can have concrete results, which heightens the irony of Jeremiah's current persecution by those he saved.

Amulek teaches that Christ's intercession is eternal and all-sufficient, pointing forward to the ultimate mediator, which contextualizes Jeremiah's intercessory role as foreshadowing Christ's perpetual advocacy.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, intercession was a recognized and valued role. Kings and priests were expected to intercede with the gods on behalf of their people. Hammurabi's Code emphasizes the king's obligation to secure divine favor for his subjects. In Israel, the prophet was the person most likely to have direct access to God's will, and therefore the most likely person to intercede. The expectation was reciprocal: the people should honor and protect the prophet because the prophet's prayers sustained the nation's covenant relationship. Jeremiah's enemies violate this ancient principle by attacking the very one whose intercession has preserved them. The pit-trap metaphor was familiar to ancient Near Eastern warfare: Mesopotamian texts describe siege tactics involving concealed pits to catch enemy soldiers.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Abinadi's experience in Mosiah 13-17 parallels Jeremiah's: Abinadi intercedes prophetically for Judah (here, the Nephites) by warning them to repent, but is condemned to death by those he sought to save. His final prayer before execution mirrors this complaint about being repaid evil for good.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 122:7-9 presents a similar theme: the Lord's servants may face persecution even when they act with integrity and good intentions. The Lord's promise is vindication, not immediate relief. D&C 124:49 emphasizes that the Lord knows the hearts of those who persecute His servants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The intercessory role Jeremiah claims—standing before God on behalf of others—is exactly the mediatorial function Christ performs in the temple covenant. Members who intercede in prayer for others and for nations are participating in the same mediatorial tradition Jeremiah practiced.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate intercessor standing before God on behalf of His people. Like Jeremiah, Christ intercedes for those who reject and attack Him. John 17 presents Christ's intercessory prayer for His disciples and for all who will believe through them. Yet unlike Jeremiah, whose intercession is limited and whose enemies triumph temporarily, Christ's intercession is eternal and efficacious. The pit that enemies dig becomes the means of Christ's redemption—His descent into death becomes the mechanism of salvation.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a profound principle about faithfulness: doing good does not guarantee that others will reciprocate with good. Jeremiah has been faithful in his prophetic intercession, yet faces betrayal. Members of the Church may experience similar injustice—serving faithfully, giving generously, interceding sincerely, only to face rejection or betrayal. The appropriate response is not bitterness but persistence in appealing to God's justice. The verse invites us to trust that God sees and remembers our faithfulness even when others forget it. Our standing before God is what matters, not others' ingratitude.

text_kjv: Therefore deliver up their children to the famine, and pour out their blood by the force of the sword; and let their wives be bereaved of their children, and be widows; and let their men be put to death; let their young men be slain by the sword in battle.

commentary.narrative:
Now Jeremiah enters into full imprecatory prayer—a prayer that calls down curses and judgment on enemies. This verse cannot be softened or spiritualized away; it must be read as Jeremiah literally requesting God to destroy his enemies' families through famine, sword, and war. Every segment of society is targeted: children starving, wives bereaved and widowed, husbands struck down by death, young men slaughtered in battle. This is a prayer for total annihilation of a people's future. To modern ears, this seems shockingly violent and vengeful. Yet to understand this passage, we must recognize that imprecatory prayers appear throughout the Psalms (35, 69, 109, 137) and were considered a legitimate form of prayer in ancient Israel—not because the psalmist was expressing private revenge fantasies, but because the conflict was understood as a cosmic struggle between God's justice and human wickedness. Jeremiah is not plotting violence; he is calling on God to enact justice. He is placing the matter entirely in God's hands and allowing God's judgment to fall where it may.

The progression of devastation in this verse mirrors the structure of ancient Near Eastern curse formulas. Just as covenants often included curses for covenant-breakers (Deuteronomy 28), so imprecatory prayers follow a pattern of total destruction—no member of the enemy's household escapes. The verb 'pour out' (hagirem) is particularly striking: it treats human lives as liquid to be spilled and wasted. The image suggests utter disposability and powerlessness. This escalation from verse 20 (the hidden pit they dug) to verse 21 (their total destruction) shows the intensity of Jeremiah's emotional and spiritual response to betrayal.

word_study.meaning: To give, to hand over, to surrender. In this context, it is a jussive (wish-form) expressing Jeremiah's urgent request that God give/hand over his enemies' children to famine. The simplicity of the verb contrasts with the terrible consequences it invokes.
word_study.significance: This is not a description of what will happen but a prayer-request for what should happen. The jussive form expresses the prophet's wish that God enact justice. The verb ten appears throughout imprecatory psalms in the same way.

word_study.meaning: To pour out, to spill, to shed. From garah, meaning to cause to flow or to spill. Here it is used with dam (blood), creating the image of blood spilled like liquid. The term emphasizes the violent dispersion and waste of life.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'pour them out' captures the sense of disposal and dehumanization. Lives are treated as commodities to be poured out and wasted. This extreme language reflects the extremity of Jeremiah's betrayal.

word_study.meaning: Bereaved, childless, deprived of children. From shakol, meaning to be robbed of children or to miscarry. This term appears in contexts of ultimate maternal tragedy (Rachel weeping for her children, Jeremiah 31:15).
word_study.significance: By praying for wives to be 'childless and widowed' simultaneously, Jeremiah is praying for the most complete family destruction imaginable in an ancient context. Women without husbands and without children had no legal protection or livelihood. This reflects the ancient understanding that a widow's status is directly connected to her children's survival and status.

word_study.term_english: young men slain by sword in battle
word_study.meaning: Their young men struck down / smitten by the sword in warfare. Bachurim (youths, young warriors) are the most valuable segment of a society. Mukkei (struck, smitten) uses the language of being struck down by weapons. Milchama refers to warfare or battle.
word_study.significance: The targeting of bachurim (young men) is deliberate: these are the soldiers, the future of the nation, the defenders and rebuilders. By praying for their destruction in battle, Jeremiah is praying for the complete collapse of his enemies' society and future capacity to resist or recover.

cross_references.connection: This imprecatory psalm contains nearly identical curse formulas ('Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow; Let his children be continually vagabonds, and beg') and provides the cultural context for Jeremiah's imprecatory language.
The curse formulas of the Deuteronomic covenant include famine, sword, death, and bereavement, establishing a biblical precedent that Jeremiah is drawing upon in his imprecatory prayer.
Jeremiah has previously prayed for judgment on his persecutors ('Let me see thy vengeance on them'), showing this imprecatory prayer is consistent with his earlier laments.

Alma prays for God to confound the Zoramites and 'cause that their hearts may be hardened,' showing Book of Mormon prophets also calling for divine judgment on those who reject truth, though using different imagery.

commentary.historical_context: Imprecatory prayer was a recognized and legitimate form of address to God in ancient Israel. Curse formulas appear in treaties and covenants throughout the ancient Near East as consequences for covenant-breaking. Egyptian texts show individuals calling on the gods to curse those who wronged them. In Israel's covenant framework, Deuteronomy 28 spells out the curses that will fall on covenant-breakers: famine, sword, destruction of family. Jeremiah is drawing on this covenantal vocabulary. The progression of destruction in verse 21—famine (agricultural collapse), sword (military defeat), family destruction (loss of heirs)—represents the total collapse of society according to ancient Near Eastern curse logic. The targeting of all family members and all age groups reflects the ancient understanding that justice required not just the punishment of the wrongdoer but the removal of the entire lineage, so that wickedness would not be perpetuated. This was not considered inhumane but just in the ancient world.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi prays for the destruction of his brethren and then implements it through the sword (2 Nephi 5). Alma calls for divine judgment on the Zoramites (Alma 31:30-35). These examples show that Book of Mormon prophets also called for God's judgment on those who rejected truth, though the outcomes differed. The pattern of imprecatory prayer as a legitimate prophetic response to rejection is consistent across scripture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76 presents God's judgment on those who reject the testimony of the prophets, with consequences that extend through eternity. The principle of proportional judgment is maintained: those who reject light and truth face specific consequences. D&C 63:32-34 shows God's justice being enacted against those who reject the prophets' words.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imprecatory prayer in verse 21 is not about personal revenge but about covenant justice. In the temple covenant, we learn that God's justice must be satisfied—that wickedness cannot go unpunished. Jeremiah's prayer is an appeal to that cosmic justice.

commentary.christological_typology: Unlike Jeremiah, who calls for the judgment and destruction of his enemies, Jesus on the cross prays, 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do' (Luke 23:34). This represents the ultimate contrast between old covenant imprecatory prayer and new covenant redemptive sacrifice. Christ does not ask for His enemies' destruction but for their salvation. Yet the judgment Jeremiah calls for in this verse does prefigure the final judgment of God on those who persistently reject truth—a judgment that will be enacted, though not necessarily through Jeremiah's enemies' destruction in his lifetime.
commentary.application: This verse is difficult for modern readers because it seems to contradict Christian principles of forgiveness. However, it teaches an important truth: God is a God of justice, and injustice is not neutral in God's sight. The prayer reminds us that wrongs done to God's servants matter to God. While we should not harbor personal revenge fantasies, we can and should trust that God sees all injustice and will eventually vindicate the righteous and judge the wicked. The imprecatory prayer invites us to place our cases in God's hands rather than taking matters into our own hands. It also reminds us that choosing to reject God's messengers has ultimate consequences. In our own lives, we can learn that calling on God for justice is appropriate when we have been betrayed, as long as we leave the implementation to God and do not try to enact revenge ourselves.

text_kjv: Let a cry be heard from their houses, when thou shalt bring a troop suddenly upon them: for they have digged a pit to take me, and hid snares for my feet.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 22 intensifies the imprecatory prayer by adding auditory imagery—the 'scream' (ze'aqah) that will be heard from houses when God brings sudden destruction. This is not a quiet judgment but a violent, visible, audible catastrophe. The verb 'bring a troop suddenly upon them' (tavi gedud pitom) suggests a military assault that comes without warning. The homes that once seemed secure will become places of terror and mourning. The genius of this verse is the circular logic: just as Jeremiah's enemies dug hidden traps for him (verse 20), so God will spring a hidden ambush on them. What was meant as a trap becomes the means of their own destruction. The snares they laid for his feet will become the occasion of their own downfall. This reflects the biblical principle that those who dig pits for others often fall into them themselves (Psalm 7:15-16, Proverbs 26:27).

The word gedud (raiding band, troop) suggests a military force—possibly Babylonian raiders in the context of Jeremiah's historical moment. But Jeremiah is not predicting a specific military campaign; he is asking God to bring sudden military assault as judgment. The adverb 'suddenly' (pitom) emphasizes that there will be no escape, no time to prepare defenses. The parallelism between trap-setting and sudden assault creates a poetic justice: those who operate in darkness and deception will face sudden, overwhelming judgment. This verse combines the threat of famine and sword from verse 21 with the specific memory of the hidden pit from verse 20, creating a complex image of divine justice responding to human wickedness.

word_study.meaning: Let a cry, scream, or shout be heard. Tishmae is from shamea (to hear, to listen). Ze'aqah refers to a loud cry, especially a cry of distress or terror. Combined, this means: let the sound of anguished screaming be heard.
word_study.significance: The focus on auditory horror emphasizes that judgment will be public, undeniable, and devastating. The 'scream' is not a call for help (which could be answered) but a shriek of terror and pain. The Covenant Rendering's 'scream' is more visceral than the KJV's 'cry.'

word_study.term_original: תָּבִיא עֲלֵיהֶם גְּדוּד פִּתְאֹם (tavi aleihem gedud pitom)
word_study.meaning: To bring upon them a raiding band / military troop suddenly / unexpectedly. Tavi (to bring, to bring upon). Gedud refers to a band of soldiers, raiders, or a troop. Pitom means suddenly, unexpectedly, without warning.
word_study.significance: Gedud specifically refers to military raids or bands of soldiers, often in the context of siege warfare. In Jeremiah's historical context, this would evoke Babylonian siege warfare. The adverb pitom emphasizes that judgment comes without warning—no time to negotiate, escape, or prepare defenses.

word_study.meaning: They hid / buried snares / traps. Pachim (plural of pach) refers to snares, traps, or nets. Tamnu is from taman (to hide, to bury, to conceal).
word_study.significance: Snares (pachim) and pits (shuchah) work together in trap-setting: the pit is the large trap, the snares are smaller traps. The verb tamnu (they hid) emphasizes the deliberate concealment and premeditation. The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'hidden snares for my feet.'

cross_references.connection: This psalm articulates the principle that 'He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head'—the exact principle Jeremiah is appealing to.
'Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him'—a wisdom principle that Jeremiah's prayer applies to his specific situation.
Jeremiah has previously warned Judah that God will 'bring a nation from the north' with horses and chariots—showing that military invasion is Jeremiah's typical language for God's judgment on Judah.
Nephi is shown that those who fight against the righteous 'shall be destroyed,' a pattern of divine judgment protecting God's servants that Jeremiah is appealing to in his prayer.

commentary.historical_context: The 'troop' (gedud) language reflects the military reality of Jeremiah's time. Judah was surrounded by predatory empires: Assyria had already conquered the northern kingdom, and Babylon was rising to power. The language of sudden military raids ('pitom') reflects actual siege warfare tactics where forces would appear suddenly to take cities. Homes in besieged cities would indeed become places of terror where families heard the screams of neighbors and loved ones dying. The image of 'a cry from their houses' is not hyperbolic but realistic for siege warfare. In ancient warfare, the homes of the conquered were often centers of atrocity. The trap metaphor (pit and snares) was familiar to military contexts as well—ancient Near Eastern texts describe siege trenches, hidden stakes, and ambush tactics.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes military judgment falling on those who reject God's prophets. When the Lamanites attack the Nephites, or when Nephites turn to wickedness and face destruction, the pattern follows this trajectory: rejection of the prophet leads to military devastation. Alma 48-49 describes battles where the righteous are preserved and the wicked destroyed.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:19-20 describes the judgments that will come on those who reject truth: 'But I say unto you, that all those who reject my gospel are under condemnation; And these signs shall follow them that believe.' The principle of judgment following rejection of truth is maintained.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The principle of justice and recompense is central to temple doctrine. In the temple, we learn that wickedness cannot go unpunished and that God's justice must be satisfied. Jeremiah's prayer appeals to this cosmic principle of divine justice.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ experienced sudden violent attack when He was arrested without warning in Gethsemane. The screams of anguish in verse 22 anticipate the cries from Golgotha—yet these were the cries of the innocent, not the guilty. Jesus' suffering reverses the logic of verse 22: instead of the wicked being brought down suddenly, the innocent are brought down suddenly so that the wicked might be saved. Yet the principle remains: God's judgment is sudden, inescapable, and comes from sources the enemy does not expect.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that hidden wickedness will eventually be exposed and judged. Those who plot in secret against God's servants should recognize that God sees all and will bring judgment. For members of the Church, this verse reassures us that persecution and injustice do not go unnoticed by God. We need not fear those who set traps for us; instead, we can trust that God will bring His judgment on those who persistently reject truth and harm His servants. The verse also invites us to examine our own lives: Are we setting traps for anyone? Are we plotting in darkness? The judgment Jeremiah calls for on his enemies should remind us that God's eye is on all our actions, whether public or hidden.

text_kjv: Yet, LORD, thou knowest all their counsel against me to slay me: forgive not their iniquity, neither blot out their sin from thy sight, but let them be overthrown before thee; deal thus with them in the time of thine anger.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 23 brings Jeremiah's imprecatory prayer to its climax and conclusion. He opens with 'Yet, LORD, thou knowest'—an appeal to God's omniscience. God knows what Jeremiah's enemies are plotting against him; their schemes are not hidden from the divine judge. This knowledge is both a comfort and a foundation for the prayer that follows. Jeremiah then makes an extraordinary request: 'Do not atone for their iniquity, and do not wipe out their sin from your sight.' This is not a prayer asking God to forgive his enemies, but literally the opposite—a prayer asking God to refuse to forgive them, to leave their guilt fully exposed before the divine throne.

The two verbs in this request are crucial: kippur (atone, cover) and machah (blot out, wipe away). Both appear in the sacrificial and redemptive language of scripture. Kippur is the root of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, when the High Priest would 'cover' (kappar) the sins of Israel by making atonement. Machah means to wipe away or erase, as in 'blotting out' sin from the record. By asking God to refuse both of these actions, Jeremiah is asking that his enemies' sins remain permanently exposed, permanently unwiped, with no sacrificial remedy available to them. This is a prayer for permanent, unmitigated guilt—not temporary judgment, but exclusion from God's mercy. The final phrase, 'deal with them in the time of your anger' (be'et appekha aseh bahem), leaves the details to God's wrath. Jeremiah has presented his case and made his request; now he leaves the execution entirely to God.

The structure of this verse is crucial: it is not a prayer that God simply judge and punish the enemies (which might happen), but that God specifically refuse the mechanisms of mercy and atonement. This raises the theological question: Can God refuse to atone? Can God deny atonement to those who reject Him? The prayer seems to acknowledge that yes, God can and does. Those who persist in wickedness and rejection of God's messengers can place themselves in a position where the normal paths to forgiveness are closed off.

word_study.meaning: You have known all their counsel / plans / schemes. Yada (to know) in the perfect tense indicates complete, comprehensive knowledge. Atzah (counsel, plan, scheme) refers to deliberate plotting.
word_study.significance: The assertion of God's omniscience is the foundation of the entire prayer. Jeremiah is saying: God, you know exactly what they are planning against me. There is no confusion, no hidden motive that escapes God. This appeal to divine omniscience grounds the prayer in justice rather than revenge.

word_study.meaning: Do not atone, do not cover, do not make atonement. Kappar (to cover, to atone) is the root of kippur (atonement). The verb literally means to cover over or to wipe clean. In cultic contexts, it means to make atonement through sacrifice. The negative form (al-tekapper) asks God NOT to perform this covering-action.
word_study.significance: This is perhaps the most extraordinary request in scripture. Instead of praying for forgiveness, Jeremiah prays for the refusal of forgiveness. The Covenant Rendering notes emphasize that kippur is the root of Yom Kippur—the Day of Atonement. By asking God not to kappar (atone/cover) for his enemies' sin, Jeremiah is asking for the exclusion of his enemies from Yom Kippur itself, from the mechanism of atonement. This is a prayer for permanent guilt.

word_study.meaning: Do not blot out, do not wipe away, do not erase. Machah means to wipe, to erase, to blot out. In biblical language, when a name is 'blotted out,' it means the person is erased from existence or memory. When sin is 'blotted out,' it means the record of sin is erased.
word_study.significance: Combined with al-tekapper, this creates a double request: not only should their sin not be covered (kappar), but it should not be wiped away (machah). The sins should remain fully visible and fully recorded before God.

word_study.meaning: Stumbling, overthrown, made to fall. From kashal (to stumble, to be made to fall). The image is of being tripped and falling helplessly.
word_study.significance: The verb carries the sense of being made to fall or stumble—not standing on firm ground but falling prostrate before God. The Covenant Rendering's 'brought down' captures the sense of being lowered, defeated, made powerless.

word_study.meaning: In the time of your anger / at the moment of your wrath. Ap (anger, wrath, fury) is often described as God's divine response to sin. The phrase 'time of anger' suggests a specific moment when God's judgment falls.
word_study.significance: By asking God to 'deal with them in the time of your anger,' Jeremiah is asking that the specific judgment he has described (famine, sword, family destruction, screams from houses) be enacted when God's wrath is kindled. He leaves the timing and full details to God, but the intensity to God's fury.

cross_references.connection: The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) is described: 'For on that day shall the priest make an atonement for you, to cleanse you, that ye may be clean from all your sins before the LORD.' Jeremiah's prayer asks that this atonement be withheld from his enemies.

The psalmist prays, 'Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me'—the opposite of Jeremiah's prayer. David prays not to be cast away from God's mercy; Jeremiah prays that his enemies will be cast away from mercy.

God says, 'I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake'—showing that God's willingness to blot out sin is an act of divine grace. Jeremiah prays for this grace to be refused to his enemies.

If we 'sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins'—which echoes the principle Jeremiah appeals to: that persistent rejection of God can result in the closing off of mercy.

Those who reject the light and truth receive according to their deeds, and for them there is 'no forgiveness in this world nor in the world to come'—establishing the Restoration principle that persistent rejection of truth results in exclusion from mercy.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite legal and cultic contexts, both the atonement (kapparah) and the blotting out of sin were understood as divine actions performed by God or God's representative. The High Priest on Yom Kippur performed the kapparah (atonement/covering) ritual. Record-keepers would 'blot out' (machah) names from records when people were to be erased or forgotten. Jeremiah's prayer reflects an understanding that God could refuse these actions—that God's mercy was not automatic but conditional on repentance. In ancient Near Eastern legal contexts, once judgment was rendered by a judge, it was final. Jeremiah is asking God to render final judgment with no avenue for appeal or remedy through sacrifice or atonement.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon's editorial comments in the Book of Mormon (especially Mormon 3:12, Mormon 8:41) suggest that those who persistently reject God's servants and God's truth can place themselves in a position where mercy is withdrawn. The Lamanites' repeated rejection of prophets eventually led to the spiritual destruction of the Nephite nation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:32-35 teaches that 'all things are spiritual unto me; and all things are to me spiritual' and 'whatever thing ye ask the Father in my name in faith, believing that ye shall receive, behold it shall be done unto you.' However, D&C 76:31-37 and D&C 132:26-27 show that those who reject the covenants and knowledge they have received face eternal consequences with 'no forgiveness in this world nor in the world to come.' The principle that mercy can be withheld from those who persistently reject is established in D&C.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant involves receiving the knowledge and power of God. Jeremiah's prayer reflects an understanding that knowledge once received creates accountability, and that those who persistently reject God after receiving knowledge face not mere temporal judgment but eternal separation from God's mercy. The garment of the holy priesthood has a specific symbolism related to covenant faithfulness; those who betray covenant and prophet face the withdrawal of covenantal protection.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's final prayer before crucifixion in John 17 stands in sharp contrast to Jeremiah's imprecatory prayer. Jeremiah prays that his enemies be denied atonement; Christ prays for His enemies' salvation: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.' Yet both prayers appeal to God the Father as the ultimate judge. Christ's sacrifice becomes the means by which atonement is offered to all, including those who reject it. However, Hebrews 10:26 affirms that there remains no sacrifice for those who 'sin willfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth'—suggesting that Jeremiah's principle is also operative in the new covenant. Christ's mercy is universal in its offer but not in its receipt; those who persistently reject it place themselves outside its operation.
commentary.application: This verse presents a difficult theological question for modern disciples: What happens when we persistently reject God's mercies and God's servants? The verse suggests that there is a point at which persistent rejection can result in the withdrawal of God's mercy—not because God is vindictive but because the person has placed themselves outside the conditions necessary for mercy to operate. For modern members, this verse teaches humility about our accountability. We should examine ourselves: Are we like Jeremiah's enemies, who plot against the Lord's servants? Or are we receiving the prophets' testimonies and repenting when corrected? The verse also teaches that God's judgments are real and serious. Mockery of the prophets, persecution of the righteous, and persistent rejection of God's word have ultimate consequences. We should never take our covenants lightly or assume that we can indefinitely reject truth without facing judgment. Finally, the verse teaches us that we can trust God's justice completely. When we have been wronged and our enemies seem to prosper, we can bring our case before the Lord and trust that God knows all counsels and will judge justly—in His own time and according to His own justice.

text_kjv: Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the LORD, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things.

commentary.narrative:
Pashhur son of Immer enters the narrative as a man of considerable institutional power. His title, paqid nagid ('chief officer'), indicates he held both administrative oversight and ruling authority over the temple compound—he was not a minor functionary but the senior official responsible for maintaining order in the sacred precincts. The Covenant Rendering clarifies that this title conveys supervisory authority (from paqad, 'to appoint, oversee') combined with ruling power (from nagid, 'ruler, leader, prince'). When Pashhur heard Jeremiah prophesying the words recorded in chapters 1-19 (likely referring to the oracles against Judah's religious leadership and the certainty of Babylonian judgment), he recognized an immediate threat to his authority and the temple's reputation.

This verse establishes the fundamental conflict: a priest invested in maintaining the status quo encounters a prophet calling for radical repentance and announcing divine judgment. Pashhur's position meant that he had personal, institutional, and possibly theological stakes in silencing Jeremiah. The structure of the sentence—'when...heard...Jeremiah prophesying these words'—flows directly into verse 2, creating syntactic unity that emphasizes how hearing the prophecy immediately prompted violent action. There is no deliberation, no prayer, no discernment. The institutional guardian of the temple responds to prophetic truth with force.

word_study.meaning: Chief officer; a compound title indicating both supervisory authority (paqid from paqad, 'to appoint, oversee') and ruling/leadership power (nagid, 'ruler, prince, leader'). This person wielded both administrative and coercive authority over temple operations and personnel.
word_study.significance: Pashhur was not a subordinate functionary but the chief administrator of the temple compound, invested with authority to discipline, restrain, and punish those who disrupted temple order. His power is institutional and absolute within his domain. This makes his violent response to Jeremiah not merely personal anger but an exercise of institutional prerogative.

word_study.meaning: He prophesied; the Niphal form of the root naba, indicating he was engaged in the act of speaking prophetic words. The Niphal voice can suggest compulsion or divine enabling—the prophet does not merely choose to speak, but is driven or empowered to do so.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah's prophecy was not a private speculation but a public proclamation. Pashhur's violence was thus not a private reprimand but a public silencing—an attempt to end Jeremiah's prophetic ministry through coercion and humiliation within the very temple where he spoke.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah is called to proclaim God's word despite fierce opposition; this encounter with Pashhur is the fulfillment of that warning that 'they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail.'
The pattern of Israel's rejection of prophets: 'But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words...until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people.'

Micaiah the prophet is struck and imprisoned by Zedekiah for refusing to prophesy smooth things; institutional religious authority historically resisted true prophecy in favor of comfortable falsehoods.

The father of Amulek, an officer in the synagogue, 'had much power and authority among the people,' similar to Pashhur's position, demonstrating how institutional authority can be wielded against those who speak uncomfortable truth.

commentary.historical_context: The role of paqid in ancient Near Eastern temple administration is well documented in Ugaritic and Egyptian temple records. Pashhur's position parallels that of temple administrators in Egypt and Mesopotamia—officials responsible not only for sacred functions but for maintaining order, managing personnel, and protecting the institution's reputation. By the late 7th century BCE, when this encounter likely occurred, Judah was experiencing the existential threat of Babylonian expansion under Nebuchadnezzar II. Optimistic prophets were telling the people that the temple would be inviolable and the monarchy would endure (cf. Jer. 23:17), while Jeremiah was prophesying the opposite. Pashhur's violent response reflects not merely personal resentment but institutional panic—the temple's chief officer was defending what he believed to be true against a prophet he dismissed as a doomsayer.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon presents repeated patterns of institutional religious authority opposing prophetic truth: the high priests of the Nephites oppressing Alma and Amulek (Alma 12-14), and Koriantumr's princes rejecting the prophetic warnings of Ether (Ether 11-13). Each case shows that proximity to institutional religious power correlates with resistance to genuine revelation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 warns that the Church president must be 'obedient to [the Lord's] commandments' and that revelation comes through 'the weak things of the world' (D&C 64:2)—a principle that guards against exactly the institutional rigidity Pashhur exemplifies. The contrast between Pashhur (who defends institutional prerogative) and Jeremiah (who speaks for God regardless of institutional cost) defines the Restoration principle that 'whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same' (D&C 1:38).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Paradoxically, Pashhur's abuse of authority occurred within the temple itself, 'in the house of the LORD.' The temple, meant to be a place of revelation and covenant renewal, became an instrument of oppression. This foreshadows the temple's destruction that Jeremiah announces—not because the building or the cult are inherently profaned, but because the people and their leadership have rejected the God the temple supposedly represented.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah prefigures Christ's experience: both were rejected by the institutional religious authorities of their time, both proclaimed a message of repentance that threatened established power, both were opposed precisely because they spoke truth that contradicted the comfortable message the institutions preferred. Christ's words in Matthew 23:29-36 about the prophets' persecution anticipates Jeremiah's experience with Pashhur.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse exposes a spiritual danger: the correlation between institutional authority and spiritual perception. Pashhur's position in the temple did not make him spiritually sensitive; it made him spiritually defensive. We must examine whether our confidence in institutional roles (whether formal or informal authority in families, communities, or wards) ever makes us resistant to uncomfortable prophetic truth. How do we respond when truth challenges our preferred narrative? Do we listen or react?

text_kjv: Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
Pashhur's response to Jeremiah's prophecy is immediate and violent. The verb vayakkeh ('he struck') indicates repeated blows, not a single blow—the same verb is used for military striking and judicial punishment throughout the Hebrew Bible. This is a beating. The deliberation takes no longer than it takes to hear the prophecy; institutional power meets prophetic speech with physical force.

Jeremiah is then placed in the mahpekhet—a wooden restraining device that twisted the body into a contorted, agonizing position. The Covenant Rendering identifies that the root hafakh means 'to turn, overturn, twist,' so the stocks were an instrument of both confinement and deliberate infliction of pain. The location—the Upper Benjamin Gate of the temple compound—is significant: this is not a distant dungeon but a public place, ensuring maximum humiliation. The phrase 'which was by the house of the LORD' underscores the shocking irony: a prophet is being tortured in the very temple that is supposed to be God's house. Pashhur uses his institutional authority not to defend the sacred precincts but to violate them by torturing a servant of God within them.

The physical punishment serves multiple purposes: it silences Jeremiah temporarily, it humiliates him publicly before the worshipers, and it warns anyone else thinking of accepting Jeremiah's message what the cost will be. It is institutional violence dressed in the language of order and propriety. Pashhur is not acting lawlessly—he is acting from his position of lawful authority.

word_study.meaning: He struck, beat, or smote; the Qal imperfect form of the root nakah ('to strike, smite, hit'). In other contexts, this verb describes military strikes (2 Sam. 2:31), judicial beatings (Deut. 25:2), and divine judgment (Exod. 12:12). The same verb describes both cosmic and corporal violence.
word_study.significance: Vayakkeh is not a gentle push or a single blow but a beating. The institutional authority behind it—Pashhur's position as chief officer—makes it an official act, not a private assault. The prophet's body becomes the canvas for institutional disapproval.

word_study.meaning: Stocks; from the root hafakh ('to turn, overturn, twist'). Unlike stocks that merely restrain (as in Acts 16:24), the mahpekhet was designed to twist and contort the body into unnatural positions, combining confinement with deliberate pain.
word_study.significance: The mahpekhet was torture equipment. The Hebrew term itself embeds the idea of inversion—turning the body against itself. Pashhur is not merely imprisoning Jeremiah but inflicting suffering. The choice of this particular instrument signals that humiliation and pain are integral to the punishment, not accidental byproducts.

word_study.meaning: The Upper Benjamin Gate; a specific location in the temple complex identified with the northern entrance and associated with access from the tribe of Benjamin's territory. The adjective 'upper' (elyon) suggests prominence—not a hidden or private location.
word_study.significance: The public location ensures that Jeremiah's suffering is witnessed. This is not punishment administered privately but public humiliation designed to intimidate others and demonstrate Pashhur's power. The association with Benjamin may also carry tribal significance—Benjamin was the tribe of the kings (Saul and David), and the Benjamin Gate may have been a ceremonial or administrative entry point where the powerful demonstrated their authority.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah is again imprisoned by Zedekiah's officials, placed 'in the dungeon, and in the cabins'; repeated persecution by institutional religious authorities characterizes Jeremiah's entire prophetic career.
Paul and Silas are beaten and placed in stocks in Philippi; the same instrument (Greek: xylo) used for torture and humiliation of those proclaiming God's word.
The Chronicler's summary: 'The LORD...sent to them by his messengers...but they mocked the messengers of God and despised his words'—a pattern of institutional resistance to prophetic truth.

Alma and Amulek are imprisoned and forced to watch the burning of believing women and children; institutional religious opposition to true prophets includes violence against both the prophets and those who hear them.

The revelation distinguishing between suffering that comes from resisting God's will and suffering that comes from standing firm: 'They who are sent forth to bear testimony of my name...are called to endure all things in all things.'

commentary.historical_context: Restraining devices called 'stocks' appear in ancient Near Eastern art and literature. The Hebrew mahpekhet belongs to a category of punishment devices designed for public display and deliberate torture. In Egypt and Mesopotamia, such devices were used to humiliate and break prisoners of war, rebellious officials, and those convicted of crimes against the state or gods. The placement of Jeremiah in the stocks at the temple gate follows a recognizable pattern: public exposure as a mechanism of social control. The temple administration had the authority to maintain order and enforce compliance through corporal punishment; what makes this event extraordinary is that they used that authority against a divinely commissioned prophet. The Babylonian threat was real enough by this period (likely the early 6th century BCE, before the final siege of 586) that prophetic words of judgment were politically dangerous—they could demoralize the population or suggest that resistance to Babylon was futile. Pashhur's violence may have seemed to him a patriotic defense of Judah's resolve.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 14:1-10 describes how Alma and Amulek are brought before the chief judge and high priests, and the institutional authorities arrange for the beating and imprisonment of believers. As in Jeremiah's case, institutional religious authority is weaponized against those proclaiming restoration. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that institutions can become tools of opposition to revelation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 122:5-8 contains the Lord's reassurance to Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail that 'all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.' Jeremiah's suffering in the stocks, like Joseph's in Liberty Jail, becomes a crucible that refines prophetic faithfulness rather than breaking it. The Lord does not promise protection from institutional violence but promises that such suffering serves redemptive purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The irony of torture occurring within 'the house of the LORD' points to a principle articulated in D&C 109:16-17: the Lord's house should be 'a place of salvation...where the glory of the Lord shall be displayed.' When institutions use their authority to silence prophetic voices or inflict suffering, they pervert the sacred into the profane. The temple should be the place where revelation is heard; instead, it becomes the place where the prophet is silenced.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's beating and confinement foreshadow Christ's scourging and imprisonment. Both are subjected to institutional religious authority; both are tortured by those claiming to serve God; both experience their suffering within or near sacred spaces (the temple). Christ's suffering is redemptive in a way Jeremiah's is not, but the pattern of institutional opposition to God's true servants reaches its culmination in Christ's passion.
commentary.application: This verse confronts us with the possibility of using institutional authority to silence or persecute those who proclaim uncomfortable truth. It asks: How do we respond when someone's prophetic word contradicts our preferred narrative or threatens our position? Do we listen or do we respond with defensiveness, social pressure, or institutional punishment? The verse also calls us to recognize and honor prophetic voices that may be unpopular or counter-institutional. In modern covenant life, we must distinguish between rightful institutional authority (which serves truth) and institutional coercion (which defends prerogative). Pashhur represents every institutional actor who uses authority to suppress rather than to serve.

text_kjv: And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then said Jeremiah unto him, The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib.
text_kjv_note: The KJV preserves the transliteration 'Magormissabib' for the Hebrew magor missabib.

commentary.narrative:
A full day passes between Jeremiah's placement in the stocks and his release. We have no record of what that day entailed—pain, prayer, despair, or renewed conviction. But when Pashhur releases him (perhaps believing the lesson has been learned), Jeremiah does not respond with gratitude, concession, or fear. Instead, he speaks a prophetic oracle that redefines Pashhur's very identity.

The renaming formula 'The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magor-Missabib' follows a prophetic tradition seen elsewhere in scripture: God calls individuals by new names when their destiny shifts or when they assume new identity and mission (Abram becomes Abraham, Saul becomes Paul, Simon becomes Peter). But Jeremiah's renaming of Pashhur is not a call to a higher calling; it is an oracle of judgment. The name 'Pashur' likely derives from Egyptian p3-šr, 'the son of Horus,' evoking protection, power, and cosmic blessing. 'Magor-Missabib' means 'Terror on Every Side,' a phrase that recurs throughout Jeremiah (6:25, 46:5, 49:29) and connotes inescapable panic, a state in which there is no safe direction to flee.

The prophetic sign-act here is profound: Pashhur, who inflicted terror and confinement, is renamed as Terror itself. He becomes a walking embodiment of the catastrophe he has refused to believe will come. The man who beat the prophet for prophesying judgment will himself become a sign of that judgment. This is not metaphorical curse but prophetic word—the name declares Pashhur's coming fate.

word_study.meaning: Called your name; literally 'he called the name.' In Hebrew thought, a name is not merely a label but an expression of identity and destiny. To 'call' a name (qara, 'to call, proclaim, name') is to define who someone is in God's economy. Only God can truly 'call' a name in this authoritative sense.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah's claim that 'the LORD hath not called thy name Pashur' means that whatever Pashhur thinks his name means or his identity is, God defines it differently. Pashhur's birth name and his self-understanding are overridden by God's designation. The prophet speaks not from personal authority but from the authority of the one who sees and shapes destinies.

word_study.meaning: Terror on Every Side; magor ('terror, dread, fear') + missabib (literally 'from around, from all sides'). The phrase conveys not a single fear but a state of inescapable panic—wherever one looks, whatever direction one tries to flee, only terror awaits. The Covenant Rendering notes that this is a 'characteristic Jeremianic phrase,' appearing also in Psalm 31:14 and in Jeremiah 6:25, 46:5, 49:29, and Lamentations 2:22.
word_study.significance: The name represents a total inversion of the meaning Pashhur's birth name may have carried (protection, divine connection). Instead of safety 'on every side,' he will experience terror 'on every side.' The phrase is not metaphorical anxiety but prophetic description of the terror Pashhur will experience when Babylon comes—a terror so complete and inescapable that it defines his existence. The phrase also echoes in the hearts of all who hear it; it becomes a byname, a reputation. Pashhur will be remembered not for his institutional power but as the embodiment of terror.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah's children are given prophetic names ('Shear-Jashub,' 'Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz') that communicate God's message; names become oracles. Jeremiah follows this prophetic convention, transforming Pashhur's identity into a proclamation.
The phrase 'magor missabib' recurs in a context of military siege: 'Go not forth into the field, nor walk by the way; for the sword of the enemy and terror are on every side.'

The pattern of name-change as identity-transformation: Abram becomes Abraham (father of nations), Jacob becomes Israel (he who wrestles with God). The renaming signals a change in destiny and role within God's economy.

The converse of Pashhur's renaming: the overcomer receives 'a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it'—a name hidden in God's knowledge, connoting dignity and restoration rather than doom.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of prophetic renaming was familiar in the ancient Near East. Both Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts record instances of oracles redefining an individual's name to proclaim coming events. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope and various cuneiform omen texts preserve the principle that a name can encode a person's fate. In Israel, the tradition is evident in the prophets: Hosea names his children with prophetic names (Hos. 1:4-8), Isaiah's sign-children carry messages about the northern kingdom's fate (Isa. 7-8). Jeremiah's renaming of Pashhur would have been recognized by his audience as a classic prophetic sign-act—the word becomes flesh, the name becomes destiny. For Pashhur specifically, hearing himself renamed before witnesses would have been devastating: it means his institutional power, his position, his self-understanding are all eclipsed by God's alternative naming. He cannot unname himself; the oracle stands.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 14:29 records that after institutional religious authorities murder believing women and children and imprison Alma and Amulek, the authorities themselves experience 'terror and amazement' and the earth shakes—a sign that terror will overtake those who persecute God's servants. Like Pashhur, they intended violence but received judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:33 expresses a principle about the limits of institutional power: 'We have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' Pashhur embodies this principle—his authority led him to abuse rather than serve. The Lord's response through Jeremiah is to declare that true authority belongs to the Lord alone, and those who wield institutional power against his servants will find their names and fates rewritten by his judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple, which should be a place of revelation and covenant renewal, was used by Pashhur as an instrument of oppression. By contrast, D&C 110 records the Lord appearing in the Kirtland Temple to accept it as his house. The contrast highlights that a building's holiness depends on whether those who serve in it align with God's will or resist it. Pashhur's occupation of a temple position did not make him holy; in fact, his abuse of his position profaned the place.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's renaming of Pashhur as Terror parallels the principle in Hebrews 10:31 and 12:29—'It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.' The terror Pashhur will experience is not random punishment but the inevitable consequence of resisting the God who works through his prophet. Christ embodies the alternative: those who come to him in faith receive a new name and new identity, but those who oppose him face judgment. The renaming is a confrontation with reality: Pashhur's terror is coming, and he will become its embodiment.
commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse raises uncomfortable questions about identity. What names do we claim for ourselves, and are they God's names for us, or names we have claimed out of pride, position, or preference? Pashhur thought his name meant something (protection, power, divine connection), but God named him differently based on his actions and fate. We must ask: How does the Lord name us? Am I becoming a vessel of his truth or a barrier to it? The verse also speaks to the power of prophetic witness: Jeremiah does not accept Pashhur's violence as the end of the conversation. He speaks one more time, reframing the entire encounter from Pashhur's perspective (I beat you into silence) to God's perspective (I have already determined your fate). In modern covenant life, we must trust that God's word will stand even when institutional authority opposes it, and we must never confuse institutional power with spiritual truth.

text_kjv: For thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will make thee a terror to thyself, and to all thy friends: and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and thine eyes shall behold it: and I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall carry them captive into Babylon, and shall slay them with the sword.

commentary.narrative:
The oracle extends outward from Pashhur to encompass the entire political and military catastrophe to come. The Lord's statement begins with an intensification: not only will Pashhur be renamed Terror, but he will become 'a terror to thyself'—he will be his own source of dread. The psychological and spiritual dissolution is as much the punishment as any external judgment. Then the oracle widens: Pashhur's friends ('all thy friends') will fall by the sword while Pashhur watches. This echoes one of the cruelest aspects of siege warfare in the ancient Near East—survivors were forced to witness the destruction of everyone they loved before experiencing their own death or captivity.

The phrase 'thine eyes shall behold it' is crucial. Pashhur will not be killed quickly or mercifully in battle; he will survive long enough to see the systematic destruction of his social world. His survival becomes its own curse. The oracle then broadens to the national scale: 'I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon.' This is the word Jeremiah has been proclaiming throughout his ministry—that Babylon's conquest is not a possibility but a certainty, not a punishment inflicted by human military might alone but the direct action of God ('I will give').
