The finality of the language leaves no room for hope or resistance: the people will be carried captive to Babylon and 'slain with the sword.' No escape, no miraculous deliverance, no last-minute reversal.

This oracle is not prediction in the sense of informed guessing but declaration. The Lord speaks as one who has already determined the outcome. Pashhur's punishment is set within this larger cosmic reality: Judah will fall because Judah—and its leaders like Pashhur—have rejected the prophetic word and clung to false assurance. Pashhur beat the prophet who proclaimed this; now the prophet declares that Pashhur will witness the very catastrophe he refused to believe.

word_study.meaning: I will make you into terror; the root natan ('to give, make, set') combined with lemagur ('for terror, as terror'). The construction uses the preposition le (often translated 'for' or 'as') to indicate transformation or identity: Pashhur will not merely experience terror but will become terror.
word_study.significance: The verb natan ('to give') places the action squarely in the divine will. God is the active agent; Pashhur is the passive subject being remade. The transformation is total and inevitable. Pashhur has no agency in determining his fate; God has already set it.

word_study.meaning: To you; the prepositional form of the second person singular pronoun. The use of 'to thyself' rather than merely 'terror to thy friends' emphasizes that Pashhur's own consciousness will be the seat of his torment. He will fear himself and his own fate.
word_study.significance: This is not external punishment alone but psychological and spiritual collapse. Pashhur will become internally divided, a source of terror to himself. The blow is aimed at his self-perception and identity—precisely what the renaming predicted.

word_study.meaning: Your eyes watching, your eyes seeing; the present participle form emphasizes ongoing, continuous witnessing. The verb ra'ah ('to see') in this form suggests an active, deliberate viewing rather than passive observation.
word_study.significance: Pashhur will not be spared the sight of destruction. In ancient siege narratives, forced witness was itself a form of torture—surviving prisoners were compelled to view the devastation they had refused to prevent or acknowledge. Pashhur's eyes will be open to the catastrophe his refusal to hear Jeremiah's warning contributed to.

word_study.meaning: The king of Babylon; at the time of Jeremiah's prophecy, this refers specifically to Nebuchadnezzar II, though Jeremiah does not name him. The phrase 'king of Babylon' appears frequently in the prophetic books as shorthand for the instrument of divine judgment against the nations.
word_study.significance: The use of 'the king of Babylon' rather than a mere generic enemy emphasizes that this is not speculation about random misfortune but specific prediction about a particular historical power. The historical accuracy of the prophecy (Babylon did conquer Judah and did deport the population) was later confirmation that Jeremiah spoke truly while Pashhur and other false prophets spoke lies.

cross_references.connection: A parallel oracle in which Jeremiah announces that Judah will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years; Pashhur is not exempt from this national judgment but trapped within it.

The Lord declares that Babylon will siege Jerusalem and Judah will fall into captivity; Jeremiah himself later imprisoned, but reaffirms the prophecy, showing prophetic faithfulness despite institutional pressure.

The covenant curse structure: 'The LORD shall bring thee, and thy king which thou shalt set over thee, unto a nation which neither thou nor thy fathers have known...and there the LORD shall give thee into the hand of thine enemies.'
The historical fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, and the king, nobles, and people are carried into captivity—exactly as Jeremiah proclaimed.

The Lord in the Americas describes how the people of Jerusalem rejected his word and were therefore given into the hands of enemies; spiritual rejection of prophetic words leads to military and political devastation.

commentary.historical_context: By the early 6th century BCE, Babylon was the ascending superpower in the ancient Near East under Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 BCE). Jeremiah's prophecy that Babylon would conquer Judah seemed unlikely to many in his own time—some still held hope that Egypt would defend Judah or that Jerusalem's fortifications were impregnable or that the temple would be divinely protected. False prophets offered reassurance (Jer. 23:16-22): 'Ye shall have peace.' Jeremiah's announcement that Babylon's conquest was determined by the Lord, not merely predicted based on military calculation, would have seemed both tactically defeatist and theologically alarming. By announcing God's gift of Judah to Babylon's king, Jeremiah was saying that the Lord actively willed the conquest. This would explain Pashhur's violent rejection of the prophecy: it was not merely bad news but apparent blasphemy—how could a priest of the Lord speak of God surrendering his people to a foreign king? For Pashhur and the Jerusalem establishment, Jeremiah's words were dangerous propaganda that could demoralize resistance and inspire surrender. They did not recognize them as the word of the Lord because they contradicted their false assurance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 14:11 records that after the high priests and judges imprison Alma and Amulek, they soon experience the very judgment those righteous men had proclaimed: 'I say unto you, they did order them take Alma and Amulek out and bring them forth to the place of execution.' The false leaders who oppose righteous prophets find themselves helpless when the judgment they dismissed actually arrives. Similarly, Pashhur will witness the judgment Jeremiah proclaimed.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:86-91 teaches that when the Lord's people are led by those who love the Lord, they prosper; but when they are led by those who seek power and ignore prophetic counsel, they are given into the hands of enemies. Pashhur represents leadership that pursues institutional prerogative rather than prophetic truth, with catastrophic consequences.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of 'giving' Judah into Babylon's hands involves a profound reversal: the Lord, who 'gave' the land to Israel as a covenant inheritance, now 'gives' it to Babylon because the people have violated covenant. The temple, which should have been the place where covenant faithfulness was renewed, became instead a place where prophetic truth was rejected. When the temple's leadership resists God's word, the land itself is forfeit.

commentary.christological_typology: The judgment announced here—loss of land, captivity, death by the sword, forced witnessing of loved ones' destruction—prefigures the judgment Christ announces in Matthew 23 on the Jerusalem establishment that rejects him. Both Jeremiah and Christ proclaim that institutional religious rejection of God's word leads to national military catastrophe. Both announce their message to those who refuse to hear and respond by persecuting the messenger.
commentary.application: This verse demands that we recognize the power of prophetic witness. Jeremiah did not speak out of anger or personal vendetta against Pashhur but out of faithful proclamation of what the Lord had revealed. The subsequent historical confirmation of the prophecy (Babylon's conquest occurred as predicted) validates Jeremiah's ministry and condemns Pashhur's opposition. For modern believers, this verse teaches that we must take seriously the prophetic word, especially when it contradicts our preferred narrative or asks us to surrender prerogative. It also teaches that there are consequences to refusing to hear the Lord's word through his servants. Finally, it teaches that the Lord's will ultimately stands despite institutional opposition. Pashhur's violence could not silence Jeremiah; it could not prevent Babylon's conquest; it could not stop the fulfillment of God's word. Our faith should rest not in institutions or power but in the Lord and his word.

text_kjv: Moreover I will deliver all the strength of this city, and all the labours thereof, and all the precious things thereof, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah will I give into the hand of their enemies, which shall spoil them, and take them, and carry them to Babylon.

commentary.narrative:
The oracle moves from personal judgment on Pashhur to material destruction of Jerusalem. The threefold accumulation of terms—'strength' (chosen, stored goods and resources), 'labours' (yegia, the fruit of labor and produce), and 'precious things' (yeqarah, valuables)—communicates totality. Nothing of value will remain. The Lord does not speak of merely partial loss or military tribute but complete dispossession. The same pattern repeats: 'all the treasures of the kings of Judah.' The repetition of 'all' creates an overwhelming rhetorical force. Jerusalem will be stripped bare.

The verbs describing the looting—'spoil them, and take them, and carry them to Babylon'—are not accidental word choices. The Covenant Rendering notes that the verb 'uvezazum' ('and they will plunder them') is onomatopoeic in Hebrew, with its buzzing z-sounds mimicking 'the swarming chaos of looting.' The language immerses the listener in the sensory experience of invasion and despoliation. This is not clinical description but visceral encounter with catastrophe. Gold, silver, vessels, implements—everything that represented wealth, power, divine favor, and national identity will be removed to a foreign land.

Why is this relevant to Pashhur's judgment? Because Pashhur himself likely benefited from this wealth. As chief officer of the temple, he may have had access to or responsibility for the treasures housed there. Those very treasures—symbols of the Lord's favor, repositories of religious meaning—will be handed to enemies. The institutional power Pashhur exercised was based partly on access to and control of these sacred valuables. When they are gone, his position becomes meaningless.

word_study.meaning: Strength, wealth, stored goods; from a root suggesting firmness or resistance. Chosen refers to accumulated resources—the material foundation of a city's power and resilience.
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes economic and material resources. Jerusalem's strength is not primarily military or political but economic. By taking this wealth, Babylon removes the material basis for Jerusalem's independence and resilience.

word_study.meaning: Labor, produce, toil, the fruit of work; from a root meaning 'to labor, toil.' Yegia represents not static resources but the ongoing productive capacity—what a people has produced through effort.
word_study.significance: The term shifts from stored wealth to active productivity. Jerusalem's yegia—its fields, harvests, manufactured goods, every product of its people's labor—will be taken. This is not merely confiscating what exists but claiming the right to future production and denying the people the fruit of their work.

word_study.meaning: Precious things, valuables, honor; from a root meaning 'to be heavy, weighty, precious, honored.' Yeqarah encompasses both material valuables and the honor/prestige they represent.
word_study.significance: The term carries both literal and symbolic weight. Precious things are both materially valuable and symbolically important—they represent divine favor, royal power, and national identity. Taking them is not only theft but a claiming of authority over what was sacred.

word_study.meaning: They will plunder them; from the root bazaz, 'to plunder, spoil, take as booty.' The verb appears frequently in descriptions of siege warfare and military conquest.
word_study.significance: The verb is almost onomatopoeic—the repeated 'z' sounds mimic the chaotic swarming of soldiers taking what they will. The Covenant Rendering notes this mimetic quality: the very sounds of the Hebrew language convey the tumultuous reality of looting. We hear what is being described.

cross_references.connection: Historical fulfillment: 'He carried out thence all the treasures of the house of the LORD...and he cut in pieces all the vessels of gold which Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD.'
The grief of the survivor: 'The adversary hath spread out his hand upon all her pleasant things: for she hath seen that the heathen entered into her sanctuary.'
Jeremiah promises that the captured treasures will eventually be restored, but only after the fulfillment of the seventy-year captivity—not a quick recovery but a long humiliation.

A principle about the consequences of rejecting the Lord's word: 'Therefore, let your hearts be deceived no longer, for a fire is kindled in my wrath, the tears of my people have come up into my ears.'  Rejection of prophecy brings material and spiritual loss.

commentary.historical_context: The despoliation of Jerusalem's treasures is historically documented. Babylonian chronicles record that Nebuchadnezzar took the temple vessels and treasures to Babylon after multiple sieges (597 BCE and 586 BCE). The temple vessels and furnishings—the implements of worship, the symbols of the covenant, the gold and silver overlay—were removed and either melted down for their materials or displayed in Babylonian temples as trophies of conquest. For a people whose identity was bound up with the temple and its treasures, this was devastation beyond military defeat. It was the violation of the sacred itself. The treasures, which had been accumulating since Solomon's time (1 Kings 10:14-25), represented centuries of royal wealth and divine blessing according to the people's understanding. The Babylonians' claim to these treasures was a claim to have superseded Israel's God in power and authority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 13:33-35 records that the Lord, through the prophet Samuel, announces the removal of treasures from the Nephites: 'Your gold and your silver shall be hid up in the earth, and ye shall not be able to bring them forth, and ye shall not be able to retain them...for they shall be hid from you.' The pattern is consistent: when a people reject prophetic warning, their treasures become sources of bondage rather than blessing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:35 contains the Lord's warning about why his word must be accepted: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled.' The treasures taken by Babylon represented a failure to heed prophetic word. D&C 64:8-10 teaches that a people's prosperity depends on faithfulness: 'I, the Lord, forgive sins, and am merciful and just; But I cannot look upon sin with allowance.'

commentary.christological_typology: The removal of Jerusalem's treasures to Babylon parallels the judgment described in Matthew 24:2, where Christ predicts the destruction of the temple: 'Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.' Both Jeremiah's prediction and Christ's prediction announce the removal of what the people believed would protect them. Both call for repentance rather than reliance on material edifices.
commentary.application: This verse challenges our relationship with material wealth and security. For Pashhur and the Jerusalem establishment, their treasures were symbols of divine favor and sources of institutional power. Yet all of it was given to enemies. The verse asks: What treasures are we holding to? What security are we building on that might be swept away? For modern covenant members, the verse teaches that true wealth is not material but spiritual—the word of the Lord, faithfulness to covenant, righteous living. Material prosperity is a blessing but can become a curse if it makes us deaf to prophetic warning. We must cultivate the ability to receive prophetic correction, even when it threatens our preferred narrative about our own righteousness or safety.

text_kjv: And thou, Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house shall go into captivity: and thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies.

commentary.narrative:
The oracle circles back to Pashhur, bringing personal and familial destruction full circle. 'Thou, Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house'—not merely Pashhur alone but his entire household, his dependents, his family. Captivity is not a solitary fate but a corporate one. The bonds that should have united them in safety instead bind them together in catastrophe. Pashhur will not be spared; he will go to Babylon, die there, and be buried in foreign soil. This is a comprehensive reversal of every covenant promise: the land of promise becomes a place of exile, the burial place of ancestors becomes a foreign grave, the legacy of the patriarchs becomes diaspora.

The final phrase reframes the entire encounter: 'to whom thou hast prophesied lies.' This is the core judgment. Pashhur was not merely a temple administrator who responded badly to an inconvenient prophet; he was himself a false prophet (navi sheqer). The Covenant Rendering clarifies that navi sheqer ('false prophet') was a functional category—these were people actively delivering oracles, making proclamations, influencing the people's religious expectations and political behavior. Pashhur had been prophesying lies, meaning he was reassuring the people when he should have been calling them to repentance. His violence toward Jeremiah was not merely administrative enforcement but a defense of his own prophetic reputation. By silencing Jeremiah through the stocks, Pashhur attempted to silence the voice that contradicted his message.

The judgment thus becomes clear: Pashhur will be exiled and buried in Babylon with all those to whom he prophesied falsely. His friends (likely the other false prophets and priests who shared his comfortable message) will accompany him into judgment. The lie he told did not protect anyone; it condemned everyone. The false security he preached became the very terror his new name announced.

word_study.meaning: Captivity, exile, the state of being carried away; from the root shaba, 'to take captive, capture, lead away.' Shevi is not merely physical confinement but the condition of being removed from one's land and subjugated to a foreign power.
word_study.significance: The term represents a total loss of agency and autonomy. To go into shevi is to have one's future determined by others, to become property or subject of a conquering power. For Pashhur, who had exercised authority ('chief officer'), shevi represents a complete inversion of his status.

word_study.meaning: You will die / you will be buried; the imperfect tense expressing what is certain to happen. Both verbs are emphatic statements of inevitable fate. Tamut (from the root mut, 'to die') and tikabir (from qabar, 'to bury') together form a merism—from death to burial, the complete arc of mortality.
word_study.significance: The finality is crushing. Pashhur will not escape Babylon through death, nor will his body be brought back to ancestral burial grounds in Judah. He will die and be buried in the land of exile, forever separated from the land of promise. This violates the deepest covenant hope: to rest in the land the Lord gave.

word_study.meaning: You prophesied to them falsely/in a lie; literally 'you prophesied to them in the lie.' The verb naba (prophesy) is combined with basheqer ('in falsehood, in the lie'), indicating that Pashhur's prophetic utterances were deliberately false or, at minimum, not grounded in genuine revelation from the Lord.
word_study.significance: This is the identifying charge against false prophets throughout Jeremiah: they speak from their own minds, not from the Lord's word (Jer. 23:16-22). Pashhur was not a confused administrator but an active false prophet. His beat-ing of Jeremiah was not merely defensive but offensive—an attack on a competitor for prophetic authority. The charge 'navi sheqer' ('false prophet') was the most serious accusation in ancient Israelite religion, potentially carrying a death penalty (Deut. 13:1-5, 18:20-22).

word_study.meaning: Those who love you; literally 'those who love you.' The term can mean friends or allies, but the root 'ahav' ('to love') suggests deeper bonds—covenant relationships, political alliances, spiritual affinity.
word_study.significance: The friends who loved Pashhur—presumably the other priests, prophets, and leaders who shared his false message—will share his fate. They are complicit in his lie. The bonds of friendship and alliance, which should have saved them, instead condemn them together. This is a teaching about the danger of surrounding oneself with those who tell you what you want to hear rather than what you need to know.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah's comprehensive denunciation of false prophets: 'They speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD...they say still unto them that despise me...I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran.'

The Torah's test for false prophecy: 'The prophet which shall presume to speak a word in my name...even that prophet shall die.' Pashhur's false prophecy renders him liable to divine judgment, which Jeremiah announces.

The Chronicler's summary of Judah's fall: 'All the chief of the priests, and the people, transgressed very much...and the LORD...sent to them by his messengers: but they mocked the messengers of God...until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy.'

Ezekiel's parallel judgment on false prophets: 'Woe unto the foolish prophets, that follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing!...Ye have not gone up into the gaps, neither made up the hedge...that it should stand in the battle.'

The Lord's identification of true vs. false teaching: 'Every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man...And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man.'

commentary.historical_context: False prophecy was endemic in late pre-exilic Judah. Jeremiah repeatedly condemns the false prophets who were telling people what they wanted to hear: that the temple would be protected, that Babylon would not conquer, that peace was coming (Jer. 6:14, 8:11, 14:13-16, 23:16-22, 27-28). These false prophets were often institutionally connected—priests like Pashhur or officials like Hananiah (Jer. 28)—who had positions to protect and comfortable narratives to defend. Their false prophecy was not necessarily conscious deliberate lying but rather the projection of their own wishes and institutional interests onto the divine will. They genuinely may have believed what they said, but the test of true prophecy is whether it comes true (Deut. 18:22). When Babylon conquered Jerusalem exactly as Jeremiah predicted and the false prophets' assurances proved hollow, the judgment became historical fact. The archaeological record and Babylonian chronicles confirm that Jerusalem fell, its treasures were taken, and its people were deported—precisely as Jeremiah had announced and Pashhur had denied.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon presents false prophets as a persistent danger. Nehor and those following him 'preach and set themselves up for a light unto the world...that they might get gain' (Alma 1:3). King Benjamin's warning about false priests (Mosiah 26:31-32) parallels Jeremiah's denunciation: those who 'preach and set themselves up for a light unto the world' are doing so 'that they might get gain and praise of the world.' The false prophets are motivated by institutional self-interest, not prophetic truth. Alma 14:18-20 records that even after institutional religious authorities fail and are destroyed, some repent, while others harden their hearts—a pattern reflected in Jeremiah's Pashhur.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:36-38 establishes the Lord's standard for true prophetic voice: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled...Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' This principle would condemn Pashhur on both counts: he did not search the true word, and his prophecies did not come to pass. D&C 46:7-8 warns against 'deceiving spirits' and calls for discernment through the Spirit. The ability to distinguish true from false prophecy is not merely an intellectual skill but a spiritual gift requiring the Holy Ghost.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Pashhur held an official position in the temple yet prophesied falsely within it. This represents a profound violation: the temple, which should be a place of revealed truth and covenant renewal, became a place where false prophecy was promoted and true prophecy was silenced. The temple should magnify God's word; Pashhur used his temple position to suppress it. D&C 97:15-16 promises that 'if my people will hearken unto my voice, and unto the voice of my servants whom I have appointed to lead my people, behold, verily I say unto you, they shall not be moved out of their place.' The converse is also true: those who reject the Lord's voice through his servants will be moved out of their place, as Pashhur was.

commentary.christological_typology: Pashhur's fate as a false prophet who opposed God's true prophet foreshadows the judgment Christ pronounces on the scribes and Pharisees in Matthew 23:29-39. Like Pashhur, the Jewish leaders claimed prophetic authority ('Ye build the tombs of the prophets'), yet resisted the ultimate Prophet sent by God. Like Pashhur, they would be scattered and destroyed. Christ's words echo Jeremiah's: those who reject the word of God through his servants face judgment that reaches beyond themselves to their children and successors. The theme of false authority being exposed and reversed through judgment runs through both Old Testament prophecy and New Testament teaching.
commentary.application: This verse confronts us with uncomfortable questions about discernment and loyalty. How do we distinguish between true and false prophetic voices? What makes us susceptible to false prophecy? The answer: we are vulnerable when (1) we want comfort rather than truth, (2) we are invested in institutional prerogatives rather than prophetic principles, (3) we surround ourselves with people who tell us what we want to hear, and (4) we mistake authority for truth. Pashhur had institutional authority but no prophetic truth. For modern believers, this verse teaches that we must value truth-telling over comfort-giving, that we must be willing to hear prophetic correction, and that we must discern voices not by their institutional position but by whether they lead us toward greater faithfulness and covenant alignment. The verse also teaches that false prophecy, however well-intentioned or carefully reasoned, ultimately leads to disaster—not because the Lord is punitive but because it cuts us off from the real guidance we need to navigate genuine threats. Pashhur's false prophecy left his household unprepared for the reality of Babylon's conquest. Our false beliefs—whether about our righteousness, our safety, or our future—leave us equally vulnerable.

text_kjv: Sing unto the LORD, praise ye the LORD: for he hath delivered the soul of the poor from the hand of evildoers.

commentary.narrative:
This verse erupts without warning—a shout of praise inserted into Jeremiah's most anguished confession cycle. The prophet has just finished recounting his abuse at Pashhur's hands (verses 7-12), and now, with apparent spontaneity, he breaks into liturgical hymn. The structure follows the ancient psalmic pattern: a lament followed by a sudden turn to praise (compare Psalm 22, which moves from "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" to "I will declare thy name unto my brethren"). But here, the rupture is unsettling. The praise does not resolve anything. Jeremiah's suffering remains unaddressed by this outburst—and worse, the text will show us that within a single breath, he will plunge into the darkest despair recorded in Scripture.

The phrase "soul of the poor" (nephesh evyon) is crucial: Jeremiah identifies himself as evyon—not merely poor in material goods but socially defenseless, stripped of protection, vulnerable to predators. In Hebrew covenant vocabulary, the evyon holds a sacred place: God has bound himself by covenant to protect the destitute (Exodus 22:22-24; Psalm 35:10). When the prophet calls himself evyon, he is claiming a covenantal status—he has been stripped of all human defenders and stands alone before God. The "hand of evildoers" (yad merei'im) represents not abstract evil but concrete human malice. This is personal: Pashhur beat him; the people mock him; his own family plots against him (12:6). Yet in this moment, Jeremiah proclaims rescue—whether that rescue has actually come or whether it remains an act of faith is precisely what the next verses will interrogate.

word_study.meaning: The destitute or vulnerable one; someone without protectors or resources. In covenant theology, the evyon is the one to whom God has pledged special obligation and care. The term carries not just economic meaning but social and spiritual vulnerability.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah's self-identification as evyon stakes a claim on God's covenantal protection. By naming himself among the defenseless, he invokes God's ancient promise to be 'a father of the fatherless' (Psalm 68:5). This same term appears throughout Proverbs and Psalms as a category God will never abandon.

word_study.meaning: To snatch away, rescue, deliver from danger or bondage. The verb carries the sense of swift, forceful removal from peril—not gradual improvement but decisive intervention.
word_study.significance: The tense is perfect (completed action): 'he has delivered.' Whether this reflects past deliverance or an act of faith claiming future deliverance is the hermeneutical hinge of the verse. In the Restoration, this language echoes D&C 109:38's language of Saints being 'delivered from all evil.'

word_study.meaning: Those who practice ra'ah (evil, wickedness, harm). Not mere wrongdoing but deliberate malice—those whose orientation is toward causing suffering.
word_study.significance: The plural form stresses that evildoers are multiple and coordinated—Jeremiah faces not isolated opposition but a network of hostility (his family, his community, the authorities). The term frames his suffering as the predictable outcome of his message: evildoers naturally oppose the prophet who exposes their wickedness.

cross_references.connection: The same liturgical structure: a devastating lament (verses 1-21) abruptly transitions to a burst of praise (verses 22+). Both psalms leave the structural rupture unhealed—the praise does not answer the agony.
The beginning of this confession cycle, where Jeremiah is first persecuted and his trust is tested. Verse 13 circles back to claim deliverance from the evildoers introduced there.
God's covenant promise to defend the widow, orphan, and poor. When Jeremiah calls himself evyon, he invokes this ancient protection.
'All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like unto thee, which deliverest the poor from him that is too strong for him?' The same claim Jeremiah makes—deliverance of the powerless from the powerful.

commentary.historical_context: The praise-after-lament structure was deeply familiar in ancient Israelite liturgy. Temple worship regularly moved from penitential complaint to thanksgiving—a rhythm embedded in the psalter itself. But Jeremiah's burst of praise occurs in a private confession, not a public liturgical moment. Whether this represents genuine spiritual breakthrough, reflexive recitation of familiar hymnic forms, or bitter irony remains deliberately unresolved. Ancient interpreters (the Targum, medieval rabbinic commentary) struggled with the rupture, with some reading verse 13 as sarcasm. The cultural context suggests Jeremiah is drawing on patterns of covenant language and psalm-form that would have been deeply embedded in any Israelite's consciousness—yet here, the form contains a theological crisis rather than resolving one.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's experience in 1 Nephi 18:15-20 mirrors this same pattern: overwhelming despair followed by sudden turn to faith and praise, though Nephi's shift is more sustained. Mormon also records moments where the Nephite people 'began to repent and began to have hope' even amid calamity (Mormon 2:26-27), suggesting that covenant faith can produce sudden reversals of emotion.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-9 records Joseph Smith's anguished questioning in Liberty Jail, followed immediately by the Lord's response 'My son, peace be unto thy soul.' Jeremiah receives no such response—the silence that follows verse 13 intensifies the prophet's isolation and raises the stakes of his despair in verses 14-18.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The language of 'praise the LORD' (hallelu-Yah) would eventually become central to temple worship. In the Restoration, Psalm 113-118 (the Hallel psalms) are associated with the temple experience, particularly the celebration of deliverance. Jeremiah's invocation of this language in a personal crisis foreshadows how individual saints claim covenantal protection through temple participation.

commentary.christological_typology: The prophet's sudden turn from despair to praise—even without resolution—anticipates Christ's own night of abandonment followed by resurrection. Jeremiah's 'I will praise' (without yet seeing vindication) mirrors the Messianic psalms (Psalm 22:22, addressed to the assembly: 'I will declare thy name unto my brethren'—words applied to Christ in Hebrews 2:12). The evyon (poor) becomes a title applied to Christ himself, the one who is utterly dependent on the Father and receives the Father's protection.
commentary.application: Modern readers often expect that emotional honesty in faith means sustained feelings. Jeremiah teaches the opposite: faith can mean praising God in the middle of unanswered agony. Verse 13 invites the reader to consider whether covenant faith requires that we *feel* delivered before we declare ourselves delivered—or whether declaring deliverance is itself an act that precedes and shapes emotional reality. For covenant members facing persecution or inexplicable suffering, this verse raises a crucial question: Is praise despite circumstances a form of denial—or is it the deepest form of faith, the claiming of God's covenantal promise when all visible evidence contradicts it?

text_kjv: Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed.

commentary.narrative:
Without transition, Jeremiah plunges into a curse of his own existence. This is not a momentary flash of despair but a programmatic rejection of life itself—the only complete reversal in the entire Hebrew Bible between praise and curse uttered by the same speaker in consecutive breaths. The Hebrew word arur ('cursed') is the covenant-curse vocabulary drawn directly from Deuteronomy's blessing-curse formula (Deuteronomy 27-28). When Jeremiah uses this word to curse the day of his birth, he is employing the most formal, irrevocable religious language available to him. He is not cursing God directly—that would be blasphemy. Instead, he curses the day itself, wishing the fabric of time undone, wishing to unwrite the day he entered existence.

The parallelism intensifies the curse: 'Cursed be the day I was born / The day my mother bore me—let it not be blessed.' The second line does not simply repeat the first; it negates the opposite condition. To curse is to invoke harm; to say 'let it not be blessed' is to strip away even the possibility of goodness. It is a more complete denial than mere curse—it is the annihilation of blessing itself from that day. The specificity of 'my mother bore me' personalizes the rejection: Jeremiah's mother brought him into existence, and he now wishes that act undone. This echoes Job 3:3-10 so closely that one wonders whether the two confessions share a literary tradition, or whether extreme suffering naturally produces this language. Both Job and Jeremiah wish not for death (which would be a release) but for non-existence—as though they could rewrite the past and prevent their own birth. The wish for non-existence is more radical than the wish for death: it denies the validity of the entire trajectory of one's life.

word_study.meaning: Placed under a curse; formally declared as the object of divine judgment and exclusion from blessing. In covenant theology, to be arur is to be cut off from the protections and provisions of the covenant community.
word_study.significance: This is the language of Deuteronomy's covenant curses—the formal vocabulary by which Israel invoked divine punishment upon violators of the Torah. When Jeremiah applies arur to the day of his own birth rather than to enemies or evildoers, he performs an act of radical self-negation. He places himself outside the covenant as if his birth itself were a violation meriting curse. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that this is 'covenant-curse vocabulary,' making clear that Jeremiah is deploying the most solemn religious language available.

word_study.meaning: A 24-hour period; also the principle of time itself, the moment of demarcation in creation (Genesis 1:5). To curse a yom is unusual—days are impersonal units of time, not agents of evil. But here, the day becomes the locus of curse because it is the day through which Jeremiah's suffering entered the world.
word_study.significance: By cursing the yom rather than God or fate, Jeremiah maintains a theological boundary: he does not curse God. Yet the curse of the day is nearly as comprehensive—it is a wish that time itself be rewritten. In the creation account, each day concludes with 'and it was good' (ki tov). Jeremiah's curse reverses that verdict: 'let this day never be good.'

word_study.meaning: To give birth, to beget; used of both the mother who births and the father who begets. The verb carries the sense of transition from non-being to being.
word_study.significance: The repetition of yalad in parallel lines ('the day I was born' / 'the day my mother bore me') emphasizes that this is precisely the moment of Jeremiah's entry into existence that he wishes reversed. The verb that should celebrate creation becomes the center of his rejection.

cross_references.connection: Job curses the day of his birth in nearly identical language: 'After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day.' Both men arrive at this extreme rejection of existence through unendurable suffering, suggesting this is a consistent response to theodicy without resolution.

The covenant-curse formula that Jeremiah invokes by using arur. In Deuteronomy, these are curses pronounced on violators of Torah; Jeremiah's use reverses the direction—he curses himself, or rather, the day that introduced him to this world.

After each day of creation, God sees 'that it was good' (ki tov). Jeremiah's curse reverses this verdict: let the day of his birth never be good. The blessing-formula of creation becomes the object of curse.
Earlier in the confessions, Jeremiah cries 'Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me'—the same complaint in lighter key. Verse 14 intensifies this earlier anguish to full curse-language.

In the context of life's futility, the Preacher declares 'Better is he that hath not yet been, than both they.' Both Jeremiah and Ecclesiastes express the dark wish that non-existence would have been preferable to existence.

commentary.historical_context: The curse-formula language (arur) is deeply embedded in Deuteronomic covenant theology and would have carried extreme weight in Jeremiah's audience. To pronounce such a curse was to invoke the full power of the covenant's sanctions. Ancient Near Eastern curse formulas often targeted specific people or acts; to curse an entire day was unusual, perhaps even shocking. The rabbinic tradition struggled with this verse—some commentators suggested that Jeremiah's words prove he was not speaking prophetically at this moment, since a true prophet would not speak such things. Others interpreted the curse as valid testimony to human suffering, but requiring divine correction or Job-like restoration. The social context matters: Jeremiah's public humiliation at Pashhur's hands (verses 7-11) would have been witnessed; his isolation from his own family (12:6) would have been known. His collapse into this curse happens within a community that has rejected him. Unlike Job, Jeremiah receives no sympathetic friends—only enemies and, later, no divine response.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma the Younger experiences something analogous when he recounts his rebellion and near-despair: 'I was tormented with an awful remorse' (Alma 36:13). Yet Alma is granted a vision that transforms his despair. Jeremiah receives no such vision. The Book of Mormon consistently moves toward redemption and course-correction; the Hebrew Bible, especially here, allows suffering to remain unresolved within the text itself.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-2 records Joseph Smith's anguished questioning in Liberty Jail: 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion that covereth thy hiding place?' This parallels Jeremiah's cry, though Joseph's question eventually receives divine response (verses 7-9 onward), whereas Jeremiah's receives none within this text.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant-curse vocabulary (arur) invoked here is the opposite pole of temple covenants, where members are blessed rather than cursed. Jeremiah's self-curse is the inversion of the endowment's promise of divine protection. In the temple context, the curse is directed against those who break covenants; Jeremiah places himself under curse for the 'crime' of existing—a transgression he did not commit.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's cry from the cross ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'—Psalm 22:1) shares Jeremiah's radical interrogation of God, though Christ's cry is directed to God rather than to the day. Yet both involve the righteous entering a state of curse-like abandonment. In Paul's theology, Christ becomes 'cursed' for humanity's sake (Galatians 3:13): 'Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.' Jeremiah's self-curse anticipates the way Christ would absorb the curse on behalf of others. Yet there is no redemptive meaning offered within Jeremiah's text itself—the typology emerges only in retrospect, from the Resurrection.
commentary.application: This verse offers permission for the most radical form of honesty before God—the wish for non-existence, the rejection of one's own life. Modern faith communities often discourage such expressions as 'giving in to despair' or 'denying God's blessings.' But the Hebrew Bible preserves Jeremiah's curse without censoring or immediately resolving it. The text honors the reality of suffering so total that it makes the sufferer wish existence itself undone. For those in clinical depression or suicidal ideation, this verse acknowledges the depth of that darkness without flinching. For those who have survived such darkness, it may validate what they endured. The verse teaches that spiritual maturity does not mean transcending despair but holding it within a covenantal relationship with God—bringing the darkest wish into speech, into the presence of the divine, even if (perhaps especially if) the divine does not immediately respond.

text_kjv: Cursed be the man who brought tidings to my father, saying, A man child is born unto thee; making him very glad.

commentary.narrative:
The curse expands outward from the day itself (verse 14) to a specific person: the unnamed messenger who announced Jeremiah's birth to his father. This figure is almost invisible in the text—he has one action, one line of dialogue—yet Jeremiah curses him with the same covenant-curse vocabulary (arur) invoked for the day. The cruelty of this curse lies in its targeting: the messenger is cursed not for anything he did wrong, but for participating in an event that brought joy. He brought 'tidings' (besorah, good news) of a son's birth, which in patriarchal Israelite culture was a signal honor. The birth of a male child was the fulfillment of divine promise (Genesis 21:2-3; 1 Samuel 1:20). The phrase 'man child' (ben zakhar) emphasizes the patriarchal significance—a son, not a daughter, was the carrier of family continuity and inheritance.

The father's response is portrayed as genuine happiness: 'making him very glad' (sammeach simmechu—an emphatic infinitive absolute in Hebrew, intensifying the emotion). This is not restrained joy but exuberant delight. Jeremiah is now cursing the moment when his father's joy was fullest, when the father believed himself blessed by God. The cruelty deepens when we consider that Jeremiah's own later suffering—his public humiliation, his family's abandonment of him (12:6)—may well have transformed this father's ancient joy into bitter regret. The father who once received the news of his son's birth with gladness may have lived to see that son become a prophet of doom, rejected and persecuted. By cursing the messenger, Jeremiah is cursing the entire chain of causation that led from that moment of paternal joy to the present anguish. He wishes that joy had never been, that the father had never received the news that would set in motion all that followed.

word_study.meaning: To bring good news, to announce tidings. The verb carries the sense of joyful proclamation. (Note: the same root produces 'gospel,' evangelion in Greek—'good message.')
word_study.significance: The messenger performs a function normally associated with blessing and celebration. He is not an evildoer or opponent; he is merely the vehicle for transmission of joy. Yet Jeremiah curses him, suggesting that the curse extends beyond agents of harm to anyone caught in the causal chain of suffering. The irony is profound: the bringer of 'good news' is cursed.

word_study.meaning: An emphatic construction using the infinitive absolute ('he made him exceedingly glad'). The doubling intensifies the emotion—this is not quiet contentment but exuberant, overflowing joy.
word_study.significance: The intensity of the father's joy is precisely what makes the curse so bitter. Jeremiah is not cursing a moment of indifference but a moment of maximum human happiness. The text suggests that the greater the joy was then, the deeper the anguish is now. This inversion of joy into suffering will dominate the remaining verses.

word_study.meaning: A male child; specifically a son. In patriarchal contexts, this designation carried covenant significance—the son is the one through whom the father's name, inheritance, and blessing are transmitted.
word_study.significance: The specificity of 'male child' emphasizes the cultural weight of Jeremiah's birth. He was not merely born but born as a son, as a carrier of family continuity. That this particular son became a prophet of despair, rejected even by his own father's house, makes the irony sharper. The promised blessing became a curse.

cross_references.connection: Abraham receives tidings of Isaac's birth and responds with joy—'God hath made me to laugh.' The contrast illustrates how Jeremiah's birth, though announced with joy, brought sorrow instead of blessing.

Hannah's joy at bearing Samuel, a son dedicated to the LORD. Like Abraham and Jeremiah's father, she receives the news of a son's birth as blessing—yet Samuel's life as prophet was also marked by isolation and conflict.

'For even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee.' The same father who received the joyful tidings of Jeremiah's birth later joined those who betrayed him—turning ancestral joy into abandonment.
The birth of John the Baptist is announced with joy, and his father's mouth is opened in praise. Like Jeremiah, John becomes a prophet whose message brings division rather than comfort.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite culture, the birth of a son was a momentous event, celebrated as divine blessing. The messenger's role was honorable—to bring such news was to participate in joy. That Jeremiah curses this role illustrates his complete inversion of values: what the culture celebrates (a son's birth, patriarchal continuity), he rejects utterly. The naming of a child typically occurred within days of birth, accompanied by celebration. Jeremiah's cursing of the messenger invokes a curse on the entire social apparatus of celebration. In some ancient Near Eastern contexts, curses could be very specific: cursing not the one who caused harm but any who participated in the causal chain. Yet even here, the messenger is innocent—he had no knowledge that this particular son would grow to be tormented. The curse is less rational argument than expression of total anguish.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records moments of joy at births of sons (Alma 63:15-16 mentions Helaman's sons), but these are consistently framed as blessings, not the sources of future sorrow. The Restoration narrative tends to move toward redemption of ancestral lines and family continuity. Jeremiah's radical rejection of these values stands outside the redemptive arc of the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 138:12-13 records that the righteous dead 'were assembled in the spirits of the just... waiting for the resurrection of the dead.' Jeremiah's curse inverts this: rather than waiting for resurrection, he wishes he had never been born. The contrast shows how Restoration theology emphasizes eternal continuity of family bonds, whereas Jeremiah's despair denies any such continuity as good.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple birth covenant language centers on the joy of bringing children into the covenant. Jeremiah's curse of the birth-messenger inverts this entirely—the moment that should be celebrated in the temple context becomes the object of curse. For modern families, the verse raises uncomfortable questions: Does the bearing of children into a world of suffering ever warrant this kind of regret?

commentary.christological_typology: The messenger who announces the birth is an innocent bystander caught in the web of another's suffering. In the Messianic tradition, those associated with Christ's birth (the shepherds, the Magi, John the Baptist) bring tidings of joy, yet they too participate in a story that moves toward crucifixion. The messenger in Jeremiah's curse is like those who would later proclaim 'Hosanna! Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord!' (Matthew 21:9) without understanding that this very figure would be rejected and killed. The joy of birth does not guarantee a joyful life—a theme that deepens in contemplation of the Incarnation itself, where God's own Son enters a world that will reject and kill him.
commentary.application: This verse presents a disturbing but important reality: the people we bless (messengers, midwives, well-wishers) are not responsible for the outcomes of the lives they help bring into being. Yet Jeremiah curses the messenger anyway—not rationally, but as an expression of total despair. The verse asks: When we regret our existence, whom do we blame? The conscious answer might be 'no one'—but the emotional answer, the truth of grief, might be everyone and anyone in the chain of causation. For those who have survived suicidal ideation or severe depression and have emerged, this verse may represent a moment they once inhabited—the irrational cursing of innocent people, the distortion of joy into a source of blame. Conversely, for those who remain in that darkness, the verse offers validation: the text preserves this moment without immediately condemning it. Recovery, when it comes, will not erase the reality of having cursed the messenger; it will contextualize it.

text_kjv: And let that man be as the cities which the LORD overthrew, and repented not: and let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide;

commentary.narrative:
The curse intensifies to apocalyptic proportions. No longer is the messenger merely to be excluded from blessing (as in verse 15); now Jeremiah wishes upon him the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah—the paradigmatic destruction in Israelite memory. The verb 'overthrew' (hafakh) is the precise technical term for what God did to Sodom (Genesis 19:21, 25, 29). When Jeremiah uses this word, he evokes the entire catastrophic narrative: the cities erased from the earth, their inhabitants annihilated, salt remaining as monument to divine wrath. The phrase 'repented not' (lo nicham) is crucial: the verb nacham usually means to relent, to have compassion, to change one's mind. The negation—'did not relent'—means the destruction was total and irreversible. God looked upon Sodom and did not soften his judgment; he did not say 'I will spare them for the sake of ten righteous people.' The destruction was complete. This is the fate Jeremiah invokes for the innocent messenger.

But the curse does not end with mere destruction. Jeremiah adds psychological torment: 'let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide.' The messenger is to live surrounded by sounds of anguish—morning and noon, the beginning and middle of the day, are mentioned (verse 17 will add evening). There is no respite. The 'cry' (ze'aqah) suggests desperate pleading; the 'shouting' (teru'ah) suggests the alarm-cry of battle or catastrophe. The messenger is to live in a state of perpetual terror, hearing without cessation the sounds of destruction. This is not instantaneous death but endless awareness of death surrounding him—a psychological hell that makes the physical destruction of Sodom almost seem merciful by comparison. The progression is significant: verses 14-15 curse temporal things (the day, the messenger); verse 16 curses a man to a fate parallel to the most catastrophic destruction recorded in Scripture, and then extends that fate into a lived experience of perpetual torment.

word_study.meaning: To overturn, overturn completely, reverse entirely. Used in Genesis 19:21, 25, 29 for God's destruction of Sodom. The verb carries the sense of complete and utter reversal—what was becomes what is not.
word_study.significance: This is not ordinary destruction but total erasure. The Covenant Rendering notes that hafakh is 'the signature verb for Sodom's destruction.' By invoking this word, Jeremiah aligns the messenger's fate with the most complete negation of human community in biblical memory. It is worth noting that Jeremiah's desire to undo his own birth (verse 14) now finds external expression: he wishes someone else utterly overturned, erased, reversed into non-being.

word_study.meaning: A loud cry, often of distress or desperation. Not mere noise but the sound of suffering humans in extremity. The verb ze'ak appears throughout laments and descriptions of persecution.
word_study.significance: Ze'aqah is the sound of the vulnerable calling out. It appears in Exodus 3:7, where God hears 'the cry of the children of Israel.' Jeremiah invokes this language to curse the messenger with a fate of perpetual exposure to the suffering of others—he will live immersed in the cries of the destroyed, unable to escape them.

word_study.meaning: A loud shout; in military contexts, the cry raised in battle or alarm. Also used of the trumpet-blast (shofar) that signaled assembly or covenant renewal.
word_study.significance: Paired with ze'aqah (desperate cry), teru'ah suggests the organized sounds of catastrophe—both the disordered screaming of the dying and the organized calls of those dealing with destruction. The messenger is to hear both kinds of sound, leaving no space for peace.

word_study.meaning: To relent, to soften, to show compassion; to change one's mind or course of action. Often used of God's willingness to spare (as in Exodus 32:14 after the golden calf).
word_study.significance: The negation 'did not relent' (lo nicham) intensifies the curse. God's destruction of Sodom was not a first impulse that he later moderated; it was a judgment that he maintained completely. The Covenant Rendering notes: 'The phrase velo nicham...means no such mercy was extended.' The messenger is to experience a divine justice that admits no compassion.

cross_references.connection: The destruction of Sodom, using the verb hafakh: 'he overthrew those cities.' Jeremiah's curse directly invokes this paradigmatic destruction, wishing the messenger to share the fate of Sodom's residents.

Amos uses the same verb (hafakh) to reference Sodom's destruction as a historical marker of total divine judgment: 'I overthrew some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.' Jeremiah echoes prophetic language for the most complete destruction imaginable.

God hears 'the cry of the children of Israel' (ze'aqah) and is moved to compassion. Jeremiah's curse is that the messenger will hear such cries perpetually, but find no divine compassion—he will experience God's judgment without mitigation.

Sodom and Gomorrah are listed as the ultimate examples of covenant violation and divine punishment: 'Like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah which the LORD overthrew in his anger.' Jeremiah's curse aligns the messenger with covenant violators.

Isaiah uses Sodom as the measure of ultimate destruction: 'And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms...shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.' The pattern is consistent across prophecy: Sodom = total erasure.

commentary.historical_context: Sodom and Gomorrah were known throughout the ancient Near East as cautionary tales—the cities whose names became synonymous with divine punishment and complete annihilation. In later Jewish tradition (Midrash, Talmud), the destruction was expanded into elaborate narratives of Sodom's depravity and God's justice. For Jeremiah's ancient audience, invoking this curse was to invoke the most severe possible fate. The mention of morning and noon emphasizes a 24-hour cycle without respite—the same language structure used of the day-curse in verse 14. In ancient Near Eastern curse formulas, it was common to call upon the gods to destroy one's enemy and scatter their remains, but to call for perpetual awareness of that destruction (as verse 16 does) is more unusual—it adds psychological torment to physical annihilation. The curse suggests Jeremiah's own experience of living amid others' suffering: he has preached doom while his people rejected him, forced to witness their refusal to repent while judgment drew near. He now wishes this experience on the messenger—not merely death, but the awareness of death all around.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records the destruction of Nephite cities (Alma 16:1-13; 3 Nephi 8-9), but even in these destructions, there is movement toward repentance and redemption. The Nephites who survive hear the cries of destruction and are moved to faith. Jeremiah's curse inverts this: the messenger is to hear cries but experience no redemptive awakening, no movement toward God—only perpetual exposure to anguish.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:32-34 describes the fate of those who refuse to hear the Lord's voice: 'But he that hath ears to hear, let him hear...for Zion shall escape if she observe to do all things whatsoever I have commanded her.' Jeremiah's curse is that the messenger will have ears but find no escape—he will hear the cries but find no Zion to flee to.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes promises of protection from evil. Jeremiah's curse removes all such protection—the messenger is to live in a state of absolute vulnerability, hearing destruction on all sides without refuge. This is the inverse of the temple's promise to clothe and protect.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's experience in Gethsemane includes hearing the cries of a suffering world—'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me' (Matthew 26:39)—without the comfort of divine response. Yet Christ endures this voluntarily, while Jeremiah's curse condemns the messenger to involuntary suffering. In the crucifixion, Christ is surrounded by sounds of mockery and anguish (the cries at Golgotha), yet he remains silent, hearing without fleeing. The typology is dark: the innocent party (like the messenger) becomes the locus of undeserved suffering.
commentary.application: Modern readers often recoil from Jeremiah's curse as unethical—how can the righteous invoke destruction on an innocent bystander? Yet the verse teaches something about how extreme suffering distorts moral reasoning. The messenger becomes a receptacle for all of Jeremiah's anguish—not because the messenger deserves it, but because he is available. For those who have worked through anger at innocents (parents, siblings, clergy, therapists) during periods of crisis, this verse may represent a landscape they have inhabited and, hopefully, moved beyond. The curse also raises the question: Is it better to suppress such emotions or to express them? By recording Jeremiah's curse without immediately condemning it, the text suggests that radical honesty about hatred and blame, even when irrational, is part of authentic covenant prayer. The curse does not resolve the anguish; it intensifies it. Yet the text preserves it, suggesting that complete emotional suppression may be a form of spiritual dishonesty.

text_kjv: Because he slew me not from the womb; or that my mother might have been my grave, and her womb to be always great with me.

commentary.narrative:
The curse now becomes surreal. Jeremiah provides the reason why the messenger deserves such a fate: 'because he did not kill me in the womb.' The logic is profoundly irrational—the messenger has no power to control whether a child is born; he is merely the announcer. Yet Jeremiah extends the curse backward through time to a moment before the messenger even arrived: the womb. He wishes the messenger cursed for failing to prevent the prophet's birth. The rage has moved beyond any logical target into pure fantasy—a fantasy of undoing existence itself by means of an act the messenger could never have performed.

The image that follows is among the most disturbing in Scripture: 'that my mother might have been my grave, and her womb to be always great with me.' The mother's womb becomes a grave (qivri); the place that should give life becomes the place of burial. Death and birth collapse into a single horrifying image—the tomb and the cradle occupy the same space. The phrase 'her womb to be always great with me' evokes eternal pregnancy—a state in which the child remains forever unborn, perpetually in gestation, never entering the light of the world. The word olam ('always, forever, unto eternity') suggests an unbounded duration, pregnancy that stretches beyond the horizon of time. It is a wish not for death but for eternal suspension between existence and non-existence—the worst of both states, neither the rest of the grave nor the engagement of life.

This image fuses two contradictory desires: to have never been born (verse 14), and to have remained in the womb forever (verse 17). The womb is simultaneously the place of origin and the place of escape—the only space where Jeremiah imagines he would have been safe. This returns us to the fundamental psychological truth underlying the entire confession: the prophet experiences the world as a realm of suffering so total that even the pre-birth state appears preferable. The Hebrew term qivri ('my grave') is remarkable—it is possessive and personal. Not 'a grave' but 'my grave,' as though Jeremiah is naming the place that belongs to him by right, the true home he should have occupied instead of this hostile world.

word_study.meaning: To put to death, to slay. In this context, the subject is ambiguous—Jeremiah seems to wish that someone (the messenger? God? fate?) had killed him in the womb, preventing his birth.
word_study.significance: The verb is in the subjunctive mood—a counterfactual wish directed at an impossible past. The messenger could not have killed the unborn Jeremiah. Yet the irrationality itself is the point: Jeremiah's rage has no rational object, so it attaches to anyone in the causal chain.

word_study.meaning: A grave, burial place. The possessive form 'my grave' is crucial—this is the place that belongs to Jeremiah, the place he should rightfully occupy.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that 'qivri' merges 'birth and death into a single horrifying image—the place that should give life becomes the place of burial.' This is the deepest inversion in the chapter: the mother's womb, source of all life in human experience, is reimagined as a tomb. It suggests that Jeremiah experiences his mother not as his creator but as his captor—the one who pulled him from the safety of non-existence into this suffering world.

word_study.term_english: was great, pregnant, heavy with child
word_study.meaning: To be or become pregnant; the state of bearing a child. The sense is of physical heaviness, the burden of gestation.
word_study.significance: The infinitive absolute construction 'harat olam' ('forever pregnant') envisions a state that never resolves. Jeremiah wishes for his mother to remain eternally pregnant with him, never delivering, never releasing him into the world. It is a paradoxical image: protection through non-delivery, safety through eternal gestation.

word_study.meaning: Eternity, forever, an unbounded duration stretching beyond the horizon of time. Used of God's eternal nature, the eternal Law, and in this context, an unbounded pregnancy.
word_study.significance: The use of olam intensifies the image: this is not temporary gestation but eternal suspension. Jeremiah wishes for a condition that transcends time—an infinite womb, a forever-pregnant state. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes: 'an unbounded duration — pregnancy stretching beyond the horizon of time.'

word_study.meaning: The womb, belly, interior of the mother. Also cognate with 'rachamim' (compassion, mercy)—suggesting that the rechem is the seat of maternal tenderness.
word_study.significance: Jeremiah perverts this etymology: the womb that should be the place of mercy and tender care becomes a grave. The mother's compassion (rachamim), which should protect the child, instead confines him eternally. This represents a complete inversion of maternal function—the mother becomes the jailer, her womb becomes the prison.

cross_references.connection: Job asks: 'Why died I not from the womb? Why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly?' The same wish to undo birth, though Job addresses it to the womb itself rather than to a messenger.

The Preacher contemplates a child born 'an hundred children, and live many years' yet ending in darkness: 'Better is he that hath not yet been, than both they...the untimely birth passeth away in darkness.' Jeremiah's wish for eternal gestation is the philosophical corollary to this observation.

God speaks to the young prophet: 'Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee.' God's claim to have known Jeremiah before his birth stands in stark contrast to Jeremiah's wish that he had never been born—the same womb that God hallowed, Jeremiah wishes to become his grave.

Isaiah recounts: 'The LORD hath called me from the womb...he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword.' God's calling from the womb is meant to be blessing; Jeremiah curses the same womb for not retaining him.

The psalmist recalls: 'I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou art my God from my mother's belly.' Here, the womb is the place from which God's relationship begins. Jeremiah's inversion makes the womb the place where God's relationship should have ended—eternally.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern sources record various curses, but the detailed psychological torture described here—eternal gestation, the womb as grave—is deeply personal and introspective. It suggests a cultural moment in which the isolated individual's inner life has become the subject of intense literary expression. The notion that the womb should be a place of safety and return appears in ancient literature (the myth of Kronos attempting to swallow his children whole, for instance), but Jeremiah's treatment is unique in its vulnerability. The mother-child relationship, which in the ancient world was often celebrated (Egyptian texts, Sumerian hymns to motherhood), is here inverted: the mother becomes the symbol of a prison, though Jeremiah does not blame her personally. He blames the messenging function that drew him from the womb. The focus on prenatal life as preferable to postnatal life is unusual in ancient literature; most ancient traditions celebrated birth as transition to human community and covenant participation. Jeremiah inverts all such celebration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon centers on the covenant of the womb—Nephi's descent as covenant son (1 Nephi 13:37), the birth of sons as blessing (Alma 63:15-16). Even in moments of despair (Alma 36:3 records Alma's torment), the solution is covenant renewal, not rejection of existence. Jeremiah's inversion of the womb's meaning stands outside the Restoration narrative.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 93:23-24 records the Father speaking to the Son: 'I give unto you these sayings that you may understand and know how to worship, and know what you worship, that you may come unto the Father in my name, and in my name you shall have access to the Father.' The doctrine of premortal existence and divine relationship stands in tension with Jeremiah's wish that he had remained forever unborn. The Restoration teaches that birth is a transition to embodied covenant participation; Jeremiah experiences it as exile from safety.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant centers on the creation of humankind in the divine image, including the role of motherhood as sacred. Jeremiah's inversion—the womb as grave, the mother as jailer—inverts temple theology entirely. Yet the preservation of Jeremiah's radical inversion within Scripture suggests that even the deepest denials of existence can be brought into covenantal dialogue with God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ speaks of being 'born again' (John 3:3-7), and Paul speaks of being 'born out of due time' (1 Corinthians 15:8). These positive reframings of birth and gestation stand in ironic contrast to Jeremiah's rejection of birth itself. Yet there is also a typology in reverse: Christ will speak of being 'in the belly of the earth' (Matthew 12:40), aligning the tomb with the womb in imagery that echoes Jeremiah's merging of the two concepts. In the crucifixion, Christ experiences a kind of reversal of birth—descent into darkness, placement in a grave—that might be seen as the fulfillment of all such death-wishes, except that it is followed by resurrection. Jeremiah has no resurrection in view; the text ends in darkness.
commentary.application: Verse 17 validates the experience of wishing one had never been born—an experience many who have suffered severe depression, trauma, or chronic suffering know intimately. The preservation of this wish in Scripture, without immediate refutation or consolation, honors the depth of that darkness. Yet it also models a way of holding that darkness: by bringing it into speech, into the form of prayer and lament, into the covenantal relationship with God. Modern pastoral care often counsels those in suicidal ideation toward alternative framings: 'You're not wishing for death; you're wishing for escape from pain.' Jeremiah offers no such reframing. He wishes for non-existence itself—to have remained in the womb forever, to have been swallowed back into nothingness. The verse teaches that such wishes are real, valid, human responses to suffering too great to bear. It also teaches, by its preservation in Scripture, that such wishes do not place one outside the covenantal relationship with God—they are part of the content of authentic prayer.

text_kjv: Wherefore came I forth out of the womb to see labour and sorrow, that my days should be consumed with shame?

commentary.narrative:
The confession ends with a question that receives no answer. The prophet has progressed from praise (verse 13) to curse of the day (verse 14), to curse of the messenger (verses 15-17), and now to the fundamental interrogation: Why? 'Why did I come out of the womb?' The question lammah ('why') is the ultimate form of lament in Hebrew—it demands a reason, a justification, an accounting. But the text provides none. God does not respond. There is no oracle of comfort, no divine assurance, no reframing that makes suffering meaningful. The text simply ends in unresolved despair.

The threefold description of Jeremiah's experience—'suffering and grief...shame'—summarizes his entire prophetic life. The word amal encompasses both external suffering and internal futility: the toil that produces no good result, the pain that serves no redemptive purpose. Yagon is the settled state of sorrow, not momentary sadness but an abiding condition. Bosheth is shame—public humiliation, social disgrace, the loss of honor before the community. For a prophet called by God to speak God's word, to be consumed by shame is particularly cruel: the very role that should confer honor instead produces contempt. Jeremiah has been beaten, imprisoned, mocked, abandoned by his own family. His message has been rejected. His predictions have not yet come true (from the perspective of the time of his speaking). He appears to be a false prophet, a man speaking words that do not come to pass, deserving of exactly the shame he experiences.

The phrase 'days...consumed with shame' uses the verb kalah (to finish, complete, consume entirely). It suggests that shame is not an occasional experience but the defining characteristic of Jeremiah's existence. His days are consumed—eaten up, used up—in this experience. The word olam (eternity, unbounded duration) from verse 17 has implicitly shifted to yamin (days, specific duration)—from the eternal womb-grave to the measured-out days of this life, all of which are consumed by shame. The confession ends here. The reader expects closure—a resolution, a return to the praise of verse 13, a divine word that explains the suffering. Instead, there is silence. This silence is itself theologically significant.

word_study.meaning: An interrogative particle demanding cause, reason, or justification. Not merely 'what' but 'why'—the deeper question of purpose and meaning.
word_study.significance: Lammah appears throughout the laments of Scripture, particularly in Psalm 22:1 ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'). It is the question that theodicy cannot answer. The Covenant Rendering notes: 'The final verse is a question with no answer.' This unresolved interrogation is the text's final word—not resolution but interrogation, not closure but rupture.

word_study.meaning: Difficult labor, suffering, trouble; also the futility of such labor when it produces no lasting result. The word encompasses both the experience of hardship and the sense that the hardship is pointless.
word_study.significance: Amal dominates Ecclesiastes ('Vanity of vanities, all is amal'). It describes work and suffering that lead nowhere. The Covenant Rendering notes: 'It encompasses both the suffering one endures and the futile labor one performs—misery and pointlessness combined.' For Jeremiah, his prophetic labor (preaching repentance, warning of judgment) has produced no visible result; he has only earned suffering and rejection. His amal is both painful and apparently futile.

word_study.meaning: Deep, persistent sorrow; not momentary sadness but a settled emotional state. The verb yagon means to grieve, mourn, grow dark. It is a sorrow that colors the entire landscape of consciousness.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes: 'Deep, persistent sorrow—not a momentary feeling but a settled state of anguish. Paired with amal, it describes a life defined entirely by pain.' Yagon suggests that Jeremiah's suffering has become his identity, his constant companion. It is not something that happens to him but something he has become.

word_study.meaning: Shame, dishonor, disgrace; the opposite of kavod (glory, honor). To experience bosheth is to lose social standing, to be publicly humiliated, to be rendered contemptible.
word_study.significance: For a prophet, bosheth is particularly cutting. The prophet is called to speak truth, to bear God's word, to occupy a place of honor in the community. That Jeremiah instead experiences bosheth—public mockery, beating, imprisonment—represents a complete inversion of his calling. He is consumed by the very condition that should have been impossible for one chosen by God.

word_study.meaning: To go out, to exit, to emerge. Used of exodus (going out of Egypt), childbirth, and the emergence of anything from containment.
word_study.significance: The verb echoes Genesis 2:24 ('leave father and mother') and the emergence of animals from the ark. The basic sense is transition from one state to another—from the womb (safety, non-existence) to the world (danger, suffering). Jeremiah wishes the transition had never happened.

word_study.meaning: To finish, complete, consume entirely. When used of a person, it means to be destroyed, used up, finished. The sense is of total expenditure with no remainder.
word_study.significance: The use of kalah intensifies the image: Jeremiah's days are not merely marked by shame; they are consumed by it, eaten up by it, finished by it. There is no part of his existence left untouched, no reservoir of experience outside the shame.

cross_references.connection: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' The same lammah ('why') question, framed as abandonment by God. Both Psalm 22 and Jeremiah 20 end with unanswered cries, though Psalm 22 eventually moves to praise (verses 22+), whereas Jeremiah does not.

'Why died I not from the womb? Why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly?' The same core question: why was I born? Both Job and Jeremiah arrive at this through unendurable suffering.

'Therefore I hated life; because the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous unto me: for all is vanity and vexation of spirit.' The same experience: life itself appears hateful because it contains only suffering and futility.

The opening of Jeremiah's call: 'But the LORD said unto me, Say not, I am a child...they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail.' The promise at his call is violated by the reality of his experience. Verse 18 circles back to the moment of his birth-curse (verse 14) and asks: Why did God allow me to be born to experience this?

Christ in Gethsemane: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.' Like Jeremiah and Job, Christ prays for release from suffering, though he ultimately accepts the Father's will. Jeremiah offers no such acceptance.
